title: Chinese HSK 2
description: The second step in Mandarin Chinese, from HSK 1 to the new HSK 2 (HSK 3.0). Grammar lessons cover comparisons with 比, the complements of result, direction, degree and quantity, 得 and 地, 过 for experiences and 着 for states, 是…的, 因为…所以 and 虽然…但是, 还是 questions, 快要…了, 已经, 就, verb and adjective reduplication and 让. The 200 new words of the level (500 in all) are learned through typed review cards and the 125 new characters (371 in all) through notecards, words and tracing, with pinyin you can turn off and a switch to traditional characters. The last lessons practise reading notices and messages, listening, writing short notes and the exam format. Requires Chinese HSK 1.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Surnames and introductions: 姓, 位, 自己
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Welcome to HSK 2. In HSK 1 you learned 300 words and 246 characters: enough to say who you are,
count, tell the time, shop, ask where things are and say what happened. This course adds 200
words and 125 **[[characters]]**, and with them longer sentences, comparisons, experiences ("have you
ever…?") and the first written answers.

This first lesson goes back to meeting people and does it more politely. You'll learn to ask
someone's family name the way adults do, to introduce other people with the respectful measure
word {位|wèi}, to talk about yourself with {自己|zì jǐ}, and to name your grandparents. You'll also
meet a pattern Chinese uses all the time: saying a verb twice, {看看|kàn kan}, for "have a quick
look".

## How this course works

The lessons have the same parts as in HSK 1, with **[[pinyin]]** over every character (the Pinyin
switch hides it) and an optional colour for each **[[tone]]** (the Tone colours switch). A few things
are new:

- **A reading text in every lesson**, 80 to 150 characters in this module and longer later, with
  questions and a translation you can open when you've tried it yourself.
- **Writing by hand.** The new HSK 2 asks for short written answers (a time, a name, a place), so
  the 100 characters of levels 1 and 2 that you should be able to write from memory are marked ✎.
  Each lesson has a "Write it" line for its ✎ characters, and each module has a "Handwriting
  review" box of HSK 1 characters to write again.
- **Traditional characters.** The Traditional switch shows the course in traditional characters.
  The character sections stay in simplified, because they explain the simplified shapes, and give
  the traditional form in brackets where it differs: {=绍=} (traditional {+绍+}). The tracing pads
  and the character notecards follow the switch.
- **Words.** The 300 words of HSK 1 and the pinyin course are already in your reviews, and every
  lesson uses them freely.

## Asking a family name: {姓|xìng}

You know {你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？ from HSK 1. It's the right question for a
classmate or a child. With a teacher, an older person or someone you meet at work, Chinese asks for
the family name first, with {姓|xìng} (to be surnamed):

{您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？ — What is your family name, please? (literally "your honourable surname")
{我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{王|Wáng}，{叫|jiào}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}。 — My family name is Wang; my name is Wang Fang.

{贵|guì} is the "expensive" of HSK 1, here meaning "honoured". It's only used to ask, and only with
{您|nín} or {你|nǐ}: you never say it about yourself, and for a third person you ask plainly:

{他|tā}{姓|xìng}{什么|shén me}？ — What's his family name?
{那位|nà wèi}{老师|lǎo shī}{姓|xìng}{什么|shén me}？ — What's that teacher's family name?

### {姓|xìng} + family name, {叫|jiào} + full name

The two verbs divide the work. {姓|xìng} takes only the family name. {叫|jiào} takes the full name,
or, among friends, the name people use for you:

| Say | Means | Not |
|---|---|---|
| {我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{李|Lǐ}。 | My family name is Li. | ~~{我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{李明|Lǐ Míng}。~~ |
| {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{李明|Lǐ Míng}。 | My name is Li Ming. | ~~{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{李|Lǐ}。~~ (sounds as if "Li" were your whole name) |
| {你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{我|wǒ}{小明|Xiǎo míng}{吧|ba}。 | Call me Xiaoming. | |

Put together, {我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{李|Lǐ}，{叫|jiào}{李明|Lǐ Míng} is the most natural polite answer,
and it's exactly what you say back to {您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？ The negative is {不|bú}{姓|xìng}:
{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{姓|xìng}{王|Wáng}，{我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{黄|Huáng}。 (I'm not a Wang, I'm a Huang: two family
names that can sound alike to a learner.)

### {姓|xìng} as a noun, and {姓名|xìng míng}

{姓|xìng} is also the noun "family name": {中国人|Zhōng guó rén}{的|de}{姓|xìng} (Chinese family
names). {姓名|xìng míng} is the full name, family name and given name together. It's the word on
forms, lists and official papers; in conversation you say {名字|míng zi}.

> **Form**
>
> {姓名|xìng míng}：{王芳|Wáng Fāng}
>
> {姓|xìng}：{王|Wáng}　　{名|míng}：{芳|Fāng}

On a form like this, {姓|xìng} is the family name and {名|míng} the given name. Write the family name
first, as Chinese always does.

## {名|míng}: name, and place in a ranking

On its own, {名|míng} appears mostly in two ways. One is "given name", on forms like the one above.
The other is as a **[[measure word]]**, a word that comes between a number and a noun (as {个|gè} does
in {三|sān}{个|gè}{人|rén}). {名|míng} counts places in a ranking, after {第|dì}:

{他|tā}{是|shì}{第一|dì yī}{名|míng}。 — He came first. / He's in first place.
{我们|wǒ men}{班|bān}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{是|shì}{第二|dì èr}{名|míng}。 — In our class, Wang Fang came second.

{第一|dì yī} keeps its first tone, *yī*, as every ordinal does. ({班|bān}, "class", is a word you'll
meet properly in lesson 16; here it's the class of students.) In notices and lists, {名|míng} also
counts people formally: {十|shí}{名|míng}{学生|xué sheng} (ten students). In speech you'd say
{十|shí}{个|gè}{学生|xué sheng}.

## {位|wèi}: the polite measure word for people

{个|gè} counts people neutrally. {位|wèi} counts them with respect, and you'll hear it whenever
someone is being polite about a guest, a teacher, a customer or an older person:

{这|zhè}{位|wèi}{老师|lǎo shī}{姓|xìng}{王|Wáng}。 — This teacher's family name is Wang.
{那|nà}{位|wèi}{先生|xiān sheng}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}。 — That gentleman is a doctor.
{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{来|lái}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{位|wèi}{客人|kè rén}。 — Two guests have come to our house.

({客人|kè rén}, guest, is an HSK 3 word.) {这位|zhè wèi} and {那位|nà wèi} also stand alone for "this
person" and "that person", and {哪位|nǎ wèi} is a polite "who":

{这|zhè}{位|wèi}{是|shì}{李|Lǐ}{医生|yī shēng}。 — This is Dr Li.
{您|nín}{是|shì}{哪|nǎ}{位|wèi}？ — Who is this, please? (on the phone or at the door)
{几|jǐ}{位|wèi}？ — How many of you? (a waiter's first question in a restaurant)

Two limits. {位|wèi} is never used about yourself: say {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}, not
~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{一|yí}{位|wèi}{学生|xué sheng}~~. And it's for people only: one book is still
{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}.

## Introducing people: {介绍|jiè shào}

{介绍|jiè shào} is "to introduce". The phrase you'll hear at any first meeting is
{我|wǒ}{介绍|jiè shào}{一下|yí xià}, "let me introduce (you)", usually with {给|gěi} + the people being
introduced (the {给|gěi} of HSK 1: {给|gěi}{朋友|péng you}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}):

{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{你们|nǐ men}{介绍|jiè shào}{一下|yí xià}：{这|zhè}{位|wèi}{是|shì}{张|Zhāng}{老师|lǎo shī}，{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{安娜|Ān nà}。
— Let me introduce you: this is Teacher Zhang, and this is my classmate Anna.

Notice {这位|zhè wèi} for the teacher and plain {这|zhè}{是|shì} for the classmate. The usual reply
is {你好|nǐ hǎo} or {您好|nín hǎo}, often followed by {认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}.

To introduce yourself, the object is {自己|zì jǐ} (below): {我|wǒ}{介绍|jiè shào}{一下|yí xià}{我|wǒ}{自己|zì jǐ}.
A self-introduction is a {自我介绍|zì wǒ jiè shào}, a phrase worth recognising (you'll be asked for
one in class and in interviews).

## Saying a verb twice: "a little, briefly"

Chinese often says a verb twice to make an action short, casual or tentative: "have a look", "ask
around", "think it over". This is **[[reduplication]]** (repeating a word or a syllable), and with
verbs it's called **[[verb reduplication]]**:

{你|nǐ}{看看|kàn kan}。 — Have a look.
{我|wǒ}{问问|wèn wen}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — I'll ask the teacher (quickly).
{我|wǒ}{想想|xiǎng xiang}。 — Let me think about it.
{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ}{介绍|jiè shào}{介绍|jiè shào}{你|nǐ}{自己|zì jǐ}。 — Please tell us a bit about yourself.

It means the same as the verb + {一下|yí xià} that you learned in HSK 1: {看看|kàn kan} =
{看|kàn}{一下|yí xià}, {介绍介绍|jiè shào jiè shào} = {介绍|jiè shào}{一下|yí xià}. Both soften a request
and make a suggestion sound easy. The forms:

| Verb | Doubled | Also |
|---|---|---|
| one syllable: {看|kàn} | {看看|kàn kan} (second syllable light) | {看|kàn}{一|yi}{看|kàn} (with a light {一|yi} in the middle) |
| one syllable: {听|tīng} | {听听|tīng ting} | {听|tīng}{一|yi}{听|tīng} |
| two syllables: {介绍|jiè shào} | {介绍介绍|jiè shào jiè shào} (the whole word twice: ABAB) | not ~~{介介绍绍|jiè jiè shào shào}~~ |
| two syllables: {休息|xiū xi} | {休息休息|xiū xi xiū xi} | |

The object follows the doubled verb, as it follows any verb: {看看|kàn kan}{这|zhè}{本|běn}{书|shū}
(have a look at this book), {介绍介绍|jiè shào jiè shào}{你|nǐ}{自己|zì jǐ}.

### Which verbs can be doubled

Only actions that someone does on purpose and that can be done "a little": look, listen, ask,
think, read, introduce, rest, find, say. Verbs of being, having and liking can't:
~~{是是|shì shì}~~, ~~{有有|yǒu yǒu}~~, ~~{喜欢喜欢|xǐ huan xǐ huan}~~. And because doubling means "a little",
it doesn't go with a large amount: not ~~{看看|kàn kan}{三|sān}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}~~.

For something already done, {了|le} goes between the two: {他|tā}{看|kàn}{了|le}{看|kàn}{我|wǒ}
(he glanced at me). That's all you need for now; the reference sheet "Reduplication" has the
details.

## {自己|zì jǐ}: oneself, one's own

{自己|zì jǐ} means "self". It goes after a pronoun or a noun, or replaces one:

{我|wǒ}{自己|zì jǐ} — myself　　{你|nǐ}{自己|zì jǐ} — yourself　　{他们|tā men}{自己|zì jǐ} — themselves

After a verb, it's the object, and it means the same person who does the action:
{介绍|jiè shào}{自己|zì jǐ} (introduce oneself).
Before a verb, it means "by oneself, without help":

{我|wǒ}{自己|zì jǐ}{做饭|zuò fàn}。 — I cook for myself. / I cook on my own.
{你|nǐ}{自己|zì jǐ}{去|qù}{吧|ba}。 — Go by yourself, then.

With {的|de} it's "one's own": {自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān} (your own room),
{他|tā}{有|yǒu}{自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{公司|gōng sī} (he has his own company). Chinese uses the same word
for every person, so there's no choice to make between "myself", "yourself" and "herself": the
pronoun in front, or the context, says who.

## Grandparents: {爷爷|yé ye} and {奶奶|nǎi nai}

Chinese kinship words say which side of the family someone is on. Your father's parents are:

{爷爷|yé ye} — grandpa, grandfather (father's father)
{奶奶|nǎi nai} — grandma, grandmother (father's mother)

Your mother's parents have different names, and they vary by region: in much of the south and in
many families everywhere they're {外公|wài gōng} and {外婆|wài pó}; in the north you'll often hear
{姥爷|lǎo ye} and {姥姥|lǎo lao}. {外|wài} is the "outside" of HSK 1: the mother's family was
traditionally the "outer" side, since a married woman joined her husband's family. These four
words are beyond HSK 2, so just recognise them.

{我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{和|hé}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}。 — My (father's) grandparents live in Beijing.
{奶奶|nǎi nai}{今年|jīn nián}{八十|bā shí}{岁|suì}{了|le}。 — Grandma is eighty this year.

Like {爸爸|bà ba}, {妈妈|mā ma} and {哥哥|gē ge}, they're doubled syllables with a light second
syllable (a **[[neutral tone]]**): *yé ye*, *nǎi nai*. That's an old habit of family words, not verb
reduplication: the meaning doesn't change. Children also call any elderly man or woman
{爷爷|yé ye} or {奶奶|nǎi nai} as a friendly title. The {奶|nǎi} in {奶奶|nǎi nai} is the one in
{牛奶|niú nǎi} (milk), which you can already write.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 姓 | family name; to be surnamed | xìng | 女 | 8 | {姓|xìng}, {姓名|xìng míng}, {贵姓|guì xìng} |
| 位 | place, position; (polite measure word for people) | wèi | 亻 | 7 | {位|wèi}, {这位|zhè wèi}, {哪位|nǎ wèi} |
| 自 | self; from | zì | 自 | 6 | {自己|zì jǐ} |
| 己 | oneself | jǐ | 己 | 3 | {自己|zì jǐ} |
| 介 | between | jiè | 人 | 4 | {介绍|jiè shào} |
| 绍 (traditional 紹) | to join, to introduce | shào | 纟 | 8 | {介绍|jiè shào} |
| 爷 (traditional 爺) | grandfather | yé | 父 | 6 | {爷爷|yé ye} |

Characters are built from **[[components]]**, smaller shapes that recur in many characters. One of
them, the **[[radical]]**, is the part a dictionary files the character under; it often hints at the
meaning. The notes:

- 姓 is 女 (woman) + 生 (to be born, as in {学生|xué sheng}; it also gives the sound): the family you
  are born into. That's
  the explanation in the Shuowen (about 100 CE), the oldest dictionary that explains how
  characters are built, and several of the oldest family names also
  contain 女, such as 姜 *Jiāng* and 姚 *Yáo*. Today 女 says nothing about whose name it is.
- 位 is 亻 (person) + 立 (to stand): the place where a person stands, a position. That's why it
  means "position" in other words, and why it became the measure word that gives each person their
  place.
- 自 began as a drawing of a nose. People in China often point to their own nose when they say "me",
  which makes it easy to remember. It's its own radical.
- 己 has three strokes and two look-alikes. A schoolroom rhyme sorts them by how far the top-left
  corner is closed: 己 is open (self, {自己|zì jǐ}), 已 is half closed (already, in {已经|yǐ jīng},
  lesson 18), and 巳 is fully closed (a rare character used in dates).
- 介 is 人 over two short legs. A memory aid: someone standing between two others, the go-between
  who introduces them. Its radical is 人 in its top form, the same "roof" you know from 今 and 会.
- 绍 is 纟 (silk) + 召 *zhào*, which gives the sound. In traditional script the silk radical has its
  full shape: 紹.
- 爷 is 父 (father) on top, as in 爸, + 卩. The traditional form 爺 has 耶 *yé* under 父 for the
  sound; simplified Chinese kept only a small part of it.

**Radical review.** Two radicals from HSK 1 come back in this lesson. 女 (woman, {女字旁|nǚ zì páng}):
姓, and from HSK 1 她, 妈, 姐, 妹, 奶, 好. 亻 (person, {单人旁|dān rén páng}): 位, and from HSK 1 你, 他,
们, 作, 住, 休, 便, 件.

### Stroke order

- 己: three strokes. The top and right side in one stroke (across, then down), the middle
  horizontal, then the vertical that bends right at the bottom and ends with an upward hook. Keep
  the top-left corner open.
- 介: the left-falling stroke and the right-falling stroke of 人 first, then the short left leg
  (a small left-falling stroke) and last the right leg (a vertical).
- 爷: 父 first (the two short dots, left then right, then the long left-falling stroke and the long
  right-falling stroke that cross), then 卩: the horizontal that turns down and hooks, and last
  the vertical through it.
- 姓, 绍: the left side first (女 in three strokes, 纟 in three), then the right side. In 女 the
  first stroke turns down and to the right, and the horizontal comes last.
- 自: the short left-falling stroke on top first, then the frame like 目: left vertical, the top and
  right side in one stroke, then the inside horizontals from top to bottom, the bottom one last.

```trace
姓位自己介绍爷
```

✎ character of the course.

## Dialogue: the new teacher

The speakers are {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī} (王老师), the new teacher {张老师|Zhāng lǎo shī}
(张老师), and the students {李明|Lǐ Míng} (李明) and {艾米|Ài mǐ} (艾米, Amy).

```dialogue
# The new teacher
王老师: {同学|tóng xué}{们|men}{好|hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{大家|dà jiā}{介绍|jiè shào}{一下|yí xià}，{这|zhè}{位|wèi}{是|shì}{张|Zhāng}{老师|lǎo shī}。
= Hello, everyone! Let me introduce someone: this is Teacher Zhang.
张老师: {大家|dà jiā}{好|hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{张|Zhāng}，{叫|jiào}{张文|Zhāng Wén}。{认识|rèn shi}{你们|nǐ men}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。
= Hello, everyone! My family name is Zhang; my name is Zhang Wen. I'm very glad to meet you.
张老师: {请|qǐng}{你们|nǐ men}{介绍|jiè shào}{介绍|jiè shào}{自己|zì jǐ}。{你|nǐ}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}？
= Please introduce yourselves. What's your name?
李明: {我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{李|Lǐ}，{叫|jiào}{李明|Lǐ Míng}，{是|shì}{北京|Běi jīng}{人|rén}。
= My family name is Li; I'm Li Ming, from Beijing.
张老师: {这|zhè}{位|wèi}{同学|tóng xué}，{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= And you (this student)?
艾米: {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{艾米|Ài mǐ}。{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{是|shì}{美国人|Měi guó rén}，{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{是|shì}{中国人|Zhōng guó rén}。
= I'm Amy. My dad is American and my mum is Chinese.
张老师: {你|nǐ}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{吗|ma}？
= Can you speak Chinese?
艾米: {会|huì}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。{我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{不|bú}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{我|wǒ}{外公|wài gōng}{外婆|wài pó}{会|huì}。
= A little. My father's parents can't speak Chinese; my mother's parents can.
张老师: {很|hěn}{好|hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{想|xiǎng}{认识|rèn shi}{认识|rèn shi}{他们|tā men}。
= Great! I'd like to meet them some time too.
```

Notice {这位同学|zhè wèi tóng xué}: a teacher being polite to a student whose name she doesn't know
yet. And Amy's family needs both pairs of grandparent words: {爷爷|yé ye}{奶奶|nǎi nai} on her
father's side, {外公|wài gōng}{外婆|wài pó} on her mother's. {认识认识|rèn shi rèn shi} is a doubled
verb: "get to know a little".

## Reading: introducing yourself

> {大家|dà jiā}{好|hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{陈|Chén}，{叫|jiào}{陈小雨|Chén Xiǎo yǔ}，{今年|jīn nián}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}，{是|shì}{大学生|dà xué shēng}。{我|wǒ}{介绍|jiè shào}{一下|yí xià}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{家|jiā}。{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{五|wǔ}{口|kǒu}{人|rén}：{爷爷|yé ye}、{奶奶|nǎi nai}、{爸爸|bà ba}、{妈妈|mā ma}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}。{爷爷|yé ye}{七十六|qī shí liù}{岁|suì}，{奶奶|nǎi nai}{七十二|qī shí èr}{岁|suì}。{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{工作|gōng zuò}，{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}。{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{唱歌|chàng gē}，{也|yě}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{自己|zì jǐ}{做饭|zuò fàn}。{我|wǒ}{会|huì}{做|zuò}{饺子|jiǎo zi}，{大家|dà jiā}{有|yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}{来|lái}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{吧|ba}！{认识|rèn shi}{大家|dà jiā}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}！

Read it twice: once for the gist, once slowly with the pinyin. Then answer:

1. How old is Chen Xiaoyu, and what does she do?
2. Who is 72?
3. What does she like doing?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Twenty; she's a university student ({大学生|dà xué shēng}).
2. Her grandmother on her father's side ({奶奶|nǎi nai}{七十二|qī shí èr}{岁|suì}).
3. Singing, and cooking for herself ({自己|zì jǐ}{做饭|zuò fàn}); she can make dumplings.

"Hello, everyone! My family name is Chen and my name is Chen Xiaoyu. I'm twenty and a university
student. Let me tell you a little about my family. There are five of us: Grandpa,
Grandma, Dad, Mum and me. Grandpa is 76 and Grandma is 72. My dad works in a hospital; he's a
doctor. My mum is a teacher. I really like singing, and I like cooking for myself. I can make dumplings: come to my place
and have some when you have time! I'm glad to meet you all!"
</details>

Notice how Xiaoyu introduces herself: family name with {姓|xìng}, full name with {叫|jiào}, then age,
studies and family, the order most self-introductions follow.

## Say it

```speak
{您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？
= What is your family name, please?
{我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{李|Lǐ}，{叫|jiào}{李明|Lǐ Míng}。
= My family name is Li; my name is Li Ming.
{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{你们|nǐ men}{介绍|jiè shào}{一下|yí xià}，{这|zhè}{位|wèi}{是|shì}{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}。
= Let me introduce you: this is Teacher Wang.
{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ}{介绍|jiè shào}{介绍|jiè shào}{你|nǐ}{自己|zì jǐ}。
= Please tell us a bit about yourself.
{我|wǒ}{想想|xiǎng xiang}。
= Let me think about it.
{我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}。
= My grandparents (on my father's side) live in Beijing.
```

## Pronunciation

- {姓|xìng} and {名|míng} both end in *-ing*, the nasal at the back of the mouth, as in English
  "sing". Don't let them slide into *-in* ({您|nín} has *-in*: say {您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng} slowly
  and feel the difference). {姓|xìng} falls, {名|míng} rises.
- {自己|zì jǐ}: *z* is like the *ds* in "beds", and the *i* after it is the buzzing vowel of
  {字|zì}, not "ee". In {己|jǐ} the *i* is a real "ee". Two different vowels spelled with one letter.
- {介绍|jiè shào}: *j* with the tongue flat behind the lower teeth, *sh* with the tongue tip curled
  back. Both syllables fall.
- {位|wèi} is spelled *wei* and said like English "way" with a falling tone.
- {爷爷|yé ye}, {奶奶|nǎi nai}: the second syllable is short and light. After the third tone of
  {奶|nǎi} it sounds a little higher than after the second tone of {爷|yé}.
- {一下|yí xià}: {一|yī} changes to *yí* before a fourth tone. This kind of change caused by the
  next syllable is **[[tone sandhi]]**; the course writes it for {一|yī} and {不|bù}: {一下|yí xià},
  {不|bú}{姓|xìng}. Two third tones together change too, but that change isn't written:
  {我|wǒ}{想想|xiǎng xiang} starts *wó xiǎng*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}~~: {姓|xìng} takes only the family name. Say {我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{王|Wáng}，
  {叫|jiào}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{贵姓|guì xìng}{王|Wáng}~~: {贵|guì} honours the other person; it's only in the question.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{一|yí}{位|wèi}{老师|lǎo shī}~~: {位|wèi} is respect for others, never for yourself.
  Say {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}.
- ~~{介介绍绍|jiè jiè shào shào}~~: a two-syllable verb doubles as a whole word, ABAB:
  {介绍介绍|jiè shào jiè shào}.
- Doubling verbs that aren't actions: ~~{喜欢喜欢|xǐ huan xǐ huan}~~, ~~{是是|shì shì}~~.
- Calling your mother's father {爷爷|yé ye}: he's {外公|wài gōng} (or {姥爷|lǎo ye}).
- Writing 己 with a closed corner (已): 己 is open at the top left.

## Key points

- Polite question: {您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？ Answer: {我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{李|Lǐ}，{叫|jiào}{李明|Lǐ Míng}。
  {姓|xìng} + family name; {叫|jiào} + full name.
- {姓名|xìng míng} is the full name on forms; {名|míng} is the given name there, and a measure word
  for places in a ranking: {第一|dì yī}{名|míng}.
- {位|wèi} is the polite measure word for people: {这位|zhè wèi}{老师|lǎo shī}, {哪位|nǎ wèi},
  {几位|jǐ wèi}. Never for yourself.
- {我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{你们|nǐ men}{介绍|jiè shào}{一下|yí xià} introduces people; {介绍|jiè shào}{自己|zì jǐ}
  is to introduce yourself.
- Verb reduplication makes an action short or casual: {看看|kàn kan}, {看|kàn}{一|yi}{看|kàn},
  {介绍介绍|jiè shào jiè shào}. Only for actions.
- {自己|zì jǐ}: oneself; before a verb "by oneself"; {自己|zì jǐ}{的|de} "one's own".
- {爷爷|yé ye} and {奶奶|nǎi nai} are your father's parents; your mother's are {外公|wài gōng} and
  {外婆|wài pó} (or {姥爷|lǎo ye}, {姥姥|lǎo lao}).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: What people look like
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 was about names. This one is about faces and figures: how tall someone is, how long or
big something is, and the body words you need to describe a person ({头|tóu}, {眼睛|yǎn jing},
{手|shǒu}, {身体|shēn tǐ}). Two pieces of grammar make descriptions sound Chinese rather than
translated: the topic-comment sentence ({他|tā}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}, "he's tall", literally
"he, height very tall"), and doubled adjectives ({大大|dà dà}{的|de}{眼睛|yǎn jing}, "big, big
eyes") that paint a picture. You'll also write your first ✎ character of the course, {=长=}.

## Height: {个子|gè zi} and {高|gāo}

{个子|gè zi} is a person's height and build, how big someone is. {高|gāo} is "tall" or "high". Put
them together and you have the usual way to say someone is tall:

{他|tā}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}。 — He's tall.
{我|wǒ}{妹妹|mèi mei}{个子|gè zi}{不|bù}{高|gāo}。 — My younger sister isn't tall.
{你|nǐ}{哥哥|gē ge}{个子|gè zi}{高|gāo}{吗|ma}？ — Is your older brother tall?

{他|tā}{很|hěn}{高|gāo} is right too, and just as common. {高|gāo} also works for things that are high
or tall: {桌子|zhuō zi}{太|tài}{高|gāo}{了|le} (the table is too high).
The opposite for people, "short", is {矮|ǎi}, an HSK 3 word; until then {个子|gè zi}{不|bù}{高|gāo} says
it kindly.

To ask how tall someone is, use {多|duō} + adjective, the pattern of {多大|duō dà} (how old):

{你|nǐ}{多|duō}{高|gāo}？ — How tall are you?
{我|wǒ}{一|yì}{米|mǐ}{七|qī}。 — I'm 1.70 m.

Heights are given in metres, {米|mǐ} (the same character as "rice"; the measuring word is HSK 3).
{一|yì}{米|mǐ}{七|qī} is "one metre seven", 1.70 m, and {一|yì}{米|mǐ}{八|bā}{五|wǔ} is 1.85 m. As in
any sentence giving an age or a measurement, no {是|shì} is needed.

## Topic-comment sentences: {他|tā}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}

Every sentence so far has had a **[[subject]]**, who or what the sentence is about, and a
**[[predicate]]**, what is said about it: in {他|tā}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}, {他|tā} is the subject and
{很|hěn}{高|gāo} the predicate. In {他|tā}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo} the predicate is a small sentence
of its own, with its own subject ({个子|gè zi}) and its own predicate ({很|hěn}{高|gāo}):

| Topic | Comment (a small sentence) | |
|---|---|---|
| {他|tā} | {个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo} | He's tall. ("Him: height, very tall") |
| {她|tā} | {眼睛|yǎn jing}{很|hěn}{大|dà} | She has big eyes. |
| {我|wǒ}{奶奶|nǎi nai} | {身体|shēn tǐ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo} | My grandma is in good health. |
| {这|zhè}{家|jiā}{饭店|fàn diàn} | {菜|cài}{很|hěn}{好吃|hǎo chī} | This restaurant's food is good. |

This is a **[[topic-comment sentence]]**: first you name what you're talking about (the topic), then
you say something about it. Chinese uses it far more than English does, and it's the natural way
to describe people by a feature. English turns it into "have" ("she has big eyes") or "'s"
("this restaurant's food"); Chinese doesn't need either.

You could also say {他|tā}{的|de}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo} with {的|de}, and it isn't wrong, but
without {的|de} the sentence sounds more natural and keeps the person in front: it's a description
of him. Questions and negatives work inside the comment:

{她|tā}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{大|dà}{不|bú}{大|dà}？ — Does she have big eyes?
{我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{身体|shēn tǐ}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}。 — My grandpa isn't in good health.
{您|nín}{身体|shēn tǐ}{好|hǎo}{吗|ma}？ — How are you keeping? (a kind question to an older person)

The last one is a greeting as much as a question. The answer is usually
{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{谢谢|xiè xie}！

## {长|cháng}: long

{长|cháng} is "long", for length and for time:

{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}{太|tài}{长|cháng}{了|le}。 — This top is too long.
{她|tā}{头发|tóu fa}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}。 — She has long hair.
{今天|jīn tiān}{的|de}{课|kè}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}。 — Today's lesson is long.

({头发|tóu fa}, hair, is an HSK 3 word: you'll see it often in this module.) The second example is
another topic-comment sentence: "her, hair very long". For people, "tall" is {高|gāo}, never
~~{长|cháng}~~.

The same character has a second reading, {长|zhǎng}, "to grow", as in {长大|zhǎng dà} (to grow up) and
{校长|xiào zhǎng} (head teacher). That's a different word with a different tone, taught in HSK 3. In
this course 长 is always *cháng*.

## Body words

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {头|tóu} | head | {他|tā}{头|tóu}{很|hěn}{大|dà}。 He has a big head. |
| {眼睛|yǎn jing} | eye, eyes | {她|tā}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{很|hěn}{大|dà}。 She has big eyes. |
| {手|shǒu} | hand | {我|wǒ}{的|de}{手|shǒu}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}。 My hands are cold. |
| {身体|shēn tǐ} | body; health | {我|wǒ}{身体|shēn tǐ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 I'm healthy. |

- {头|tóu} is the head. It's also a measure word for cattle and other big animals,
  {一|yì}{头|tóu}{牛|niú} (a cow), but you'll mostly meet it in {头疼|tóu téng} (headache, lesson 05)
  and {头发|tóu fa} (hair).
- {眼睛|yǎn jing} has a light second syllable. One eye is {一|yì}{只|zhī}{眼睛|yǎn jing} and two
  are {两|liǎng}{只|zhī}{眼睛|yǎn jing}, with the measure word for animals, which also counts one
  of a pair. Chinese doesn't mark the plural, so
  {她|tā}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{很|hěn}{大|dà} is "her eyes are big".
- {手|shǒu} is in a word you know, {手机|shǒu jī} (mobile phone, "hand machine"), and in one you'll
  learn next lesson, {手表|shǒu biǎo} (wristwatch).
- {身体|shēn tǐ} is the body, and, as in {身体|shēn tǐ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}, a person's health. Chinese
  speakers ask about it often, especially with older people.

Other parts of the face come in HSK 3. You may meet them before then, so here they are to
recognise: {脸|liǎn} face, {嘴|zuǐ} mouth (you know {口|kǒu} as a measure word; {嘴|zuǐ} is the
everyday word for the mouth), {耳朵|ěr duo} ear, {鼻子|bí zi} nose, {脚|jiǎo} foot.

## Doubled adjectives: {高高|gāo gāo}{的|de}, {大大|dà dà}{的|de}

In lesson 01 you doubled verbs to make an action short. Adjectives double too, with a different
effect: they become vivid and descriptive, the way a storyteller describes someone. This is
**[[adjective reduplication]]**:

{她|tā}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{双|shuāng}{大大|dà dà}{的|de}{眼睛|yǎn jing}。 — She has big, big eyes.
{那|nà}{个|gè}{男|nán}{孩子|hái zi}{个子|gè zi}{高高|gāo gāo}{的|de}。 — That boy is nice and tall.
{我|wǒ}{妹妹|mèi mei}{的|de}{头发|tóu fa}{长长|cháng cháng}{的|de}。 — My younger sister's hair is long.

({双|shuāng}, a pair, is an HSK 3 measure word; {一|yì}{双|shuāng}{眼睛|yǎn jing} is "a pair of eyes".)

The rules:

| Adjective | Doubled | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| {大|dà} | {大大|dà dà}{的|de} | AA + {的|de} |
| {小|xiǎo} | {小小|xiǎo xiǎo}{的|de} | AA + {的|de} |
| {长|cháng} | {长长|cháng cháng}{的|de} | AA + {的|de} |
| {漂亮|piào liang} | {漂漂亮亮|piào piào liàng liàng}{的|de} | AABB + {的|de} |
| {高兴|gāo xìng} | {高高兴兴|gāo gāo xìng xìng}{的|de} | AABB + {的|de} |

- One syllable: AA. Two syllables: AABB, each syllable doubled in place (not ABAB, which is for
  verbs: compare {介绍介绍|jiè shào jiè shào}). In AABB, a light syllable such as the *liang* of
  {漂亮|piào liang} gets its full tone back.
- Add {的|de}, before a noun ({大大|dà dà}{的|de}{眼睛|yǎn jing}) and usually at the end of a sentence
  too ({个子|gè zi}{高高|gāo gāo}{的|de}).
- **No {很|hěn}.** {很|hěn}, {太|tài} and {非常|fēi cháng} are **[[adverbs]]** of degree, words that go
  before an adjective or a verb to say how much. A doubled adjective already says "very" in its own
  way, so it never takes them: not ~~{很|hěn}{高高|gāo gāo}{的|de}~~, and no {不|bù} either.
- It's for description: looks, colours, sizes, moods. You won't double every adjective; the
  common ones of shape and size are the safest: {大|dà}, {小|xiǎo}, {高|gāo}, {长|cháng}.

In Beijing speech the second syllable of a doubled one-syllable adjective often turns into a first
tone with *-r*: {好好儿|hǎo hāor}{的|de}. You'll hear it; you don't need to say it.

A doubled adjective in front of a noun is a **[[modifier]]**, a word or phrase that describes a noun and
comes before it, as {中国|Zhōng guó} does in {中国|Zhōng guó}{菜|cài} and {新|xīn} in
{新|xīn}{衣服|yī fu}. In Chinese a modifier always comes first, however long it is.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 长 (traditional 長) ✎ | long | cháng (and zhǎng) | 长 | 4 | {长|cháng}, {长长|cháng cháng}{的|de} |
| 头 (traditional 頭) | head | tóu | 大 | 5 | {头|tóu}, {头发|tóu fa} (hair, HSK 3) |
| 眼 | eye | yǎn | 目 | 11 | {眼睛|yǎn jing} |
| 睛 | eyeball | jing (jīng) | 目 | 13 | {眼睛|yǎn jing} |
| 身 | body | shēn | 身 | 7 | {身体|shēn tǐ} |
| 体 (traditional 體) | body, form | tǐ | 亻 | 7 | {身体|shēn tǐ} |

- 长 is usually explained as a drawing of a person with long hair. The traditional form 長 keeps
  more of the drawing; simplified 长 has only four strokes.
- 头: the traditional form 頭 is 頁 (an old character for the head) + 豆 *dòu*, which once gave the
  sound. Simplified 头 is a new shape made from the handwritten form. Make Me a Hanzi files it under
  大; many dictionaries put it under 丶 (the dot).
- 眼 and 睛 both have 目 (eye) on the left. In 睛 the right side is 青 *qīng*, which gives the
  sound, as it does in {请|qǐng} (please). {眼睛|yǎn jing} is two "eye" characters, and 睛 has a
  light tone in this word.
- 身 is traditionally explained as a drawing of a person with a big belly, a body seen from the
  side. It's its own radical.
- 体 is 亻 (person) + 本 (root, as in {本|běn}). A memory aid: a person's root is their body.
  The traditional form 體 is quite different: 骨 (bone) + 豊, 23 strokes in all.

**Radical review.** 目 (eye, {目字旁|mù zì páng}): 眼, 睛, and from HSK 1 看 (a hand over an eye:
looking), 睡 and 真. 大 (big, {大字头|dà zì tóu}): 头, and from HSK 1 天 and 太.

### Stroke order

- 长: four strokes. The short left-falling stroke at the top left, then the long horizontal, then
  the vertical that flicks up to the right at the bottom, and last the right-falling stroke.
- 头: the two dots first, from the top down, then the horizontal, then the long left-falling
  stroke, and the big dot at the bottom right last.
- 身: the short left-falling stroke on top, the vertical on the left, the stroke that goes across
  and down and hooks left, the two short horizontals inside, then the long horizontal that rises to
  the right, and last the long left-falling stroke through everything.
- 眼, 睛: 目 first, narrow on the left (its bottom horizontal last), then the right side.
- 体: 亻 first, then 本: horizontal, vertical, the two falling strokes, and the short horizontal near
  the bottom last.

```trace
长头眼睛身体
```

Write it: 长 is on the handwriting list. Write it three times from memory, on paper or on the pad:
four strokes, and the third one flicks up at the bottom.

=}

## Dialogue: an old photo

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) is looking at a family photo ({照片|zhào piàn}, HSK 3) at {王芳|Wáng Fāng}'s
(王芳) house.

```dialogue
# An old photo
安娜: {这|zhè}{是|shì}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{家人|jiā rén}{吗|ma}？
= Is this your family?
王芳: {对|duì}。{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}，{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{奶奶|nǎi nai}。
= Yes. This is my grandpa, and this is my grandma.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{爷爷|yé ye}{个子|gè zi}{真|zhēn}{高|gāo}！
= Your grandpa is really tall!
王芳: {对|duì}，{他|tā}{一|yì}{米|mǐ}{八|bā}{五|wǔ}。{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{个子|gè zi}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}。
= Yes, he's 1.85 m. My dad is tall too.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{大大|dà dà}{的|de}，{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。
= Your grandma has big eyes. She's very pretty.
王芳: {谢谢|xiè xie}！{她|tā}{今年|jīn nián}{七十|qī shí}{岁|suì}{了|le}，{身体|shēn tǐ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。
= Thank you! She's seventy this year, and she's in good health.
安娜: {这|zhè}{个|gè}{孩子|hái zi}{是|shì}{谁|shéi}？{她|tā}{的|de}{头发|tóu fa}{长长|cháng cháng}{的|de}。
= Who's this child? Her hair is so long.
王芳: {那|nà}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}！{那|nà}{时候|shí hou}{我|wǒ}{五|wǔ}{岁|suì}。
= That's me! I was five then.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{的|de}{头|tóu}{小小|xiǎo xiǎo}{的|de}，{眼睛|yǎn jing}{大大|dà dà}{的|de}！
= Your head is so small, and your eyes are so big!
```

Count the topic-comment sentences: {你|nǐ}{爷爷|yé ye}{个子|gè zi}{真|zhēn}{高|gāo},
{你|nǐ}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{大大|dà dà}{的|de}, {身体|shēn tǐ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}. And notice that
{那|nà}{时候|shí hou} ("at that time") is all Chinese needs for the past: the verb doesn't change.

## Reading: my brother

> {我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge}{今年|jīn nián}{二十五|èr shí wǔ}{岁|suì}，{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}，{一|yì}{米|mǐ}{八|bā}{五|wǔ}。{他|tā}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{大大|dà dà}{的|de}，{手|shǒu}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{大|dà}。{他|tā}{身体|shēn tǐ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}{生病|shēng bìng}。{哥哥|gē ge}{在|zài}{一|yì}{家|jiā}{电脑|diàn nǎo}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}，{工作|gōng zuò}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}。{他|tā}{女朋友|nǚ péng you}{叫|jiào}{李文|Lǐ Wén}，{个子|gè zi}{不|bù}{高|gāo}，{头发|tóu fa}{长长|cháng cháng}{的|de}，{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。{他们|tā men}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}。{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{她|tā}。

Read it twice: once for the gist, once slowly with the pinyin. Then answer:

1. How tall is the writer's brother?
2. Is he often ill?
3. What does his girlfriend look like?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. 1.85 m ({一|yì}{米|mǐ}{八|bā}{五|wǔ}).
2. No: {他|tā}{身体|shēn tǐ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}{生病|shēng bìng}, he's healthy and seldom ill.
3. She isn't tall, she has long hair and she's very pretty.

"My older brother is 25 this year. He's tall: 1.85 m. He has big eyes, and his hands are big too.
He's in good health and is seldom ill. My brother works at a computer company, and his job is very
busy. His girlfriend is called Li Wen. She isn't tall, she has long hair, and she's very pretty.
They both love watching films. I like her a lot too."
</details>

{很|hěn}{少|shǎo} + verb is "seldom": {少|shǎo} (few, little) is HSK 1's. And {工作|gōng zuò}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}
is one more topic-comment sentence: "him, work very busy".

## Say it

```speak
{他|tā}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}。
= He's tall.
{你|nǐ}{多|duō}{高|gāo}？
= How tall are you?
{她|tā}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{大大|dà dà}{的|de}。
= She has big eyes.
{您|nín}{身体|shēn tǐ}{好|hǎo}{吗|ma}？
= How are you keeping? (to an older person)
{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}{太|tài}{长|cháng}{了|le}。
= This top is too long.
```

## Pronunciation

- {个子|gè zi}: the *zi* is light and short, with the buzzing vowel. Compare {个|gè} in
  {一|yí}{个|gè}{人|rén}, which keeps its tone.
- {高|gāo} is high and level. {个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo} ends on a high note; don't let it fall.
- {长|cháng} rises, and it starts with *ch* (tongue tip curled back, with a puff of air). Its other
  reading, *zhǎng*, starts with *zh* and dips: two different words.
- {头|tóu}: *ou* as in English "toe", rising.
- {眼睛|yǎn jing}: *yǎn* rhymes with "yen", not "yarn"; *jing* is light.
- {手|shǒu} and {身体|shēn tǐ}: *sh* both times. In {身|shēn} the *e* is the "uh" of "the"; *-n*, not
  *-ng*.
- Doubled adjectives keep both tones: {大大|dà dà}{的|de}, two falls. {小小|xiǎo xiǎo}{的|de} is two third
  tones, so the first one rises: said *xiáo xiǎo de*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{他|tā}{是|shì}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}~~: no {是|shì} before an adjective comment.
  {他|tā}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}.
- ~~{他|tā}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}~~ for "he's tall": people are {高|gāo}; {长|cháng} is for
  hair, clothes, time and roads.
- ~~{很|hěn}{大大|dà dà}{的|de}~~, ~~{非常|fēi cháng}{高高|gāo gāo}{的|de}~~: a doubled adjective takes no
  degree adverb.
- ~~{漂亮漂亮|piào liang piào liang}{的|de}~~: two-syllable adjectives double AABB,
  {漂漂亮亮|piào piào liàng liàng}{的|de}. ABAB is for verbs.
- English word order with "have": ~~{她|tā}{有|yǒu}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{很|hěn}{大|dà}~~. Say
  {她|tā}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{很|hěn}{大|dà}.
- Writing the third stroke of {=长=} as a plain vertical: it flicks up to the right at the bottom.

## Key points

- {他|tā}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}: a topic-comment sentence, a topic followed by a small sentence
  about it. Chinese uses it to describe people by a feature: {她|tā}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{很|hěn}{大|dà},
  {我|wǒ}{身体|shēn tǐ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}.
- {高|gāo} tall, high; {多|duō}{高|gāo} how tall; heights in metres: {一|yì}{米|mǐ}{七|qī}.
- {长|cháng} long, for length and time; {长|zhǎng} (to grow) is HSK 3's.
- Body words: {头|tóu}, {眼睛|yǎn jing}, {手|shǒu}, {身体|shēn tǐ} (body; health).
- Adjective reduplication: AA{的|de} ({大大|dà dà}{的|de}) and AABB{的|de}
  ({漂漂亮亮|piào piào liàng liàng}{的|de}): vivid description, never with {很|hěn}.
- Modifiers come before the noun: {大大|dà dà}{的|de}{眼睛|yǎn jing}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Colours and what people wear: 着
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 02 described faces and figures. This one adds colours and clothes, so you can say what
someone is wearing and pick out "the red one" in a shop. The grammar point is the particle
{着|zhe}, which turns an action into a state you can see: {他|tā}{穿|chuān}{着|zhe}{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}
(he's in red, he has red clothes on), {电视|diàn shì}{开|kāi}{着|zhe} (the TV is on). You'll also
learn a new radical, 衤, the clothing radical.

## Colours: {颜色|yán sè}

{颜色|yán sè} is "colour". A colour word is a character + {色|sè} ("colour"):

| Colour | Meaning | Also in |
|---|---|---|
| {红色|hóng sè} | red | {红茶|hóng chá} (black tea: "red tea" in Chinese) |
| {白色|bái sè} | white | {白天|bái tiān} (daytime) |
| {黑色|hēi sè} | black | {天|tiān}{黑|hēi}{了|le} (it's got dark) |
| {绿色|lǜ sè} | green | {绿茶|lǜ chá} (green tea) |

Two more you'll want come in HSK 3: {黄色|huáng sè} (yellow) and {蓝色|lán sè} (blue).

Ask about colour with {什么|shén me}{颜色|yán sè}:

{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{什么|shén me}{颜色|yán sè}？ — What colour do you like?
{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{绿色|lǜ sè}。 — I like green.
{你|nǐ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{颜色|yán sè}{的|de}？ — What colour is your phone?
{黑色|hēi sè}{的|de}。 — Black.

Here the colour words are nouns ("red, the colour red"), so they can follow {是|shì} and
{喜欢|xǐ huan}. The first character on its own is an adjective: {红|hóng}, {白|bái}, {黑|hēi},
{绿|lǜ}. You'll see it in compound words ({红茶|hóng chá}), in doubled form
({红红|hóng hóng}{的|de}, lesson 02's pattern) and in {天|tiān}{黑|hēi}{了|le}.

### Colour + noun

There are two ways to put a colour before a noun:

{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu} — red clothes (the usual written and spoken form)
{红|hóng}{衣服|yī fu} — red clothes (shorter, everyday)

With the two-syllable word, add {的|de}: {白色|bái sè}{的|de}{裤子|kù zi}, {黑色|hēi sè}{的|de}{手表|shǒu biǎo}.
The one-character form joins the noun directly: {白|bái}{裤子|kù zi}. Both are fine; this course uses
the {色|sè} forms, which are this lesson's words.

## Clothes: {裤子|kù zi} and {手表|shǒu biǎo}

You know {衣服|yī fu} (clothes; a top) and {穿|chuān} (to wear, put on) from HSK 1. Two new things to
wear:

{裤子|kù zi} — trousers (one pair: {一|yì}{条|tiáo}{裤子|kù zi})
{手表|shǒu biǎo} — wristwatch ({一|yí}{块|kuài}{手表|shǒu biǎo})

{条|tiáo} is the measure word for long thin things, from lesson 22; for now learn
{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{裤子|kù zi} as a phrase. Watches are counted with {块|kuài}, the "piece" of
{块|kuài} (and the money word). Trousers and a watch are both "worn" in English; in Chinese
trousers take {穿|chuān}, and a watch takes {戴|dài} (to wear an accessory: HSK 3), or you just say
where it is: {他|tā}{手|shǒu}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{块|kuài}{手表|shǒu biǎo} (he has a watch on his
wrist, literally "on his hand").

{手表|shǒu biǎo} is "hand" + "watch". In simplified Chinese the second character, {=表=}, also means a
table or a form; traditional Chinese writes "watch" with a character of its own, 錶 (see the
character notes).

## "The red one": colour or adjective + {的|de}

A noun can drop out after {的|de} when everyone knows what you mean. What's left, the {的|de}
phrase, stands for the whole thing:

{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}。 — I'll have the red one.
{黑色|hēi sè}{的|de}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}，{白色|bái sè}{的|de}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{妹妹|mèi mei}{的|de}。 — The black one is mine; the white one is my sister's.
{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}{有|yǒu}{绿色|lǜ sè}{的|de}{吗|ma}？ — Does this top come in green?
{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{大|dà}{的|de}，{不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{小|xiǎo}{的|de}。 — I like big ones, not small ones.

You already know one kind: {我|wǒ}{的|de} (mine), {老师|lǎo shī}{的|de} (the teacher's). It works with
colours, adjectives ({新|xīn}{的|de}, the new one) and nouns ({中国|Zhōng guó}{的|de}, the Chinese
one). In a shop it saves repeating the noun every time.

## {着|zhe}: a state that continues

### The form

{着|zhe} goes straight after a verb and says that the result of the action is there and lasting:
the clothes are on, the TV is on, the person is seated. It's a light, toneless syllable.

{他|tā}{穿|chuān}{着|zhe}{一|yí}{件|jiàn}{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}。 — He's wearing a red top.
{电视|diàn shì}{开|kāi}{着|zhe}。 — The TV is on.
{奶奶|nǎi nai}{坐|zuò}{着|zhe}。 — Grandma is sitting down.
{书|shū}{上|shàng}{写|xiě}{着|zhe}{他|tā}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}。 — His name is written in the book.

This is **[[durative 着]]**. "Durative" means lasting: {着|zhe} shows how a situation is going on, not
when it happened. Chinese has several words of this kind, called **[[aspect]]** markers: they show
how an action unfolds (finished, going on, lasting) rather than its time. You know {了|le} for
completed actions and {在|zài} for actions in progress; {着|zhe} is the third, and {过|guo} (for
experiences, lesson 10) completes the set.

In {书|shū}{上|shàng}{写|xiě}{着|zhe}…, the place comes first, with {上|shàng} after the noun: a
**[[locative]]**, the position word ({上|shàng}, {里|lǐ}, {下|xià}…) that turns a thing into a place,
as in HSK 1's {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}. Sentences that describe a scene often start like this: place,
verb + {着|zhe}, what is there.

### {着|zhe} or {在|zài}?

{在|zài} + verb is an action in progress; verb + {着|zhe} is the state it leaves behind:

| {在|zài} + verb: the action is happening | verb + {着|zhe}: the state lasts |
|---|---|
| {他|tā}{在|zài}{穿|chuān}{衣服|yī fu}。 He's getting dressed. | {他|tā}{穿|chuān}{着|zhe}{新|xīn}{衣服|yī fu}。 He's wearing new clothes. |
| {她|tā}{在|zài}{写|xiě}{名字|míng zi}。 She's writing her name. | {书|shū}{上|shàng}{写|xiě}{着|zhe}{名字|míng zi}。 The name is written in the book. |
| {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{开|kāi}{电脑|diàn nǎo}。 I'm switching the computer on. | {电脑|diàn nǎo}{开|kāi}{着|zhe}。 The computer is on. |

Clothes show the difference best: {穿|chuān} is "to put on", so {在|zài}{穿|chuān} is the putting
on, and {穿着|chuān zhe} is having it on. English "wear" covers both, which is why learners reach
for {在|zài} when Chinese wants {着|zhe}.

### {着|zhe} with {呢|ne}, and the negative

{呢|ne} at the end makes it chattier, "you know, it's on": {电视|diàn shì}{开|kāi}{着|zhe}{呢|ne}。

The negative is {没|méi} + verb, usually without {着|zhe}: {电视|diàn shì}{没|méi}{开|kāi} (the TV isn't
on). Questions: {电视|diàn shì}{开|kāi}{着|zhe}{吗|ma}？ or {门|mén}{开|kāi}{着|zhe}{没有|méi yǒu}？ (Is the
door open? {门|mén}, door, is lesson 09's word.)

### Doing one thing in a certain way: verb + {着|zhe} + verb

With two verbs, the first + {着|zhe} says how the second is done:

{奶奶|nǎi nai}{坐|zuò}{着|zhe}{看|kàn}{电视|diàn shì}。 — Grandma watches TV sitting down.
{他|tā}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{坐|zuò}{着|zhe}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}。 — He likes to eat sitting down.

### What {着|zhe} doesn't do

- It isn't a tense. {着|zhe} describes a state you can see now or at the time you're talking about.
  For tomorrow's clothes, say {明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{穿|chuān}{白色|bái sè}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}, with no
  {着|zhe}.
- It needs a verb whose result can last: {穿|chuān}, {开|kāi}, {坐|zuò}, {写|xiě}, {住|zhù}. Verbs of
  being, having, knowing or moving somewhere don't take it: not ~~{是着|shì zhe}~~, ~~{有着|yǒu zhe}~~
  (in everyday speech), ~~{去着|qù zhe}~~.
- The character 着 has other readings in a few words, such as *zháo* in {着急|zháo jí} (anxious,
  HSK 3). As a particle it's always light *zhe*.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 着 (traditional 著) | (particle: lasting state) | zhe (and zháo) | 目 | 11 | {着|zhe}, {穿着|chuān zhe} |
| 颜 (traditional 顏) | colour; face | yán | 页 | 15 | {颜色|yán sè} |
| 色 | colour | sè | 色 | 6 | {颜色|yán sè}, {红色|hóng sè}, {白色|bái sè} |
| 红 (traditional 紅) | red | hóng | 纟 | 6 | {红色|hóng sè}, {红茶|hóng chá} |
| 黑 | black, dark | hēi | 黑 | 12 | {黑色|hēi sè}, {天|tiān}{黑|hēi}{了|le} |
| 绿 (traditional 綠) | green | lǜ | 纟 | 11 | {绿色|lǜ sè}, {绿茶|lǜ chá} |
| 裤 (traditional 褲) | trousers | kù | 衤 | 12 | {裤子|kù zi} |
| 表 (traditional 錶 for "watch"; 表 otherwise) | outside; table, form; watch | biǎo | 衣 | 8 | {手表|shǒu biǎo} |

- 着 began as a handwritten form of 著, which is how the traditional switch shows it (in
  Taiwan the particle is written 著: 穿著). Its parts today are a form of 羊 (sheep) on top and 目
  (eye) below; Make Me a Hanzi files it under 目.
- 颜: 彦 *yàn* gives the sound, and 页 (head, as in {题|tí} from {问题|wèn tí}) the meaning: the
  word first meant the face or forehead, and then its colour.
- 红 and 绿 are both 纟 (silk) + a sound part: 工 *gōng* in 红, 录 *lù* in 绿. Dyed silk gave many
  colour words their radical.
- 黑 is traditionally explained as soot: a window or chimney over a fire, with the fire as the four
  dots 灬 at the bottom. It's its own radical.
- 色 is its own radical. A memory aid: a person (the hat on top) bending over 巴.
- 裤 is 衤 (clothing) + 库 *kù* (storehouse), which gives the sound. Same sound, same tone.
- 表 first meant the outer garment, the one on the outside: that's why it's filed under 衣 (the
  lower part comes from 衣) and why it still means "outside, surface". Watches came much
  later. Traditional script gave them their own character, 錶, with 金 (metal) on the left, so
  the switch shows {手表|shǒu biǎo} as 手錶 but keeps 表 in other words.

### New radical: 衤

衤, the clothing radical ({衣字旁|yī zì páng}, "clothes at the side"), is the side form of 衣, the
first character of {衣服|yī fu}. Characters with it are usually things to wear: 裤 now, and in HSK 3
衬 and 衫 ({衬衫|chèn shān}, shirt), 裙 ({裙子|qún zi}, skirt) and 被 (a quilt, also "by"). Five
characters of the track have it.

Don't mix it up with 礻, the radical of 视 in {电视|diàn shì} (HSK 1). They differ by one stroke: 衤
has five strokes, with two short strokes at the bottom right; 礻 has four, with one. A memory aid:
clothes have an extra fold.

**Radical review.** 纟 (silk, {绞丝旁|jiǎo sī páng}): 红 and 绿 here, 绍 in lesson 01, and 给 from HSK 1.
页 (head, {页字旁|yè zì páng}): 颜, and 题 from HSK 1.

### Stroke order

- 黑: start like 里 but with the inside dots: the left vertical, the top and right side in one
  stroke, the two short strokes inside (a dot, then a short left-falling stroke), the horizontal,
  the vertical, two horizontals (the second one long), and last the four dots from left to right.
- 着: the two short strokes on top (a dot, then a short left-falling stroke), three horizontals (the
  third one longest), the long left-falling stroke through them, then 目.
- 表: the top part first: two horizontals, the vertical, then the long third horizontal; then the
  left-falling stroke, the vertical that flicks up, a short left-falling stroke and the long
  right-falling stroke.
- 裤: 衤 first: the dot, the horizontal that turns down to the left, the vertical, then the two
  short strokes. Then 库: dot, horizontal, the long left-falling stroke (广), then 车.
- 红, 绿: 纟 first (three strokes: two bends, then the rising stroke), then the right side.

```trace
着颜色红黑绿裤表
```

None of these eight is on the handwriting list.

=}

## Dialogue: who's who at the party

At a friend's birthday party, {安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) asks {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) about the guests.

```dialogue
# Who's who at the party
安娜: {李明|Lǐ Míng}{呢|ne}？{他|tā}{来|lái}{了|le}{吗|ma}？
= Where's Li Ming? Has he come?
王芳: {来|lái}{了|le}。{你|nǐ}{看|kàn}，{他|tā}{在|zài}{那儿|nàr}{坐|zuò}{着|zhe}{呢|ne}。
= Yes. Look, he's sitting over there.
安娜: {哪|nǎ}{个|gè}{是|shì}{他|tā}？{那儿|nàr}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{人|rén}。
= Which one is he? There are lots of people there.
王芳: {他|tā}{穿|chuān}{着|zhe}{黑色|hēi sè}{的|de}{裤子|kù zi}{和|hé}{白色|bái sè}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}。
= He's wearing black trousers and a white top.
安娜: {啊|à}，{我|wǒ}{看见|kàn jiàn}{了|le}。{他|tā}{手|shǒu}{上|shàng}{的|de}{手表|shǒu biǎo}{真|zhēn}{漂亮|piào liang}！
= Ah, I see him. The watch on his wrist is really nice!
王芳: {那|nà}{是|shì}{他|tā}{爷爷|yé ye}{的|de}。
= That's his grandpa's.
安娜: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{想|xiǎng}{买|mǎi}{一|yí}{块|kuài}{手表|shǒu biǎo}。{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}{好看|hǎo kàn}{吗|ma}？
= I'd like to buy a watch too. Do red ones look nice?
王芳: {红色|hóng sè}{的|de}、{白色|bái sè}{的|de}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{好看|hǎo kàn}。{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{什么|shén me}{颜色|yán sè}？
= Red and white ones both look nice. What colour do you like?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{绿色|lǜ sè}。{你|nǐ}{看|kàn}，{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{穿|chuān}{着|zhe}{绿色|lǜ sè}{的|de}{裤子|kù zi}！
= I like green. Look, I'm wearing green trousers today!
```

{啊|à} here is a short "ah!" of realising; the particle {啊|a} is lesson 13's. {穿|chuān}{着|zhe} three
times describes what people have on, and every {红色|hóng sè}{的|de} / {白色|bái sè}{的|de} stands for
"a red / white watch".

## Reading: a message before meeting

{安娜|Ān nà} sends {王芳|Wáng Fāng} a message the evening before they meet.

> {王芳|Wáng Fāng}，{你好|nǐ hǎo}！{明天|míng tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{三|sān}{点|diǎn}{我们|wǒ men}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{的|de}{书店|shū diàn}{见|jiàn}{吧|ba}。{我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge}{也|yě}{来|lái}，{他|tā}{想|xiǎng}{认识|rèn shi}{认识|rèn shi}{你|nǐ}。{他|tā}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}，{明天|míng tiān}{穿|chuān}{黑色|hēi sè}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}{和|hé}{白色|bái sè}{的|de}{裤子|kù zi}，{手|shǒu}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{块|kuài}{绿色|lǜ sè}{的|de}{手表|shǒu biǎo}。{我|wǒ}{呢|ne}？{我|wǒ}{穿|chuān}{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}，{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{红色|hóng sè}！{明天|míng tiān}{见|jiàn}！{安娜|Ān nà}

Answer:

1. When and where will they meet?
2. How will Wang Fang recognise Anna's brother?
3. Why does the message say {明天|míng tiān}{穿|chuān}, not {穿着|chuān zhe}?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Tomorrow at three in the afternoon, at the school bookshop.
2. He's tall, he'll be wearing a black top and white trousers, and he has a green watch on his
   wrist.
3. Because it's about tomorrow. {着|zhe} describes a state that is there now (or at the time you're
   describing); for plans, use the plain verb.

"Hi Wang Fang! Let's meet at the school bookshop at three tomorrow afternoon. My older brother is
coming too; he'd like to meet you. He's tall. Tomorrow he's wearing a black top and white trousers,
and he has a green watch on his wrist. And me? I'm wearing red. I really like red! See you
tomorrow! Anna"
</details>

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{什么|shén me}{颜色|yán sè}？
= What colour do you like?
{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}。
= I'll have the red one.
{他|tā}{穿|chuān}{着|zhe}{白色|bái sè}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}。
= He's wearing a white top.
{电视|diàn shì}{开|kāi}{着|zhe}{呢|ne}。
= The TV is on.
{这|zhè}{块|kuài}{手表|shǒu biǎo}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{的|de}。
= This watch is my grandpa's.
```

## Pronunciation

- The four colours give you three of the four tones: {黑|hēi} 1, {红|hóng} and {白|bái} 2, {绿|lǜ} 4.
  Say {黑色|hēi sè}, {红色|hóng sè}, {白色|bái sè}, {绿色|lǜ sè} in a row, then add the third
  tone with {手表|shǒu biǎo}, two third tones together: said *shóu biǎo*.
- {色|sè}: *s* + the back vowel *e* ("uh"), falling. Don't say "say".
- {绿|lǜ}: the ü sound (say "ee" with rounded lips). After *l* the two dots are written:
  *lǜ*, not *lù* ({路|lù}, road, lesson 07, is a different word).
- {颜|yán}: rhymes with "yen", rising.
- {着|zhe} is light and short, like the *zi* of {裤子|kù zi}.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{他|tā}{在|zài}{穿|chuān}{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}~~ for "he's wearing red" (as a
  description): that's "he's putting on red clothes". Say {他|tā}{穿|chuān}{着|zhe}…
- ~~{明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{穿|chuān}{着|zhe}{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}~~: {着|zhe} isn't a future. Say
  {明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{穿|chuān}{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}.
- ~~{电视|diàn shì}{不|bù}{开|kāi}{着|zhe}~~: the negative is {没|méi}: {电视|diàn shì}{没|méi}{开|kāi}.
- Repeating the noun when {的|de} can carry it: {我|wǒ}{要|yào}{红色|hóng sè}{的|de} is enough.
- ~~{红色|hóng sè}{衣服|yī fu}{的|de}~~: the colour comes first, then {的|de}, then the noun.
- Writing 裤 with 礻 (four strokes, as in 视): clothing is 衤, with five.

## Key points

- {颜色|yán sè}: colour. {红色|hóng sè}, {白色|bái sè}, {黑色|hēi sè}, {绿色|lǜ sè}; ask
  {什么|shén me}{颜色|yán sè}？
- Colour + {的|de} + noun: {白色|bái sè}{的|de}{裤子|kù zi}. Without the noun, the {的|de} phrase means
  "the white one".
- {裤子|kù zi} (trousers, {一|yì}{条|tiáo}); {手表|shǒu biǎo} (wristwatch, {一|yí}{块|kuài}; traditional 手錶).
- Durative {着|zhe}: verb + {着|zhe} = a state that lasts: {穿着|chuān zhe}, {开着|kāi zhe},
  {坐着|zuò zhe}, {书|shū}{上|shàng}{写|xiě}{着|zhe}…. {在|zài} + verb is the action; verb + {着|zhe} the
  state.
- Negative {没|méi} + verb; not for future plans; verb + {着|zhe} + verb = doing something in a way.
- New radical 衤 (clothing), five strokes; 礻 has four.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Family life: 每, 经常, 有时
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

HSK 1 gave you the family: parents, brothers and sisters, sons and daughters. Lesson 01 added the
grandparents. This lesson completes the picture with husbands, wives and children, and moves from
who is in a family to what they do: who cooks, who does the washing, what happens every day and
what happens only sometimes. The grammar is about how often: {每|měi} (every) with {都|dōu}, and the
adverbs {经常|jīng cháng} (often) and {有时|yǒu shí} (sometimes).

## Husband and wife: {丈夫|zhàng fu} and {妻子|qī zi}

{丈夫|zhàng fu} — husband
{妻子|qī zi} — wife

Both have a light second syllable: *zhàng fu*, *qī zi*. They're the clear, neutral words, right for
talking about anyone's spouse and for forms:

{她|tā}{丈夫|zhàng fu}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}。 — Her husband is a doctor.
{我|wǒ}{妻子|qī zi}{在|zài}{大学|dà xué}{工作|gōng zuò}。 — My wife works at a university.
{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}{的|de}{丈夫|zhàng fu}{姓|xìng}{李|Lǐ}。 — Teacher Wang's husband's family name is Li.

The last example is a reminder from HSK 1's honors lesson on Chinese names: in mainland China a married
woman keeps her own family name, so husband and wife usually have different ones.

You'll hear other words for spouses too. {先生|xiān sheng} (HSK 1) also means "husband":
{我|wǒ}{先生|xiān sheng} is a polite way for a woman to say "my husband", and {太太|tài tai} (Mrs; wife)
is its partner, common in polite speech. Between couples and friends, {老公|lǎo gōng} (hubby) and
{老婆|lǎo po} (wife) are very common and informal; {爱人|ài ren} (spouse, HSK 3) is used for either,
especially by older people on the mainland. Learn {丈夫|zhàng fu} and {妻子|qī zi} first; the others
you'll recognise.

## Children: {小孩儿|xiǎo háir}, {男孩儿|nán háir}, {女孩儿|nǚ háir}

{孩子|hái zi} (HSK 1) is a child, and also somebody's son or daughter at any age:
{他们|tā men}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{孩子|hái zi}. These three are for young people:

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {小孩儿|xiǎo háir} | child, kid | everyday speech: {那|nà}{个|gè}{小孩儿|xiǎo háir}{真|zhēn}{漂亮|piào liang}！ |
| {男孩儿|nán háir} | boy | |
| {女孩儿|nǚ háir} | girl | also used loosely for young women |

{我|wǒ}{姐姐|jiě jie}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{孩子|hái zi}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{男孩儿|nán háir}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{女孩儿|nǚ háir}。
— My older sister has two children, a boy and a girl.

### The -r syllable

All three end in *-r*, the erhua of the north that you met in {一点儿|yì diǎnr} and {哪儿|nǎr}. The 儿
isn't a syllable of its own: it adds an *r* to the syllable before it, and the spelling shows that,
*háir*. In speech the *i* drops out before the *r*, so *háir* sounds like "har" with a rising
tone. Many speakers, especially in the south, say {小孩|xiǎo hái}, {男孩|nán hái}, {女孩|nǚ hái} without
the *-r*, or {男孩子|nán hái zi}, {女孩子|nǚ hái zi}; all of these are right. Type the words either way
when you review them.

## Every: {每|měi} + measure word (+ noun) + {都|dōu}

{每|měi} is "every, each". Like {这|zhè} and {那|nà}, it comes before a measure word:

{每|měi}{个|gè}{人|rén} — every person, everyone
{每|měi}{本|běn}{书|shū} — every book
{每|měi}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī} — every week
{每|měi}{个|gè}{月|yuè} — every month

Words that are measures themselves, such as {天|tiān} (day) and {年|nián} (year), need no {个|gè}:
{每天|měi tiān}, {每年|měi nián}. ~~{每|měi}{个|gè}{天|tiān}~~ is a mistake, as ~~{一|yí}{个|gè}{天|tiān}~~
would be.

Then, in a sentence, {都|dōu} goes before the verb: "every …, without exception".

{我|wǒ}{每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}。 — I get up at seven every day.
{每|měi}{个|gè}{人|rén}{都|dōu}{有|yǒu}{自己|zì jǐ}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}。 — Everyone has their own name.
{我们|wǒ men}{每|měi}{个|gè}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{都|dōu}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{爷爷|yé ye}{奶奶|nǎi nai}。 — We go to see Grandpa and Grandma every Saturday.

{每天|měi tiān} and the other {每|měi} time phrases are time words, so they go where time words go:
after the subject or at the start, never at the end (~~{我|wǒ}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}{每天|měi tiān}~~).
In speech the {都|dōu} is sometimes left out, but keep it: it's almost always there.

### {天天|tiān tiān}, {人人|rén rén}: doubled measure words

Here's one more kind of reduplication. A few measure words and nouns double to mean "every":
{天天|tiān tiān} (every day), {人人|rén rén} (everybody), {年年|nián nián} (every year). They also take
{都|dōu}: {他|tā}{天天|tiān tiān}{都|dōu}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}. They sound a little more lively than {每天|měi tiān},
which is the everyday word.

## How often: {经常|jīng cháng} and {有时|yǒu shí}

{经常|jīng cháng} is "often", {有时|yǒu shí} is "sometimes". They're **[[frequency adverbs]]**, adverbs that
say how often something happens, and like other adverbs ({也|yě}, {都|dōu}, {很|hěn}) they go after the
subject and before the verb:

{他|tā}{经常|jīng cháng}{做饭|zuò fàn}。 — He often cooks.
{我|wǒ}{妻子|qī zi}{有时|yǒu shí}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}。 — My wife is sometimes very busy.
{我们|wǒ men}{经常|jīng cháng}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}。 — We often eat at home.

The last one shows the order with a place: the adverb comes before {在|zài} + place, which comes
before the verb. English puts "often" in the same place ("we often eat"), but "sometimes" can go
anywhere in English. In Chinese, {有时|yǒu shí} goes before the verb or at the very start:

{有时|yǒu shí}{我们|wǒ men}{在|zài}{饭店|fàn diàn}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}。 — Sometimes we eat in a restaurant.

Never at the end: not ~~{我|wǒ}{做饭|zuò fàn}{经常|jīng cháng}~~, not ~~{我们|wǒ men}{在|zài}{饭店|fàn diàn}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{有时|yǒu shí}~~.

| How often | Chinese | Example |
|---|---|---|
| every day | {每天|měi tiān}…{都|dōu} | {他|tā}{每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu}。 |
| often | {经常|jīng cháng} | {他|tā}{经常|jīng cháng}{洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu}。 |
| sometimes | {有时|yǒu shí}, {有时候|yǒu shí hou} | {他|tā}{有时|yǒu shí}{洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu}。 |
| seldom | {很|hěn}{少|shǎo} | {他|tā}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}{洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu}。 |
| not often | {不|bù}{经常|jīng cháng} | {他|tā}{不|bù}{经常|jīng cháng}{洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu}。 |

- {有时|yǒu shí} and {有时候|yǒu shí hou} mean the same; {有时候|yǒu shí hou} (built from HSK 1's
  {时候|shí hou}) is a little more relaxed. Both are fine anywhere in this course.
- {有时|yǒu shí}…，{有时|yǒu shí}… is "sometimes…, sometimes…", a handy way to describe a varied
  routine: {星期天|xīng qī tiān}{我|wǒ}{有时|yǒu shí}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}，{有时|yǒu shí}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{休息|xiū xi}。
- {很|hěn}{少|shǎo} + verb (seldom) came up in lesson 02's reading: {很|hěn}{少|shǎo}{生病|shēng bìng}.

## Washing: {洗|xǐ}

{洗|xǐ} is "to wash". Its object is what gets washed, and the phrases are the everyday words for
housework and hygiene:

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu} | to do the washing, wash clothes |
| {洗|xǐ}{手|shǒu} | to wash your hands |
| {洗|xǐ}{碗|wǎn} | to do the dishes ({碗|wǎn}, bowl: HSK 3) |
| {洗|xǐ}{苹果|píng guǒ} | to wash an apple |
| {洗澡|xǐ zǎo} | to have a bath or a shower (HSK 3) |

{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{前|qián}{要|yào}{洗|xǐ}{手|shǒu}。 — You should wash your hands before eating.
{在|zài}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}，{丈夫|zhàng fu}{做饭|zuò fàn}，{妻子|qī zi}{洗|xǐ}{碗|wǎn}。 — In our house the husband cooks and the wife does the dishes.

The {洗|xǐ} of {洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān}, the polite word for a toilet ("wash-hand room"), is this one;
that word comes in lesson 11.

### Verb + object words, and doubling them

{洗澡|xǐ zǎo} is a **[[separable verb]]**: a verb made of a verb and its object, which can come apart when
something goes between them, as {睡觉|shuì jiào} and {起床|qǐ chuáng} do. "Have a quick shower" is
{洗|xǐ}{个|gè}{澡|zǎo}, with {个|gè} in the middle. {洗|xǐ}{手|shǒu} and {洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu} are
looser still: verb + object phrases.

That matters when you double them (lesson 01): only the verb doubles, AAB, not the whole thing:

{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{洗洗|xǐ xi}{手|shǒu}。 — Go and wash your hands.
{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{休息|xiū xi}{休息|xiū xi}。 — I'd like to have a little rest. (one verb: ABAB)

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 丈 | (old unit of length); husband | zhàng | 一 | 3 | {丈夫|zhàng fu} |
| 夫 | man; husband | fu (fū) | 大 | 4 | {丈夫|zhàng fu}, {夫妻|fū qī} (husband and wife, HSK 3) |
| 妻 | wife | qī | 女 | 8 | {妻子|qī zi} |
| 每 | every | měi | 母 | 7 | {每|měi}, {每天|měi tiān} |
| 经 (traditional 經) | warp (of cloth); to pass through; regular | jīng | 纟 | 8 | {经常|jīng cháng}, {已经|yǐ jīng} (already, lesson 18) |
| 洗 | to wash | xǐ | 氵 | 9 | {洗|xǐ}, {洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān} (toilet, lesson 11) |

- 丈 is an old unit of length, ten {尺|chǐ} (about 3.3 m today), and in {丈夫|zhàng fu} it first meant
  a grown man. It has only three strokes; don't add a dot.
- 夫 is 大 (a person with arms spread) with a second horizontal through the top. The traditional
  explanation: the pin in a grown man's hair. Four look-alikes are worth sorting now: 大 (big), 太
  (too: a dot underneath), 天 (day: the extra line on top, not crossing) and 夫 (the extra line
  crossing the top). In {丈夫|zhàng fu} 夫 is light, *fu*; in other words, *fū*.
- 妻 has 女 (woman) at the bottom, under a shape that once showed a hand. Its radical is 女.
- 每 is 𠂉 (a figure on top) over 母 (mother), its radical. Keep the two dots inside 母 as dots:
  with a stroke through instead, it becomes 毋, an old word for "don't".
- 经 is 纟 (silk) + a part that showed the threads stretched on a loom: 经 first meant the warp, the
  long threads of a cloth. From "running straight through" it came to mean "to pass through" and
  "regular", the sense in {经常|jīng cháng}. The traditional form is 經.
- 洗 is 氵 (water) + 先, which gives the sound (the 先 of {先生|xiān sheng}): *xiān* and *xǐ* share
  the *x*.

**Radical review.** 氵 (water, {三点水|sān diǎn shuǐ}, "three drops of water"): 洗, and from HSK 1 汉,
没 and 漂. 一 (the horizontal, filed alone as a radical): 丈, and from HSK 1 七, 三, 上, 下, 不, 两 and
东. Characters filed under 一 often have nothing to do with "one": the stroke is just their most
visible part.

### Stroke order

- 丈: the horizontal, then the left-falling stroke, then the right-falling stroke that crosses it.
- 夫: the two horizontals (the short top one first), then the left-falling stroke, then the
  right-falling stroke.
- 每: the short left-falling stroke and the short horizontal on top, then 母: the left side going
  down and right in one stroke, the top and right side with its hook, the upper dot, the long
  horizontal, and the lower dot last.
- 妻: the top part first (horizontal, the stroke that turns down, the long horizontal, the short
  horizontal, then the vertical through them), then 女.
- 洗: 氵 (two dots and the rising stroke), then 先: the short left-falling stroke, the horizontal,
  the vertical, the long horizontal, the left-falling stroke and the last stroke, which bends right
  and up.

```trace
丈夫妻每经洗
```

None of these six is on the handwriting list.

=}

## Dialogue: who does what?

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) asks {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) about her older sister's family.

```dialogue
# Who does what?
安娜: {你|nǐ}{姐姐|jiě jie}{有|yǒu}{孩子|hái zi}{吗|ma}？
= Does your older sister have children?
王芳: {有|yǒu}，{她|tā}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{孩子|hái zi}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{男孩儿|nán háir}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{女孩儿|nǚ háir}。
= Yes, she has two, a boy and a girl.
安娜: {她|tā}{丈夫|zhàng fu}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}{工作|gōng zuò}？
= What does her husband do?
王芳: {他|tā}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}，{经常|jīng cháng}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}，{有时|yǒu shí}{晚上|wǎn shang}{也|yě}{工作|gōng zuò}。
= He's a doctor. He's often very busy, and sometimes he works in the evening too.
安娜: {谁|shéi}{做饭|zuò fàn}？
= Who does the cooking?
王芳: {每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{姐姐|jiě jie}{做饭|zuò fàn}，{她|tā}{丈夫|zhàng fu}{洗|xǐ}{碗|wǎn}。
= My sister cooks every day, and her husband does the dishes.
安娜: {星期天|xīng qī tiān}{呢|ne}？
= What about Sundays?
王芳: {星期天|xīng qī tiān}{她|tā}{丈夫|zhàng fu}{休息|xiū xi}，{他|tā}{经常|jīng cháng}{给|gěi}{孩子们|hái zi men}{做饭|zuò fàn}。
= On Sundays her husband is off, and he often cooks for the children.
安娜: {你们|nǐ men}{家|jiā}{呢|ne}？{谁|shéi}{洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu}？
= What about your family? Who does the washing?
王芳: {我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu}，{我|wǒ}{有时|yǒu shí}{也|yě}{洗|xǐ}。
= My mum does the washing every day, and sometimes I do it too.
```

{每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{姐姐|jiě jie}{做饭|zuò fàn}: putting {是|shì} before the person
stresses who it is, "it's my sister who cooks". And {孩子们|hái zi men} shows {们|men} after a noun
for people, as in {同学们|tóng xué men}; nouns for things don't take it.

## Reading: our week

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{马东|Mǎ Dōng}。{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}{妻子|qī zi}{都|dōu}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{工作|gōng zuò}，{每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}。{我们|wǒ men}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{女儿|nǚ ér}，{今年|jīn nián}{六|liù}{岁|suì}。{早上|zǎo shang}{我|wǒ}{妻子|qī zi}{做|zuò}{早饭|zǎo fàn}，{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{女儿|nǚ ér}{穿|chuān}{衣服|yī fu}。{晚上|wǎn shang}{我|wǒ}{做饭|zuò fàn}，{我|wǒ}{妻子|qī zi}{洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu}。{星期六|xīng qī liù}{我们|wǒ men}{经常|jīng cháng}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{妈妈|mā ma}。{我|wǒ}{女儿|nǚ ér}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{爷爷|yé ye}{奶奶|nǎi nai}，{每|měi}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī}{都|dōu}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{他们|tā men}{家|jiā}。{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{我们|wǒ men}{有时|yǒu shí}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{休息|xiū xi}，{有时|yǒu shí}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}。

Answer:

1. Where do Ma Dong and his wife work?
2. Who does the washing?
3. What does the family often do on Saturdays?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Both at a hospital ({都|dōu}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{工作|gōng zuò}).
2. His wife, in the evening.
3. They go to see Ma Dong's parents (his daughter's {爷爷|yé ye} and {奶奶|nǎi nai}).

"My name is Ma Dong. My wife and I both work at a hospital, and we're busy every day. We have a
daughter who is six this year. In the morning my wife makes breakfast and I get our daughter
dressed. In the evening I cook and my wife does the washing. On Saturdays we often go to see my mum
and dad. My daughter loves her grandparents and wants to go to their house every week. On Sundays
we sometimes stay at home and rest, and sometimes go to see a film."
</details>

Notice that the grandparents are {爷爷|yé ye} and {奶奶|nǎi nai} because they're the father's parents.

## Say it

```speak
{我|wǒ}{每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}。
= I get up at seven every day.
{他|tā}{经常|jīng cháng}{做饭|zuò fàn}。
= He often cooks.
{有时|yǒu shí}{我们|wǒ men}{在|zài}{饭店|fàn diàn}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}。
= Sometimes we eat in a restaurant.
{她|tā}{丈夫|zhàng fu}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}。
= Her husband is a doctor.
{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{洗洗|xǐ xi}{手|shǒu}。
= Go and wash your hands.
```

## Pronunciation

- {丈夫|zhàng fu} and {妻子|qī zi}: a full tone, then a light one. {丈|zhàng} has *zh* and *-ang*;
  {妻|qī} has *q*, a puffed "ch" with the tongue flat, and a real "ee".
- {小孩儿|xiǎo háir}: said *xiǎo hár*; {小|xiǎo} keeps its low dip because a second tone follows.
- {每|měi} is the *mei* of "May" with a dip. {每天|měi tiān}: low, then high and level.
- {经常|jīng cháng}: two different finals, *-ing* and *-ang*; the first is level, the second rises.
  The *ch* is curled back with a puff of air.
- {有时|yǒu shí}: the *sh* + buzzing *i* of {是|shì} and {十|shí}, here rising.
- {洗|xǐ} and {洗手|xǐ shǒu}: two third tones, so the first one rises: said *xí shǒu*. {洗|xǐ} sounds
  exactly like the {喜|xǐ} of {喜欢|xǐ huan}; only the character tells them apart.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{每|měi}{个|gè}{天|tiān}~~: {天|tiān} and {年|nián} need no measure word: {每天|měi tiān}, {每年|měi nián}.
- Leaving out the measure word: {每|měi}{个|gè}{人|rén}, {每|měi}{本|běn}{书|shū}. ({每|měi}{人|rén}
  without {个|gè} exists, but mostly in notices and set phrases: {每|měi}{人|rén}{一|yí}{个|gè}, one each.)
- Forgetting {都|dōu}: {每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu} sounds natural; without {都|dōu} it
  sounds clipped.
- Frequency at the end, English-style: ~~{我|wǒ}{做饭|zuò fàn}{经常|jīng cháng}~~. Say
  {我|wǒ}{经常|jīng cháng}{做饭|zuò fàn}.
- {经常|jīng cháng} at the very start sounds odd: {有时|yǒu shí} can start a sentence, but
  {经常|jīng cháng} goes after the subject, {我|wǒ}{经常|jīng cháng}{做饭|zuò fàn}.
- ~~{洗手洗手|xǐ shǒu xǐ shǒu}~~ for "wash your hands quickly": only the verb doubles:
  {洗洗|xǐ xi}{手|shǒu}.
- Writing 夫 like 天: in 夫 the top horizontal is crossed by the left-falling stroke.

## Key points

- {丈夫|zhàng fu} husband, {妻子|qī zi} wife; {先生|xiān sheng}, {太太|tài tai}, {老公|lǎo gōng},
  {老婆|lǎo po} and {爱人|ài ren} are other words you'll hear.
- {小孩儿|xiǎo háir}, {男孩儿|nán háir}, {女孩儿|nǚ háir}: the -r syllable (*háir*, said *hár*); also
  {小孩|xiǎo hái}, {男孩|nán hái}, {女孩|nǚ hái}.
- {每|měi} + measure word (+ noun) … {都|dōu} + verb: {每|měi}{个|gè}{人|rén}{都|dōu}…, {每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}….
  Doubled {天天|tiān tiān}, {人人|rén rén} also mean "every".
- Frequency adverbs go after the subject, before the verb: {经常|jīng cháng} (often), {有时|yǒu shí}
  (sometimes, also at the start), {很|hěn}{少|shǎo} (seldom), {不|bù}{经常|jīng cháng} (not often).
- {洗|xǐ} + what you wash: {洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu}, {洗|xǐ}{手|shǒu}; doubled: {洗洗|xǐ xi}{手|shǒu}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: How you feel: 因为…所以
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In HSK 1 you learned to say you're ill ({我|wǒ}{病|bìng}{了|le}), to see a doctor and to rest. This
lesson lets you say how you feel and why: tired, unwell, aching somewhere, and better after some
medicine. The grammar point is the pair {因为|yīn wèi}…{所以|suǒ yǐ}… (because…, so…), which joins a
cause to its effect. You'll also learn the character 店 at last, the one in {饭店|fàn diàn},
{商店|shāng diàn} and {书店|shū diàn}, and the module ends with a handwriting review.

## How you feel: {舒服|shū fu}, {累|lèi}, {疼|téng}

### {舒服|shū fu}: comfortable, well

{舒服|shū fu} is "comfortable" for things and "well, feeling good" for people. The negative,
{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}, is the everyday way to say you feel unwell:

{这|zhè}{个|gè}{椅子|yǐ zi}{很|hěn}{舒服|shū fu}。 — This chair is comfortable.
{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}。 — I don't feel well today.
{我|wǒ}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}。 — I'm feeling a bit unwell.
{你|nǐ}{哪儿|nǎr}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}？ — Where don't you feel well? (what's wrong?)

{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr} (HSK 1) fits here perfectly: it's for things you'd rather not have, a little.

### {累|lèi}: tired

{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{累|lèi}。 — I'm (very) tired.
{你|nǐ}{累|lèi}{了|le}{吧|ba}？ — You must be tired. (change-of-state {了|le}: you've got tired)
{这|zhè}{个|gè}{工作|gōng zuò}{很|hěn}{累|lèi}。 — This job is tiring.

The same word describes the person ("tired") and the thing that tires them ("tiring"), so
{很|hěn}{累|lèi} can be either: context tells you which.

### {疼|téng}: to ache, sore

{疼|téng} says a part of the body hurts. Name the part, then {疼|téng}. That's a topic-comment
sentence from lesson 02, with the person as topic:

{我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{疼|téng}。 — I have a headache. ("me, head aches")
{她|tā}{手|shǒu}{很|hěn}{疼|téng}。 — Her hand hurts a lot.
{你|nǐ}{哪儿|nǎr}{疼|téng}？ — Where does it hurt?

{头疼|tóu téng} is so common it's almost one word, "headache". {疼|téng} can also take {很|hěn} or
{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}: {我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{疼|téng}. You'll also see {痛|tòng}, a more formal
word for "pain", in writing and on medicine boxes. And {疼|téng} has a warm second meaning, "to dote
on": {奶奶|nǎi nai}{很|hěn}{疼|téng}{我|wǒ} (Grandma dotes on me).

## Medicine: {药|yào} and {药店|yào diàn}

{药|yào} is medicine, and you "eat" it: {吃|chī}{药|yào} is "to take medicine", the everyday phrase for
pills and most other medicine. ({喝|hē}{药|yào}, "drink medicine", is also said for medicine you
drink, such as Chinese herbal medicine.)

{你|nǐ}{要|yào}{吃|chī}{药|yào}。 — You should take some medicine.
{这|zhè}{个|gè}{药|yào}{一|yì}{天|tiān}{吃|chī}{三|sān}{次|cì}。 — Take this medicine three times a day.

({次|cì}, "times", is lesson 10's word; it's on every medicine label.) {药店|yào diàn} is a
pharmacy, built like the shop words you know: {书店|shū diàn} (bookshop), {饭店|fàn diàn}
(restaurant), {商店|shāng diàn} (shop). {中药|zhōng yào} is traditional Chinese medicine, which many
pharmacies sell beside {西药|xī yào}, Western medicine.

### {要|yào} and {能|néng}: what you should do, what you can't

The first example used {要|yào} for "should, need to". {要|yào}, {能|néng}, {会|huì}, {可以|kě yǐ} and
{想|xiǎng} are **[[modal verbs]]**: verbs that go before another verb to add need, ability, permission or
wish. When you're ill, two of them do most of the work:

{你|nǐ}{要|yào}{多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}。 — You need to rest more. ({多|duō} before a verb: "more")
{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bù}{能|néng}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}。 — I can't go to class today.

{不|bù}{能|néng} is "can't (because of circumstances)", the right word for being too ill to go.
{不|bú}{会|huì} would mean you never learned how.

## Laughing and smiling: {笑|xiào}

{笑|xiào} is both "to laugh" and "to smile":

{她|tā}{笑|xiào}{了|le}。 — She laughed. / She smiled.
{你|nǐ}{笑|xiào}{什么|shén me}？ — What are you laughing at?
{爷爷|yé ye}{笑|xiào}{着|zhe}{说|shuō}：“{没事|méi shì}！” — Grandpa said with a smile, "It's nothing!"

The last example is lesson 03's verb + {着|zhe} + verb: smiling while saying it. The character 笑 is
taught in lesson 06, so for now it always has its pinyin.

## Because…, so…: {因为|yīn wèi}…{所以|suǒ yǐ}…

### The pattern

{因为|yīn wèi} (because) introduces a cause, {所以|suǒ yǐ} (so, therefore) its result. Together they
make a sentence of **[[cause and effect]]**:

{因为|yīn wèi}{我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{疼|téng}，{所以|suǒ yǐ}{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}。
— Because I had a headache, I didn't go to class.

{因为|yīn wèi}{今天|jīn tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{所以|suǒ yǐ}{他|tā}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{休息|xiū xi}。
— Because it's cold today, he's resting at home.

In English you say "because" or "so", never both: "because I had a headache, so I didn't go" is a
mistake. In Chinese the pair is normal and, in careful speech and writing, usual. The cause comes
first, as it happened.

### One half alone

Either word also works alone:

{我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{疼|téng}，{所以|suǒ yǐ}{没|méi}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}。 — I had a headache, so I didn't go to class.
{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}，{因为|yīn wèi}{我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{疼|téng}。 — I didn't go to class because I had a headache.

The second order, result first and then {因为|yīn wèi}…, is how you give a reason after the fact,
as English does. Don't add {所以|suǒ yǐ} to it: there's nothing after the cause for it to introduce.

### Where the subject goes

{因为|yīn wèi} can come before or after the subject: {因为|yīn wèi}{我|wǒ}{病|bìng}{了|le}… and
{我|wǒ}{因为|yīn wèi}{病|bìng}{了|le}… are both fine. {所以|suǒ yǐ} starts its clause, before the
subject: {所以|suǒ yǐ}{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}, never ~~{我|wǒ}{所以|suǒ yǐ}{没|méi}{去|qù}~~. When both
clauses have the same subject, the second can drop it: {所以|suǒ yǐ}{没|méi}{去|qù}.

### Answering "why?"

The question "why?" is {为什么|wèi shén me} (lesson 15's word), and the answer starts with
{因为|yīn wèi}:

{你|nǐ}{为什么|wèi shén me}{没|méi}{来|lái}？ — Why didn't you come?
{因为|yīn wèi}{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}。 — Because I wasn't feeling well.

The 为 of {为什么|wèi shén me} is the one you learn in this lesson.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 因 | cause, reason | yīn | 囗 | 6 | {因为|yīn wèi} |
| 为 (traditional 為) ✎ | for; to do | wèi (and wéi) | 丶 | 4 | {因为|yīn wèi}, {为什么|wèi shén me} (why, lesson 15) |
| 所 | place; (in {所以|suǒ yǐ}) | suǒ | 户 | 8 | {所以|suǒ yǐ} |
| 舒 | to stretch, relax | shū | 舌 | 12 | {舒服|shū fu} |
| 累 | tired | lèi (and others) | 糸 | 11 | {累|lèi} |
| 疼 | to ache | téng | 疒 | 10 | {疼|téng}, {头疼|tóu téng} |
| 药 (traditional 藥) | medicine | yào | 艹 | 9 | {药|yào}, {药店|yào diàn}, {吃|chī}{药|yào} |
| 店 | shop | diàn | 广 | 8 | {药店|yào diàn}, {饭店|fàn diàn}, {商店|shāng diàn}, {书店|shū diàn} |

- 因 is 大 inside 囗, the enclosure. One old explanation sees a person lying on a mat, something to
  rely on; from "rely on, follow from" it came to mean "cause".
- 为 is a simplified form of 為, which began as a drawing of a hand leading an elephant: "to do, to
  make". In {因为|yīn wèi} and {为什么|wèi shén me} it's read *wèi* ("for"); in a few HSK 3 words such as
  {认为|rèn wéi} (to think that) it's *wéi*.
- 所 is 户 (a door) + 斤 (an axe). Its own meaning is "place"; in {所以|suǒ yǐ} it's just part of the
  word.
- 舒: 舍 (a house) + 予 *yǔ*. Make Me a Hanzi files it under 舌 (tongue), the top part of 舍; other
  dictionaries use 人 or 予. In {舒服|shū fu} the second syllable is light.
- 累 is 田 (field) over 糸 (silk), the full form of the 纟 of 红 and 给. As in 系 from {没关系|méi guān xi},
  糸 stands at the bottom when it's not at the side. The character has other readings (*lěi*, *léi*)
  in words beyond HSK 3.
- 疼 is 疒 (illness, as in {病|bìng}) + 冬 *dōng*, which once gave the sound.
- 药 is 艹 (plants: many medicines were herbs) + 约 *yuē*, the sound part. The traditional form 藥 has
  樂 *yuè* under 艹 instead.
- 店 is 广 (a building open on one side) + 占 *zhàn*. You've been reading it with pinyin since HSK 1;
  now {饭店|fàn diàn}, {商店|shāng diàn}, {书店|shū diàn} and {店|diàn} are all fully yours.

**Radical review.** 疒 (illness, {病字旁|bìng zì páng}): 疼, and 病 from HSK 1. 广 (a building,
{广字旁|guǎng zì páng}): 店, and 床 from HSK 1's {起床|qǐ chuáng}. 艹 (grass): 药, and 茶, 菜, 苹 from HSK 1.

### Stroke order

- 为: four strokes in mainland order: the dot at the top left, the long left-falling stroke, the
  stroke that goes across, down and hooks left, and the dot inside last.
- 因: 囗 is written "go in, then shut the door": the left vertical, the top and right side in one
  stroke, then everything inside (大), and the bottom horizontal last.
