- 疼: 疒 first: the dot, the horizontal, the long left-falling stroke, then the short dot and the
  rising stroke on the left. Then 冬 inside: two dots at the bottom last.
- 药: 艹 (horizontal first), then 纟, then 勺: the short left-falling stroke, the turning hook, and the
  dot inside.
- 店: 广 (dot, horizontal, long left-falling stroke), then 占: vertical, short horizontal, then 口.

```trace
因为所舒累疼药店
```

Write it: 为 is on the handwriting list. Write it three times from memory: the dot first, and the
inside dot last.

=}

## Handwriting review: HSK 1
{=

These sixteen ✎ characters from HSK 1 (小 and 好 from the pinyin course) are all used in this
module. Write each one twice from
memory, on paper or on the pad, then check it against the tracing pad.

> **Handwriting review, module 1**
>
> 名 ({姓名|xìng míng}) · 字 ({名字|míng zi}) · 个 ({个子|gè zi}) · 子 ({裤子|kù zi}, {妻子|qī zi}) · 女 ({女孩儿|nǚ háir}) · 男 ({男孩儿|nán háir}) · 儿 ({小孩儿|xiǎo háir}) · 小 ({小孩儿|xiǎo háir})
>
> 有 ({有时|yǒu shí}) · 时 ({有时|yǒu shí}) · 家 ({家人|jiā rén}) · 爸 ({爸爸|bà ba}) · 妈 ({妈妈|mā ma}) · 好 ({你好|nǐ hǎo}) · 学 ({学生|xué sheng}) · 生 ({学生|xué sheng})

```trace
名字个子女男儿小
```

```trace
有时家爸妈好学生
```

Two to watch: 女 starts with the stroke that turns down and to the right, and the horizontal comes
last; 儿 is only two strokes, the left-falling stroke and then the vertical that bends right and
hooks up.

=}

## Dialogue: not feeling well

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) meets {李明|Lǐ Míng} (李明) before class.

```dialogue
# Not feeling well
安娜: {李明|Lǐ Míng}，{你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{了|le}？
= Li Ming, what's the matter?
李明: {我|wǒ}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}，{头|tóu}{很|hěn}{疼|téng}。
= I'm not feeling very well. I've got a bad headache.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{累|lèi}{了|le}{吧|ba}？
= You must be tired.
李明: {对|duì}。{因为|yīn wèi}{我|wǒ}{昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{一|yī}{点|diǎn}{睡觉|shuì jiào}，{所以|suǒ yǐ}{今天|jīn tiān}{很|hěn}{累|lèi}。
= Yes. I went to bed at one last night, so I'm very tired today.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{要|yào}{吃|chī}{药|yào}{吗|ma}？
= Do you want to take something for it?
李明: {我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{药|yào}。
= I haven't got any medicine.
安娜: {学校|xué xiào}{外边|wài bian}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{家|jiā}{药店|yào diàn}，{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{买|mǎi}{药|yào}{吧|ba}。
= There's a pharmacy outside the school. Let's go and buy some.
李明: {好|hǎo}，{谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}！{你|nǐ}{真|zhēn}{好|hǎo}。
= OK, thank you! You're so kind.
安娜: {不|bú}{客气|kè qi}。{你|nǐ}{今天|jīn tiān}{要|yào}{早|zǎo}{点儿|diǎnr}{睡觉|shuì jiào}！
= You're welcome. You need to go to bed early tonight!
```

{一|yī}{点|diǎn} here is one o'clock, so {一|yī} keeps its first tone, as in all times and dates.
{你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{了|le}？ (What's the matter?) is a phrase to remember: {怎么|zěn me} (HSK 1) +
change-of-state {了|le}, "what has happened to you?". And {早|zǎo}{点儿|diǎnr} is "a bit early": {早|zǎo}
+ the short form of {一点儿|yì diǎnr}.

## Reading: a message to the teacher

{安娜|Ān nà} can't come to class and writes to her teacher.

> {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}：{您好|nín hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{安娜|Ān nà}。{因为|yīn wèi}{我|wǒ}{生病|shēng bìng}{了|le}，{头|tóu}{很|hěn}{疼|téng}，{也|yě}{很|hěn}{累|lèi}，{所以|suǒ yǐ}{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bù}{能|néng}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}{了|le}。{昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}{看|kàn}{了|le}{医生|yī shēng}，{医生|yī shēng}{给|gěi}{了|le}{我|wǒ}{一些|yì xiē}{药|yào}，{说|shuō}{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}。{我|wǒ}{现在|xiàn zài}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{休息|xiū xi}，{明天|míng tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}。{真|zhēn}{对不起|duì bu qǐ}，{谢谢|xiè xie}{您|nín}！{安娜|Ān nà}

Answer:

1. Why can't Anna come to class?
2. What did the doctor say?
3. What does she hope to do tomorrow?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. She's ill, with a headache, and she's very tired.
2. That she needs to rest more ({要|yào}{多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}); the doctor also gave her some medicine.
3. Go to class in the morning ({明天|míng tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}).

"Dear Teacher Wang, I'm Anna. Because I'm ill, with a bad headache, and I'm very tired, I can't
come to class today. Last night I went to the hospital to see a doctor. The doctor gave me some
medicine and said I need to rest more. I'm resting at home now, and I'd like to come to class
tomorrow morning. I'm really sorry, and thank you! Anna"
</details>

A note like this is one of the writing tasks of HSK 2: a greeting ({王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}：{您好|nín hǎo}！),
who you are, the reason with {因为|yīn wèi}…{所以|suǒ yǐ}…, what happens next, an apology and thanks.

## Say it

```speak
{我|wǒ}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}。
= I'm feeling a bit unwell.
{我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{疼|téng}。
= I have a headache.
{你|nǐ}{哪儿|nǎr}{疼|téng}？
= Where does it hurt?
{因为|yīn wèi}{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{累|lèi}，{所以|suǒ yǐ}{今天|jīn tiān}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{休息|xiū xi}。
= Because I'm very tired, I'm resting at home today.
{附近|fù jìn}{有|yǒu}{药店|yào diàn}{吗|ma}？
= Is there a pharmacy nearby?
```

{附近|fù jìn} (nearby) is an HSK 3 word, worth having ready.

## Pronunciation

- {因为|yīn wèi}: level, then falling. *yīn* ends in *-n* (front), not *-ng*.
- {所以|suǒ yǐ}: two third tones, so the first one rises: said *suó yǐ*. Written *suǒ yǐ*.
- {舒服|shū fu}: *sh* + *u*, level, then a light *fu*.
- {累|lèi} falls sharply, like {位|wèi} with an *l*.
- {疼|téng}: *t* with a puff of air, *-eng* as in "sung" said with "uh"; rising.
- {药|yào} sounds exactly like {要|yào} (want; should). In {你|nǐ}{要|yào}{吃|chī}{药|yào} you hear
  *yào* twice: the first is "need to", the second "medicine".
- {笑|xiào}: *x* (tongue flat behind the lower teeth, like a thin "sh") + *iao*, falling.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{我|wǒ}{所以|suǒ yǐ}{没|méi}{去|qù}~~: {所以|suǒ yǐ} starts its clause: {所以|suǒ yǐ}{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}，{所以|suǒ yǐ}{因为|yīn wèi}{我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{疼|téng}~~: when the reason comes
  second, use {因为|yīn wèi} alone.
- Thinking "because…, so…" is wrong in Chinese because it's wrong in English: {因为|yīn wèi}…，
  {所以|suǒ yǐ}… is normal.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{的|de}{头|tóu}{是|shì}{疼|téng}~~: {疼|téng} is the verb; say {我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{疼|téng}.
- ~~{喝|hē}{药|yào}~~ for taking pills: you "eat" them, {吃|chī}{药|yào}. {喝|hē} is only for medicine
  you drink.
- {不|bú}{会|huì}{去|qù} for "can't go (I'm ill)": that's "won't go" or "doesn't know how". Say
  {不|bù}{能|néng}{去|qù}.
- Writing {=为=} with the dots in the wrong order: the outer dot first, the inner dot last.

## Key points

- {舒服|shū fu} comfortable, well; {不|bù}{舒服|shū fu} unwell. {累|lèi} tired, tiring.
- {疼|téng}: body part + {疼|téng}: {我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{疼|téng}, {你|nǐ}{哪儿|nǎr}{疼|téng}？
- {吃|chī}{药|yào} takes medicine; {药店|yào diàn} is a pharmacy.
- {笑|xiào} laugh, smile; {笑|xiào}{着|zhe}{说|shuō} said with a smile.
- Cause and effect: {因为|yīn wèi} (cause), {所以|suǒ yǐ} (result): both together, or either alone.
  {所以|suǒ yǐ} starts its clause; {因为|yīn wèi} goes before or after the subject.
- Modal verbs when you're ill: {要|yào} (need to, should), {不|bù}{能|néng} (can't).
- 店 is now taught: {饭店|fàn diàn}, {商店|shāng diàn}, {书店|shū diàn}, {药店|yào diàn}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: What to call people
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 taught you to ask a family name politely and to introduce people with {位|wèi}. This
honors lesson is about the next step: what to call someone once you've met them, or before you
know their name at all. A taxi driver, a waiter, a friend's mother, a colleague a little older
than you: each has a usual form of address, and choosing well is part of sounding polite in
Chinese. Customs vary by region and generation, so read the advice below as what is common, not
as rules. It's optional, for extra depth.

## The safe choice: family name + title

You met this in HSK 1: the family name comes first and the title after it.

| Form | Meaning | When |
|---|---|---|
| {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī} | Teacher Wang | teachers, and many people in education and the arts |
| {李|Lǐ}{医生|yī shēng} | Dr Li | doctors |
| {张|Zhāng}{先生|xiān sheng} | Mr Zhang | men, in formal and business settings |
| {刘|Liú}{女士|nǚ shì} | Ms Liu | women, in formal and business settings |

{先生|xiān sheng} and {女士|nǚ shì} are what you'll hear in offices, hotels and on the phone with a
company. In everyday life they can sound stiff, but they're never rude, and with someone you're
meeting for work they're usually expected.

{老师|lǎo shī} has spread well beyond schools. In many workplaces people call colleagues they respect
{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī} even if they've never taught anyone. When you don't know someone's job, age or exact role, {老师|lǎo shī} is a polite compromise.

## When you don't know the name

### {师傅|shī fu}: drivers and skilled workers

{师傅|shī fu} means "master (of a trade)". It's the usual polite way to address a taxi or bus
driver, a repair person, a cook or a craftsman, mostly men in manual jobs:

{师傅|shī fu}，{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}{大学|dà xué}。 — (to a taxi driver) Beijing University, please.
{师傅|shī fu}，{这|zhè}{个|gè}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？ — (to someone repairing your bike) How much is it?

Don't confuse it with {师父|shī fu}, written with 父 (father): the same sound, meaning one's own
master in a martial art or a religious order.

### Waiters and shop staff

In a restaurant, {服务员|fú wù yuán} (waiter, server) is the standard way to call someone over, and
it's what most guidebooks recommend. Many people today simply say {你好|nǐ hǎo}！ to get attention.
You'll also hear {美女|měi nǚ} ("beautiful woman") and {帅哥|shuài gē} ("handsome guy") used to
address service staff and other strangers. They were most popular some years ago; they're friendly
and informal, but can sound over-familiar, so leave them to others until you have a feel for them.

### Why not {小姐|xiǎo jie}?

{小姐|xiǎo jie} once meant "Miss", and with a family name it still can: hotel staff may address a
guest as {王|Wáng}{小姐|xiǎo jie}, and in Taiwan it's ordinary. But on the mainland, calling out
{小姐|xiǎo jie}！ to a waitress or a young woman you don't know is widely avoided, because in slang the
word has come to refer to women working in the sex industry. This is one reason {服务员|fú wù yuán}
became the usual word for staff. If you want to be safe, use {女士|nǚ shì} with a family name, or
{你好|nǐ hǎo}.

## Family words for people outside the family

Chinese often uses kinship words as friendly titles for people who aren't relatives:

| Word | Literally | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| {叔叔|shū shu} | uncle (father's younger brother) | a man of your parents' generation, said by children and young people, and to a friend's father |
| {阿姨|ā yí} | auntie (mother's sister) | a woman of your parents' generation, the same way; also a common name for a cleaner or a nanny |
| {爷爷|yé ye}, {奶奶|nǎi nai} | grandpa, grandma | elderly people, said by children (lesson 01) |
| {大哥|dà gē}, {大姐|dà jiě} | big brother, big sister | a man or woman a bit older than you: friendly, informal |
| {王|Wáng}{哥|gē}, {李|Lǐ}{姐|jiě} | brother Wang, sister Li | colleagues and friends a little older than you |
| {小朋友|xiǎo péng you} | little friend | any child (HSK 1) |

So when Anna visits a classmate, she greets the parents with {叔叔|shū shu}{好|hǎo}！ and
{阿姨|ā yí}{好|hǎo}！, not with their names. Children are taught to do this from an early age: it's
polite to greet adults first and to use the right word. Some adults find {叔叔|shū shu} and
{阿姨|ā yí} a little too cosy when an adult stranger uses them, and prefer {先生|xiān sheng} or
{女士|nǚ shì}; context and age matter.

{哥|gē} and {姐|jiě} after a family name are common between colleagues: {王|Wáng}{哥|gē} for a male
colleague a few years older, {李|Lǐ}{姐|jiě} for a female one. They show warmth and a little respect
for age.

## Names among friends

From HSK 1's honors lesson: full names ({王芳|Wáng Fāng}) are normal and friendly in Chinese, not cold
as in English. Close friends and family may use the given name alone, especially a two-character one,
or a doubled nickname ({芳芳|Fāng fāng}: reduplication again). {小|xiǎo} + family name ({小王|Xiǎo Wáng})
is for someone younger whom you know well, {老|lǎo} + family name ({老王|Lǎo Wáng}) for someone older,
with respect. Neither is used with strangers.

## Relatives on both sides

Lesson 01 showed that grandparents have different words on the father's and the mother's side.
The same goes for aunts, uncles and cousins. None of these is an HSK 2 word: recognise them, and look
them up when you need them.

| | Father's side | Mother's side |
|---|---|---|
| grandfather | {爷爷|yé ye} | {外公|wài gōng} (south), {姥爷|lǎo ye} (north) |
| grandmother | {奶奶|nǎi nai} | {外婆|wài pó} (south), {姥姥|lǎo lao} (north) |
| uncle | {伯伯|bó bo} (father's older brother), {叔叔|shū shu} (father's younger brother) | {舅舅|jiù jiu} (mother's brother) |
| aunt | {姑姑|gū gu} (father's sister) | {阿姨|ā yí} or {姨妈|yí mā} (mother's sister) |
| cousins | {堂哥|táng gē}, {堂姐|táng jiě}… (children of father's brothers) | {表哥|biǎo gē}, {表姐|biǎo jiě}… (all other cousins) |

- The north–south split for maternal grandparents is a broad tendency: many northern families say
  {姥姥|lǎo lao} and many southern ones {外婆|wài pó}, and plenty of families mix them.
- Cousins are {堂|táng} only when they're the children of your father's brothers, who traditionally
  share your family name and your family line. All other cousins, on the mother's side or
  through your father's sisters, are {表|biǎo}. Then comes the usual {哥|gē} / {姐|jiě} / {弟|dì} /
  {妹|mèi} for age and sex: {表哥|biǎo gē} is an older male cousin.
- The {表|biǎo} of {表哥|biǎo gē} keeps the old meaning of the character 表 from lesson 03,
  "outside": the "outer" relatives.

## Dialogue: a busy Saturday

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) takes a taxi, has lunch and visits {王芳|Wáng Fāng}'s family. The other speakers
are a taxi driver ({司机|sī jī}, 司机), a waiter ({服务员|fú wù yuán}, 服务员) and Wang Fang's mother
({王芳|Wáng Fāng}{妈妈|mā ma}, 王芳妈妈).

```dialogue
# A busy Saturday
安娜: {师傅|shī fu}，{您好|nín hǎo}！{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}{大学|dà xué}。
= Hello! Beijing University, please.
司机: {好|hǎo}{的|de}。
= Right.
安娜: {服务员|fú wù yuán}！{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{茶|chá}。
= Excuse me! I'd like a cup of tea.
服务员: {好|hǎo}{的|de}，{请|qǐng}{等|děng}{一下|yí xià}。
= Certainly, just a moment.
安娜: {阿姨|ā yí}{好|hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}，{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}。
= Hello! I'm Wang Fang's classmate; my name is Anna.
王芳妈妈: {你好|nǐ hǎo}，{安娜|Ān nà}！{快|kuài}{请|qǐng}{进|jìn}。{叔叔|shū shu}{在|zài}{做饭|zuò fàn}{呢|ne}。
= Hello, Anna! Come in, come in. Uncle (Wang Fang's dad) is cooking.
安娜: {谢谢|xiè xie}{阿姨|ā yí}！
= Thank you!
```

{等|děng} (to wait, lesson 20), {快|kuài} (quick, lesson 14) and {进|jìn} (to come in, lesson 09) come
later in the course; {快|kuài}{请|qǐng}{进|jìn} is a warm "do come in". Notice that Wang Fang's mother
calls her own husband {叔叔|shū shu} when speaking to Anna: she uses the title Anna would use. The
speaker label 王芳妈妈 ("Wang Fang's mum") is how parents are often referred to among families
and at school: the child's name + {妈妈|mā ma} or {爸爸|bà ba}.

## Say it

```speak
{师傅|shī fu}，{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}{大学|dà xué}。
= Beijing University, please. (to a taxi driver)
{服务员|fú wù yuán}！
= Excuse me! (calling a waiter)
{叔叔|shū shu}{好|hǎo}！{阿姨|ā yí}{好|hǎo}！
= Hello! (to a friend's father and mother)
{王|Wáng}{先生|xiān sheng}，{您好|nín hǎo}！
= Hello, Mr Wang!
```

## Key points

- Family name + title is always safe: {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}, {李|Lǐ}{医生|yī shēng},
  {张|Zhāng}{先生|xiān sheng}, {刘|Liú}{女士|nǚ shì}. {老师|lǎo shī} is also a polite title well beyond
  schools.
- {师傅|shī fu} for drivers and skilled workers; {服务员|fú wù yuán} or {你好|nǐ hǎo} for waiters.
- On the mainland, avoid calling out {小姐|xiǎo jie} to a stranger; with a family name in formal
  service settings it's still heard.
- Kinship words as titles: {叔叔|shū shu}, {阿姨|ā yí}, {爷爷|yé ye}, {奶奶|nǎi nai}, {大哥|dà gē},
  {大姐|dà jiě}; {王|Wáng}{哥|gē}, {李|Lǐ}{姐|jiě} between colleagues.
- Relatives differ by side: {爷爷|yé ye} / {外公|wài gōng}, {叔叔|shū shu} / {舅舅|jiù jiu},
  {姑姑|gū gu} / {阿姨|ā yí}; cousins are {堂|táng} (father's brothers' children) or {表|biǎo}.

lessons.title: Colours in Chinese culture
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 03 taught the colour words {红色|hóng sè}, {白色|bái sè}, {黑色|hēi sè} and {绿色|lǜ sè}. This honors
lesson looks at what those colours mean in Chinese life: red for celebrations, white for mourning
(and for brides today), yellow for emperors, and a green hat you should never give anyone. These are
customs, not laws: they vary by region and family, and younger people often treat them lightly. The
lesson is optional, for extra depth.

## Red: joy and good luck

Red is the colour of celebrations. It's on lanterns and decorations at the Spring Festival
({春节|Chūn jié}), on the paper of the couplets pasted around doors at New Year ({春联|chūn lián}: more in
the honors lesson "The Spring Festival", lesson 15h1) and all over a traditional wedding.

- **Red envelopes.** Money given as a gift goes in a red envelope, a {红包|hóng bāo} ("red packet"):
  to children at New Year, to a couple at their wedding, on other happy occasions. Today many people
  also send "red packets" through phone apps. The amount matters to some families: many prefer even
  numbers for weddings, and amounts with 4 ({四|sì}, which sounds like the word for
  "death") are often avoided.
- **Weddings.** Traditionally the bride wore red, and red decorations carry the character 囍
  ({双喜|shuāng xǐ}, "double happiness": two 喜, the first character of {喜欢|xǐ huan}, side by side).
- **The stock market.** On Chinese share-price displays, red means a price has gone up and green that
  it has gone down: the opposite of the convention in the United States, and a nice example of red
  as the colour of good news.

So {红|hóng} words are often positive: {走红|zǒu hóng} is to become popular, a {红人|hóng rén} is a popular
person or a favourite, and {开门红|kāi mén hóng} ("red when the door opens") is a good start to the year
or to a business.

## White: mourning, and brides today

White is the traditional colour of mourning. Mourners at a traditional funeral wore white, and a
funeral is still called a {白事|bái shì} ("white event"), as opposed to a wedding, a {喜事|xǐ shì}
("happy event"). Together they make the phrase {红白喜事|hóng bái xǐ shì}, weddings and funerals, the
big family occasions. Mourning colours also include black and other dark or plain shades, depending
on the region.

Because of that, women once avoided white at weddings. The taboo has largely faded: many brides now
wear a white Western-style wedding dress, often for the photos or the ceremony, and change into a
red {旗袍|qí páo} (a close-fitting traditional dress) or another red outfit later in the day. Guests,
on the other hand, are usually advised not to wear all white or all black to a wedding; red and
other bright colours are welcome.

{白|bái} also has an everyday meaning that has nothing to do with mourning: "for nothing, in vain".
{白吃|bái chī} is to eat without paying.

## Yellow and gold: the emperor's colours

In the Ming and Qing dynasties a bright "imperial yellow" was reserved for the emperor and the
imperial family. That's why almost all the roofs of the Forbidden City, the palace in Beijing, have
yellow glazed tiles. Gold, {金色|jīn sè}, is the colour of wealth: {黄金|huáng jīn} is the metal gold.

{黄色|huáng sè} (yellow, HSK 3) has a modern second meaning to know about: "indecent, pornographic"
when it describes a film or a book, as "blue" can in English. Ordinary yellow things, like a yellow
top or a yellow flower, are just yellow.

## Green: nature, go, and the green hat

Green is the colour of plants and of going: {绿灯|lǜ dēng} is a green traffic light, and
{红绿灯|hóng lǜ dēng} is a traffic light (HSK 3). {绿色|lǜ sè} also means "green" in the
environmental sense, as in English: {绿色食品|lǜ sè shí pǐn} is clean or organic food.

But never give a Chinese man a green hat. {戴|dài}{绿帽子|lǜ mào zi}, "to wear a green hat", means that
his partner has been unfaithful. A green hat as a gift, or a green hat in a photo, makes people
laugh, or wince. Green clothes are fine; it's the hat.

## Black: dark, and unofficial

{黑|hēi} is dark: {天|tiān}{黑|hēi}{了|le}, it's got dark (lesson 03). It also means "unofficial, illegal":
a {黑车|hēi chē} is an unlicensed taxi, the kind of car to avoid at a station.

## Colour words to recognise

| Expression | Literally | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {红包|hóng bāo} | red packet | money given as a gift |
| {走红|zǒu hóng} | walk red | to become popular |
| {眼红|yǎn hóng} | red eyes | jealous, envious |
| {脸红|liǎn hóng} | red face | to blush |
| {红白喜事|hóng bái xǐ shì} | red and white happy events | weddings and funerals |
| {白吃|bái chī} | white eat | to eat without paying |
| {黑车|hēi chē} | black car | unlicensed taxi |
| {绿帽子|lǜ mào zi} | green hat | a sign that one's partner has been unfaithful |

Notice {眼红|yǎn hóng}: English says "green with envy", Chinese "red-eyed".

## Dialogue: a present for Grandpa Li

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) tells {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) about a present she wants to buy for {李明|Lǐ Míng}'s
grandfather.

```dialogue
# A present for Grandpa Li
安娜: {王芳|Wáng Fāng}，{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{给|gěi}{李明|Lǐ Míng}{的|de}{爷爷|yé ye}{买|mǎi}{一|yí}{个|gè}{帽子|mào zi}。
= Wang Fang, I'd like to buy a hat for Li Ming's grandpa.
王芳: {很|hěn}{好|hǎo}{啊|a}。{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{买|mǎi}{什么|shén me}{颜色|yán sè}{的|de}？
= Good idea. What colour are you thinking of?
安娜: {绿色|lǜ sè}{的|de}。{他|tā}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{绿色|lǜ sè}。
= Green. He really likes green.
王芳: {绿色|lǜ sè}{的|de}{帽子|mào zi}？{不|bù}{好|hǎo}，{不|bù}{好|hǎo}！
= A green hat? No, no!
安娜: {是|shì}{吗|ma}？{那|nà}{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}{呢|ne}？
= Really? Then how about a red one?
王芳: {红色|hóng sè}{的|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{爷爷|yé ye}{会|huì}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}{的|de}。{绿色|lǜ sè}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}{也|yě}{可以|kě yǐ}。
= Red is fine; Grandpa will be pleased. A green top would be OK too.
```

{帽子|mào zi} (hat) is an HSK 3 word, and {啊|a} (lesson 13) softens {很|hěn}{好|hǎo}. Wang Fang doesn't
explain the green hat: it isn't a thing you say aloud in front of the family. {会|huì}…{的|de} is
"will surely": {爷爷|yé ye}{会|huì}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}{的|de}.

## Say it

```speak
{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。
= Red is good.
{这|zhè}{是|shì}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{红包|hóng bāo}。
= This red envelope is for you.
{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{什么|shén me}{颜色|yán sè}？
= What colour do you like?
```

## Key points

- Red ({红|hóng}) is for joy and luck: weddings, the Spring Festival, {红包|hóng bāo} (money gifts),
  and rising share prices.
- White ({白|bái}) is the traditional colour of mourning ({白事|bái shì}); many brides now wear a
  white dress and change into red.
- Imperial yellow was reserved for the emperor in the Ming and Qing dynasties; {黄色|huáng sè} today
  can also mean "indecent".
- Green ({绿|lǜ}) is nature and "go", but a green hat ({绿帽子|lǜ mào zi}) means a partner has been
  unfaithful.
- Black ({黑|hēi}) is dark, and in some words unofficial: {黑车|hēi chē}.
- These are customs with variation, not rules.

lessons.title: Left, right and next to: 左, 右, 旁边
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 was about people: names, looks, clothes, family life and feelings. Module 2 takes you out
of the house: where things are, how far they are, how you get there, coming in and going out,
and the places you have been. It starts where HSK 1 left off. You know the position words {上|shàng}, {下|xià},
{里|lǐ}, {外|wài}, {前|qián} and {后|hòu} after a noun ({桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}, {学校|xué xiào}{里|lǐ}), the -{边|biān} words ({外边|wài bian}, {这边|zhè biān}, {那边|nà biān}), and the two ways to
say where something is: {书|shū}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng} and {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}.

This lesson adds the rest of what you need to describe a room or a street:

- {左|zuǒ} (left) and {右|yòu} (right), and {左边|zuǒ bian} / {右边|yòu bian} (the left / right side);
- {旁边|páng biān} (beside, next to);
- the suffix -{面|miàn}, which makes {前面|qián miàn} (in front) and {后面|hòu miàn} (behind) and means the same as -{边|biān};
- {面|miàn} on its own: a side or a surface;
- the three sentence patterns with a place ({在|zài}, {有|yǒu} and {是|shì}), used to describe a map and a room.

## {左|zuǒ} and {右|yòu}: left and right

{左|zuǒ} is "left" and {右|yòu} is "right". On their own they're used mostly in set phrases and directions
(lesson 07: {往|wǎng}{左|zuǒ}{走|zǒu}, go left). Before a noun they say which one of a pair:

{左手|zuǒ shǒu} — the left hand

{右手|yòu shǒu} — the right hand

{左边|zuǒ bian} — the left side; on the left

{右边|yòu bian} — the right side; on the right

{左边|zuǒ bian} and {右边|yòu bian} are built like {外边|wài bian} from HSK 1: a position + {边|biān} (side). As there, {边|biān} is said
lightly: zuǒ bian, yòu bian. They work as place words:

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{右边|yòu bian}。 — My phone is on the right.

{左边|zuǒ bian}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{学校|xué xiào}。 — On the left is my school.

To say "to the left of something", put the thing first and {左边|zuǒ bian} / {右边|yòu bian} after it, the way you put {里|lǐ}
after {杯子|bēi zi} in {杯子|bēi zi}{里|lǐ}. A {的|de} between them is optional:

{超市|chāo shì}{左边|zuǒ bian} / {超市|chāo shì}{的|de}{左边|zuǒ bian} — to the left of the supermarket

{学校|xué xiào}{右边|yòu bian} / {学校|xué xiào}{的|de}{右边|yòu bian} — to the right of the school

This is the opposite of English, where "left" comes first and "of the supermarket" after. The
Chinese order is always: the thing you measure from, then the position.

You'll also meet {左面|zuǒ miàn} and {右面|yòu miàn}. They mean the same as {左边|zuǒ bian} and {右边|yòu bian}, but {左边|zuǒ bian} and {右边|yòu bian} are what you'll
hear most, so use those.

## {旁边|páng biān}: next to

{旁边|páng biān} is "the side, beside, next to". Unlike the {边|biān} in {左边|zuǒ bian}, the {边|biān} here keeps its tone: páng biān.

{医院|yī yuàn}{旁边|páng biān}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{药店|yào diàn}。 — There's a pharmacy next to the hospital.

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{旁边|páng biān}{是|shì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{超市|chāo shì}。 — Next to my home is a supermarket.

{你|nǐ}{坐|zuò}{我|wǒ}{旁边|páng biān}{吧|ba}。 — Sit next to me.

The last sentence shows something useful: with -{边|biān} words you can put a person straight in front.
In HSK 1 "at my place" needed {这儿|zhèr} ({在|zài}{我|wǒ}{这儿|zhèr}), but "next to me", "on my left" and "behind
him" are simply {我|wǒ}{旁边|páng biān}, {我|wǒ}{左边|zuǒ bian} and {他|tā}{后边|hòu bian}.

{旁边|páng biān} can also stand alone: {旁边|páng biān}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{书店|shū diàn} (there's a bookshop nearby, next to it).

## The suffix -{面|miàn}: {前面|qián miàn} and {后面|hòu miàn}

{面|miàn} is "face, side". As a suffix it makes position words just as {边|biān} does, and in most words the
two mean exactly the same:

| With -{边|biān} | With -{面|miàn} | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {前边|qián bian} | {前面|qián miàn} | in front; ahead |
| {后边|hòu bian} | {后面|hòu miàn} | behind; at the back |
| {左边|zuǒ bian} | {左面|zuǒ miàn} | on the left |
| {右边|yòu bian} | {右面|yòu miàn} | on the right |
| {外边|wài bian} | {外面|wài miàn} | outside |
| {里边|lǐ bian} | {里面|lǐ miàn} | inside |
| {上边|shàng bian} | {上面|shàng miàn} | on top; above |
| {下边|xià bian} | {下面|xià miàn} | underneath; below |
| {旁边|páng biān} | — | beside |

{前面|qián miàn} and {后面|hòu miàn} are this lesson's words; {里面|lǐ miàn}, {外面|wài miàn}, {上面|shàng miàn} and {下面|xià miàn} are lesson 11's, so you only need
to recognise them now. {旁边|páng biān} has no -{面|miàn} form: ~~{旁面|páng miàn}~~ isn't a word.

Which one should you say? Both are standard everywhere. -{面|miàn} is often said to be a little more frequent in writing, and
-{边|biān} a little more spoken. If you're not sure, either
is right. {面|miàn} is often said lightly in these words too (qián mian), though dictionaries and this
course write miàn.

{前面|qián miàn}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{书店|shū diàn}。 — There's a bookshop ahead.

{电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn}{在|zài}{超市|chāo shì}{后面|hòu miàn}。 — The cinema is behind the supermarket.

{你|nǐ}{前面|qián miàn}{的|de}{人|rén}{是|shì}{谁|shéi}？ — Who's the person in front of you?

{前面|qián miàn} and {后面|hòu miàn} also work for order in a queue or a list: {他|tā}{在|zài}{我|wǒ}{前面|qián miàn} is "he's in front of me" or
"he's ahead of me".

## {面|miàn} on its own: a side, a surface

{面|miàn} alone is a word for a flat side or surface, such as the face of a wall or the top of a table.
It's also a measure word for flat things such as mirrors and flags: {一|yí}{面|miàn}{镜子|jìng zi} is "a
mirror" ({镜子|jìng zi}, mirror, isn't a course word). You'll need {面|miàn} mostly as the suffix, so recognise this
use and move on.

{=One script note. In HSK 1 you learned {面|miàn} in {面条儿|miàn tiáor} and {面包|miàn bāo}, where it means flour and noodles. The
traditional script writes that meaning {麵|miàn}. The {面|miàn} of {前面|qián miàn}, {后面|hòu miàn} and "side, surface" stays {面|miàn} in
traditional script too: with the script switch, {后面|hòu miàn} becomes {後面|hòu miàn}, but its {面|miàn} doesn't change.=}

## Saying where things are: {在|zài}, {有|yǒu} and {是|shì}

With a place word you have three patterns. You know the first two from HSK 1; the third is new.

| Pattern | Use it when | Example |
|---|---|---|
| thing + {在|zài} + place | you know the thing and ask or say where it is | {药店|yào diàn}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{旁边|páng biān}。 The pharmacy is next to the hospital. |
| place + {有|yǒu} + thing | you tell someone that something is there (new information) | {医院|yī yuàn}{旁边|páng biān}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{药店|yào diàn}。 There's a pharmacy next to the hospital. |
| place + {是|shì} + thing | you say what the thing in that place is | {医院|yī yuàn}{旁边|páng biān}{是|shì}{药店|yào diàn}。 Next to the hospital is the pharmacy. |

{有|yǒu} introduces something: "there's a pharmacy (and you didn't know)". {是|shì} identifies: you know
something is there, and you say what it is. So when you walk down a street and name the shops one
by one, {是|shì} is the natural choice:

{超市|chāo shì}{左边|zuǒ bian}{是|shì}{书店|shū diàn}，{右边|yòu bian}{是|shì}{饭店|fàn diàn}。 — To the left of the supermarket is the bookshop; to the right is the restaurant.

Questions follow the same patterns. With {在|zài} you ask where; with {有|yǒu} you ask whether; with {是|shì} you
ask what:

{请问|qǐng wèn}，{药店|yào diàn}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？ — Excuse me, where's the pharmacy?

{这儿|zhèr}{有|yǒu}{药店|yào diàn}{吗|ma}？ — Is there a pharmacy here?

{超市|chāo shì}{旁边|páng biān}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}？ — What's next to the supermarket?

To ask "on which side?", use {哪边|nǎ biān}: {在|zài}{哪边|nǎ biān}？

## Describing a street

Here's a street, from left to right. The sentences under it describe it in the three ways.

| ← left | | | | right → |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| {医院|yī yuàn} | {药店|yào diàn} | {超市|chāo shì} | {书店|shū diàn} | {饭店|fàn diàn} |

{医院|yī yuàn}{在|zài}{药店|yào diàn}{的|de}{左边|zuǒ bian}。 — The hospital is to the left of the pharmacy.

{药店|yào diàn}{旁边|páng biān}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{超市|chāo shì}。 — There's a supermarket next to the pharmacy.

{超市|chāo shì}{右边|yòu bian}{是|shì}{书店|shū diàn}，{书店|shū diàn}{右边|yòu bian}{是|shì}{饭店|fàn diàn}。 — To the right of the supermarket is the bookshop, and to the
right of the bookshop is the restaurant.

{饭店|fàn diàn}{在|zài}{右边|yòu bian}。 — The restaurant is on the right.

Notice that {旁边|páng biān} doesn't say which side. If it matters, say {左边|zuǒ bian} or {右边|yòu bian}.

## Dialogue: where's the pharmacy?

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) isn't feeling well. She asks her classmate {李明|Lǐ Míng} (李明).

```dialogue
# Where's the pharmacy?
安娜: {李明|Lǐ Míng}，{请问|qǐng wèn}，{这儿|zhèr}{有|yǒu}{药店|yào diàn}{吗|ma}？
= Li Ming, excuse me, is there a pharmacy around here?
李明: {有|yǒu}。{你|nǐ}{看|kàn}，{前面|qián miàn}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{超市|chāo shì}，{药店|yào diàn}{在|zài}{超市|chāo shì}{旁边|páng biān}。
= Yes. Look, there's a supermarket ahead; the pharmacy is next to it.
安娜: {在|zài}{超市|chāo shì}{左边|zuǒ bian}{吗|ma}？
= Is it to the left of the supermarket?
李明: {不|bú}{在|zài}{左边|zuǒ bian}，{在|zài}{右边|yòu bian}。{超市|chāo shì}{左边|zuǒ bian}{是|shì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{饭店|fàn diàn}。
= Not the left, the right. To the left of the supermarket is a restaurant.
安娜: {书店|shū diàn}{也|yě}{在|zài}{那儿|nàr}{吗|ma}？{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{买|mǎi}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}。
= Is the bookshop there too? I'd like to buy a book.
李明: {书店|shū diàn}{在|zài}{药店|yào diàn}{后面|hòu miàn}，{很|hěn}{近|jìn}。
= The bookshop is behind the pharmacy, very close.
安娜: {太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！{你|nǐ}{也|yě}{去|qù}{吗|ma}？
= Great! Are you going too?
李明: {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}，{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}{看病|kàn bìng}。{医院|yī yuàn}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{左边|zuǒ bian}。
= No, I'm going to the hospital to see a doctor. The hospital is to the left of the school.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{也|yě}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}{吗|ma}？
= Are you unwell too?
李明: {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{累|lèi}，{没事儿|méi shìr}。
= A bit tired, it's nothing.
```

Anna's first question, {这儿|zhèr}{有|yǒu}{药店|yào diàn}{吗|ma}, asks whether there is one, so it uses {有|yǒu}. Li Ming answers with
both patterns: {前面|qián miàn}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{超市|chāo shì} (new: there's a supermarket) and {药店|yào diàn}{在|zài}{超市|chāo shì}{旁边|páng biān} (where the pharmacy
is). {近|jìn} is "near, close" (lesson 07's word). {没事儿|méi shìr} is the northern form of {没事|méi shì} (it's nothing), with the -r ending.

## Reading: my room

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}，{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}。{我|wǒ}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}{不|bú}{大|dà}，{可是|kě shì}{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}。{桌子|zhuō zi}{在|zài}{左边|zuǒ bian}，{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{电脑|diàn nǎo}{和|hé}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{书|shū}。{椅子|yǐ zi}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{前面|qián miàn}。{右边|yòu bian}{是|shì}{床|chuáng}，{床|chuáng}{旁边|páng biān}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{小|xiǎo}{桌子|zhuō zi}，{小|xiǎo}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{和|hé}{手表|shǒu biǎo}。{电视|diàn shì}{在|zài}{床|chuáng}{的|de}{前面|qián miàn}。{我|wǒ}{的|de}{猫|māo}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{床|chuáng}，{它|tā}{每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{在|zài}{床|chuáng}{上|shàng}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。

{床|chuáng} is "bed" (a lesson 11 word; you know the character from {起床|qǐ chuáng}), and {可是|kě shì} is
"but".

1. Where is the computer?
2. What is next to the bed, and what's on it?
3. Where does the cat sleep?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. On the desk, which is on the left ({桌子|zhuō zi}{在|zài}{左边|zuǒ bian}，{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{电脑|diàn nǎo}…).
2. Her small table, with her phone and watch on it.
3. On the bed, every day ({每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{在|zài}{床|chuáng}{上|shàng}{睡觉|shuì jiào}).

"My name is Wang Fang, and this is my room. My room isn't big, but I like it a lot. The desk is on
the left; on the desk there are a computer and lots of books. The chair is in front of the desk. On
the right is the bed; next to the bed is my small table, and on the small table are my phone and
my watch. The TV is in front of the bed. My cat really likes the bed: it sleeps on it every
day."
</details>

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 笑 | laugh, smile | xiào | ⺮ | 10 | {笑|xiào} (lesson 05) |
| 左 | left | zuǒ | 工 | 5 | {左|zuǒ}, {左边|zuǒ bian}, {左手|zuǒ shǒu} |
| 右 | right | yòu | 口 | 5 | {右|yòu}, {右边|yòu bian}, {右手|yòu shǒu} |
| 旁 | side | páng | 方 | 10 | {旁边|páng biān} |

All four are written the same in traditional script.

- {笑|xiào} was lesson 05's word, shown there with pinyin; here is its character. ⺮ (bamboo) is on top
  and 夭 below. Memory aid: the drooping bamboo leaves are the curve of a smiling face.
- {左|zuǒ} and {右|yòu} both began as drawings of a hand: an old form of {左|zuǒ} was a left hand and of {右|yòu} a right
  hand, which is why the top of both looks the same (a horizontal and a long left-falling
  stroke). {左|zuǒ} later added 工 and {右|yòu} added {口|kǒu}. That's the usual explanation of the two shapes.
  Memory aid to keep them apart: {右|yòu} has a mouth {口|kǒu}, and the right hand is the one many people eat
  with.
- {右|yòu} (yòu, right) and {有|yǒu} (yǒu, to have) look and sound alike: {有|yǒu} has {月|yuè} under the top part.
- {旁|páng}: the top is a dot, a horizontal, two short strokes and a small cover; 方 below gave the sound
  (fāng in {方|fāng}, páng here).

### New radical: 方

方 ({方|fāng}, "square; direction"). It's a character of its own, which you'll learn as a word in HSK 3
({方便|fāng biàn}, convenient). As a radical it's at the bottom of {旁|páng}, and on the left of {旅|lǚ} (in
{旅游|lǚ yóu}, to travel, lesson 10), where it is squeezed narrow. Three characters in this track have
it. On the left it's called {方字旁|fāng zì páng}.

Radical review: {口|kǒu} (mouth, HSK 1 lesson 01), here in {右|yòu} where it has nothing to do with the mouth;
工 (work, HSK 1 lesson 12), in {左|zuǒ}; and ⺮ (bamboo, HSK 1 lesson 14), in {笑|xiào} and {第|dì}.

### Stroke order

- **左** and **右** start the same way: the horizontal first, then the long left-falling stroke.
  That's the mainland standard, and the Taiwan standard agrees. Japanese school order writes
  {右|yòu}'s left-falling stroke first, so you may see both. Then {左|zuǒ} adds 工
  (horizontal, vertical, horizontal) and {右|yòu} adds {口|kǒu} (left vertical, the top-and-right stroke, the
  bottom).
- **笑**: ⺮ first, as two small halves (each a left-falling stroke, a short horizontal and a
  dot), then 夭: the short left-falling stroke at the top, the horizontal, the long left-falling
  stroke, and the right-falling stroke last.
- **旁**: from the top down: dot, horizontal, the two short strokes, the cover (a short vertical
  and a horizontal with a hook), then 方: dot, horizontal, the hooked turn, the left-falling
  stroke.

```trace
笑左右旁
```
=}

## Say it

```speak
{请问|qǐng wèn}，{药店|yào diàn}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Excuse me, where's the pharmacy?
{在|zài}{超市|chāo shì}{旁边|páng biān}。
= Next to the supermarket.
{在|zài}{左边|zuǒ bian}{还是|hái shi}{在|zài}{右边|yòu bian}？
= On the left or on the right?
{书店|shū diàn}{在|zài}{前面|qián miàn}。
= The bookshop is ahead.
{你|nǐ}{坐|zuò}{我|wǒ}{旁边|páng biān}{吧|ba}。
= Sit next to me.
```

({还是|hái shi}, "or" in questions, is lesson 21's word; here it's just part of a useful phrase.)

## Pronunciation

- {左|zuǒ} zuǒ dips (third tone); {坐|zuò} zuò (to sit) and {做|zuò} zuò (to do) fall. Say {左边|zuǒ bian} and {坐|zuò}{这儿|zhèr} in a row
  to hear the difference.
- {右|yòu} yòu falls; {有|yǒu} yǒu dips. {右边|yòu bian}{有|yǒu} is yòu bian yǒu: fall, light, dip.
- {左边|zuǒ bian}, {右边|yòu bian}: the {边|biān} is light. {旁边|páng biān}: the {边|biān} keeps its first tone, páng biān.
- {左手|zuǒ shǒu} is two third tones in a row: said zuó shǒu, as {你好|nǐ hǎo} is said ní hǎo. {左手|zuǒ shǒu} and {右手|yòu shǒu} then
  sound quite different: rise-dip and fall-dip.
- {前面|qián miàn}, {后面|hòu miàn}: the {面|miàn} is often light in speech (qián mian, hòu mian).

## Common mistakes

- English order: ~~{左边|zuǒ bian}{超市|chāo shì}~~ for "to the left of the supermarket". The thing comes first: {超市|chāo shì}{左边|zuǒ bian}
  (or {超市|chāo shì}{的|de}{左边|zuǒ bian}).
- ~~{旁面|páng miàn}~~: only {旁边|páng biān}.
- {有|yǒu} where you mean "what's there": when both people can see the shops, name them with {是|shì}:
  {左边|zuǒ bian}{是|shì}{书店|shū diàn}. {有|yǒu} says "there is a…".
- {在|zài}{超市|chāo shì}{旁边|páng biān}{有|yǒu}{药店|yào diàn} for "there's a pharmacy next to the supermarket": you'll hear it in
  speech, but it's less natural. In a {有|yǒu} sentence the place usually comes first with no {在|zài}, as in HSK 1: {超市|chāo shì}{旁边|páng biān}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{药店|yào diàn}.
- Writing {右|yòu} for {有|yǒu} or the other way round: {有|yǒu} has {月|yuè}, {右|yòu} has {口|kǒu}.
- Mixing up the tones of {左|zuǒ} and {坐|zuò} / {做|zuò}, and of {右|yòu} and {有|yǒu}.

## Key points

- {左|zuǒ} / {右|yòu}: left / right; {左边|zuǒ bian} / {右边|yòu bian} (light {边|biān}): on the left / right; {左手|zuǒ shǒu}, {右手|yòu shǒu}.
- {旁边|páng biān} (páng biān): beside, next to; X {旁边|páng biān}, {我|wǒ}{旁边|páng biān}.
- -{面|miàn} = -{边|biān} in position words: {前面|qián miàn} = {前边|qián bian}, {后面|hòu miàn} = {后边|hòu bian} (also {左面|zuǒ miàn}, {外面|wài miàn}, {里面|lǐ miàn}…); no ~~{旁面|páng miàn}~~.
- The thing you measure from comes first: {超市|chāo shì}{左边|zuǒ bian}, {学校|xué xiào}{后面|hòu miàn}, {我|wǒ}{旁边|páng biān}.
- thing + {在|zài} + place (where?); place + {有|yǒu} + thing (is there a…?); place + {是|shì} + thing (what's there?).
- New radical: {方|fāng} ({旁|páng}, {旅|lǚ}).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: How far is it? 离, 从, 往
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 06 put things on a map: {左边|zuǒ bian}, {右边|yòu bian}, {旁边|páng biān}, {前面|qián miàn}, {后面|hòu miàn}. Now you'll move across it. This lesson
teaches three small words that come before a place, and the verb you'll use for every step you
take:

- {离|lí}: how far one place is from another (A {离|lí} B {远|yuǎn} / {近|jìn});
- {从|cóng}…{到|dào}…: from… to…, for places and for times;
- {往|wǎng} + direction + verb: go this way ({往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}, {往|wǎng}{左|zuǒ}{走|zǒu});
- {走|zǒu} (to walk; to leave) and {走路|zǒu lù} (to go on foot);
- {路|lù} (road; route) and {路上|lù shang} (on the way).

At the end you can ask the way, understand the answer, and say how long the walk is.

## {离|lí}: how far is it?

{离|lí} measures the distance between two places. The pattern is A {离|lí} B + {远|yuǎn} (far) or {近|jìn} (near):

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{离|lí}{学校|xué xiào}{很|hěn}{近|jìn}。 — My home is very close to school.

{医院|yī yuàn}{离|lí}{这儿|zhèr}{不|bù}{远|yuǎn}。 — The hospital isn't far from here.

{他|tā}{家|jiā}{离|lí}{公司|gōng sī}{太|tài}{远|yuǎn}{了|le}。 — His home is too far from his company.

A is the place you're talking about, B the point you measure from. English says "A is near B" or
"A is far from B"; Chinese puts B straight after {离|lí} and the adjective at the end, as an
adjective predicate: no {是|shì}. Degree words go before the adjective as usual: {很|hěn}{近|jìn}, {不|bù}{远|yuǎn}, {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{远|yuǎn},
{太|tài}{远|yuǎn}{了|le}.

Ask with {吗|ma} or with A-not-A, or with {多|duō}{远|yuǎn} (how far), built like {多|duō}{大|dà} (how old):

{超市|chāo shì}{离|lí}{这儿|zhèr}{远|yuǎn}{吗|ma}？ — Is the supermarket far from here?

{书店|shū diàn}{离|lí}{这儿|zhèr}{远|yuǎn}{不|bù}{远|yuǎn}？ — Is the bookshop far from here or not?

{机场|jī chǎng}{离|lí}{这儿|zhèr}{有|yǒu}{多|duō}{远|yuǎn}？ — How far is the airport from here? ({机场|jī chǎng}: airport, lesson 08)

The usual answer gives a time instead of a distance: walking or driving time is how most people
think of it. Put {走路|zǒu lù} (on foot) or {坐车|zuò chē} / {开车|kāi chē} before the time:

{不|bù}{远|yuǎn}，{走路|zǒu lù}{五|wǔ}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。 — Not far, five minutes on foot.

{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{远|yuǎn}，{坐车|zuò chē}{要|yào}{半|bàn}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — A bit far: it takes half an hour by car.

**{离|lí} is not "from" as a starting point, in time or in movement.** It measures the gap: usually a
distance, sometimes a time ({离|lí}{考试|kǎo shì}{还有|hái yǒu}{三|sān}{天|tiān}, "three days to go before the exam", is for later). For "I come from Beijing",
"from eight o'clock" or "go from here", use {从|cóng} (next section). ~~{我|wǒ}{从|cóng}{学校|xué xiào}{很|hěn}{远|yuǎn}~~ is a typical
mistake for {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{离|lí}{学校|xué xiào}{很|hěn}{远|yuǎn}.

## {从|cóng}…{到|dào}…: from… to…

{从|cóng} marks a starting point and {到|dào} (to, arrive: HSK 1 lesson 18) the end. Together they cover
places and times:

{从|cóng}{北京|Běi jīng}{到|dào}{上海|Shàng hǎi} — from Beijing to Shanghai

{从|cóng}{这儿|zhèr}{到|dào}{那儿|nàr} — from here to there

{从|cóng}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}{十二|shí èr}{点|diǎn} — from eight to twelve

{从|cóng}{星期|xīng qī}{一|yī}{到|dào}{星期|xīng qī}{五|wǔ} — from Monday to Friday

The phrase goes before the verb, like every place and time phrase:

{我|wǒ}{从|cóng}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}{十二|shí èr}{点|diǎn}{上课|shàng kè}。 — I have classes from eight to twelve.

{从|cóng}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{到|dào}{学校|xué xiào}{要|yào}{二十|èr shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。 — It takes twenty minutes from my home to school.

The second sentence uses {要|yào} + time ("it takes") from HSK 1, with the whole {从|cóng}…{到|dào}… phrase as the
subject.

{从|cóng} works alone too, before a place and a verb of movement:

{我|wǒ}{从|cóng}{北京|Běi jīng}{来|lái}。 — I've come from Beijing. / I'm coming from Beijing.

{她|tā}{从|cóng}{学校|xué xiào}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。 — She's going home from school.

{你|nǐ}{从|cóng}{这儿|zhèr}{走|zǒu}，{很|hěn}{近|jìn}。 — Go from here; it's very close.

{我|wǒ}{从|cóng}{北京|Běi jīng}{来|lái} is about the journey; to say where you're from as a person, HSK 1's {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{北京|Běi jīng}{人|rén} is still the
natural sentence.

Compare the two "from"s once more:

| | Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {离|lí} | A {离|lí} B {远|yuǎn} / {近|jìn} | how far A is from B (the gap) |
| {从|cóng} | {从|cóng} A ({到|dào} B) + verb | starting at A (and going to B): places and times |

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{离|lí}{学校|xué xiào}{很|hěn}{远|yuǎn}，{从|cóng}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{到|dào}{学校|xué xiào}{要|yào}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — My home is far from school: it takes an hour from my home
to school.

## {往|wǎng} + direction + verb: go this way

{往|wǎng} means "towards, in the direction of". It goes before a direction, and the verb of movement
follows:

{往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu} — go straight ahead (walk forwards)

{往|wǎng}{左|zuǒ}{走|zǒu} — go left

{往|wǎng}{右|yòu}{走|zǒu} — go right

{往|wǎng}{后|hòu}{看|kàn} — look back (look behind you)

{往|wǎng}{这边|zhè biān}{走|zǒu} — come this way

{往|wǎng}{那边|nà biān}{走|zǒu} — go that way

A full set of directions strings them together. You'll often hear {一直|yì zhí} (straight on: an HSK 3
word) before {往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}, and {拐|guǎi} (to turn) instead of {走|zǒu} for a turn:

{从|cóng}{这儿|zhèr}{一直|yì zhí}{往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}，{到|dào}{了|le}{超市|chāo shì}{往|wǎng}{右|yòu}{拐|guǎi}。 — Go straight on from here, and at the supermarket turn right.

{到|dào}{了|le}{超市|chāo shì} (when you get to the supermarket) uses {到|dào} + {了|le} for a completed step (HSK 1 lesson 25).

{往|wǎng} is third tone, wǎng. Don't confuse it with {忘|wàng} (to forget, lesson 17), fourth tone.

## {走|zǒu} and {走路|zǒu lù}: walking and leaving

{走|zǒu} is the movement of walking, and it also means "to leave, to go away". {去|qù} is "go (to a place)";
{走|zǒu} says nothing about where:

{我们|wǒ men}{走|zǒu}{吧|ba}！ — Let's go! (Let's be off.)

{他|tā}{走|zǒu}{了|le}。 — He's left. (He's gone.)

{我|wǒ}{走|zǒu}{了|le}，{明天|míng tiān}{见|jiàn}！ — I'm off: see you tomorrow!

{你|nǐ}{走|zǒu}{得|de}{太|tài}{快|kuài}{了|le} would be "you walk too fast"; that {得|de} is lesson 18's. For now use {走|zǒu} with a direction
({往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}), with {吧|ba} or {了|le}, or with a length of time after it, which says how long the walk is:

{走|zǒu}{十|shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}{就|jiù}{到|dào}{了|le}。 — It's a ten-minute walk. ({就|jiù}, "then", is lesson 18's word.)

{走路|zǒu lù} is {走|zǒu} + {路|lù} (road), a verb with its own object, like {睡觉|shuì jiào} or {吃|chī}{饭|fàn}. It means "to walk, to go on
foot", and it's how you say the means of travel, in the slot where {坐车|zuò chē} goes:

{我|wǒ}{每天|měi tiān}{走路|zǒu lù}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}。 — I walk to school every day.

{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{坐车|zuò chē}，{我|wǒ}{走路|zǒu lù}{去|qù}。 — I'm not taking a car; I'll walk.

Because {走路|zǒu lù} already has its object, don't add a place to it: "walk to school" is {走路|zǒu lù}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}, with
{去|qù} + place after it (a serial verb, like {坐车|zuò chē}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}).

## {路|lù} and {路上|lù shang}

{路|lù} is a road or a way. {路上|lù shang} is "on the road, on the way", with a light {上|shàng} (lù shang):

{这儿|zhèr}{的|de}{路|lù}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{新|xīn}。 — The roads here are all new.

{路上|lù shang}{车|chē}{很|hěn}{多|duō}。 — There's lots of traffic on the way. (On the road there are many cars.)

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{路上|lù shang}，{十|shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}{到|dào}。 — I'm on my way; I'll be there in ten minutes.

That last sentence is one of the most useful messages you can send in Chinese. {路上|lù shang} also comes in
the friendly {路上|lù shang}{小心|xiǎo xīn}！ (take care on the way: {小心|xiǎo xīn} is HSK 3's "careful"), said to someone leaving.

{路|lù} also numbers bus routes. A bus line is a "road": {八|bā}{路|lù} is the No. 8 bus, and {三十二|sān shí èr}{路|lù} the No. 32. You'll
use it with {公交车|gōng jiāo chē} (bus) in lesson 08.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 离 (traditional 離) | leave; away from | lí | 禸 | 10 | {离|lí} |
| 远 (traditional 遠) | far | yuǎn | 辶 | 7 | {远|yuǎn} |
| 近 | near | jìn | 辶 | 7 | {近|jìn} |
| 往 | towards | wǎng | 彳 | 8 | {往|wǎng} |
| 从 (traditional 從) | from; follow | cóng | 人 | 4 | {从|cóng} |
| 走 | walk; leave | zǒu | 走 | 7 | {走|zǒu}, {走路|zǒu lù} |
| 路 | road | lù | 足 | 13 | {路|lù}, {走路|zǒu lù}, {路上|lù shang} |

- {离|lí} ({離|lí}): Make Me a Hanzi files it under 禸 (the bottom part); some dictionaries file it under
  亠, the "lid" on top. The traditional form adds 隹 (a bird) on the right.
- {远|yuǎn} and {近|jìn}: both have 辶, the "walking" radical you know from {这|zhè}, {边|biān}, {还|hái} and {道|dào}. In {远|yuǎn} the inside
  is {元|yuán} (the yuan of money), which gives the sound: yuǎn. In {近|jìn} it's {斤|jīn} (a unit of weight), which
  gives the sound jìn. Traditional {遠|yuǎn} has a different inside, {袁|yuán}, which is also read yuán.
- {往|wǎng}: 彳 (double person, "step") on the left, as in {很|hěn} and {得|de}. The right side looks like {主|zhǔ}
  (master), but that is a later change of shape: treat it as a memory aid, not as history.
- {从|cóng} is two people {人人|rén rén}, one walking behind the other: "to follow". That's what the character
  first meant, and "from" came later. Traditional {從|cóng} adds 彳 and 止 (both about walking).
- {走|zǒu}: 土 on top and a short "foot" below. In old Chinese {走|zǒu} meant "to run"; "to walk" is its
  modern meaning. {走|zǒu} is also the radical of {起|qǐ} and {超|chāo} ({起床|qǐ chuáng}, {超市|chāo shì}).
- {路|lù}: {足|zú} (foot) on the left gives the meaning; {各|gè} (each) is the other part. You know its shape
  from {客|kè} (in {不客气|bú kè qi}).

### New radical: 足

足 ({足|zú}, foot). On the left of a character it becomes ⻊: its last strokes are squeezed, and
the bottom horizontal turns into a rising stroke. Characters with it have to do with the feet
and legs: {路|lù} (road), and in later lessons {跑|pǎo} (to run), {跳|tiào} (to jump), {踢|tī} (to kick) and {跟|gēn} (to
follow; with). {足|zú} itself is in {足球|zú qiú} (football, lesson 19). Six characters in this track have it.
Its name on the left is {足字旁|zú zì páng}.

Radical review: 辶 (walking, HSK 1 lesson 03) in {远|yuǎn} and {近|jìn}; 彳 (step, HSK 1 lesson 11) in {往|wǎng}; and
走 (HSK 1 lesson 08) as a character of its own. All three have to do with going somewhere.

### Stroke order

- **远, 近**: the inside first, 辶 last (dot, the bent stroke, then the long sweep along the
  bottom), as in {这|zhè} and {边|biān}.
- **从**: the left {人|rén} first, then the right one. The left {人|rén}'s second stroke is cut short to a
  dot so that the right {人|rén} fits.
- **走**: 土 first (horizontal, vertical, horizontal), then the bottom: a short vertical, a short
  horizontal, the left-falling stroke and the long right-falling stroke.
- **路**: ⻊ first: {口|kǒu}, then the vertical, a short horizontal, the left vertical and the rising
  stroke at the bottom. Then {各|gè}: 夂 on top and {口|kǒu} below.
- **往**: 彳 (two left-falling strokes and a vertical), then the right side: dot, horizontal,
  horizontal, the vertical, and the long horizontal at the bottom.

```trace
离远近往从走路
```
=}

## Dialogue: asking the way

{大卫|Dà wèi} (大卫) is looking for a cinema. He asks a woman in the street, whom he calls {阿姨|ā yí} (阿姨),
"auntie": a friendly way to address a woman of your parents' age.

```dialogue
# Asking the way
大卫: {阿姨|ā yí}，{您|nín}{好|hǎo}！{请问|qǐng wèn}，{电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn}{离|lí}{这儿|zhèr}{远|yuǎn}{吗|ma}？
= Excuse me, madam, is the cinema far from here?
阿姨: {不|bù}{远|yuǎn}，{走路|zǒu lù}{十|shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。
= Not far, ten minutes on foot.
大卫: {怎么|zěn me}{走|zǒu}？
= How do I get there?
阿姨: {你|nǐ}{从|cóng}{这儿|zhèr}{往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}，{到|dào}{了|le}{超市|chāo shì}{往|wǎng}{右|yòu}{走|zǒu}。{电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn}{在|zài}{书店|shū diàn}{旁边|páng biān}。
= Go straight ahead from here, and when you get to the supermarket, go right. The cinema is next to the bookshop.
大卫: {往|wǎng}{右|yòu}{走|zǒu}，{书店|shū diàn}{旁边|páng biān}。{谢谢|xiè xie}{您|nín}！
= Right, next to the bookshop. Thank you!
阿姨: {不客气|bú kè qi}。{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{外国人|wài guó rén}{吧|ba}？{你|nǐ}{的|de}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}！
= You're welcome. You're from abroad, aren't you? Your Chinese is very good!
大卫: {哪里哪里|nǎ lǐ nǎ lǐ}。{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{学习|xué xí}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。
= Oh, not really. I'm studying Chinese in Beijing.
阿姨: {电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{开门|kāi mén}，{现在|xiàn zài}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{五十|wǔ shí}，{你|nǐ}{快|kuài}{走|zǒu}{吧|ba}！
= The cinema opens at eight. It's seven-fifty now; you'd better hurry!
大卫: {好|hǎo}，{我|wǒ}{走|zǒu}{了|le}。{再见|zài jiàn}！
= OK, I'm off. Goodbye!
```

{怎么|zěn me}{走|zǒu}？ (how do you walk it?) is the everyday way to ask for directions: {怎么|zěn me} + verb from HSK 1.

{外国人|wài guó rén} (foreigner) is lesson 10's word, and {快|kuài} (quickly) lesson 14's. {哪里哪里|nǎ lǐ nǎ lǐ} ("where? where?") is a modest way to brush off a compliment; you'll also hear a simple {谢谢|xiè xie}. {开门|kāi mén} is "to
open the door": here, the cinema opens.

## Reading: on the way to work

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{张伟|Zhāng Wěi}，{在|zài}{一|yí}{个|gè}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}。{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{离|lí}{公司|gōng sī}{不|bù}{远|yuǎn}，{走路|zǒu lù}{二十|èr shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。{我|wǒ}{每天|měi tiān}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{半|bàn}{从|cóng}{家|jiā}{里|lǐ}{走|zǒu}，{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}{公司|gōng sī}。{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{坐车|zuò chē}，{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{走路|zǒu lù}。{从|cóng}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}，{路上|lù shang}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{商店|shāng diàn}{和|hé}{一|yí}{个|gè}{饭店|fàn diàn}。{到|dào}{了|le}{饭店|fàn diàn}{往|wǎng}{左|zuǒ}{走|zǒu}，{就|jiù}{是|shì}{我们|wǒ men}{公司|gōng sī}。{我|wǒ}{妻子|qī zi}{的|de}{公司|gōng sī}{很|hěn}{远|yuǎn}，{她|tā}{每天|měi tiān}{开车|kāi chē}{去|qù}，{路上|lù shang}{要|yào}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。

{就|jiù}{是|shì}{我们|wǒ men}{公司|gōng sī} is "and there's our company" ({就|jiù}: lesson 18). {妻子|qī zi} (wife) is a lesson 04 word.

1. How long does Zhang Wei's walk to work take?
2. What's on the way?
3. How does his wife get to work?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Twenty minutes ({走路|zǒu lù}{二十|èr shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}): he leaves at half past seven and gets there at eight.
2. A shop and a restaurant ({路上|lù shang}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{商店|shāng diàn}{和|hé}{一|yí}{个|gè}{饭店|fàn diàn}).
3. She drives; it takes an hour ({开车|kāi chē}{去|qù}，{路上|lù shang}{要|yào}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}).

"My name is Zhang Wei and I work for a company. My home isn't far from the company: twenty minutes on
foot. Every day I leave home at half past seven and get to the company at eight. I don't take a
car; I really like walking. From my home you go straight ahead, and on the way there's a shop and
a restaurant. At the restaurant you turn left, and there's our company. My wife's company is a
long way away: she drives there every day, and it takes an hour on the road."
</details>

## Say it

```speak
{请问|qǐng wèn}，{地铁站|dì tiě zhàn}{离|lí}{这儿|zhèr}{远|yuǎn}{吗|ma}？
= Excuse me, is the metro station far from here?
{不|bù}{远|yuǎn}，{走路|zǒu lù}{五|wǔ}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。
= Not far: five minutes on foot.
{怎么|zěn me}{走|zǒu}？
= How do I get there?
{往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}，{到|dào}{了|le}{超市|chāo shì}{往|wǎng}{右|yòu}{走|zǒu}。
= Go straight ahead, and at the supermarket go right.
{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{路上|lù shang}，{十|shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}{到|dào}。
= I'm on my way; I'll be there in ten minutes.
{我|wǒ}{走|zǒu}{了|le}，{明天|míng tiān}{见|jiàn}！
= I'm off: see you tomorrow!
```

({地铁站|dì tiě zhàn}, metro station, comes in lesson 08.)

## Pronunciation

- {远|yuǎn}: the *yu* is ü, lips rounded as for "oo" while the tongue says "ee". {元|yuán} rises.
- {近|jìn} and {进|jìn} (to enter, lesson 09) are the same syllable; {斤|jīn} is level.
- {走|zǒu}: *ou* as in "so", with a dip. Don't let it become zuǒ ({左|zuǒ}, left).
- {往|wǎng}{左|zuǒ}{走|zǒu} wǎng zuǒ zǒu is three third tones in a row. Say the first two as rising tones,
  *wáng zuó zǒu*, and keep the full dip for {走|zǒu}.
- {路上|lù shang}: a falling {路|lù}, then a light *shang*.
- {从|cóng}: the *c* is "ts" with a puff of air, as in "cats".

## Common mistakes

- ~~{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{从|cóng}{学校|xué xiào}{很|hěn}{远|yuǎn}~~: the distance between places takes {离|lí}: {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{离|lí}{学校|xué xiào}{很|hěn}{远|yuǎn}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{离|lí}{北京|Běi jīng}{来|lái}~~: a starting point takes {从|cóng}: {我|wǒ}{从|cóng}{北京|Běi jīng}{来|lái}.
- ~~{走|zǒu}{前|qián}~~ or ~~{往|wǎng}{走|zǒu}{前|qián}~~ for "go straight ahead": {往|wǎng} + direction + verb, {往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}.
- English order: ~~{我|wǒ}{走路|zǒu lù}{学校|xué xiào}~~ or ~~{我|wǒ}{走路|zǒu lù}{到|dào}{学校|xué xiào}{每天|měi tiān}~~. Say {我|wǒ}{每天|měi tiān}{走路|zǒu lù}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}: time first, then the
  means ({走路|zǒu lù}), then {去|qù} + place.
- {是|shì} before {远|yuǎn} / {近|jìn}: ~~{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{离|lí}{学校|xué xiào}{是|shì}{很|hěn}{近|jìn}~~. {近|jìn} is an adjective predicate: {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{离|lí}{学校|xué xiào}{很|hěn}{近|jìn}.
- {=Writing {远|yuǎn} with {斤|jīn} and {近|jìn} with {元|yuán}, the wrong way round: {远|yuǎn} has the *yuán* part, {近|jìn} the
  *jīn* part.=}

## Key points

- A {离|lí} B {远|yuǎn} / {近|jìn}: how far A is from B; {多|duō}{远|yuǎn}？ how far?; answer with a time: {走路|zǒu lù}{五|wǔ}{分钟|fēn zhōng}.
- {从|cóng} A {到|dào} B (+ verb): from A to B, for places and times; {从|cóng} + place + {来|lái} / {去|qù} / {走|zǒu}.
- {往|wǎng} + direction + verb: {往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}, {往|wǎng}{左|zuǒ}{走|zǒu}, {往|wǎng}{右|yòu}{走|zǒu}.
- {走|zǒu}: to walk; to leave ({我|wǒ}{走|zǒu}{了|le}). {走路|zǒu lù}: to go on foot ({走路|zǒu lù}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}).
- {路|lù}: road; bus route ({八|bā}{路|lù}). {路上|lù shang}: on the way ({我|wǒ}{在|zài}{路上|lù shang}).
- New radical: 足 (⻊ on the left: {路|lù}, {跑|pǎo}, {跳|tiào}…).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: By metro, bus and taxi: 是…的
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In HSK 1 you learned {坐|zuò} + vehicle ({坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}) with {火车|huǒ chē}, {飞机|fēi jī} and {出租车|chū zū chē}. In lesson 07 you walked. This
lesson adds the rest of city transport: the metro, the bus, taking a taxi, stations, stops,
tickets and the airport.

It also teaches one of the most useful patterns of the level. When someone has arrived, Chinese
speakers don't ask "Did you come?" (that's obvious). They ask "*How* did you come? *When* did you
get here? Who did you come *with*?" For that there's a special frame, {是|shì}…{的|de}:

{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{怎么|zěn me}{来|lái}{的|de}？ — How did you get here?

{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{来|lái}{的|de}。 — I came by metro.

## Getting around town

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {地铁|dì tiě} | metro, underground, subway | "ground iron": {地|dì} (ground) + {铁|tiě} (iron) |
| {公交车|gōng jiāo chē} | (city) bus | short for "public transport vehicle" |
| {打车|dǎ chē} | to take a taxi | {打|dǎ} + {车|chē}; HSK 1's {出租车|chū zū chē} is the taxi itself |
| {车站|chē zhàn} | station; stop | for buses, trains and coaches |
| {站|zhàn} | stop; station | {地铁站|dì tiě zhàn} (metro station), {下|xià}{一|yí}{站|zhàn} (the next stop) |
| {机场|jī chǎng} | airport | {机|jī} (machine, as in {飞机|fēi jī}) + {场|chǎng} (an open space) |
| {票|piào} | ticket | {买|mǎi}{票|piào}, buy a ticket |
| {机票|jī piào} | plane ticket | {飞机|fēi jī} + {票|piào} |
| {飞|fēi} | to fly | you know it from {飞机|fēi jī} |

All of them work with what you know from HSK 1. Vehicles take {坐|zuò} (you sit in them), and the means
of travel comes before the going:

{我|wǒ}{每天|měi tiān}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{上班|shàng bān}。 — I go to work by metro every day.

{我们|wǒ men}{坐|zuò}{公交车|gōng jiāo chē}{去|qù}{吧|ba}。 — Let's take the bus.

{从|cóng}{这儿|zhèr}{到|dào}{机场|jī chǎng}，{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{要|yào}{四十|sì shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。 — From here to the airport takes forty minutes by metro.

A bus line is a "road", {路|lù} (lesson 07): {八|bā}{路|lù}{公交车|gōng jiāo chē} is the No. 8 bus, and people often just say {八|bā}{路|lù}:
{你|nǐ}{坐|zuò}{几|jǐ}{路|lù}？ "Which number (bus) are you taking?"

## {打车|dǎ chē}: taking a taxi

{打车|dǎ chē} is the everyday verb for "take a taxi", in a city street or with a phone app. It's a verb with
its object ({打|dǎ} + {车|chē}) like {开车|kāi chē}, and it goes where {坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē} goes:

{我们|wǒ men}{打车|dǎ chē}{去|qù}{机场|jī chǎng}{吧|ba}。 — Let's take a taxi to the airport.

{太|tài}{晚|wǎn}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{打车|dǎ chē}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。 — It's late: I'll get a taxi home.

{打|dǎ} is "to hit", the {打|dǎ} of {打电话|dǎ diàn huà} (to make a phone call). Here it has lost that meaning: you don't hit
the car! Lesson 23 collects the other uses of {打|dǎ}.

## {站|zhàn} and {车站|chē zhàn}: stations and stops

{车站|chē zhàn} is a station or a stop for any vehicle: {车站|chē zhàn}{在|zài}{前面|qián miàn} (the stop is just ahead). {站|zhàn} is the same
word in short, and it goes after another noun to say what kind:

| | |
|---|---|
| {地铁站|dì tiě zhàn} | metro station |
| {火车站|huǒ chē zhàn} | railway station ({火车|huǒ chē} + {站|zhàn}) |
| {公交车站|gōng jiāo chē zhàn} | bus stop (people also say just {车站|chē zhàn}) |

{站|zhàn} also counts stops, like a measure word: {坐|zuò}{三|sān}{站|zhàn} is "ride three stops". On the metro you'll hear the
next stop announced:

{下|xià}{一|yí}{站|zhàn}，{机场|jī chǎng}。 — Next stop: the airport.

{坐|zuò}{两|liǎng}{站|zhàn}{就|jiù}{到|dào}{了|le}。 — It's just two stops. ({就|jiù}, "then, just", is lesson 18's.)

In HSK 3 you'll meet {站|zhàn} as a verb, "to stand". Here it's only the noun.

## {票|piào}, {机票|jī piào} and {飞|fēi}

{票|piào} is any ticket. {买|mǎi}{票|piào} is "buy a ticket"; {机票|jī piào} is a plane ticket; a bus or train ticket is {车票|chē piào} (not a
course word), and lesson 10's {门票|mén piào} gets you into a park or museum. Tickets are
counted with {张|zhāng} (an HSK 3 measure word for flat things): {两张|liǎng zhāng}{票|piào}, two tickets.

{你|nǐ}{买|mǎi}{票|piào}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Have you bought the tickets?

{机票|jī piào}{很|hěn}{贵|guì}。 — Plane tickets are expensive.

{飞|fēi} is "to fly". With {从|cóng} or a destination right after it, it's the everyday way to talk about
flights:

{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{从|cóng}{北京|Běi jīng}{飞|fēi}{上海|Shàng hǎi}。 — Tomorrow I'm flying from Beijing to Shanghai.

## {是|shì}…{的|de}: how, when, where, who with

The **[[是…的 construction]]** frames one detail of something that has already happened. Everyone
knows the event took place; the question or the answer is about *how*, *when*, *where*, *with
whom* or *from where*. {是|shì} goes right before that detail, and {的|de} at the end:

| Detail | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| how | {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{怎么|zěn me}{来|lái}{的|de}？ | {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{来|lái}{的|de}。 I came by metro. |
| when | {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{到|dào}{的|de}？ | {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{昨天|zuó tiān}{到|dào}{的|de}。 I arrived yesterday. |
| where | {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}{买|mǎi}{的|de}？ | {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{在|zài}{机场|jī chǎng}{买|mǎi}{的|de}。 I bought it at the airport. |
| from where | {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{从|cóng}{哪儿|nǎr}{来|lái}{的|de}？ | {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{从|cóng}{上海|Shàng hǎi}{来|lái}{的|de}。 I came from Shanghai. |
| who with | {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{和|hé}{谁|shéi}{一起|yì qǐ}{来|lái}{的|de}？ | {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{和|hé}{朋友|péng you}{一起|yì qǐ}{来|lái}{的|de}。 I came with a friend. |

({一起|yì qǐ}, together, is lesson 20's word; {和|hé}…{一起|yì qǐ} is "together with".)

The verb inside is an ordinary verb, with no {了|le}: the frame already says it happened. Compare:

| | Sentence | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| {了|le} | {他|tā}{来|lái}{了|le}。 | He's come. (news: it happened) |
| {是|shì}…{的|de} | {他|tā}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{来|lái}{的|de}。 | He came by plane. (we know he came; this is how) |

So the usual conversation goes from one to the other: first the news with {了|le}, then the details
with {是|shì}…{的|de}.

{你|nǐ}{到|dào}{北京|Běi jīng}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Have you arrived in Beijing?

{到|dào}{了|le}。 — Yes, I have.

{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{怎么|zěn me}{去|qù}{机场|jī chǎng}{的|de}？ — How did you get to the airport?

{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{打车|dǎ chē}{去|qù}{的|de}。 — I took a taxi.

**Dropping {是|shì}.** In a positive sentence {是|shì} is often left out in speech: {我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{来|lái}{的|de} means the same as
{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{来|lái}{的|de}. {的|de} always stays.

**The negative** keeps {是|shì} and puts {不|bù} before it. Very often a correction follows:

{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{来|lái}{的|de}，{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{来|lái}{的|de}。 — I didn't come by plane; I came by train.

{他|tā}{不|bú}{是|shì}{昨天|zuó tiān}{到|dào}{的|de}，{是|shì}{今天|jīn tiān}{到|dào}{的|de}。 — He didn't arrive yesterday; he arrived today.

**With an object.** If the verb has an object, {的|de} can go at the end or just before the object.
Both are correct; in everyday speech the second is more common:

{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{在|zài}{机场|jī chǎng}{买|mǎi}{票|piào}{的|de}。 / {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{在|zài}{机场|jī chǎng}{买|mǎi}{的|de}{票|piào}。 — I bought the ticket at the airport.

With a pronoun as the object, put {的|de} at the end: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{认识|rèn shi}{他|tā}{的|de} (I met him in Beijing).

**Only for the past.** {是|shì}…{的|de} is about events that have happened. Plans and habits take plain
sentences: {我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{去|qù} (tomorrow I'm going by plane), never ~~{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{去|qù}{的|de}~~.

Don't mix this frame up with {是|shì} + noun + {的|de} as "it's someone's": {这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de} (this is mine) has no
event in it at all.

## Dialogue: you made it!

{大卫|Dà wèi} ({大卫|Dà wèi}) arrived in Beijing yesterday for a new term. {王芳|Wáng Fāng} ({王芳|Wáng Fāng}) meets him at a
café near the university.

```dialogue
# You made it!
王芳: {大卫|Dà wèi}！{你|nǐ}{到|dào}{了|le}！{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{到|dào}{的|de}？
= David! You're here! When did you arrive?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{到|dào}{的|de}。
= I got in last night.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{从|cóng}{上海|Shàng hǎi}{来|lái}{的|de}{吗|ma}？
= Did you come from Shanghai?
大卫: {不|bú}{是|shì}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{从|cóng}{英国|Yīng guó}{来|lái}{的|de}，{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{要|yào}{十|shí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。
= No, I came from Britain: ten hours by plane.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{怎么|zěn me}{从|cóng}{机场|jī chǎng}{来|lái}{的|de}？{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{来|lái}{的|de}{吗|ma}？
= How did you get here from the airport? By metro?
大卫: {不|bú}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{来|lái}{的|de}，{太|tài}{晚|wǎn}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{打车|dǎ chē}{来|lái}{的|de}。
= Not by metro: it was too late. I took a taxi.
王芳: {今天|jīn tiān}{呢|ne}？{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{怎么|zěn me}{来|lái}{的|de}？
= And today? How did you get here?
大卫: {今天|jīn tiān}{我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{公交车|gōng jiāo chē}{来|lái}{的|de}。{车站|chē zhàn}{就在|jiù zài}{学校|xué xiào}{门口|mén kǒu}。
= Today I came by bus. The stop is right by the school gate.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{的|de}{机票|jī piào}{贵|guì}{吗|ma}？
= Was your plane ticket expensive?
大卫: {不|bú}{太|tài}{贵|guì}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{买|mǎi}{的|de}。
= Not too bad: I bought it online.
```

Wang Fang starts with the news, {你|nǐ}{到|dào}{了|le}！, and then asks only about details with {是|shì}…{的|de}. David's
answer {今天|jīn tiān}{我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{公交车|gōng jiāo chē}{来|lái}{的|de} drops {是|shì}, as speakers often do. {英国|Yīng guó} is Britain, {门口|mén kǒu} (the gate,
the doorway) is lesson 09's word and {网上|wǎng shàng} (online) lesson 24's, and {就在|jiù zài} is "right at".

## Reading: a message from David

> {王芳|Wáng Fāng}，{你好|nǐ hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{大卫|Dà wèi}。{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{到|dào}{北京|Běi jīng}{的|de}，{现在|xiàn zài}{在|zài}{一|yí}{个|gè}{酒店|jiǔ diàn}。{今天|jīn tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{学校|xué xiào}{看|kàn}{看|kàn}。{请问|qǐng wèn}，{从|cóng}{酒店|jiǔ diàn}{到|dào}{学校|xué xiào}，{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{还是|hái shi}{坐|zuò}{公交车|gōng jiāo chē}？{地铁站|dì tiě zhàn}{离|lí}{酒店|jiǔ diàn}{很|hěn}{近|jìn}，{走路|zǒu lù}{五|wǔ}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。{公交车站|gōng jiāo chē zhàn}{在|zài}{酒店|jiǔ diàn}{门口|mén kǒu}，{可是|kě shì}{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}{坐|zuò}{几|jǐ}{路|lù}。{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{打车|dǎ chē}，{打车|dǎ chē}{太|tài}{贵|guì}{了|le}！{谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}！

{还是|hái shi} ("or" in a question) is lesson 21's word, {酒店|jiǔ diàn} (hotel) lesson 10's, and {门口|mén kǒu} (doorway) lesson
09's. {看|kàn}{看|kàn} (have a look) is the verb reduplication of module 1.

1. When did David arrive in Beijing?
2. How far is the metro station from his hotel?
3. Why doesn't he want to take a taxi?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Last night ({我|wǒ}{是|shì}{昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{到|dào}{北京|Běi jīng}{的|de}).
2. Five minutes' walk ({走路|zǒu lù}{五|wǔ}{分钟|fēn zhōng}).
3. It's too expensive ({打车|dǎ chē}{太|tài}{贵|guì}{了|le}).

"Hi Wang Fang! It's David. I arrived in Beijing last night and I'm at a hotel. This afternoon
I'd like to go and see the university. Could you tell me: from the hotel to the university, should I take the metro or the bus? The metro station is close to the hotel,
five minutes on foot. The bus stop is right outside the hotel, but I don't know which number to
take. I don't want to get a taxi: taxis are too expensive! Thanks!"
</details>

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 地 ✎ | ground, land, place | dì (and de) | 土 | 6 | {地铁|dì tiě} |
| 铁 (traditional 鐵) | iron | tiě | 钅 | 10 | {地铁|dì tiě} |
| 交 | cross; hand over | jiāo | 亠 | 6 | {公交车|gōng jiāo chē} |
| 站 | station; stand | zhàn | 立 | 10 | {站|zhàn}, {车站|chē zhàn} |
| 场 (traditional 場) | open space, ground | chǎng | 土 | 6 | {机场|jī chǎng} |
| 票 | ticket | piào | 示 | 11 | {票|piào}, {机票|jī piào} |

- {地|dì} has two readings. In {地铁|dì tiě} it's dì (ground, earth); in lesson 18 it's the light particle {地|de}
  that turns an adjective into an adverb ({慢慢|màn màn}{地|de}{说|shuō}, speak slowly). {土|tǔ} (earth) on the left gives the
  meaning; {也|yě} (also) is the right side.
- {铁|tiě}: 钅, the metal radical you know from {钱|qián} and {钟|zhōng}, gives the meaning. The traditional form {鐵|tiě} is
  much more complicated; the simplified right side {失|shī} is a shortcut.
- {交|jiāo}: the usual explanation is a person with crossed legs, hence "to cross". It's in {公交车|gōng jiāo chē}
  because buses are "public transport" ({公共交通|gōng gòng jiāo tōng}).
- {站|zhàn}: {立|lì} (to stand, a person standing on the ground) gives the meaning, and {占|zhàn} gives the sound,
  zhàn. The first meaning was "to stand"; a station is where vehicles stop and stand.
- {场|chǎng}: an open area such as a square, a field, a ground: {机场|jī chǎng} is "machine ground". {土|tǔ} on the left
  again, as in {地|dì}. In lesson 23 it's in {商场|shāng chǎng} (shopping centre).
- {票|piào}: on top is {西|xī} squeezed flat; below is {示|shì} (to show). Memory aid: a ticket is what you show at
  the gate.

Radical review: {土|tǔ} (earth, HSK 1 lesson 05), which you know from {在|zài}, {块|kuài} and {坐|zuò}, here in {地|dì} and {场|chǎng};
钅 (metal, HSK 1 lesson 07) in {铁|tiě}. {立|lì} (stand) and {示|shì} (show) are named in the table; this track has
only one character with each, so they don't get their own section.

### Stroke order

- **地, 场**: {土|tǔ} first, with its last stroke rising to the right (it's on the left side, as in {块|kuài}).
  Then {也|yě}: the turning stroke with a hook, the short vertical, and the long stroke that curves
  along the bottom and hooks up. In {场|chǎng} the right side starts with one long stroke that zigzags down
  and hooks, then two left-falling strokes.
- **铁**: 钅 (five strokes: the left-falling stroke, three short horizontals, the vertical that
  rises at the bottom), then {失|shī} (left-falling stroke, two horizontals, the long left-falling
  stroke, the right-falling stroke).
- **站**: {立|lì} first (dot, horizontal, dot, left-falling stroke, the rising stroke at the bottom),
  then {占|zhàn} (vertical, short horizontal, then {口|kǒu}).
- **票**: top part (horizontal, then the box with two verticals inside, then the bottom
  horizontal), then {示|shì} (two horizontals, the hooked vertical, a short left-falling stroke on the left and a dot on
  the right).
- **交**: dot and horizontal, then the two short strokes below, then the long left-falling stroke
  and the right-falling stroke that cross.

```trace
地铁交站场票
```

Write it: {地|dì} is one of the characters to know by hand. Write it three times on paper or on the
pad, from memory, then check its strokes against the pad.
=}

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{怎么|zěn me}{来|lái}{的|de}？
= How did you get here?
{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{来|lái}{的|de}。
= I came by metro.
{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{到|dào}{的|de}？
= When did you arrive?
{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{来|lái}{的|de}，{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{来|lái}{的|de}。
= I didn't come by plane; I came by train.
{我们|wǒ men}{打车|dǎ chē}{去|qù}{机场|jī chǎng}{吧|ba}。
= Let's take a taxi to the airport.
{下|xià}{一|yí}{站|zhàn}{是|shì}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= What's the next stop?
```

## Pronunciation

- {地铁|dì tiě}: a falling tone, then a dip. {铁|tiě} has the *ie* of {写|xiě} (xiě): "yeh", not "ee".
- {车站|chē zhàn} and {机场|jī chǎng}: *ch* and *zh* are the curled-tongue sounds; *ch* has a puff of
  air, *zh* has none. {场|chǎng} is chǎng with a dip.
- {公交车|gōng jiāo chē}: three first tones, all high and level. Keep them level to the end.
- {票|piào} falls; *p* has a strong puff of air.
- In {是|shì}…{的|de}, {的|de} is light and {是|shì} is often light too: *wǒ shi zuò dì tiě lái de*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{来|lái}{了|le}~~: {是|shì}…{的|de} never takes {了|le}. Say {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{来|lái}{的|de}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{来|lái}{的|de}~~ or ~~{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{来|lái}{的|de}~~: the negative is {不|bú}{是|shì}…{的|de}: {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{飞机|fēi jī}{来|lái}{的|de}.
- {是|shì}…{的|de} for the future: ~~{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}{的|de}~~. Plans are plain: {我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}.
- {了|le} when you mean {是|shì}…{的|de}: to "When did you arrive?", ~~{你|nǐ}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{到|dào}{了|le}？~~ sounds odd. Ask {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{到|dào}{的|de}？
- {开车|kāi chē} for a taxi passenger: you {打车|dǎ chē} or {坐|zuò}{出租车|chū zū chē}; the driver {开车|kāi chē}.
- Mixing up {站|zhàn} and {场|chǎng}: {站|zhàn} is a station or stop ({车站|chē zhàn}), {场|chǎng} an open area ({机场|jī chǎng}).

## Key points

- {坐|zuò} + {地铁|dì tiě} / {公交车|gōng jiāo chē} / {出租车|chū zū chē}; {打车|dǎ chē} (take a taxi); {车站|chē zhàn}, {地铁站|dì tiě zhàn}, {火车站|huǒ chē zhàn}; {站|zhàn} for stops ({坐|zuò}{三|sān}{站|zhàn}, {下|xià}{一|yí}{站|zhàn}).
- {票|piào} (ticket), {机票|jī piào} (plane ticket), {机场|jī chǎng} (airport), {飞|fēi} (fly: {从|cóng}{北京|Běi jīng}{飞|fēi}{上海|Shàng hǎi}).
- {是|shì}…{的|de} for how, when, where and who with of a past event: {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{怎么|zěn me}{来|lái}{的|de}？{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{来|lái}{的|de}。
- {是|shì} can drop in a positive sentence; the negative is {不|bú}{是|shì}…{的|de}; no {了|le}; not for plans.
- With an object: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{在|zài}{机场|jī chǎng}{买|mǎi}{的|de}{票|piào} or {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{在|zài}{机场|jī chǎng}{买|mǎi}{票|piào}{的|de}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Coming in and going out: 进来, 出去, 回来
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now say where places are, how far they are and how you got there. This lesson is about
the moment you cross a doorway: coming in, going out, coming back home. English uses "come" and
"go" with "in", "out" and "back"; Chinese has the same idea, with the verbs {进|jìn} (to enter), {出|chū} (to
exit) and {回|huí} (to return), followed by {来|lái} or {去|qù}:

- {进来|jìn lái} / {进去|jìn qù}: to come in / to go in;
- {出来|chū lái} / {出去|chū qù}: to come out / to go out;
- {回来|huí lái} / {回去|huí qù}: to come back / to go back;
- where the place goes ({回家|huí jiā}{去|qù}, {进|jìn}{房间|fáng jiān}{来|lái});
- {门|mén} (door, gate) and {门口|mén kǒu} (the doorway, the entrance).

The choice between {来|lái} and {去|qù} depends mainly on one thing: where the speaker is.

## {进|jìn} and {出|chū}: in and out

{进|jìn} is "to enter, to go or come in", and {出|chū} is "to exit, to go or come out". Both can take the place
straight after them:

{我们|wǒ men}{进|jìn}{商店|shāng diàn}{看|kàn}{看|kàn}{吧|ba}。 — Let's go into the shop and have a look.

{出|chū}{了|le}{学校|xué xiào}，{往|wǎng}{右|yòu}{走|zǒu}。 — When you come out of the school, go right.

You'll meet {出|chū} in two very common words in lesson 10: {出门|chū mén} (to leave the house) and {出国|chū guó} (to go
abroad). On their own, {进|jìn} and {出|chū} sound a little bare in speech; most of the time they come with {来|lái}
or {去|qù}.

## {来|lái} and {去|qù}: towards the speaker or away

Put {来|lái} or {去|qù} after {进|jìn}, {出|chū} or {回|huí} and you add a direction: {来|lái} means "towards me, the speaker", {去|qù}
means "away from me". This {来|lái} / {去|qù} is a **[[direction complement]]**: a word after the verb that says
which way the action goes.

| | Towards the speaker ({来|lái}) | Away from the speaker ({去|qù}) |
|---|---|---|
| {进|jìn} in | {进来|jìn lái} come in | {进去|jìn qù} go in |
| {出|chū} out | {出来|chū lái} come out | {出去|chū qù} go out |
| {回|huí} back | {回来|huí lái} come back | {回去|huí qù} go back |

So the same door gives four sentences, depending on which side you're on:

| You are | Someone comes in | Someone goes out |
|---|---|---|
| inside the room | {请|qǐng}{进来|jìn lái}！ Come in! | {他|tā}{出去|chū qù}{了|le}。 He's gone out. |
| outside the room | {我们|wǒ men}{进去|jìn qù}{吧|ba}。 Let's go in. | {你|nǐ}{出来|chū lái}{吧|ba}！ Come out! |

The rule: measure from where the speaker is. There is one common exception: when you talk about
your own movement towards the person you're speaking to, you can measure from where *they* are.
If a friend is waiting outside and calls you, you'll hear both {我|wǒ}{出去|chū qù} (from your side of the door)
and {我|wǒ}{马上|mǎ shàng}{出来|chū lái} ("I'll be right out", from your friend's side; {马上|mǎ shàng}, right away, is an HSK 3
word). {来|lái} on its own works the same way: {我|wǒ}{来|lái}{了|le}！ "Coming!", {我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{来|lái}{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}, I'll come to your place
tomorrow. When you're not sure, measure from where you are.

**{回来|huí lái} and {回去|huí qù}** work the same way. {回来|huí lái} is "come back here", {回去|huí qù} "go back there":

{我|wǒ}{回来|huí lái}{了|le}！ — I'm back! (I'm home!)

{你|nǐ}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{回来|huí lái}？ — What time will you be back? (said by someone at home)

{太|tài}{晚|wǎn}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{回去|huí qù}{了|le}。 — It's late; I'm heading back. (said by someone who is out)

{我|wǒ}{回来|huí lái}{了|le} is what many people call out as they come through their own front door, like "I'm home!".
Someone at home might answer {回来|huí lái}{了|le}？ or {回来|huí lái}{了|le}！ (you're back!).

## Where the place goes

If you name the place, it goes **between** the verb and {来|lái} / {去|qù}:

{回家|huí jiā}{去|qù} — go back home

{回|huí}{中国|Zhōng guó}{来|lái} — come back to China

{进|jìn}{房间|fáng jiān}{来|lái} — come into the room

{进|jìn}{商店|shāng diàn}{去|qù} — go into the shop

Never at the end: ~~{回去|huí qù}{家|jiā}~~, ~~{进来|jìn lái}{房间|fáng jiān}~~. Many speakers leave {来|lái} / {去|qù} out when the place is named:
{回家|huí jiā} and {进|jìn}{商店|shāng diàn} are complete and very common. So the easiest choice is:

- with a place: {回家|huí jiā}, {进|jìn}{商店|shāng diàn} (or {回家|huí jiā}{去|qù}, {进|jìn}{商店|shāng diàn}{去|qù});
- without a place: {回来|huí lái}, {回去|huí qù}, {进来|jìn lái}, {进去|jìn qù}.

{请|qǐng}{进|jìn}！ (please come in) is a short form you'll hear at the door, and {请|qǐng}{进来|jìn lái} is the full one.

## With {了|le}, {吧|ba} and time words

These verbs behave like any other verb. {了|le} for a change or a completed action, {吧|ba} for a
suggestion, time words before the verb:

{他|tā}{出去|chū qù}{了|le}。 — He's gone out. (and isn't back yet)

{他|tā}{回来|huí lái}{了|le}。 — He's back.

{你|nǐ}{进来|jìn lái}{吧|ba}。 — Come on in.

{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{回去|huí qù}。 — I'm going back tomorrow.

{你|nǐ}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{回来|huí lái}？ — When are you coming back?

{出去|chū qù} and {回来|huí lái} often have a purpose after them, just like {去|qù} in a serial verb: {我|wǒ}{出去|chū qù}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi} (I'm going out
to buy some things), {他|tā}{回家|huí jiā}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn} (he's going home to eat).

## Light {来|lái} and {去|qù}

When {来|lái} and {去|qù} follow another verb as a direction, they're usually said lightly: jìn lai, chū qu,
