huí lai. Dictionaries, and this course, write the full tones (jìn lái, chū qù), but listen for the
light syllable. The first verb keeps its tone.

## {门|mén} and {门口|mén kǒu}

{门|mén} is a door or a gate: {开门|kāi mén} is "to open the door", and also "to open" for a shop or a museum.

{请|qǐng}{开门|kāi mén}！ — Please open the door!

{商店|shāng diàn}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{开门|kāi mén}？ — What time does the shop open?

{门口|mén kǒu} is "the door's mouth": the doorway, the entrance, the space just outside a door or gate. It's a
place word, so it goes after {在|zài} and can follow another noun:

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{门口|mén kǒu}。 — I'm at the door. / I'm outside.

{学校|xué xiào}{门口|mén kǒu}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{书店|shū diàn}。 — There's a bookshop at the school gate.

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{你|nǐ}{家|jiā}{门口|mén kǒu}。 — I'm outside your place.

{门口|mén kǒu} is one of the most useful words for meeting people: {我们|wǒ men}{在|zài}{电影院|diàn yǐng yuàn}{门口|mén kǒu}{见|jiàn}{吧|ba} (let's meet at the entrance
of the cinema). {见|jiàn} is "to see, to meet", as in {再见|zài jiàn}.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 进 (traditional 進) | enter | jìn | 辶 | 7 | {进|jìn}, {进来|jìn lái}, {进去|jìn qù} |
| 门 (traditional 門) | door, gate | mén | 门 | 3 | {门|mén}, {门口|mén kǒu}, {门票|mén piào} (lesson 10) |

- {进|jìn}: the walking radical 辶 again, as in {远|yuǎn} and {近|jìn} (lesson 07). The inside of the simplified form is
  {井|jǐng} (jǐng, a well), chosen for its sound, which is close to jìn. Traditional {進|jìn} has {隹|zhuī} (a bird)
  inside; a well-known memory aid says a bird can only move forwards. {进|jìn} and {近|jìn} sound exactly the
  same: tell them apart by their insides, {井|jǐng} for "enter" and {斤|jīn} for "near".
- {门|mén} is the simplified form of {門|mén}, a picture of a double door with two swinging leaves. The
  simplified shape comes from the quick handwritten form of {門|mén}. As a radical it wraps round the
  top and sides of a character: you know it from {问|wèn} (to ask) and {时间|shí jiān} (time). In {们|men} (the plural
  suffix) it's on the right and gives the sound, next to 亻.

Radical review: 辶 (walking) and {门|mén} (door). Both are radicals that go round part of the
character: 辶 along the bottom left, written last; {门|mén} over the top, written first.

### Stroke order

- **门**: the dot, the left vertical, then the long stroke across the top and down the right,
  ending in a hook. Three strokes, and nothing closes the bottom.
- **进**: {井|jǐng} first, the way a grid is written: the two horizontals, then the left-falling stroke and
  the vertical. Then 辶 last: dot, the bent stroke, the long sweep along the bottom.

```trace
进门
```

| 去 | qù | go | {进去|jìn qù}, {出去|chū qù}, {回去|huí qù} |

## Dialogue: I'm home!

{李明|Lǐ Míng} (李明) comes home from university for the weekend. His mother (妈妈) is in the kitchen, and his father (爸爸) comes back later.

```dialogue
# I'm home!
李明: {妈|mā}，{我|wǒ}{回来|huí lái}{了|le}！
= Mum, I'm home!
妈妈: {回来|huí lái}{了|le}？{进来|jìn lái}{吧|ba}，{外边|wài bian}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}。
= You're back? Come in, it's cold outside.
李明: {爸爸|bà ba}{呢|ne}？
= Where's Dad?
妈妈: {他|tā}{出去|chū qù}{了|le}，{去|qù}{超市|chāo shì}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。
= He's gone out, to the supermarket to buy some things.
李明: {他|tā}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{回来|huí lái}？
= When will he be back?
妈妈: {六|liù}{点|diǎn}{回来|huí lái}。{你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？
= At six. Have you eaten?
李明: {还|hái}{没|méi}{吃|chī}。……{妈|mā}，{有|yǒu}{人|rén}{在|zài}{门口|mén kǒu}！
= Not yet. … Mum, there's someone at the door!
妈妈: {是|shì}{你|nǐ}{爸爸|bà ba}{吧|ba}？{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{开门|kāi mén}。
= It must be your dad. You go and open the door.
李明: {爸|bà}，{你|nǐ}{回来|huí lái}{了|le}！{进来|jìn lái}{吧|ba}！
= Dad, you're back! Come in!
爸爸: {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{菜|cài}。{小明|Xiǎo Míng}，{你|nǐ}{明天|míng tiān}{回|huí}{学校|xué xiào}{去|qù}{吗|ma}？
= I've bought lots of food. Xiaoming, are you going back to university tomorrow?
李明: {不|bù}{回去|huí qù}，{后天|hòu tiān}{回去|huí qù}。
= No, I'm going back the day after tomorrow.
```

Every {来|lái} / {去|qù} is chosen from the speaker's position. Mum, inside, says {进来|jìn lái}{吧|ba}; Li Ming, also inside,
says {进来|jìn lái}{吧|ba} to his father. Dad asks about going back to the university: Li Ming isn't there now,
so it's {回|huí}{学校|xué xiào}{去|qù} and {回去|huí qù}. {小明|Xiǎo Míng} is a family nickname: {小|xiǎo} + the last syllable of his given name. {后天|hòu tiān}
is "the day after tomorrow".

## Reading: a note on the door

Chen Xiaoyu leaves a note for her roommate Anna.

> {安娜|Ān nà}：{我|wǒ}{出去|chū qù}{了|le}，{去|qù}{超市|chāo shì}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}，{六|liù}{点|diǎn}{回来|huí lái}。{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{今天|jīn tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{从|cóng}{上海|Shàng hǎi}{回来|huí lái}，{她|tā}{说|shuō}{晚上|wǎn shang}{来|lái}{学校|xué xiào}{看|kàn}{我们|wǒ men}。{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{出去|chū qù}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}，{你|nǐ}{也|yě}{来|lái}{吧|ba}！{饭店|fàn diàn}{就在|jiù zài}{学校|xué xiào}{门口|mén kǒu}，{很|hěn}{近|jìn}。{你|nǐ}{回来|huí lái}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{请|qǐng}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{打|dǎ}{个|gè}{电话|diàn huà}。{我|wǒ}{带|dài}{着|zhe}{手机|shǒu jī}{呢|ne}。——{陈小雨|Chén Xiǎo yǔ}

{一起|yì qǐ} (together) is lesson 20's word and {就在|jiù zài} "right at"; {打|dǎ}{个|gè}{电话|diàn huà} is short for {打|dǎ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{电话|diàn huà}, and {带|dài}{着|zhe} is "have with you" ({带|dài}, to take along, is an HSK 3 word).

1. Where has Chen Xiaoyu gone, and when will she be back?
2. Who is coming to the school this evening?
3. What should Anna do when she gets back?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. To the supermarket, to buy some things; she'll be back at six ({六|liù}{点|diǎn}{回来|huí lái}).
2. Chen Xiaoyu's mother ({我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}…{晚上|wǎn shang}{来|lái}{学校|xué xiào}{看|kàn}{我们|wǒ men}).
3. Phone Chen Xiaoyu ({请|qǐng}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{打|dǎ}{个|gè}{电话|diàn huà}).

"Anna: I've gone out to the supermarket to buy a few things; I'll be back at six. My mum gets back
from Shanghai this afternoon, and she says she'll come to the school this evening to see us. At
seven we're all going out to eat together: you come too! The restaurant is right at the school
gate, very close. When you get back, please give me a call. I've got my phone with me. — Chen
Xiaoyu"
</details>

## Say it

```speak
{请|qǐng}{进来|jìn lái}！
= Please come in!
{我|wǒ}{回来|huí lái}{了|le}！
= I'm home!
{他|tā}{出去|chū qù}{了|le}。
= He's gone out.
{你|nǐ}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{回来|huí lái}？
= When will you be back?
{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{门口|mén kǒu}。
= I'm at the door.
{商店|shāng diàn}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{开门|kāi mén}？
= What time does the shop open?
```

## Pronunciation

- {进|jìn} falls. {进来|jìn lái} and {回来|huí lái} are said with a light {来|lái} after a full first syllable: *jìn lai*,
  *huí lai*.
- {出|chū}: the curled *ch* with a puff of air, then a level tone. Keep *chū qu* apart from *qù*
  alone: the {去|qù} after {出|chū} is short.
- {门|mén} rises; the plural suffix {们|men} is light (*wǒ men*). Same letters, different tone.
- {门口|mén kǒu}: rise, then dip.

## Common mistakes

- {来|lái} / {去|qù} from the wrong side: you're in your room and someone knocks, so it's {请|qǐng}{进来|jìn lái}, not
  ~~{请|qǐng}{进去|jìn qù}~~. Measure from where you are.
- The place at the end: ~~{回去|huí qù}{家|jiā}~~, ~~{进来|jìn lái}{房间|fáng jiān}~~. Say {回家|huí jiā} ({去|qù}), {进|jìn}{房间|fáng jiān} ({来|lái}).
- ~~{我|wǒ}{回去|huí qù}{来|lái}{了|le}~~: one direction at a time. {来|lái} and {去|qù} don't go together.
- Writing {们|men} for {门|mén} or the other way round: {门|mén} is the door; {们|men} has 亻 on the left.
- {=Writing {近|jìn} for {进|jìn}: {进|jìn} (enter) has {井|jǐng} inside, {近|jìn} (near) has {斤|jīn}.=}

## Key points

- {进|jìn} (enter), {出|chū} (exit), {回|huí} (return) + {来|lái} (towards the speaker) or {去|qù} (away from the speaker): the
  direction complement. Measure from where the speaker is.
- {进来|jìn lái} / {进去|jìn qù}, {出来|chū lái} / {出去|chū qù}, {回来|huí lái} / {回去|huí qù}; {我|wǒ}{回来|huí lái}{了|le}！ "I'm home!"
- A place goes between: {回家|huí jiā}{去|qù}, {进|jìn}{房间|fáng jiān}{来|lái}; or drop {来|lái} / {去|qù}: {回家|huí jiā}, {进|jìn}{商店|shāng diàn}.
- After a verb, {来|lái} and {去|qù} are often light.
- {门|mén}: door, gate ({开门|kāi mén}: open; a shop opens). {门口|mén kǒu}: the doorway, the entrance ({我|wǒ}{在|zài}{门口|mén kǒu}).

lessons.title: Have you ever been? 过 and 次
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This module has taken you round town: left and right, near and far, by metro and taxi, in and out
of doors. The last core lesson goes further, to travel: the places you've been, how many times,
and what you did there. Two grammar points carry it:

- {过|guo} after a verb: you've done something at some time in your life, as an experience
  ({我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}, I've been to Beijing);
- {次|cì} after a verb: how many times ({去|qù}{过|guo}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}, been twice).

And six travel words: {旅游|lǚ yóu} (to travel for pleasure), {外国|wài guó} (a foreign country), {出国|chū guó} (to go abroad),
{酒店|jiǔ diàn} (hotel), {门票|mén piào} (admission ticket) and {出门|chū mén} (to go out, to leave the house).

## {过|guo}: have you ever…?

Put {过|guo} straight after a verb and the sentence says that this has happened at least once, at some
time in the past: it's part of your experience. This is **[[experiential 过]]**. It's always light
(guo), and it doesn't change the verb:

{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}。 — I've been to Beijing.

{我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{过|guo}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。 — I've had dumplings (before).

{他|tā}{学|xué}{过|guo}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — He has studied Chinese (at some point).

English often uses "have ever…" or "have… before" for the same idea. The time is vague: once in
your life, last year, as a child; {过|guo} doesn't say when, only that it happened.

**Questions** take {吗|ma} or end in {没有|méi yǒu}:

{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}{吗|ma}？ — Have you ever been to Beijing?

{你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{过|guo}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{没有|méi yǒu}？ — Have you ever had dumplings?

The short answer repeats the verb with {过|guo}: {去|qù}{过|guo}。 (Yes, I have.) or {没|méi}{去|qù}{过|guo}。 (No, I haven't.)

**The negative** is {没|méi} (or {没有|méi yǒu}) + verb + {过|guo}, and {过|guo} stays. That's different from completed-action
{了|le}, which disappears in the negative:

{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}。 — I've never been to Beijing.

{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{吃|chī}{过|guo}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。 — I've never had dumplings.

Never ~~{不|bú}{去|qù}{过|guo}~~: experiences are about what has or hasn't happened, so they take {没|méi}.

A word of warning: the same character is also {过|guò}, a full verb, "to pass, to spend (time)",
in {过年|guò nián} (to celebrate the New Year) and {过|guò}{生日|shēng rì} (to have a birthday), lesson 13, and in the {过来|guò lái} /
{过去|guò qù} of lesson 12. The {过|guo} of this lesson is the light particle after another verb.

## {过|guo} or {了|le}?

You know completed-action {了|le} from HSK 1 ({我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}). Both are about the past, but they answer
different questions:

| | {了|le} | {过|guo} |
|---|---|---|
| What it says | one particular event happened | this is part of your experience |
| Example | {我|wǒ}{昨天|zuó tiān}{去|qù}{了|le}{超市|chāo shì}。 I went to the supermarket yesterday. | {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{那个|nà ge}{超市|chāo shì}。 I've been to that supermarket. |
| With a time | usually a definite time: {昨天|zuó tiān}, {上午|shàng wǔ} | often no time, or a loose one: {去年|qù nián} |
| Negative | {没|méi}{去|qù} (didn't go) | {没|méi}{去|qù}{过|guo} (have never been) |
| Is it still true? | {他|tā}{去|qù}{了|le}{北京|Běi jīng}。 He went to Beijing (and may still be there). | {他|tā}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}。 He has been to Beijing (and came back). |

The last row is a good test: {他|tā}{去|qù}{了|le}{上海|Shàng hǎi} can mean he's in Shanghai now; {他|tā}{去|qù}{过|guo}{上海|Shàng hǎi} says the trip is
over and is now part of his past.

The reference sheet for this module sets {了|le}, {过|guo} and lesson 03's {着|zhe} side by side.

## {次|cì}: how many times

To say how many times, put number + {次|cì} after the verb (and after {过|guo} or {了|le}). Like the duration in
{学习|xué xí}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí} (HSK 1), this number phrase after the verb is a **[[quantity complement]]**: it tells you
how many times or how long:

{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}。 — I've been twice.

{他|tā}{来|lái}{过|guo}{三|sān}{次|cì}。 — He has been here three times.

{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{几|jǐ}{次|cì}？ — How many times have you been?

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{住|zhù}{了|le}{三|sān}{天|tiān}。 — I stayed in Beijing for three days.

Time words that say *when* go before the verb ({我|wǒ}{去年|qù nián}{去|qù}{过|guo}); quantity complements that say *how
many times* or *how long* go after it.

**With an object**, where the object goes depends on what it is:

| Object | Order | Example |
|---|---|---|
| a place name | either side of {次|cì} | {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}{北京|Běi jīng}。 / {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}。 |
| an ordinary noun | after {次|cì} | {我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{过|guo}{一|yí}{次|cì}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。 I've had dumplings once. |
| a pronoun (me, him…) | before {次|cì} | {我|wǒ}{见|jiàn}{过|guo}{他|tā}{一|yí}{次|cì}。 I've met him once. |

{一|yí}{次|cì} is said yí cì: {次|cì} is fourth tone, so {一|yī} rises.

{次|cì} can also come before a noun, with {这|zhè}, {上|shàng}, {下|xià} and {第|dì}, to talk about a particular time:

{这|zhè}{次|cì} — this time

{上|shàng}{次|cì} — last time

{下|xià}{次|cì} — next time

{第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì} — the first time

{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì}{来|lái}{中国|Zhōng guó}。 — This is my first time in China.

{下|xià}{次|cì}{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{吧|ba}！ — Let's go together next time! ({一起|yì qǐ}, together, is lesson 20's word.)

## Travel words

{旅游|lǚ yóu} is "to travel for pleasure, to go sightseeing". It usually comes after {去|qù} + place, as the purpose
of a serial verb:

{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}{旅游|lǚ yóu}。 — I'd like to go to Beijing on holiday.

{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{旅游|lǚ yóu}。 — I love travelling.

{外国|wài guó} is a foreign country, any country other than your own. With {人|rén} it's a foreigner; before a noun
it means "foreign":

{外国人|wài guó rén} — a foreigner

{外国|wài guó}{朋友|péng you} — friends from abroad

{外国|wài guó}{菜|cài} — foreign food

{出国|chū guó} is "to go abroad": {出|chū} (exit) + {国|guó} (country). It's a verb with its own object, like {出门|chū mén} below, so {过|guo}
goes in the middle and so does the number of times:

{你|nǐ}{出|chū}{过|guo}{国|guó}{吗|ma}？ — Have you ever been abroad?

{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{出|chū}{过|guo}{国|guó}。 — I've never been abroad.

{我|wǒ}{出|chū}{过|guo}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}{国|guó}。 — I've been abroad twice.

{出国|chū guó}{旅游|lǚ yóu} is "to travel abroad".

{出门|chū mén} is "to go out, to leave the house": {出|chū} (exit) + {门|mén} (door). It's about leaving home for the day or
for a trip, and it's often used for being away from home:

{今天|jīn tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{出门|chū mén}。 — It's cold today; I don't want to go out.

{我|wǒ}{早上|zǎo shang}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{出门|chū mén}。 — I leave the house at eight in the morning.

Compare {出去|chū qù} (lesson 09), "to go out" from wherever you are right now: a room, an office, a shop.

{酒店|jiǔ diàn} is a hotel. {酒|jiǔ} is alcohol (an HSK 3 word), but a {酒店|jiǔ diàn} is not a bar: it's where you stay.

{我们|wǒ men}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{一|yí}{个|gè}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}{的|de}{酒店|jiǔ diàn}。 — We're staying in a very nice hotel.

{酒店|jiǔ diàn}{离|lí}{机场|jī chǎng}{很|hěn}{近|jìn}。 — The hotel is very close to the airport.

You know {饭店|fàn diàn} from HSK 1 as "restaurant"; some big hotels also have {饭店|fàn diàn} in their names, so read the
sign.

{门票|mén piào} is an admission ticket, the "gate ticket" for a park, a museum or a historic site. It's
counted with {张|zhāng} (an HSK 3 measure word) like other tickets:

{门票|mén piào}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？ — How much is admission?

{两张|liǎng zhāng}{门票|mén piào}，{谢谢|xiè xie}。 — Two admission tickets, please.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 旅 | travel; journey | lǚ | 方 | 10 | {旅游|lǚ yóu} |
| 游 (traditional 遊 in 旅游; 游 in 游泳) | travel; swim | yóu | 氵 | 12 | {旅游|lǚ yóu}, {游泳|yóu yǒng} (lesson 19) |
| 过 ✎ (traditional 過) | pass; (particle) | guo, guò | 辶 | 6 | {过|guo} (have done), {过年|guò nián} (lesson 13) |
| 次 | time (occurrence); next | cì | 欠 | 6 | {次|cì}, {这|zhè}{次|cì}, {第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì} |
| 酒 | alcohol, wine | jiǔ | 酉 | 10 | {酒店|jiǔ diàn} |

- {旅|lǚ}: {方|fāng} on the left, the radical you met in {旁|páng} (lesson 06). The usual explanation of its old form
  is a flag with people walking under it: a band of soldiers on the move, and then "to travel".
- {游|yóu} stands for two words in traditional script. For "to travel, to wander" ({旅游|lǚ yóu}) Taiwan writes {遊|yóu},
  with the walking radical 辶; for "to swim" ({游泳|yóu yǒng}) it writes {游|yóu}, with water 氵. Simplified Chinese
  uses {游|yóu} for both. With the script switch, {旅游|lǚ yóu} becomes {旅|lǚ}{遊|yóu} and {游泳|yóu yǒng} stays {游泳|yóu yǒng}.
- {过|guò}: 辶 (walking) and {寸|cùn} (an old unit of length). Traditional {過|guò} has {咼|guō} inside instead of
  {寸|cùn}. The particle guo and the verb guò are the same character; the verb is lesson 13's.
- {次|cì}: two dots (冫, "ice", but only a shape here) and 欠 (a person with an open mouth), the
  radical of {欢|huān} and {歌|gē}. An old meaning of {次|cì} is "next, second in order", still found in some
  words; "time, occurrence" came later.
- {酒|jiǔ}: water 氵 and {酉|yǒu}, a drawing of a wine jar. Characters with {酉|yǒu} often have to do with
  fermenting.

Radical review: {方|fāng} (lesson 06) in {旅|lǚ}; 氵 (water, HSK 1 lesson 02) in {游|yóu} and {酒|jiǔ}; 辶 (walking) in {过|guo};
欠 (open mouth, HSK 1 lesson 14) in {次|cì}.

### Stroke order

- **过**: {寸|cùn} first (horizontal, the vertical with a hook, the dot), then 辶 last: dot, the bent
  stroke, and the long sweep along the bottom.
- **旅**: {方|fāng} first (dot, horizontal, the turning stroke with a hook, the left-falling stroke), then
  the right side: the short left-falling stroke and the horizontal on top, then the rest from the
  top down.
- **游**: 氵, then {方|fāng} (four strokes), then the short left-falling stroke and horizontal, then {子|zǐ}
  (the turning stroke, the hooked vertical, the horizontal).
- **次**: the two dots of 冫 (the second one rises), then 欠: the left-falling stroke, the
  horizontal turning into a short left-falling stroke, then the long left-falling stroke and the
  right-falling one.
- **酒**: 氵 (three strokes), then {酉|yǒu}: the top horizontal, the frame (left vertical, then the
  top-and-right stroke), the two short strokes inside, and the two bottom horizontals.

```trace
旅游过次酒
```

Write it: {过|guò} is one of the characters to know by hand. Write it three times on paper or on the
pad, from memory, then check its strokes against the pad.
=}

## Dialogue: have you ever been?

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) has been in China for a year. Her classmate {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) asks
about her travels.

```dialogue
# Have you ever been?
王芳: {安娜|Ān nà}，{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{长城|Cháng chéng}{吗|ma}？
= Anna, have you been to the Great Wall?
安娜: {去|qù}{过|guo}，{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}。{第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì}{是|shì}{和|hé}{同学|tóng xué}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{的|de}，{第|dì}{二|èr}{次|cì}{是|shì}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{的|de}。
= Yes, twice. The first time I went with classmates, the second time with my mum.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{妈妈|mā ma}{也|yě}{来|lái}{过|guo}{中国|Zhōng guó}？
= Your mum has been to China too?
安娜: {对|duì}，{她|tā}{是|shì}{去年|qù nián}{来|lái}{的|de}，{那|nà}{是|shì}{她|tā}{第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì}{出国|chū guó}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？{你|nǐ}{出|chū}{过|guo}{国|guó}{吗|ma}？
= Yes, she came last year. It was her first time abroad. And you? Have you ever been abroad?
王芳: {没|méi}{出|chū}{过|guo}。{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{想|xiǎng}{出国|chū guó}{旅游|lǚ yóu}，{可是|kě shì}{机票|jī piào}{太|tài}{贵|guì}{了|le}。
= Never. I'd love to travel abroad, but plane tickets are too expensive.
安娜: {上海|Shàng hǎi}{呢|ne}？{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{上海|Shàng hǎi}{吗|ma}？
= What about Shanghai? Have you been?
王芳: {去|qù}{过|guo}{一|yí}{次|cì}。{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{那儿|nàr}{住|zhù}{了|le}{三|sān}{天|tiān}，{住|zhù}{在|zài}{一|yí}{个|gè}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}{的|de}{酒店|jiǔ diàn}。
= Once. I stayed there three days, in a very nice hotel.
安娜: {下|xià}{次|cì}{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{旅游|lǚ yóu}{吧|ba}！
= Let's travel together next time!
王芳: {好|hǎo}{啊|a}！
= Good idea!
```

Notice how Anna mixes the grammar of the module. {第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì}{是|shì}{和|hé}{同学|tóng xué}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{的|de} uses {是|shì}…{的|de} (lesson 08) for a
detail of a known trip; {她|tā}{是|shì}{去年|qù nián}{来|lái}{的|de} does the same. {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{那儿|nàr}{住|zhù}{了|le}{三|sān}{天|tiān} is a duration after the verb.
{啊|a} at the end of {好|hǎo}{啊|a} makes the reply warmer (lesson 13), and {可是|kě shì} is "but". {长城|Cháng chéng} is the Great Wall: honors lesson
10h1 is about it.

## Reading: Anna's travel post

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{安娜|Ān nà}，{是|shì}{外国人|wài guó rén}，{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{学习|xué xí}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{旅游|lǚ yóu}。{来|lái}{中国|Zhōng guó}{以前|yǐ qián}，{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{出|chū}{过|guo}{国|guó}。{现在|xiàn zài}{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{地方|dì fang}：{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{三|sān}{次|cì}{上海|Shàng hǎi}，{两|liǎng}{次|cì}{长城|Cháng chéng}，{还|hái}{去|qù}{过|guo}{一|yí}{次|cì}{西安|Xī'ān}。{上个月|shàng gè yuè}{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{朋友|péng you}{去|qù}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{公园|gōng yuán}，{门票|mén piào}{不|bú}{贵|guì}，{二十|èr shí}{块|kuài}。{我们|wǒ men}{住|zhù}{的|de}{酒店|jiǔ diàn}{离|lí}{公园|gōng yuán}{很|hěn}{近|jìn}，{走路|zǒu lù}{十|shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。{下|xià}{次|cì}{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}{别的|bié de}{城市|chéng shì}{看|kàn}{看|kàn}。

{以前|yǐ qián} (before), {地方|dì fang} (place), {公园|gōng yuán} (park) and {城市|chéng shì} (city) are HSK 3 words; {西安|Xī'ān} is the city of
Xi'an, and {别的|bié de} is "other". {上个月|shàng gè yuè} is "last month".

1. Had Anna been abroad before she came to China?
2. How many times has she been to Shanghai?
3. How much was the admission ticket, and how far was the hotel?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. No ({来|lái}{中国|Zhōng guó}{以前|yǐ qián}，{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{出|chū}{过|guo}{国|guó}).
2. Three times ({我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{三|sān}{次|cì}{上海|Shàng hǎi}).
3. Twenty yuan; ten minutes' walk.

"My name is Anna; I'm from abroad and I'm studying Chinese in Beijing. I love travelling. Before I
came to China I'd never been abroad. Now I've been to lots of places: I've been to Shanghai three
times and the Great Wall twice, and I've also been to Xi'an once. Last month my friends and I went
to a park; the admission ticket wasn't expensive, twenty yuan. The hotel we stayed in was very
close to the park, ten minutes on foot. Next time I'd like to take the train to another city and
have a look round."
</details>

The text uses both past markers: {去|qù}{过|guo} for her experiences, and {去|qù}{了|le} for one trip last month.

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{长城|Cháng chéng}{吗|ma}？
= Have you been to the Great Wall?
{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}。
= I've been twice.
{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{出|chū}{过|guo}{国|guó}。
= I've never been abroad.
{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì}{来|lái}{中国|Zhōng guó}。
= This is my first time in China.
{门票|mén piào}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？
= How much is admission?
{下|xià}{次|cì}{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{吧|ba}！
= Let's go together next time!
```

## Pronunciation

- {旅游|lǚ yóu}: ü after l is written with the dots (lǚ). Round your lips as for "oo" and say "ee".
  Then a rising {游|yóu}.
- {过|guo} after a verb is short and light: {去|qù}{过|guo} *qù guo*, {吃|chī}{过|guo} *chī guo*.
- {次|cì}: *c* is "ts" with a puff of air, and the vowel is the buzzing *-i*. {词|cí} (word, lesson
  17) rises; {次|cì} falls.
- {酒店|jiǔ diàn}: a dip, then a fall. *iu* is said *iou*: "jyoh".
- {一|yí}{次|cì} yí cì, {两|liǎng}{次|cì} liǎng cì, {第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì} dì yī cì: {一|yī} rises before {次|cì}, except in the ordinal {第|dì}{一|yī}.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}~~: experiences take {没|méi}: {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}{过|guo}{了|le}~~ or ~~{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{了|le}{过|guo}~~: {过|guo} and {了|le} don't go together like this. Choose one. (You will
  hear {我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{过|guo}{了|le}, "I've already eaten": there {过|guo} means "done, finished", a use for later.)
- Dropping {过|guo} in the negative: ~~{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}~~ is "I didn't go to Beijing (that time)". "I've never
  been" keeps {过|guo}: {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}.
- {次|cì} before the verb, English-style: ~~{我|wǒ}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}{去|qù}{过|guo}{上海|Shàng hǎi}~~. The number of times follows the verb:
  {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}{上海|Shàng hǎi} (or {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{上海|Shàng hǎi}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}).
- ~~{我|wǒ}{出国|chū guó}{过|guo}~~: in {出国|chū guó} and {出门|chū mén}, {过|guo} goes between the two parts: {出|chū}{过|guo}{国|guó}.
- {酒店|jiǔ diàn} as a bar: it's a hotel.

## Key points

- Verb + {过|guo} (light guo): an experience, "have (ever) done". Questions …{过|guo}{吗|ma}？ / …{过|guo}{没有|méi yǒu}？
- Negative: {没|méi} + verb + {过|guo} ({过|guo} stays). Never {不|bù}…{过|guo}.
- {了|le} is one event; {过|guo} is experience. {他|tā}{去|qù}{了|le}{北京|Běi jīng} (he went) vs {他|tā}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng} (he has been).
- Verb + number + {次|cì}: how many times ({去|qù}{过|guo}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}); {这|zhè}{次|cì}, {上|shàng}{次|cì}, {下|xià}{次|cì}, {第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì}.
- Objects: place names either side of {次|cì}, ordinary nouns after it, pronouns before it.
- {旅游|lǚ yóu} ({去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}{旅游|lǚ yóu}), {外国|wài guó} / {外国人|wài guó rén}, {出国|chū guó} and {出门|chū mén} ({过|guo} in the middle), {酒店|jiǔ diàn} (hotel), {门票|mén piào}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The Great Wall
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{长城|Cháng chéng}{吗|ma}？ is one of the first questions a visitor to Beijing is asked, and after lesson 10 you can
answer it. This honors lesson is about the wall itself: what it is (many walls, not one), how long
it is (it depends what you count), the famous claim that you can see it from space, and the
sections you can visit from Beijing. It ends with a short text about a visit. New words are
glossed; none join your vocabulary reviews.

## The name: {长城|Cháng chéng}

In Chinese the Great Wall is {长城|Cháng chéng}, "the long wall": {长|cháng} (long, from lesson 02) + {城|chéng} (a city
wall; in HSK 3 you'll meet it in {城市|chéng shì}, city). Its fuller name is {万里长城|Wàn lǐ Cháng chéng}, "the long wall of ten
thousand li": {万|wàn} is ten thousand (lesson 23), and the li is an old Chinese unit of distance,
about half a kilometre, so {万里|wàn lǐ} is "ten thousand li". It's a way of saying "endless", not
a measurement.

{长城|Cháng chéng}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}。 — The Great Wall is very long.

## Not one wall, but many

The Great Wall isn't a single wall built at one time. It's a long series of walls, built,
rebuilt and abandoned over more than two thousand years:

- The first walls go back to about the 7th century BC, when different states in what is now China
  walled their borders against each other and against peoples from the north.
- After the first emperor, {秦始皇|Qín Shǐ huáng}, united China in 221 BC, walls were linked into
  a longer line, around 220 BC.
- Many later dynasties repaired and extended them.
- Most of the wall that stands today was rebuilt under the Ming dynasty ({明朝|Míng cháo},
  1368–1644), much of it in brick and stone. The famous sections near Beijing, with their
  watchtowers on the mountain ridges, are Ming.

Much of the wall is now a ruin. Only a small share of the Ming wall is still in good condition; the
rest has worn away, been taken apart for building stone, or survives as earth ridges in the
desert. In 1987 the Great Wall became a UNESCO World Heritage site.

## How long is it?

That depends on what you count. In 2012, after a five-year survey, China's State Administration
of Cultural Heritage gave a length of **21,196 km** for all the walls of all periods together,
including sections that are only traces today. An earlier survey had put the Ming walls alone at
about 8,850 km. Both numbers appear in books and on signs, and they measure different things, so
neither is "wrong". Either way, it's far longer than any traveller could walk in a holiday.

## Can you see it from space?

You may have read that the Great Wall is the only human-made structure you can see from space, or
even from the Moon. It isn't true:

- From the Moon, no human-made structure on Earth can be seen with the naked eye.
- From a low orbit (a few hundred kilometres up), the wall is very hard to see: it's long but
  narrow, and about the same colour as the land around it. Some astronauts say they've glimpsed it
  in a low sun, when it casts a shadow; many say they never saw it.
- China's first astronaut, {杨利伟|Yáng Lì wěi}, was asked about it after his flight in October
  2003 and said he didn't see the Great Wall.

The myth is older than space flight, which may be why it's so hard to kill. In Chinese you'd ask:

{从|cóng}{太空|tài kōng}{能|néng}{看见|kàn jiàn}{长城|Cháng chéng}{吗|ma}？ — Can you see the Great Wall from space? ({太空|tài kōng}: outer space)

## Visiting from Beijing

Several restored Ming sections are a day trip from the city. Distances are rough, by road from
central Beijing:

| Section | Pinyin | About | What it's known for |
|---|---|---|---|
| {八达岭|Bā dá lǐng} | Bā dá lǐng | 70 km | the most famous and the busiest; the first section restored and opened to visitors; trains go there |
| {慕田峪|Mù tián yù} | Mù tián yù | 75 km | restored, with a cable car; usually quieter than {八达岭|Bā dá lǐng} |
| {金山岭|Jīn shān lǐng} | Jīn shān lǐng | 130 km | for walkers: restored stretches and wild, unrestored ones |
| {司马台|Sī mǎ tái} | Sī mǎ tái | 120 km | steep, much of it original Ming work; one of the few sections open at night |

Weekends and holidays are crowded, especially at {八达岭|Bā dá lǐng}. Wear good shoes: the wall follows the
mountain ridges, so much of a visit is climbing steps.

{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{怎么|zěn me}{去|qù}{八达岭|Bā dá lǐng}{的|de}？ — How did you get to Badaling?

{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}{的|de}。 — I went by train.

## A visit to the Great Wall

> {上|shàng}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī}{六|liù}，{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{同学|tóng xué}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{了|le}{长城|Cháng chéng}。{我们|wǒ men}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}{的|de}，{路上|lù shang}{要|yào}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。{长城上|Cháng chéng shang}{的|de}{人|rén}{很|hěn}{多|duō}，{有|yǒu}{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}，{也|yě}{有|yǒu}{外国人|wài guó rén}。{我们|wǒ men}{走|zǒu}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}，{很|hěn}{累|lèi}，{可是|kě shì}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。{在|zài}{长城上|Cháng chéng shang}，{我们|wǒ men}{看见|kàn jiàn}{了|le}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{山|shān}。{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì}{去|qù}{长城|Cháng chéng}，{下|xià}{次|cì}{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{妈妈|mā ma}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}。

{一起|yì qǐ} (together) is lesson 20's word, {可是|kě shì} is "but", and {山|shān} is "mountain", an HSK 3 word.

1. How did the writer get to the Great Wall?
2. How long did they walk?
3. Who does the writer want to go with next time?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. By train ({我们|wǒ men}{是|shì}{坐|zuò}{火车|huǒ chē}{去|qù}{的|de}).
2. Two hours ({我们|wǒ men}{走|zǒu}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}).
3. Their mum and dad ({下|xià}{次|cì}{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{妈妈|mā ma}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}).

"Last Saturday my classmates and I went to the Great Wall. We went by train; the journey took an
hour. There were lots of people on the wall, Chinese and foreign. We walked for two hours: we were
tired, but very happy. From the wall we could see lots of mountains. This was my first time at
the Great Wall; next time I'd like to go with my mum and dad."
</details>

## Words in this lesson (glossed, not for review)

| Word | Pinyin | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {长城|Cháng chéng} | Cháng chéng | the Great Wall |
| {万里长城|Wàn lǐ Cháng chéng} | Wàn lǐ Cháng chéng | the Great Wall ("long wall of ten thousand li") |
| {城|chéng} | chéng | city wall; city (HSK 3: {城市|chéng shì}) |
| {秦始皇|Qín Shǐ huáng} | Qín Shǐ huáng | the first emperor of China (reigned 221–210 BC as emperor) |
| {明朝|Míng cháo} | Míng cháo | the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) |
| {太空|tài kōng} | tài kōng | outer space |
| {山|shān} | shān | mountain (HSK 3) |

## Key points

- {长城|Cháng chéng} is many walls from many periods; most of what visitors see is Ming (1368–1644).
- The 2012 survey counted 21,196 km for all walls of all periods; the Ming walls are about 8,850 km.
- It can't be seen from the Moon, and from orbit only rarely, if at all.
- Near Beijing: {八达岭|Bā dá lǐng} (busiest), {慕田峪|Mù tián yù}, {金山岭|Jīn shān lǐng}, {司马台|Sī mǎ tái}.
- {你|nǐ}{去|qù}{过|guo}{长城|Cháng chéng}{吗|ma}？ — {去|qù}{过|guo}，{去|qù}{过|guo}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}。 / {没|méi}{去|qù}{过|guo}。

lessons.title: Travelling by train
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

For most long trips inside China, people take the train. This honors lesson follows a journey
from start to finish: buying the ticket, getting through the station, the kinds of train and seat,
and the busiest travel season of the year, around the Spring Festival. It uses this module's words
({车站|chē zhàn}, {站|zhàn}, {票|piào}, {进去|jìn qù}, {是|shì}…{的|de}) in a new setting. New words are glossed; none join your vocabulary
reviews.

## Buying a ticket

Train tickets are sold through the railway's official website and app, **12306** (named after its
customer-service phone number), and at station ticket offices. Many travellers book online:

{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{买|mǎi}{的|de}{火车票|huǒ chē piào}。 — I bought my train ticket online. ({火车票|huǒ chē piào}: train ticket; {网上|wǎng shàng}: online, lesson 24)

Tickets are **real-name** tickets: each one is tied to the passenger's ID. Chinese citizens use their
identity card ({身份证|shēn fèn zhèng}); foreign visitors use their passport ({护照|hù zhào}, an HSK 3 word). Today the ticket
itself is usually electronic, stored against that ID, so the ID is what you show at the station.
Bring the same document you booked with, and arrive early: ticket sales and boarding close a little
before the train leaves.

Big cities have several stations, so read the ticket carefully. Beijing, for example, has {北京站|Běi jīng zhàn},
{北京南站|Běi jīng Nán zhàn} (South), {北京西站|Běi jīng Xī zhàn} (West) and others, far apart from each other.

## At the station

| Step | In Chinese | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| security check | {安检|ān jiǎn} | bags go through a scanner at the entrance, as at an airport |
| ID check | | staff or a machine check your ID against your ticket |
| waiting hall | {候车室|hòu chē shì} | you wait for your train; boards show the trains and their gates |
| ticket gate | {检票口|jiǎn piào kǒu} | it opens shortly before departure; your ID is checked again |
| platform | {站台|zhàn tái} | you find your coach number ({车厢|chē xiāng}) and get on |

In traditional script this course writes {站台|zhàn tái} just as in simplified: Taiwan's official
form uses a more complex character for its second syllable, but this one is common in everyday
writing.

The {进|jìn} and {出|chū} of lesson 09 are everywhere here: {进站|jìn zhàn} (to enter the station) and {出站|chū zhàn} (to leave the
station), and signs at the exits say {出口|chū kǒu} (exit; {入口|rù kǒu} is "entrance").

{我们|wǒ men}{进站|jìn zhàn}{吧|ba}。 — Let's go into the station.

## Fast and slow trains

The fastest trains are the high-speed trains, {高铁|gāo tiě} (an HSK 3 word: "high iron", the {铁|tiě} of {地铁|dì tiě}).
Their train numbers start with a letter that tells you the kind of train:

| Letter | Kind | Roughly |
|---|---|---|
| G | high-speed ({高铁|gāo tiě}) | the fastest, up to 350 km/h on some lines |
| D | {动车|dòng chē} | fast, around 250 km/h; some run overnight with sleepers |
| C | intercity | short hops between neighbouring cities |
| Z, T, K | conventional trains | slower, cheaper, often overnight |

China's high-speed network is very large and still growing: in December 2024 the National
Railway Administration put it at about 47,000 km.

## Seats and sleepers

| Train | Class | In Chinese | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| high-speed | second class | {二等座|èr děng zuò} | the usual seat, five across (3 + 2) |
| high-speed | first class | {一等座|yī děng zuò} | four across, more room |
| high-speed | business class | {商务座|shāng wù zuò} | the most expensive, seats that lie almost flat |
| conventional | hard seat | {硬座|yìng zuò} | the cheapest seat, often crowded |
| conventional | hard sleeper | {硬卧|yìng wò} | an open bay with six bunks, three on each side |
| conventional | soft sleeper | {软卧|ruǎn wò} | a closed compartment with four bunks |
| any | standing | {无座|wú zuò} | "no seat": a ticket without a seat, when the seats are sold out |

At the end of each coach there's usually a hot-water tap ({开水|kāi shuǐ}, boiled water), and many
passengers bring a cup for tea or a pot of instant noodles.

## The Spring Festival rush: {春运|chūn yùn}

Every winter, around the Spring Festival (the lunar New Year, honors lesson 15h1), hundreds of
millions of people travel home to spend the holiday with their families, and then back to the
cities where they work or study. The travel season is called {春运|chūn yùn}, "spring transport",
and it lasts about forty days. Official figures for 2025 counted 513 million railway trips in the
forty days and about nine billion trips between regions by every kind of transport, both records
at the time. Tickets for the busiest days sell out fast, and stations are packed.

## Dialogue: at the station

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) and {李明|Lǐ Míng} (李明) are taking the high-speed train to Shanghai.

```dialogue
# At the station
安娜: {李明|Lǐ Míng}，{我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{火车|huǒ chē}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{开|kāi}？
= Li Ming, what time does our train leave?
李明: {十|shí}{点|diǎn}{二十|èr shí}。{现在|xiàn zài}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}{半|bàn}，{我们|wǒ men}{进站|jìn zhàn}{吧|ba}。
= Ten twenty. It's half past nine; let's go into the station.
安娜: {我们|wǒ men}{没有|méi yǒu}{票|piào}，{怎么|zěn me}{进去|jìn qù}？
= We haven't got tickets: how do we get in?
李明: {我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{票|piào}{是|shì}{在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{买|mǎi}{的|de}，{看|kàn}{护照|hù zhào}{就|jiù}{可以|kě yǐ}。{你|nǐ}{的|de}{护照|hù zhào}{呢|ne}？
= We bought them online; they just check your passport. Where's your passport?
安娜: {在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}。{我们|wǒ men}{坐|zuò}{几号|jǐ hào}{车厢|chē xiāng}？
= Here. Which coach are we in?
李明: {五|wǔ}{号|hào}{车厢|chē xiāng}，{二等座|èr děng zuò}。
= Coach five, second class.
安娜: {火车|huǒ chē}{上|shàng}{能|néng}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吗|ma}？
= Can you eat on the train?
李明: {能|néng}。{火车|huǒ chē}{上|shàng}{也|yě}{有|yǒu}{开水|kāi shuǐ}，{我们|wǒ men}{可以|kě yǐ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}。
= Yes. There's boiled water on the train too, so we can have tea.
安娜: {太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{第|dì}{一|yī}{次|cì}{坐|zuò}{高铁|gāo tiě}。
= Great! It's my first time on a high-speed train.
```

{火车|huǒ chē}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{开|kāi}？ uses {开|kāi} in its sense "to set off" (for a train or a bus). {看|kàn}{护照|hù zhào}{就|jiù}{可以|kě yǐ} is "checking the
passport is enough" ({就|jiù}, lesson 18; {可以|kě yǐ}, HSK 1). {几号|jǐ hào}{车厢|chē xiāng} asks for the coach number, like {几号|jǐ hào} for a
date.

## Reading: a message about the tickets

> {王芳|Wáng Fāng}：{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{火车票|huǒ chē piào}！{我们|wǒ men}{是|shì}{十二|shí èr}{月|yuè}{二十|èr shí}{号|hào}{早上|zǎo shang}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{的|de}{火车|huǒ chē}，{从|cóng}{北京南站|Běi jīng Nán zhàn}{开|kāi}，{下午|xià wǔ}{一|yī}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}{上海|Shàng hǎi}。{是|shì}{二等座|èr děng zuò}，{五|wǔ}{号|hào}{车厢|chē xiāng}。{北京南站|Běi jīng Nán zhàn}{离|lí}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{远|yuǎn}，{我们|wǒ men}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{去|qù}{吧|ba}。{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{在|zài}{地铁站|dì tiě zhàn}{门口|mén kǒu}{见|jiàn}！——{李明|Lǐ Míng}

1. When does the train leave, and when does it arrive?
2. Which class are the seats?
3. Where and when will they meet?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. It leaves at eight in the morning on 20 December and arrives at one in the afternoon.
2. Second class ({二等座|èr děng zuò}), coach five.
3. At the entrance of the metro station, at seven ({七|qī}{点|diǎn}{在|zài}{地铁站|dì tiě zhàn}{门口|mén kǒu}{见|jiàn}).

"Wang Fang: I've bought our train tickets! Ours is the eight o'clock train on the morning of 20
December, leaving from Beijing South, arriving in Shanghai at one in the afternoon. Second class,
coach five. Beijing South is a bit far from my home, so let's take the metro there. See you at the
entrance of the metro station at seven! — Li Ming"
</details>

## Words in this lesson (glossed, not for review)

| Word | Pinyin | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {火车票|huǒ chē piào} | huǒ chē piào | train ticket |
| {身份证|shēn fèn zhèng} | shēn fèn zhèng | identity card |
| {护照|hù zhào} | hù zhào | passport (HSK 3) |
| {安检|ān jiǎn} | ān jiǎn | security check |
| {候车室|hòu chē shì} | hòu chē shì | waiting hall |
| {检票口|jiǎn piào kǒu} | jiǎn piào kǒu | ticket gate |
| {站台|zhàn tái} | zhàn tái | platform |
| {车厢|chē xiāng} | chē xiāng | railway coach, carriage |
| {进站|jìn zhàn} / {出站|chū zhàn} | jìn zhàn / chū zhàn | enter / leave the station |
| {出口|chū kǒu} / {入口|rù kǒu} | chū kǒu / rù kǒu | exit / entrance |
| {高铁|gāo tiě} | gāo tiě | high-speed rail (HSK 3) |
| {动车|dòng chē} | dòng chē | fast (D) train |
| {二等座|èr děng zuò} / {一等座|yī děng zuò} / {商务座|shāng wù zuò} | èr děng zuò / yī děng zuò / shāng wù zuò | second / first / business class |
| {硬座|yìng zuò} / {硬卧|yìng wò} / {软卧|ruǎn wò} | yìng zuò / yìng wò / ruǎn wò | hard seat / hard sleeper / soft sleeper |
| {无座|wú zuò} | wú zuò | standing ticket ("no seat") |
| {开水|kāi shuǐ} | kāi shuǐ | boiled water |
| {春运|chūn yùn} | chūn yùn | the Spring Festival travel season |

## Key points

- Tickets: online (12306) or at the station; real-name, tied to your ID ({身份证|shēn fèn zhèng} or {护照|hù zhào}).
- At the station: {安检|ān jiǎn}, the waiting hall {候车室|hòu chē shì}, the gate {检票口|jiǎn piào kǒu}, the platform {站台|zhàn tái}; {进站|jìn zhàn} / {出站|chū zhàn}.
- G = {高铁|gāo tiě} (fastest), D = {动车|dòng chē}, Z / T / K = conventional trains.
- {二等座|èr děng zuò}, {一等座|yī děng zuò}, {商务座|shāng wù zuò} on high-speed trains; {硬座|yìng zuò}, {硬卧|yìng wò}, {软卧|ruǎn wò} on conventional ones.
- {春运|chūn yùn}: about forty days of travel around the Spring Festival.

lessons.title: Upstairs, downstairs, inside and outside: 上面, 里面, 楼
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 2 took you out of the house: left and right, how far, the metro, coming in and going out,
and travel. Module 3 comes home. You'll describe a flat (rooms, floors, the bed, the toilet),
then in the next lessons move things up and down the stairs, celebrate a birthday, compare things
and ask why.

This lesson finishes the set of position words. In HSK 1 you put {上|shàng}, {下|xià}, {里|lǐ} and
{外|wài} after a noun ({桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}, on the table), and lesson 06 gave you the suffix
-{面|miàn} in {前面|qián miàn} and {后面|hòu miàn}. Now come {上面|shàng miàn}, {下面|xià miàn},
{里面|lǐ miàn} and {外面|wài miàn}, which can stand on their own. You'll also learn to say which
floor you live on with {楼|lóu}, to count rooms with {间|jiān}, and to ask for the
{洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān}.

## Four position words: {上面|shàng miàn}, {下面|xià miàn}, {里面|lǐ miàn}, {外面|wài miàn}

| Word | Meaning | After a noun | Short form after a noun |
|---|---|---|---|
| {上面|shàng miàn} | on top, above | {桌子|zhuō zi}{上面|shàng miàn} | {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng} |
| {下面|xià miàn} | below, underneath | {床|chuáng}{下面|xià miàn} | {床|chuáng}{下|xià} |
| {里面|lǐ miàn} | inside, in | {房间|fáng jiān}{里面|lǐ miàn} | {房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ} |
| {外面|wài miàn} | outside | {门|mén}{外面|wài miàn} | {门|mén}{外|wài} |

They are the same as the -{边|biān} forms you met in HSK 1 ({上边|shàng bian}, {里边|lǐ bian},
{外边|wài bian}): -{面|miàn} and -{边|biān} mean the same here, and both are common. Like
{前面|qián miàn} and {后面|hòu miàn}, these are **[[locatives]]**, words for a position, and they
work as place words: after {在|zài}, at the start of a sentence with {有|yǒu}, or before {的|de}.

*On their own.* The big difference from the one-syllable forms: {上面|shàng miàn},
{里面|lǐ miàn} and the others can stand alone, with no noun in front. The short forms can't.

{里面|lǐ miàn}{有|yǒu}{人|rén}{吗|ma}？ — Is there anyone in there? (knocking on a door)
{外面|wài miàn}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{里面|lǐ miàn}{很|hěn}{热|rè}。 — It's cold outside and warm inside.
{你|nǐ}{的|de}{书|shū}{在|zài}{上面|shàng miàn}。 — Your book is up there / on top.

You can't say ~~{里|lǐ}{很|hěn}{热|rè}~~ or ~~{外|wài}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}~~: alone, the short forms
need a noun in front of them ({房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}, {门|mén}{外|wài}).

*After a noun.* Both forms work, and the short one is more usual in speech for {上|shàng} and
{里|lǐ}:

{手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}。 / {手机|shǒu jī}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上面|shàng miàn}。 — The phone is on the table.
{房间|fáng jiān}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}。 — There are two people in the room.
{床|chuáng}{下面|xià miàn}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}。 — There's a cat under the bed.

*"On" or "above"?* {上面|shàng miàn} covers both. {书|shū}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上面|shàng miàn}
is a book lying on the table; for a lamp hanging over it, the same words mean "above". Context
decides, just as {下面|xià miàn} is both "under" and "below".

*With {的|de}.* Before a noun, add {的|de}: {上面|shàng miàn}{的|de}{书|shū} (the book on top),
{外面|wài miàn}{的|de}{人|rén} (the people outside). {上面|shàng miàn}{的|de}{字|zì} can also mean
"the words above" in a text, as in an exam instruction.

## Which floor? {楼|lóu}

{楼|lóu} is a building with storeys: a block of flats, an office building, a school building. It's
also a floor of one. Put a number before it and you have a floor, with no {第|dì}:

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{在|zài}{五|wǔ}{楼|lóu}。 — We live on the fifth floor.
{你|nǐ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{几|jǐ}{楼|lóu}？ — Which floor do you live on?
{洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān}{在|zài}{二|èr}{楼|lóu}。 — The toilets are on the second floor.

{五|wǔ}{楼|lóu} is already "the fifth floor": the number works as an ordinal here, the way
{三|sān}{月|yuè} is March, not "three months". So {一|yī} keeps its first tone ({一|yī}{楼|lóu},
like {第|dì}{一|yī}), and 2 is {二|èr}, never {两|liǎng}: {二|èr}{楼|lóu}. Ask with {几|jǐ}{楼|lóu}.

*Counting floors.* {一|yī}{楼|lóu} is the floor at street level. In the US that's the first floor
too; in Britain it's the ground floor, so British {二|èr}{楼|lóu} is the "first floor". When you
visit a Chinese building, count the street level as one.

{楼|lóu} combines with {上|shàng} and {下|xià}: {楼上|lóu shàng} is upstairs (a higher floor) and
{楼下|lóu xià} downstairs, or at the foot of your building:

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{楼下|lóu xià}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{超市|chāo shì}。 — There's a supermarket at the bottom of our building.
{楼上|lóu shàng}{的|de}{人|rén}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{只|zhī}{狗|gǒu}。 — The people upstairs have a dog.

The lift is {电梯|diàn tī} (an HSK 3 word). You'll also see {层|céng} for floors in buildings and
on signs; it's HSK 3's too.

## Rooms: {间|jiān} and {洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān}

{间|jiān} is a **[[measure word]]** for rooms. You already know the character from
{时间|shí jiān} (time) and {房间|fáng jiān} (room); as a measure word it means "a space between
walls":

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{三|sān}{间|jiān}{房间|fáng jiān}。 — Our flat has three rooms.
{这|zhè}{间|jiān}{房间|fáng jiān}{很|hěn}{大|dà}。 — This room is big.
{我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{那|nà}{间|jiān}。 — I'm in that room. (the noun left out, as with any measure word)

{个|gè} works too ({三|sān}{个|gè}{房间|fáng jiān}), so you won't be wrong with it, but {间|jiān}
is the precise word, the one you'll read in notices for flats and hotel rooms. {一|yì}{间|jiān}
has *yì*, because {间|jiān} is a first tone.

{洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān}: "wash-hands room", the polite everyday word for a toilet or restroom,
at home and in public. You know {洗|xǐ} (wash) and {手|shǒu} (hand) from module 1.

{请问|qǐng wèn}，{洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？ — Excuse me, where's the toilet?

On signs you'll also see {卫生间|wèi shēng jiān} (HSK 3) and {厕所|cè suǒ} (a plainer word for the
toilet itself).

## {床|chuáng}: the bed

You've seen the character in {起床|qǐ chuáng} (to get up). On its own, {床|chuáng} is a bed:

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{床|chuáng}{很|hěn}{舒服|shū fu}。 — My bed is comfortable.
{孩子|hái zi}{在|zài}{床|chuáng}{上|shàng}{看|kàn}{书|shū}。 — The child is reading in bed.

"In bed" is {床|chuáng}{上|shàng}, "on the bed": a bed is something you lie on, not in.

## Describing a flat

Put it together with the existential {有|yǒu} (place + {有|yǒu} + thing) and {在|zài} (thing +
{在|zài} + place), as in HSK 1:

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{在|zài}{八|bā}{楼|lóu}，{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{间|jiān}{房间|fáng jiān}{和|hé}{一|yí}{个|gè}{洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān}。
— Our flat is on the eighth floor, with two rooms and a bathroom.

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}{不|bú}{大|dà}，{里面|lǐ miàn}{有|yǒu}{一|yì}{张|zhāng}{床|chuáng}、{一|yì}{张|zhāng}{桌子|zhuō zi}。
— My room isn't big; there's a bed and a desk in it.

({张|zhāng} is the measure word for flat things such as beds, tables and paper: HSK 3. You can
say {里面|lǐ miàn}{有|yǒu}{床|chuáng}{和|hé}{桌子|zhuō zi} without counting.)

A flat or house is {房子|fáng zi} (HSK 3); the kitchen is {厨房|chú fáng} and the living room
{客厅|kè tīng}. {房子|fáng zi} comes in HSK 3, the other two later; here they're just for recognising.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 楼 (traditional 樓) | storeyed building; floor | lóu | 木 | 13 | {楼|lóu}, {楼上|lóu shàng}, {楼下|lóu xià} |

The other words of the lesson use characters you know: 间, 手, 床, 上 下 里 外 and 面 (HSK 1),
and 洗 (lesson 04).

- 楼 is a sound-and-meaning character: 木 (wood, tree) for the meaning, since buildings were
  once built of timber, and 娄 (*lóu*) on the right for the sound. Traditional 樓 has the older
  form of the same sound part, 婁.
- 里 and 面 in {里面|lǐ miàn} are two of the characters with two traditional forms: "inside" is
  裡 and "side" is 面, so {里面|lǐ miàn} becomes 裡面 in traditional script.

Radical review: 木 (wood) on the left, written narrow, is the radical of 楼, and of 校, 机, 杯,
桌 (on the bottom) and 椅, which you know. Several of them name things made of wood.

### Stroke order

- 楼: 木 first, as a narrow left side: horizontal, vertical, the left-falling stroke, and its last
  stroke shortened to a dot. Then the right side from top to bottom: the top part (like a
  flattened 米) and 女 underneath. 4 + 6 + 3 = 13 strokes.

```trace
楼
```

> **Handwriting review.** By the end of HSK 2 you should be able to write 100 characters by hand.
> This module's lessons use these 18 from HSK 1: 上 下 间 来 去 打 年 什 么 是 没 对 边 后 多 两 岁 点.
> Write each one three times from memory, then check it on a pad. Words to think of:
> {上面|shàng miàn}, {下面|xià miàn}, {房间|fáng jiān}, {回来|huí lái}, {出去|chū qù},
> {打车|dǎ chē}, {今年|jīn nián}, {什么|shén me}, {是|shì}, {没有|méi yǒu}, {对|duì},
> {旁边|páng biān}, {后面|hòu miàn}, {多|duō}, {两|liǎng}{岁|suì}, {一点儿|yì diǎnr}.

```trace
上下间来去打
```

```trace
年什么是没对
```

```trace
边后多两岁点
```
