lessons.title: The Spring Festival
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 13 you learned {过年|guò nián}, "to celebrate the New Year". In China that means the
lunar New Year, called {春节|Chūn jié}, the Spring Festival: the biggest holiday of the year, when
millions of people travel home to be with their families. This lesson walks through the festival
from the cleaning beforehand to the lanterns at the end, with the words and greetings you'll hear.
Customs differ between regions and families; what follows is what is widely done, not a rule for
everyone.

## When is it?

{春节|Chūn jié} is the first day of the first month of the lunar calendar ({正月|zhēng yuè}{初一|chū yī}).
Because the lunar months follow the moon, its date in the ordinary calendar moves from year to
year: it always falls on a new moon between 21 January and 20 February. The festive season
starts a little before it, on New Year's Eve, and traditionally ends on the fifteenth day of the
month with the Lantern Festival ({元宵节|Yuán xiāo jié}), when the moon is full.

In mainland China, {春节|Chūn jié} is the official name, and the everyday words are {过年|guò nián}
and {新年|xīn nián} (the New Year).

## Getting ready

In the days before the festival, families clean the whole home ({大扫除|dà sǎo chú}, the "big
sweep"): the old idea is to sweep away the bad luck of the old year and make room for the new.

Then come the decorations, almost all of them red, the colour of luck and celebration:

- *Spring couplets* ({春联|chūn lián}): two lines of good wishes written on long strips of red
  paper, one on each side of the front door, often with a short line across the top.
- The character {福|fú} (good fortune) on a square of red paper, on the door or the wall. Many
  people hang it *upside down*. "Upside down" is {倒|dào}, which sounds exactly like {到|dào},
  "to arrive". Seeing it, people say {福|fú}{倒|dào}{了|le}, "the fortune is upside down", which
  sounds like {福|fú}{到|dào}{了|le}, "good fortune has arrived".

Puns like this are everywhere at New Year, because Chinese has many words that sound alike.

## New Year's Eve: the reunion dinner

New Year's Eve is {除夕|chú xī}. Its centre is the reunion dinner, {年夜饭|nián yè fàn} (the "New
Year's night meal"), the most important family meal of the year. People travel a long way not to
miss it.

Two foods carry their own wishes:
- *Fish* ({鱼|yú}, lesson 22's word). The phrase {年年有余|nián nián yǒu yú} means "may there be
  plenty left over every year", and its {余|yú} (surplus) sounds like {鱼|yú} (fish). So a fish is
  served, and often some of it is left on purpose.
- *Dumplings* ({饺子|jiǎo zi}), especially in the north, where families make them together and
  eat them around midnight. Their shape is said to look like the gold and silver ingots once used
  as money.

After dinner many families watch the *Spring Festival Gala* ({春晚|Chūn wǎn}) on television, a
show of songs, dances, comedy sketches ({小品|xiǎo pǐn}) and comic dialogues ({相声|xiàng sheng})
that has been broadcast on New Year's Eve every year since 1983.

## Red envelopes

A {红包|hóng bāo} is a small red envelope with money inside. Older, married relatives give them to
children and to younger relatives who aren't married yet; some employers give them too. The money
is in new banknotes, and it's polite not to open the envelope in front of the giver. Since the
middle of the 2010s, many {红包|hóng bāo} are sent by phone through messaging apps, often as a game
in a family chat group.

## Fireworks

Firecrackers ({鞭炮|biān pào}) and fireworks ({烟花|yān huā}) are an old part of New Year's Eve.
A story often told to children explains why: a monster called {年|Nián} came every New Year to
attack the villages, until people found that it was afraid of the colour red and of loud noises.
So they put up red paper and set off firecrackers to drive it away.

Today many cities limit or ban fireworks, at least in their central areas, so what you see and
hear depends on where you are.

## Going home: the travel rush

Because so many people work far from their home towns, the weeks around the festival see an
enormous wave of travel, called {春运|chūn yùn} (the "Spring Festival transport" season). It lasts
about forty days and is often described as the largest yearly human migration in the world. Train
and plane tickets are hard to get, and many people book weeks ahead (see honors lesson 10h2 on
trains).

## Greetings

| Greeting | Meaning | When |
|---|---|---|
| {过年好|guò nián hǎo}！ | Happy New Year! | in speech, during the holiday |
| {新年|xīn nián}{好|hǎo}！ / {新年|xīn nián}{快乐|kuài lè}！ | Happy New Year! | any New Year, in speech or writing |
| {春节|Chūn jié}{快乐|kuài lè}！ | Happy Spring Festival! | messages and cards |
| {恭喜发财|gōng xǐ fā cái}！ | Wishing you prosperity! | to friends and colleagues; children say it hoping for a {红包|hóng bāo} |

Visiting relatives and friends in the first days of the year to wish them well is {拜年|bài nián}.
Today much of it is done by phone and message too.

## Reading: our New Year

> {王芳|Wáng Fāng}{家|jiā}{每|měi}{年|nián}{都|dōu}{在|zài}{外婆|wài pó}{家|jiā}{过年|guò nián}。{过年|guò nián}{以前|yǐ qián}，{妈妈|mā ma}{和|hé}{她|tā}{打开|dǎ kāi}{门|mén}{和|hé}{窗户|chuāng hu}，{打扫|dǎ sǎo}{房间|fáng jiān}。{爸爸|bà ba}{在|zài}{门|mén}{上|shàng}{贴|tiē}{春联|chūn lián}，{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{贴|tiē}{一|yí}{个|gè}{倒|dào}{着|zhe}{的|de}{福|fú}{字|zì}。{除夕|chú xī}{晚上|wǎn shang}，{大家|dà jiā}{一起|yì qǐ}{吃|chī}{年夜饭|nián yè fàn}，{有|yǒu}{鱼|yú}，{也|yě}{有|yǒu}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。{外婆|wài pó}{送|sòng}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{一|yí}{个|gè}{红包|hóng bāo}。{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{说|shuō}：“{外婆|wài pó}，{过年|guò nián}{好|hǎo}！”{她|tā}{觉得|jué de}{过年|guò nián}{比|bǐ}{过|guò}{生日|shēng rì}{还|hái}{有意思|yǒu yì si}！

({以前|yǐ qián}: before. {窗户|chuāng hu}: window. {打扫|dǎ sǎo}: to clean. {贴|tiē}: to stick, put up.
{一起|yì qǐ}: together, lesson 20. {外婆|wài pó}: grandma on your mother's side, lesson 01. {比|bǐ}…{还|hái}…: even more… than.)

1. Where does Wang Fang's family spend the New Year?
2. What does Wang Fang put up?
3. What does her grandmother give her?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. At her grandmother's on her mother's side ({在|zài}{外婆|wài pó}{家|jiā}).
2. A {福|fú} character, upside down ({倒|dào}{着|zhe}{的|de}: "turned upside down", with the
   lasting-state {着|zhe} of lesson 03).
3. A red envelope.

"Every year Wang Fang's family spends the New Year at her mother's mother's. Before New Year, she and
her mother open the doors and windows and clean the rooms. Her father puts up the couplets on the
door, and Wang Fang puts up a {福|fú} character, upside down. On New Year's Eve everyone has the reunion
dinner together: there's fish, and dumplings too. Grandma gives Wang Fang a red envelope. Wang
Fang says, 'Happy New Year, Grandma!' She thinks New Year is even more fun than a birthday!"
</details>

## Key points

- {春节|Chūn jié}: the first day of the lunar year, between 21 January and 20 February; the season
  ends with the Lantern Festival ({元宵节|Yuán xiāo jié}) on the fifteenth.
- Before: cleaning, red couplets ({春联|chūn lián}) and an upside-down {福|fú} ({倒|dào} sounds like {到|dào}).
- New Year's Eve ({除夕|chú xī}): the reunion dinner ({年夜饭|nián yè fàn}), fish for {年年有余|nián nián yǒu yú},
  dumplings in the north, the TV gala ({春晚|Chūn wǎn}).
- {红包|hóng bāo}: money in red envelopes from older relatives, now often sent by phone.
- Fireworks, limited in many cities; the {春运|chūn yùn} travel rush; {过年好|guò nián hǎo}！ {拜年|bài nián}.

lessons.title: Birthdays and long-life noodles
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 13 gave you {生日快乐|shēng rì kuài lè} and {过|guò}{生日|shēng rì}. Today a birthday in a
Chinese city often looks much like one anywhere else: a cake ({蛋糕|dàn gāo}), candles, presents
and the birthday song. Older customs live on beside these, especially for children and for older
people: long-life noodles, peach-shaped buns, a baby's first-birthday "pick", and a traditional
way of counting age. As always with customs, families differ; these are traditions some families
keep, not rules.

## The birthday song

The Chinese birthday song is the familiar tune with the words {祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{生日快乐|shēng rì kuài lè}
usually sung four times. Singing a song at birthdays wasn't a Chinese tradition: like the cake, it came
from abroad, and it's now everywhere.

## Long-life noodles

The traditional birthday dish is {长寿面|cháng shòu miàn}, "long-life noodles" ({长寿|cháng shòu}
is a long life; {寿|shòu} is the character for longevity). The idea is simple: long noodles,
long life. So the noodles are kept as long as possible, and you try not to cut or bite them
short. Some families eat a bowl of them on every birthday; others at New Year too.

In traditional script, {长寿面|cháng shòu miàn} ends in 麵 (noodles), not 面 (face, side), just as
{面条儿|miàn tiáor} does (HSK 1, lesson 11).

## Peach-shaped buns

At the birthdays of older people you may see {寿桃|shòu táo}, "longevity peaches": soft white
steamed buns shaped like a peach, with a pink or red tip, usually filled with a sweet paste of
lotus seeds or beans. The peach has stood for long life in China for a very long time. In a
well-known legend, the Queen Mother of the West ({西王母|Xī wáng mǔ}) grows peaches of
immortality that ripen only once in thousands of years, and the god of longevity is often shown
holding a peach.

## Birthdays of older people

Traditionally, birthdays weren't celebrated with much fuss every year; the big celebrations were
for small children and for older people, at certain ages such as 60 and 70. Celebrating an
older relative's birthday is {祝寿|zhù shòu}, and the whole family comes.

The greetings change with the age of the person:

| Greeting | Meaning | Said to |
|---|---|---|
| {生日快乐|shēng rì kuài lè}！ | Happy birthday! | anyone |
| {祝|zhù}{您|nín}{生日快乐|shēng rì kuài lè}！ | Wishing you a happy birthday! | someone older (with {您|nín}) |
| {长命百岁|cháng mìng bǎi suì}！ | Live to a hundred! | mostly children and older people: a wish for a long life |
| {福如东海|fú rú dōng hǎi}，{寿比南山|shòu bǐ nán shān}！ | Fortune as wide as the Eastern Sea, a life as long as the Southern Mountains! | older people, on a big birthday |

The last one is a fixed pair of four-character phrases. Notice {比|bǐ} in it: it's the {比|bǐ} of
lesson 14, in an old use, "to compare with".

## A child's first birthday: {抓周|zhuā zhōu}

A baby's first birthday is a big occasion. Some families keep a custom called {抓周|zhuā zhōu}
(roughly "the first-year grab"): they put a few objects in front of the child and watch which one
the child picks up first. Each object stands for a future:

| Object | The future it stands for |
|---|---|
| a book ({书|shū}) | a scholar |
| a pen ({笔|bǐ}, lesson 16) | a writer |
| an abacus or calculator | business |
| money ({钱|qián}) | wealth |
| a stethoscope | a doctor |

Some families add foods for their sounds: celery ({芹菜|qín cài}), because {芹|qín} sounds like
{勤|qín} (hard-working), and spring onion ({葱|cōng}), because it sounds like the {聪|cōng} of
{聪明|cōng ming} (clever). New objects join the list: a phone, a computer mouse.

The custom is old: written records of it go back to the Song dynasty (960–1279), and a book of
family advice from the 6th century already describes a very similar custom. Few
parents take it as a real prediction today. It's kept as a tradition and as a happy moment for the
family, with plenty of photos.

## How old are you? Two ways to count

Traditionally, a child was one year old at birth and became a year older at every lunar New
Year, not on the birthday. This is the *nominal age*, {虚岁|xū suì}. The everyday modern count,
from birthdays, is {周岁|zhōu suì} (actual age), and it's the only age used officially in
mainland China.

Because of the New Year step, the two can differ by two years: a baby born a few days before
the lunar New Year is "one" at birth and "two" a few days later, at the New Year, when only a few days old.

Some older people, and some families in certain regions, still give their age in {虚岁|xū suì},
and it can matter for traditional birthday celebrations. Younger people mostly use
{周岁|zhōu suì}. If someone's age surprises you, they may be counting the old way. To be clear,
you can ask: {周岁|zhōu suì}{还是|hái shi}{虚岁|xū suì}？ ({还是|hái shi}, "or", is lesson 21's.)

## Reading: Grandma's birthday

> {今天|jīn tiān}{是|shì}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{的|de}{生日|shēng rì}，{她|tā}{八十|bā shí}{岁|suì}{了|le}。{我们|wǒ men}{一|yì}{家|jiā}{人|rén}{都|dōu}{回来|huí lái}{给|gěi}{她|tā}{过|guò}{生日|shēng rì}。{妈妈|mā ma}{准备|zhǔn bèi}{了|le}{长寿面|cháng shòu miàn}，{爸爸|bà ba}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{寿桃|shòu táo}。{我|wǒ}{送|sòng}{了|le}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{一|yí}{件|jiàn}{红|hóng}{衣服|yī fu}，{她|tā}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{我们|wǒ men}{跟|gēn}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{说|shuō}：“{祝|zhù}{您|nín}{福如东海|fú rú dōng hǎi}，{寿比南山|shòu bǐ nán shān}！”{奶奶|nǎi nai}{笑|xiào}{了|le}，{说|shuō}：“{你们|nǐ men}{都|dōu}{回来|huí lái}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{太|tài}{高兴|gāo xìng}{了|le}！”

1. How old is Grandma?
2. What did Mum and Dad prepare?
3. What did the writer give Grandma?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Eighty ({八十|bā shí}{岁|suì}{了|le}: "she's eighty now").
2. Mum made long-life noodles; Dad bought peach-shaped buns.
3. A red top ({一|yí}{件|jiàn}{红|hóng}{衣服|yī fu}).

"Today is Grandma's birthday; she's eighty. Our whole family has come back to celebrate her
birthday. Mum has made long-life noodles, and Dad has bought longevity peach buns. I gave Grandma
a red top, and she was very pleased. During the meal we said to her, 'May your fortune be as
wide as the Eastern Sea and your life as long as the Southern Mountains!' Grandma laughed and
said, 'You've all come home: I'm so happy!'"
</details>

Red is a happy colour for an older person's birthday, as at New Year.

## Key points

- Cake and the song ({祝|zhù}{你|nǐ}{生日快乐|shēng rì kuài lè}) are recent arrivals; long-life
  noodles ({长寿面|cháng shòu miàn}) are the traditional birthday dish: long noodles, long life.
- {寿桃|shòu táo}: peach-shaped buns for older people's birthdays; the peach stands for long life.
- Big birthdays: small children and older people ({祝寿|zhù shòu}); greet elders with {您|nín} and
  {福如东海|fú rú dōng hǎi}，{寿比南山|shòu bǐ nán shān}.
- {抓周|zhuā zhōu}: the first-birthday pick, kept as a tradition rather than a prediction.
- {虚岁|xū suì} (nominal age, one at birth, plus one each New Year) vs {周岁|zhōu suì} (actual age,
  the official one).

lessons.title: School and classes: 教, 班, 开学
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This module is about school, sport and hobbies: what you study, how exams go, how well you do
things, and what you like doing in your free time. It starts in the classroom. In HSK 1 you
learned {学|xué} and {学习|xué xí} (to learn, to study), {上课|shàng kè} and {下课|xià kè}, {课|kè} (a class,
a lesson) and {同学|tóng xué} (classmate). Now you get the other side, the teacher's verb {教|jiāo}
(to teach), and the words for the place and the things: the classroom, your class, your school
bag, your pen and notebook, and the day school starts.

You'll learn:

- {教|jiāo} + person + subject: {老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{我们|wǒ men}{汉语|Hàn yǔ} (two objects, like {给|gěi}
  and {送|sòng});
- {教|jiāo} *jiāo* (to teach) and {教室|jiào shì} *jiàoshì* (classroom): one character, two tones;
- {班|bān}: a class, the group of students you belong to;
- {高中|gāo zhōng}, {开学|kāi xué}, {书包|shū bāo}, {笔|bǐ}, {本子|běn zi};
- the character 留 (to stay), which you'll meet in the phrase {留|liú}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}.

## Teaching: {教|jiāo}

{教|jiāo} is "to teach". Like {给|gěi} (HSK 1, lesson 23) and {送|sòng} and {告诉|gào su} (lesson 13), it
can take two objects: first the person, then what they learn.

| Subject | {教|jiāo} | Person | What |
|---|---|---|---|
| {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī} | {教|jiāo} | {我们|wǒ men} | {汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 |
| {谁|shéi} | {教|jiāo} | {你们|nǐ men} | {汉字|hàn zì}？ |
| {我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma} | {教|jiāo} | {我|wǒ} | {做饭|zuò fàn}。 |

{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{我们|wǒ men}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — Teacher Wang teaches us Chinese.

{谁|shéi}{教|jiāo}{你们|nǐ men}{汉字|hàn zì}？ — Who teaches you characters?

{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{教|jiāo}{我|wǒ}{做饭|zuò fàn}。 — My mum is teaching me to cook.

The person always comes first, the subject second, the same order as {给|gěi}{他|tā}{一|yì}{本|běn}{书|shū}
(give him a book). English sometimes lets you say "teach Chinese to us"; Chinese doesn't:
~~{老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{我们|wǒ men}~~ is wrong.

What is taught can also be an action, a verb phrase, as in the last example:

{你|nǐ}{能|néng}{教|jiāo}{我|wǒ}{写|xiě}{这个|zhè ge}{字|zì}{吗|ma}？ — Can you teach me to write this character?

{爸爸|bà ba}{教|jiāo}{我|wǒ}{开车|kāi chē}。 — Dad's teaching me to drive.

Either object can be left out when it's clear:

{她|tā}{在|zài}{高中|gāo zhōng}{教|jiāo}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — She teaches Chinese at a senior high school.

{李|Lǐ}{老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{我们|wǒ men}。 — Teacher Li teaches us.

And {教书|jiāo shū} ("teach books") is "to teach for a living, be a teacher": {我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{在|zài}{大学|dà xué}{教书|jiāo shū}, "My dad teaches at a university."

### The learner's side: {跟|gēn}…{学|xué}

To say who you learn from, use {跟|gēn} (with, lesson 14) + the teacher + {学|xué}:

{我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — I'm learning Chinese with Teacher Wang.

{你|nǐ}{跟|gēn}{谁|shéi}{学|xué}{画|huà}？ — Who are you learning to draw with? ({画|huà}, to draw: lesson 20)

So the same lesson can be said from both sides: {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{我|wǒ} = {我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}{学|xué}.

## One character, two tones: {教|jiāo} and {教室|jiào shì}

The verb "to teach" is first tone, {教|jiāo}. In {教室|jiào shì} (classroom: a "teaching room") the
same character is read *jiào*, fourth tone. That fourth-tone reading belongs to words about
teaching as a thing rather than an action; at this level {教室|jiào shì} is the one you need.

{我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{教室|jiào shì}{在|zài}{三|sān}{楼|lóu}。 — Our classroom is on the third floor.

{教室|jiào shì}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{学生|xué sheng}。 — There are a lot of students in the classroom.

{老师|lǎo shī}{在|zài}{教室|jiào shì}{里|lǐ}{等|děng}{你|nǐ}。 — The teacher is waiting for you in the classroom. ({等|děng}, to wait: lesson 20)

A quick check: if you can put a person after it, it's *jiāo*; if it names a place, it's *jiào*.

## {班|bān}: your class

English "class" covers two things Chinese keeps apart:

| Chinese | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {课|kè} | a class as a lesson, a period of teaching | {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{课|kè}, a Chinese lesson; {上课|shàng kè}, have class |
| {班|bān} | a class as a group of students | {我们|wǒ men}{班|bān}, our class; {三|sān}{班|bān}, Class 3 |

{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪个|nǎ ge}{班|bān}？ — Which class are you in?
— {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{三|sān}{班|bān}。 — I'm in Class 3.

{我们|wǒ men}{班|bān}{有|yǒu}{三十|sān shí}{个|gè}{学生|xué sheng}。 — There are thirty students in our class.

{她|tā}{是|shì}{我们|wǒ men}{班|bān}{的|de}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — She's our class's Chinese teacher.

Classes are named by number: {一|yī}{班|bān} (Class 1), {二|èr}{班|bān}, {三|sān}{班|bān}. As in other names
and ordinals, {一|yī} keeps its first tone here. {我们|wǒ men}{班|bān} needs no {的|de}: it's a group
you belong to, like {我|wǒ}{家|jiā} and {我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}.

You've met the character before, in {上班|shàng bān} and {下班|xià bān} (go to and leave work): there
{班|bān} is a work shift. The idea in both is a group or slot that you're part of.

## Stages of school: {高中|gāo zhōng}

HSK 1 gave you {小学|xiǎo xué} (primary school), {中学|zhōng xué} (secondary school) and {大学|dà xué}
(university). Secondary school in China has two parts, a lower one, {初中|chū zhōng} (junior high
school; an HSK 3 word), and an upper one, {高中|gāo zhōng} (senior high school): {高|gāo} (high) +
{中|zhōng} (from {中学|zhōng xué}).

| Stage | Word | A student there |
|---|---|---|
| primary school | {小学|xiǎo xué} | {小学生|xiǎo xué shēng} |
| junior high school | {初中|chū zhōng} (HSK 3) | {初中生|chū zhōng shēng} |
| senior high school | {高中|gāo zhōng} | {高中生|gāo zhōng shēng} |
| university | {大学|dà xué} | {大学生|dà xué shēng} |

{我|wǒ}{弟弟|dì di}{是|shì}{高中生|gāo zhōng shēng}。 — My younger brother is a senior high school student.

{她|tā}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{上|shàng}{高中|gāo zhōng}。 — She goes to senior high school in Beijing.

{上|shàng} + a school stage is "to attend": {上|shàng}{小学|xiǎo xué}, {上|shàng}{高中|gāo zhōng}, {上|shàng}{大学|dà xué}, the
same {上|shàng} as in {上学|shàng xué} (go to school). The honors lesson "School in China" says more
about the stages.

## The start of term: {开学|kāi xué}

{开学|kāi xué} is "school starts": {开|kāi} (open, start) + {学|xué}. It's what a school does at the
beginning of a term, so its subject is the school, the students or a time, and it takes no object.

{我们|wǒ men}{学校|xué xiào}{九|jiǔ}{月|yuè}{一|yī}{号|hào}{开学|kāi xué}。 — Our school starts on 1 September.

{你们|nǐ men}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{开学|kāi xué}？ — When does your term start?

{开学|kāi xué}{了|le}！ — School has started (again)! (change-of-state {了|le})

Don't add an object: "the first day of school" is {开学|kāi xué}{的|de}{第一|dì yī}{天|tiān}, not
~~{开学|kāi xué}{学校|xué xiào}~~. Compare {上课|shàng kè}, which is each class starting; {开学|kāi xué} is the
whole term.

## In your school bag: {书包|shū bāo}, {笔|bǐ}, {本子|běn zi}

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {书包|shū bāo} | school bag | "book bag": {书|shū} + {包|bāo} (bag) |
| {笔|bǐ} | pen; anything you write with | a pencil is {铅笔|qiān bǐ} (HSK 3) |
| {本子|běn zi} | notebook, exercise book | {本|běn} is also the measure word for books |

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{书包|shū bāo}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{本|běn}{书|shū}{和|hé}{三|sān}{个|gè}{本子|běn zi}。 — In my school bag
there are two books and three notebooks.

{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{笔|bǐ}{吗|ma}？{我|wǒ}{的|de}{笔|bǐ}{不|bú}{在|zài}{书包|shū bāo}{里|lǐ}。 — Have you got a pen? My pen
isn't in my bag.

Measure words: {一|yí}{个|gè}{书包|shū bāo}, {一|yí}{个|gè}{本子|běn zi} (or {一|yì}{本|běn}{本子|běn zi}). Pens have their
own measure word, {支|zhī}, which isn't in the HSK 1–3 word lists, so this course uses {笔|bǐ}
without a number. ({笔|bǐ} is also a measure word for sums of money, a use for later levels.)

## Staying behind: 留

The character 留 *liú* means "to stay, to remain". It's taught now as a character; the words built
on it come in HSK 3 ({留学|liú xué}, to study abroad; {留学生|liú xué shēng}, an overseas student).
You'll see it in phrases like these, always with pinyin:

{下课|xià kè}{以后|yǐ hòu}{我|wǒ}{留|liú}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{学习|xué xí}。 — After class I stay at school and study.
({以后|yǐ hòu}, after: HSK 3)

{你|nǐ}{留|liú}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{里|lǐ}{吧|ba}。 — Stay at home.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 留 | stay, remain; keep | liú | 田 | 10 | {留|liú}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào} (stay at school), {留学|liú xué} (HSK 3) |
| 教 | teach | jiāo; jiào | 攵 | 11 | {教|jiāo}, {教室|jiào shì}, {教书|jiāo shū} (teach for a living) |
| 室 | room | shì | 宀 | 9 | {教室|jiào shì} |
| 笔 (traditional 筆) | pen, brush | bǐ | ⺮ | 10 | {笔|bǐ}, {铅笔|qiān bǐ} (pencil, HSK 3) |

- 留: the top has two small parts side by side (three short strokes on the left, a shape like 刀
  on the right), and 田 (field) sits underneath. Make Me a Hanzi and most dictionaries file it
  under 田, although 田 has nothing to do with the meaning.
- 教: two halves. The right half is the new radical 攵 (below). The left half today looks like
  孝 (耂 over 子), with the same top as 老 (old) and 考 (test, next lesson). Old forms of 教 show
  子 (child) with a hand holding a stick; a common reading is that teaching, in the old view,
  came with discipline.
- 室: 宀 (roof) on top of 至 (to arrive). A memory aid: a room is where you arrive and stop, under
  a roof.
- 笔: the simplified form is ⺮ (bamboo) on top of 毛 (hair): a Chinese writing brush is hair set in
  a bamboo handle. The traditional form 筆 has 聿 underneath instead, an old drawing of a hand
  holding a brush.

### New radical: 攵, "tapping hand"

攵 is called {反文|fǎn wén} or {反文旁|fǎn wén páng} ("reversed 文"), because it looks a little like
文 (writing) with its top changed. It is really the short form of an old radical 攴, a hand holding
a stick, and characters with it often describe an action done to something: striking, making,
arranging. It usually stands on the right. 教 is the first of five characters with it in this track;
the others come in HSK 3 ({放|fàng}, put; {收|shōu}, receive; {数|shù}, number; {故|gù}, old, reason).
Four strokes: a short slash, a horizontal, a long slash, and a long falling stroke to the right.

### Radical review: 宀, the roof

宀 ("roof on top", HSK 1 lesson 03) covers 家 (home), 客 (guest), 宜 (suitable, in {便宜|pián yi}) and 它
(it). Now add 室 (room), and next lesson 完 (to finish). A roof over a character often means a
building or something inside one: 家 and 室 still fit; 它 and 完 don't any more.

### Stroke order

- **留**: the top left part first (a short slash, a stroke that goes down and turns right, and a
  dot), then the top right part (the horizontal-turn-hook, then the slash inside it), and 田 last:
  left side, top and right side, the middle horizontal and vertical, the bottom.
- **教**: the left half first: 土 (horizontal, vertical, long horizontal), then the long slash from
  top right to bottom left, then 子 (the turning stroke, the hooked vertical, and a rising stroke
  instead of a horizontal). Then 攵 on the right.
- **室**: 宀 (dot, the left side, the hooked top), then 至: the top horizontal, the slash that turns,
  the dot, and 土 at the bottom.
- **笔**: ⺮ first: two little "people" of three strokes each (a slash, a short horizontal, a dot).
  Then 毛: the slash, two horizontals, and the long vertical that bends right and hooks up, last.

```trace
留教室笔
```

### Handwriting review

These HSK 1 handwriting characters are all over this lesson. Write each three times from
memory, then check it on the pad: 学 (8 strokes), 书 (4), 写 (5), 字 (6).

```trace
学书写字
```
=}

In traditional script the pads show {+学+} (16 strokes), {+书+} (10) and {+写+} (15); {字|zì} is the same.

## Dialogue: the first day of term

{保罗|Bǎo luó} (Paul) is new at a senior high school in Beijing. On the first morning he meets
{赵雪|Zhào Xuě} (Zhao Xue).

```dialogue
# The first day of term
赵雪: {保罗|Bǎo luó}，{你好|nǐ hǎo}！{今天|jīn tiān}{开学|kāi xué}，{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪个|nǎ ge}{班|bān}？
= Hi, Paul! It's the first day of term. Which class are you in?
保罗: {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{三|sān}{班|bān}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= I'm in Class 3. And you?
赵雪: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{在|zài}{三|sān}{班|bān}！{我们|wǒ men}{是|shì}{同学|tóng xué}{了|le}。
= I'm in Class 3 too! So we're classmates now.
保罗: {太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！{我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{教室|jiào shì}{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
= Great! Where's our classroom?
赵雪: {在|zài}{二|èr}{楼|lóu}。{走|zǒu}，{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{教室|jiào shì}{吧|ba}。
= On the second floor. Come on, let's go to the classroom.
保罗: {谁|shéi}{教|jiāo}{我们|wǒ men}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}？
= Who teaches us Chinese?
赵雪: {何|Hé}{老师|lǎo shī}。{她|tā}{是|shì}{一|yí}{位|wèi}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}{的|de}{老师|lǎo shī}。
= Teacher He. She's a very good teacher.
保罗: {不好意思|bù hǎo yì si}，{我|wǒ}{的|de}{书包|shū bāo}{里|lǐ}{没有|méi yǒu}{笔|bǐ}。{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{笔|bǐ}{吗|ma}？
= Sorry, there's no pen in my school bag. Have you got a pen?
赵雪: {有|yǒu}，{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}。
= Yes, here you are.
保罗: {谢谢|xiè xie}！{下午|xià wǔ}{下课|xià kè}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{你|nǐ}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{吗|ma}？
= Thanks! When class finishes this afternoon, are you going home?
赵雪: {不|bù}{回|huí}，{我|wǒ}{留|liú}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{学习|xué xí}。
= No, I'm staying at school to study.
```

{我们|wǒ men}{是|shì}{同学|tóng xué}{了|le}: the {了|le} at the end is the change-of-state {了|le}: they
weren't classmates before and now they are. {给|gěi}{你|nǐ} ("to you") is what you say as you hand
something over. {以后|yǐ hòu} (after) is an HSK 3 word.

## Reading: a message from the class teacher

The evening before school starts, the class teacher posts this in the class chat group.

> {三|sān}{班|bān}{的|de}{同学们|tóng xué men}：{你们|nǐ men}{好|hǎo}！{明天|míng tiān}{九|jiǔ}{月|yuè}{一|yī}{号|hào}，{我们|wǒ men}{开学|kāi xué}。{请|qǐng}{大家|dà jiā}{早上|zǎo shang}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{半|bàn}{到|dào}{教室|jiào shì}，{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{上课|shàng kè}。{我们|wǒ men}{班|bān}{的|de}{教室|jiào shì}{在|zài}{二|èr}{楼|lóu}，{洗手间|xǐ shǒu jiān}{在|zài}{旁边|páng biān}。{上午|shàng wǔ}{是|shì}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{课|kè}，{何|Hé}{老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{我们|wǒ men}；{下午|xià wǔ}{是|shì}{数学|shù xué}{课|kè}。{你们|nǐ men}{的|de}{书包|shū bāo}{里|lǐ}{要|yào}{有|yǒu}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{书|shū}、{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{本子|běn zi}{和|hé}{笔|bǐ}。{下午|xià wǔ}{四|sì}{点|diǎn}{下课|xià kè}。{想|xiǎng}{留|liú}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{学习|xué xí}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}，{可以|kě yǐ}{在|zài}{教室|jiào shì}{里|lǐ}{看|kàn}{书|shū}。——{孙|Sūn}{老师|lǎo shī}

{数学|shù xué}: maths (HSK 3).

1. What time should the students be in the classroom?
2. What should they have in their school bags?
3. What can students do after four o'clock?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. At half past seven ({七|qī}{点|diǎn}{半|bàn}); class starts at eight.
2. Their Chinese book, two notebooks and a pen.
3. Those who want to stay at school and study can read in the classroom.

"Class 3, hello everyone! Tomorrow, 1 September, school starts. Please be in the classroom at half
past seven in the morning; class begins at eight. Our classroom is on the second floor, and the
toilets are next to it. In the morning there's Chinese, taught by Teacher He; in the afternoon
there's maths. In your school bags you need your Chinese book, two notebooks and a pen. Classes end
at four in the afternoon. Anyone who wants to stay at school and study can read in the classroom.
— Teacher Sun"
</details>

{想|xiǎng}{留|liú}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{学习|xué xí}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué} is a long modifier with {的|de}: "the students
who want to stay at school and study". Everything before {的|de} describes {同学|tóng xué}.

## Say it

```speak
{谁|shéi}{教|jiāo}{你们|nǐ men}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}？
= Who teaches you Chinese?
{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{我们|wǒ men}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。
= Teacher Wang teaches us Chinese.
{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{哪个|nǎ ge}{班|bān}？
= Which class are you in?
{我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{教室|jiào shì}{在|zài}{三|sān}{楼|lóu}。
= Our classroom is on the third floor.
{你们|nǐ men}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{开学|kāi xué}？
= When does your term start?
{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{笔|bǐ}{吗|ma}？
= Have you got a pen?
```

## Pronunciation

- {教|jiāo} (high, level) vs {教室|jiào shì} (falling, then falling): say {老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{我们|wǒ men} and
  {我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{教室|jiào shì} one after the other.
- {书包|shū bāo}, {高中|gāo zhōng}: two first tones, both high and level; don't let the second one drop.
- {本子|běn zi}: a low third tone and a light *zi*. {笔|bǐ} is third tone too; before a pause it dips
  and rises a little.
- {开学|kāi xué}: *xué* has the *üe* sound (lips rounded as for *ü*), spelled *ue* after *x*.
- {班|bān} rhymes with {半|bàn} (half) but is high and level.

## Common mistakes

- The two objects of {教|jiāo} swapped: ~~{老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{我们|wǒ men}~~. The person first:
  {老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{我们|wǒ men}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}.
- Reading the verb as *jiào*: "to teach" is {教|jiāo}; only {教室|jiào shì} has the fourth tone here.
- {课|kè} for a group of students: "our class" (the people) is {我们|wǒ men}{班|bān}; {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{课|kè} is the
  lesson.
- An object after {开学|kāi xué}: ~~{开学|kāi xué}{学校|xué xiào}~~. Say {学校|xué xiào}{开学|kāi xué}.
- {学|xué} with the teacher as its object: ~~{我|wǒ}{学|xué}{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}~~. Say
  {我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}{学|xué}, or {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{我|wǒ}.
- {=Writing the bottom of 笔 as 手 or 毛 without its last hook: 毛 ends in a long stroke that bends
  right and hooks up.=}

## Key points

- {教|jiāo} + person + subject or action: {老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{我们|wǒ men}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}, {妈妈|mā ma}{教|jiāo}{我|wǒ}{做饭|zuò fàn}.
  From the learner's side: {跟|gēn} + teacher + {学|xué}.
- {教|jiāo} *jiāo* teach; {教室|jiào shì} *jiàoshì* classroom.
- {班|bān} is a class of students ({三|sān}{班|bān}, {我们|wǒ men}{班|bān}); {课|kè} is a lesson.
- {高中|gāo zhōng} senior high school; {上|shàng}{高中|gāo zhōng}, attend it.
- {开学|kāi xué}: school starts; no object.
- {书包|shū bāo}, {笔|bǐ}, {本子|běn zi}; 留 *liú*, to stay ({留|liú}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}).
- New radical 攵 (tapping hand); 宀 reviewed.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Exams and results: 看完, 听懂, 做错
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

English often needs two words to say what an action achieved: "I *read* it *through*", "I
*heard* you but didn't *understand*", "she *got* the answer *wrong*". Chinese does the same thing
more tightly: it puts a second word straight after the verb to say how the action came out.
{看|kàn} (read) + {完|wán} (finish) is {看完|kàn wán}, "read to the end"; {听|tīng} (listen) + {懂|dǒng}
(understand) is {听懂|tīng dǒng}, "understand what you hear". These pairs are everywhere in
Chinese, and they're what this lesson is about, set in the place where you need them most: exams.

You'll learn:

- verb + result: {看完|kàn wán}, {听懂|tīng dǒng}, {做错|zuò cuò}, {写好|xiě hǎo}, {找到|zhǎo dào}, {学会|xué huì};
- the negative with {没|méi}: {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{听懂|tīng dǒng} (never with {不|bù});
- questions: {你|nǐ}{听懂|tīng dǒng}{了|le}{吗|ma}？;
- {考|kǎo} and {考试|kǎo shì}, {题|tí} and {词|cí};
- {记得|jì de} (remember) and {忘|wàng} (forget).

You've met two of these pairs already: {看见|kàn jiàn} and {听见|tīng jiàn} in HSK 1 (lesson 24), and
{打开|dǎ kāi} (open) in lesson 12. Now you'll see the pattern behind them.

## Result complements: verb + what happened

A **[[result complement]]** is a verb or adjective placed right after the main verb to say what the
action led to. The main verb says what you did; the complement says how it turned out.

| Verb | + result | Together | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {看|kàn} read, look | {完|wán} finish | {看完|kàn wán} | read to the end, finish reading |
| {听|tīng} listen | {懂|dǒng} understand | {听懂|tīng dǒng} | understand (what you hear) |
| {做|zuò} do | {错|cuò} wrong | {做错|zuò cuò} | do wrong, get wrong |
| {写|xiě} write | {好|hǎo} well, properly | {写好|xiě hǎo} | finish writing (it's ready) |
| {找|zhǎo} look for | {到|dào} reach | {找到|zhǎo dào} | find |
| {学|xué} learn | {会|huì} can | {学会|xué huì} | learn (and now can) |
| {看|kàn} look | {见|jiàn} perceive | {看见|kàn jiàn} | see |

{我|wǒ}{看完|kàn wán}{了|le}。 — I've finished reading it.

{你|nǐ}{听懂|tīng dǒng}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Did you understand (what you heard)?

{我|wǒ}{做错|zuò cuò}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{题|tí}。 — I got two questions wrong.

{我|wǒ}{找到|zhǎo dào}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{笔|bǐ}{了|le}！ — I've found my pen!

{我|wǒ}{学会|xué huì}{了|le}{游泳|yóu yǒng}。 — I've learned to swim. ({游泳|yóu yǒng}: lesson 19)

The two parts don't separate: nothing goes between {看|kàn} and {完|wán} (except {得|de} or {不|bu}
in a form you'll meet in HSK 3, as in {听不懂|tīng bu dǒng}). The difference between
the verb alone and the verb + complement is the difference between trying and succeeding:

| Just the action | The action + its result |
|---|---|
| {我|wǒ}{找|zhǎo}{了|le}，{没|méi}{找到|zhǎo dào}。 I looked, but didn't find it. | {我|wǒ}{找到|zhǎo dào}{了|le}。 I found it. |
| {我|wǒ}{听|tīng}{了|le}，{没|méi}{听懂|tīng dǒng}。 I listened, but didn't understand. | {我|wǒ}{听懂|tīng dǒng}{了|le}。 I understood. |
| {他|tā}{在|zài}{看|kàn}{书|shū}。 He's reading. | {他|tā}{看完|kàn wán}{了|le}。 He's finished reading. |

English "find" and "understand" pack the result into one word; Chinese builds them from look-for
+ reach and listen + understand. That's why {找|zhǎo} alone is "look for", not "find".

### Which complement?

Each complement adds its own kind of result. These are the ones you can use now:

- {完|wán}, finished, to the end: {看完|kàn wán}, {做完|zuò wán}, {写完|xiě wán}, {吃完|chī wán}, {考完|kǎo wán}.
- {懂|dǒng}, understood: {听懂|tīng dǒng} (by listening), {看懂|kàn dǒng} (by reading).
- {错|cuò}, wrong: {做错|zuò cuò}, {写错|xiě cuò}, {听错|tīng cuò} (mishear), {说错|shuō cuò}; and the opposite,
  {对|duì}, right: {做对|zuò duì}, {说对|shuō duì}.
- {好|hǎo}, done properly, ready: {写好|xiě hǎo}, {做好|zuò hǎo}, {准备好|zhǔn bèi hǎo} (get ready).
- {到|dào}, reached, got: {找到|zhǎo dào} (find), {买到|mǎi dào} (manage to buy), {看到|kàn dào}, {听到|tīng dào}.
- {见|jiàn}, perceived: {看见|kàn jiàn}, {听见|tīng jiàn}.
- {会|huì}, now able: {学会|xué huì}.
- {开|kāi}, open: {打开|dǎ kāi}.

{完|wán} and {好|hǎo} are close: {写完|xiě wán} says you reached the end; {写好|xiě hǎo} says it's done and
ready, done properly.

{作业|zuò yè}{我|wǒ}{写完|xiě wán}{了|le}，{但是|dàn shì}{没|méi}{写好|xiě hǎo}。 — I've finished my homework, but I
haven't done it well. ({作业|zuò yè}: homework, HSK 3)

## Saying it didn't happen: {没|méi} + verb + complement

A result either happened or it didn't, so the negative is {没|méi} (or {没有|méi yǒu}), as for any
completed action (HSK 1, lesson 25). The {了|le} goes.

{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{听懂|tīng dǒng}。 — I didn't understand.

{他|tā}{还|hái}{没|méi}{做完|zuò wán}。 — He hasn't finished yet.

{我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{找到|zhǎo dào}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{本子|běn zi}。 — I haven't found my notebook.

Not ~~{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{听懂|tīng dǒng}~~ and not ~~{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{听懂|tīng dǒng}{了|le}~~. (You'll hear
{听不懂|tīng bu dǒng}, "can't understand", with {不|bu} *inside* the pair: that's a different form,
taught in HSK 3. For "I don't understand" in general, plain {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{懂|dǒng} works.)

## Asking about results

Add {吗|ma}, or {没有|méi yǒu} at the end:

{你|nǐ}{看完|kàn wán}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Have you finished reading it?

{你|nǐ}{听懂|tīng dǒng}{了|le}{没有|méi yǒu}？ — Did you understand or not?

Answer with the verb + complement: {看完|kàn wán}{了|le}。/ {没|méi}{看完|kàn wán}。 — Yes, I have. / No,
I haven't.

## Where the object goes

The object follows the whole verb + complement, and {了|le} can come right after the complement or
at the end of the sentence:

{我|wǒ}{看完|kàn wán}{了|le}{那|nà}{本|běn}{书|shū}。 / {我|wǒ}{看完|kàn wán}{那|nà}{本|běn}{书|shū}{了|le}。 — I've finished
that book.

When the object is something you both know about, Chinese often puts it first, as the topic
(lesson 02's topic-comment sentences):

{那|nà}{本|běn}{书|shū}{我|wǒ}{看完|kàn wán}{了|le}。 — That book, I've finished it.

{今天|jīn tiān}{的|de}{题|tí}{你|nǐ}{做完|zuò wán}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Have you finished today's questions?

## Exams: {考|kǎo} and {考试|kǎo shì}

{考试|kǎo shì} is "an exam" and "to take an exam". At this level keep it whole, with no object:

{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{考试|kǎo shì}。 — I've got an exam tomorrow.

{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{考试|kǎo shì}{在|zài}{星期五|xīng qī wǔ}。 — The Chinese exam is on Friday.

{考|kǎo} alone is the verb "to test, to sit a test in", and it takes the subject as its object:

{明天|míng tiān}{考|kǎo}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — Tomorrow there's a Chinese exam (we're tested in Chinese).

{老师|lǎo shī}{考|kǎo}{我们|wǒ men}{三十|sān shí}{个|gè}{词|cí}。 — The teacher tested us on thirty words.

{考完|kǎo wán}{了|le}！ — The exam's over! (finished taking it)

And the score: {我|wǒ}{考|kǎo}{了|le}{九十|jiǔ shí}{分|fēn}。 — I got 90 (points). Here {分|fēn} is a
point, the same character as the minute and the cent: {分|fēn} is a small unit of something
bigger, a minute of an hour, a cent of a yuan, a point of the full mark.

(You'll often hear {考试|kǎo shì} split, {考|kǎo}{了|le}{一|yí}{次|cì}{试|shì}, "took an exam once": that's
HSK 3 grammar. Keep {考试|kǎo shì} whole for now.)

## Questions and words: {题|tí}, {词|cí}

{题|tí} is a question in an exam or an exercise, something to answer or solve. You met the
character in {问题|wèn tí} (question, problem: HSK 1). Questions are numbered with {第|dì}:

{第三|dì sān}{题|tí}{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{看懂|kàn dǒng}。 — I didn't understand question 3.

{这个|zhè ge}{题|tí}{你|nǐ}{做对|zuò duì}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Did you get this question right?

{问题|wèn tí} is a question you ask (or a problem); {题|tí} is a question you answer in a test:
{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{问题|wèn tí} (I've got a question) vs {考试|kǎo shì}{有|yǒu}{五十|wǔ shí}{个|gè}{题|tí}
(the exam has fifty questions).

{词|cí} is a word. In HSK 1 you learned {字|zì}, a written character. A {词|cí} can be one {字|zì} or
more: {书|shū} is one character and one word; {书包|shū bāo} is one word written with two characters.

{这个|zhè ge}{词|cí}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{意思|yì si}？ — What does this word mean?

{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{学会|xué huì}{了|le}{十|shí}{个|gè}{新|xīn}{词|cí}。 — Today I learned ten new words.

## Remembering and forgetting: {记得|jì de}, {忘|wàng}

{记得|jì de} is "to remember", to still have something in your mind; its {得|de} is light. It takes
a noun or a whole clause.

{你|nǐ}{记得|jì de}{他|tā}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}{吗|ma}？ — Do you remember his name?

{我|wǒ}{记得|jì de}{考试|kǎo shì}{在|zài}{星期五|xīng qī wǔ}。 — I remember the exam's on Friday.

{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{记得|jì de}{了|le}。 — I don't remember (any more).

{记得|jì de} is a state, so its negative is {不|bù}: {不|bú}{记得|jì de}.

{忘|wàng} is "to forget". It's nearly always followed by {了|le}, because forgetting is something
that has happened:

{我|wǒ}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{他|tā}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}。 — I've forgotten his name.

{我|wǒ}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{笔|bǐ}！ — I've forgotten my pen!

{不要|bú yào}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{明天|míng tiān}{考试|kǎo shì}。 — Don't forget the exam tomorrow.

With a verb after it, {忘|wàng}{了|le} is "forgot to": {我|wǒ}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{写|xiě}{名字|míng zi}, "I forgot to write
my name". (A longer verb, {忘记|wàng jì}, means the same and comes in HSK 3.)

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 考 | test, examine | kǎo | 耂 | 6 | {考|kǎo}, {考试|kǎo shì} |
| 试 (traditional 試) | try; test | shì | 讠 | 8 | {考试|kǎo shì} |
| 词 (traditional 詞) | word | cí | 讠 | 7 | {词|cí} |
| 懂 | understand | dǒng | 忄 | 15 | {懂|dǒng}, {听懂|tīng dǒng}, {看懂|kàn dǒng} |
| 完 | finish, whole | wán | 宀 | 7 | {完|wán}, {看完|kàn wán} |
| 记 (traditional 記) | note down; remember | jì | 讠 | 5 | {记得|jì de} |
| 忘 | forget | wàng | 心 | 7 | {忘|wàng} |

Most of today's characters are built the common way: a part for the meaning and a part for the
sound.

- 试: 讠 (speech) + 式 *shì* (form, style), which gives the sound.
- 词: 讠 + 司 *sī* (as in {公司|gōng sī}), an old sound hint.
- 记: 讠 + 己 *jǐ* (self, as in {自己|zì jǐ}), the sound hint.
- 懂: 忄 (heart, mind: understanding happens there) + 董 *dǒng*, which gives the sound exactly.
- 完: 宀 (roof) + 元 *yuán*, an old sound hint.
- 忘: 亡 *wáng* (to lose, be gone) over 心 (heart, mind): gone from the mind. 亡 gives the sound
  too.
- 考: 耂 on top, the same as in 老 (old). In the oldest writing 考 and 老 were closely related,
  both drawings of an old person with a walking stick; "to test" is a later meaning of 考.

### Radical review: 讠, 忄 and 心

讠 (speech, HSK 1 lesson 02) is on the left of a lot of words about language: 语 说 话 请 谢 课 读
认 识 谁. Today adds three: 试, 词 and 记; next lesson brings 让. In traditional script all of them
have the full form 言: 試 詞 記.

忄 and 心 are the same radical, "heart", in two shapes: 忄 on the left (忙, now 懂), 心 at the bottom
(想, 您, 怎, now 忘). The Chinese tradition placed thinking and feeling in the heart, so both shapes
often mark words about the mind.

### Stroke order

- **考**: 耂 first (horizontal, vertical, the long horizontal, the long slash), then a short
  horizontal and the last stroke, which zigzags: down, across to the right, then down again with
  a hook to the left.
- **懂**: 忄 first, and in the mainland order the two dots come before the vertical (left dot,
  right dot, then the long vertical). Then 董, top to bottom: 艹, then the rest of 重 down to the
  long bottom horizontal.
- **试**: after 讠, the top horizontal of 式, then 工 (horizontal, vertical, rising stroke), then
  the long slanting hook, and the dot at the top right last.
- **记**, **词**: 讠, then the right side. 己 ends with a stroke that goes down, along the bottom and
  hooks up.
- **完**: 宀, then 元: two horizontals, the slash, and the bottom stroke that bends right and hooks
  up.
- **忘**: 亡 (dot, horizontal, the stroke that goes down and turns right), then 心: the left dot,
  the long curved hook, and the two dots inside.

```trace
考试词懂完记忘
```

### Handwriting review

Four HSK 1 handwriting characters about language: 汉 (5 strokes), 语 (9), 文 (4), 说 (9). Write
each three times from memory.

```trace
汉语文说
```
=}

In traditional script the pads show {+汉+} (14 strokes), {+语+} (14) and {+说+} (14); {文|wén} is the same.

## Dialogue: after the exam

{安娜|Ān nà} (Anna) meets {大卫|Dà wèi} (David) outside the exam room.

```dialogue
# After the exam
安娜: {大卫|Dà wèi}，{你|nǐ}{考完|kǎo wán}{了|le}{吗|ma}？
= David, have you finished your exam?
大卫: {考完|kǎo wán}{了|le}！{上午|shàng wǔ}{考|kǎo}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{下午|xià wǔ}{考|kǎo}{数学|shù xué}。
= Finished! Chinese in the morning, maths in the afternoon.
安娜: {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{考试|kǎo shì}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= How was the Chinese exam?
大卫: {听|tīng}{的|de}{题|tí}{我|wǒ}{都|dōu}{听懂|tīng dǒng}{了|le}，{但是|dàn shì}{有|yǒu}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{词|cí}{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{看懂|kàn dǒng}。
= I understood all the listening questions, but there were two words I couldn't read.
安娜: {哪|nǎ}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{词|cí}？
= Which two words?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{忘|wàng}{了|le}……{啊|a}，{我|wǒ}{记得|jì de}{一|yí}{个|gè}：{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{字|zì}{是|shì}“{懂|dǒng}”。
= I've forgotten… Ah, I remember one: one of the characters was dǒng, "understand".
安娜: {你|nǐ}{不|bù}{懂|dǒng}“{懂|dǒng}”{字|zì}？
= You don't understand the character for "understand"?
大卫: {现在|xiàn zài}{懂|dǒng}{了|le}！
= I do now!
安娜: {你|nǐ}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}{的|de}{题|tí}{做完|zuò wán}{了|le}{吗|ma}？
= Did you finish the character-writing questions?
大卫: {做完|zuò wán}{了|le}，{可能|kě néng}{写错|xiě cuò}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}。{不|bù}{说|shuō}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{吃饭|chī fàn}{吧|ba}！
= Yes, though I may have written one wrong. Enough of that, let's go and eat!
```

{数学|shù xué}: maths (HSK 3). {可能|kě néng} (maybe) is next lesson's word. {不|bù}{说|shuō}{了|le}, "let's
not talk about it any more", uses the change-of-state {了|le}: from now on, no more talking.

Notice the objects at the front: {听|tīng}{的|de}{题|tí}{我|wǒ}{都|dōu}{听懂|tīng dǒng}{了|le}, "the listening
questions, I understood them all". {都|dōu} (all) refers back to the topic before it.

## Reading: a note on the classroom door

> {同学们|tóng xué men}：{下|xià}{星期一|xīng qī yī}{上午|shàng wǔ}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}{考|kǎo}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{考试|kǎo shì}{在|zài}{二|èr}{楼|lóu}{的|de}{大|dà}{教室|jiào shì}。{考试|kǎo shì}{有|yǒu}{五十|wǔ shí}{个|gè}{题|tí}：{有|yǒu}{的|de}{题|tí}{要|yào}{听|tīng}，{有|yǒu}{的|de}{要|yào}{看|kàn}，{也|yě}{有|yǒu}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}{的|de}。{请|qǐng}{大家|dà jiā}{看完|kàn wán}{第一|dì yī}{课|kè}{到|dào}{第十|dì shí}{课|kè}，{记得|jì de}{每|měi}{课|kè}{的|de}{新|xīn}{词|cí}。{考试|kǎo shì}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{没|méi}{听懂|tīng dǒng}{的|de}{题|tí}{可以|kě yǐ}{先|xiān}{不|bú}{做|zuò}，{做完|zuò wán}{别|bié}{的|de}{再|zài}{回来|huí lái}{做|zuò}。{不要|bú yào}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{写|xiě}{名字|míng zi}！——{王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}

{先|xiān}: first (HSK 3). {别|bié}{的|de}: the others ({别|bié} is lesson 21's word).

1. When and where is the exam?
2. What kinds of question are there?
3. What should you do with a listening question you didn't understand?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Next Monday at nine in the morning, in the big classroom on the second floor.
2. Some to listen to, some to read, and some where you write characters.
3. Leave it for now ({先|xiān}{不|bú}{做|zuò}), finish the others, then come back to it.

"Everyone: the Chinese exam is next Monday at 9 a.m., in the big classroom on the second floor.
The exam has fifty questions: some you listen to, some you read, and there are also some where
you write characters. Please read through lessons 1 to 10 and remember the new words of each
lesson. During the exam, you can skip any question you didn't understand at first, finish the
others and then come back to it. Don't forget to write your name! — Teacher Wang"
</details>

{做完|zuò wán}{别|bié}{的|de}{再|zài}{回来|huí lái}{做|zuò}: "finish the others, *then* come back": {再|zài} here is
"and only then", a use you'll see more of. {回来|huí lái} (come back) is from lesson 09.

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{听懂|tīng dǒng}{了|le}{吗|ma}？
= Did you understand?
{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{听懂|tīng dǒng}，{请|qǐng}{再|zài}{说|shuō}{一下|yí xià}。
= I didn't understand; please say it again.
{这个|zhè ge}{词|cí}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}{意思|yì si}？
= What does this word mean?
{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{考试|kǎo shì}。
= I've got an exam tomorrow.
{我|wǒ}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{他|tā}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}。
= I've forgotten his name.
{你|nǐ}{还|hái}{记得|jì de}{我|wǒ}{吗|ma}？
= Do you still remember me?
```

## Pronunciation

- {考试|kǎo shì}: a low third tone, then a sharp fall. {考|kǎo} rhymes with {好|hǎo}.
- {词|cí} and {字|zì}: both have the buzzing *-i* after *c* / *z*, but {词|cí} rises and has a puff of
  air (*c* is like "ts" in "cats"); {字|zì} falls, with no puff.
- {懂|dǒng}: third tone; {听懂|tīng dǒng} is high, then low. {不懂|bù dǒng} keeps {不|bù} fourth (before a
  third tone).
- {忘|wàng} and {完|wán}: both start with *w*; {完|wán} rises, {忘|wàng} falls and ends in *-ng*.
- {记得|jì de}: the *de* is short and light. {不记得|bú jì de}: {不|bú} rises before the fourth-tone {记|jì}.
- In result pairs the complement keeps its tone: {看完|kàn wán}, {做错|zuò cuò}, {找到|zhǎo dào}.

## Common mistakes

- {不|bù} before a result: ~~{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{听懂|tīng dǒng}~~. The result didn't happen: {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{听懂|tīng dǒng}.
- {了|le} after {没|méi}: ~~{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{看完|kàn wán}{了|le}~~. Drop {了|le}: {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{看完|kàn wán}.
- {找|zhǎo} for "find": ~~{我|wǒ}{找|zhǎo}{了|le}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{笔|bǐ}~~ only says you looked. "I found my pen" is
  {我|wǒ}{找到|zhǎo dào}{了|le}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{笔|bǐ}.
- The object between verb and complement: ~~{看|kàn}{书|shū}{完|wán}~~. Keep the pair together:
  {看完|kàn wán}{书|shū}.
- {问题|wèn tí} for a test question: in an exam you do {题|tí}; a {问题|wèn tí} is a question you ask.
- {字|zì} for a word of two characters: {书包|shū bāo} is one {词|cí}, two {字|zì}.
- {忘|wàng} without {了|le}: ~~{我|wǒ}{忘|wàng}{他|tā}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}~~ sounds unfinished. Say
  {我|wǒ}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{他|tā}{的|de}{名字|míng zi}.

## Key points

- Result complement: verb + result, side by side: {看完|kàn wán}, {听懂|tīng dǒng}, {做错|zuò cuò}, {写好|xiě hǎo},
  {找到|zhǎo dào}, {学会|xué huì}. The verb is the action; the complement is how it came out.
- Negative: {没|méi} + verb + complement, no {了|le}. Questions: …{了|le}{吗|ma}？ / …{了|le}{没有|méi yǒu}？
- The object follows the pair, or goes first as the topic.
- {考试|kǎo shì} exam (kept whole); {考|kǎo} + subject; {考|kǎo}{了|le}{九十|jiǔ shí}{分|fēn}.
- {题|tí} a test question; {词|cí} a word; {字|zì} a character.
- {记得|jì de} remember ({不|bú}{记得|jì de}); {忘|wàng}{了|le} forgot.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: How well? 得, 地 and 让
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Last lesson's result complements say what an action achieved: {听懂|tīng dǒng}, {做完|zuò wán}. This
lesson adds the other question you ask about an action: *how well* was it done? {他|tā}{说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo},
"he speaks well". It also gives you the way to say *how* someone does something, {慢慢|màn màn}{地|de}{说|shuō}
("speak slowly"), and how to make or let someone do something: {老师|lǎo shī}{让|ràng}{我们|wǒ men}{读|dú}{书|shū}.

You'll learn:

- verb + {得|de} + description: {说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}, {来|lái}{得|de}{很|hěn}{早|zǎo};
- verb + object + verb + {得|de}…: {他|tā}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo};
- description + {地|de} + verb: {慢慢|màn màn}{地|de}{说|shuō}; the three *de*: {的|de}, {地|de}, {得|de};
- {让|ràng} + person + verb: let someone, make someone;
- {帮|bāng} and {帮忙|bāng máng} ({帮|bāng}{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{忙|máng});
- {希望|xī wàng} (hope), {可能|kě néng} (maybe), {已经|yǐ jīng}…{了|le} (already), {就|jiù} (right away; then).

## How well: verb + {得|de} + description

A **[[degree complement]]** comes after the verb, joined to it by the particle {得|de}, and describes how
the action is (or was) done: how well, how fast, how early.

| Subject | Verb | {得|de} | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| {她|tā} | {说|shuō} | {得|de} | {很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 |
| {他|tā} | {写|xiě} | {得|de} | {很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。 |
| {你|nǐ} | {来|lái} | {得|de} | {真|zhēn}{早|zǎo}！ |
| {老师|lǎo shī} | {说|shuō} | {得|de} | {太|tài}{快|kuài}{了|le}。 |

{她|tā}{说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 — She speaks well.

{他|tā}{写|xiě}{得|de}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。 — He writes beautifully.

{你|nǐ}{来|lái}{得|de}{真|zhēn}{早|zǎo}！ — You're early!

{老师|lǎo shī}{说|shuō}{得|de}{太|tài}{快|kuài}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{听懂|tīng dǒng}。 — The teacher spoke too fast; I
didn't understand.

The part after {得|de} works exactly like an adjective predicate (HSK 1, lesson 15): it usually has
{很|hěn}, {非常|fēi cháng}, {真|zhēn} or {太|tài}…{了|le} before the adjective, and a bare adjective
sounds like a comparison. English puts an adverb after the verb ("speaks well"); Chinese puts the
description after {得|de}, as a little sentence about the action.

**Negative and questions.** {不|bù} goes after {得|de}, before the adjective, because it's the
description that's negative, not the action:

{他|tā}{说|shuō}{得|de}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}。 — He doesn't speak well. (not ~~{他|tā}{不|bù}{说|shuō}{得|de}{好|hǎo}~~)

{你|nǐ}{说|shuō}{得|de}{好|hǎo}{不|bu}{好|hǎo}？ — Do you speak well?

{她|tā}{唱|chàng}{得|de}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？ — How does she sing? / How well did she sing?

### With an object: say the verb twice

{得|de} must follow the verb directly, so an object can't sit between them. Chinese solves this by
saying the verb twice: once with the object, once with {得|de}.

{他|tā}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 — He speaks Chinese well.

{她|tā}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}{写|xiě}{得|de}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。 — She writes characters beautifully.

In speech the first verb is often dropped and the object moves to the front, as a topic:

{他|tā}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 — His Chinese is good. (He, Chinese, speaks well.)

{汉字|hàn zì}{她|tā}{写|xiě}{得|de}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。 — Characters, she writes beautifully.

What you can't say is ~~{他|tā}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}~~: {得|de} would follow the object, not the
verb.

### Degree or result?

| Result complement (lesson 17) | Degree complement |
|---|---|
| {我|wǒ}{写好|xiě hǎo}{了|le}。 I've finished writing it (it's done). | {我|wǒ}{写|xiě}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 I write well. |
| one result, right after the verb | a description, after {得|de} |
| negative {没|méi}{写好|xiě hǎo} | negative {写|xiě}{得|de}{不|bù}{好|hǎo} |

## How you do it: description + {地|de} + verb

The other side of the action is the manner, put *before* the verb with {地|de}. This is
**[[adverbial 地]]**: it turns a description into a word that modifies the verb, like English -ly.

{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ}{慢慢|màn màn}{地|de}{说|shuō}。 — Please speak slowly.

{孩子们|hái zi men}{高高兴兴|gāo gāo xìng xìng}{地|de}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{了|le}。 — The children went home happily.

{他|tā}{很|hěn}{快|kuài}{地|de}{吃|chī}{了|le}{早饭|zǎo fàn}。 — He ate his breakfast quickly.

Doubled adjectives (lesson 02: {慢慢|màn màn}, {高高兴兴|gāo gāo xìng xìng}) and adjectives with {很|hěn} are
the usual forms before {地|de}. In speech you'll hear {慢慢|màn màn} without {地|de}, and often said
*mànmānr*, especially in the north: {慢慢|màn màn}{说|shuō}, {慢慢|màn màn}{吃|chī} ("take your time eating" is
also what a host says to guests).

{地|de} and {得|de} both say *how*, but they point different ways:

{他|tā}{慢慢|màn màn}{地|de}{走|zǒu}。 — He walks slowly. (the manner, as he does it)

{他|tā}{走|zǒu}{得|de}{很|hěn}{慢|màn}。 — He walks slowly. / He's a slow walker. (a comment on the result)

### The three *de*

All three are said *de*, light, and they are often confused even by Chinese speakers when they
write. The rule is simple once you look at the word that follows or comes before:

| Particle | Where | Joins | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {的|de} | before a noun | description + a noun | {漂亮|piào liang}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}, pretty clothes |
| {地|de} | before a verb | description + a verb | {慢慢|màn màn}{地|de}{说|shuō}, speak slowly |
| {得|de} | after a verb | a verb + description | {说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{慢|màn}, speak slowly |

The character {地|de} is the {地|dì} of {地铁|dì tiě} (lesson 08) and {得|de} is the {得|de} of {觉得|jué de}
(HSK 1). Both have other readings; as particles they're always light *de*.

## Making and letting: {让|ràng} + person + verb

{让|ràng} is "to let" and "to make (someone do)". The person after it is the one who then does
the next verb:

{老师|lǎo shī}{让|ràng}{我们|wǒ men}{读|dú}{课文|kè wén}。 — The teacher has us read the text aloud. ({课文|kè wén}: the
text of a lesson, HSK 3)

{妈妈|mā ma}{不|bú}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{看|kàn}{电视|diàn shì}。 — Mum won't let me watch TV.

{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{看看|kàn kan}。 — Let me have a look.

{对不起|duì bu qǐ}，{让|ràng}{你|nǐ}{等|děng}{了|le}{这么|zhè me}{长|cháng}{时间|shí jiān}。 — Sorry to keep you waiting so long.
({等|děng}, wait: lesson 20; {这么|zhè me}, so: lesson 22)

A sentence like this is a **[[pivotal sentence]]**: {我们|wǒ men} is the object of {让|ràng} and at the same
time the subject of {读|dú}. It "pivots" from one verb to the next. {请|qǐng} works the same way:
{我|wǒ}{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ}{吃饭|chī fàn} ("I invite you to eat", I'm treating you), {老师|lǎo shī}{请|qǐng}{我们|wǒ men}{进来|jìn lái}
(the teacher asks us to come in). {让|ràng} is "let, make, have"; {请|qǐng} is the polite "invite,
ask".

The negative goes before {让|ràng}: {不|bú}{让|ràng}, {没|méi}{让|ràng}. Whether {让|ràng} is "let" or "make" depends
on the situation; Chinese doesn't separate them.

## Helping: {帮|bāng} and {帮忙|bāng máng}

{帮|bāng} is "to help", and it's usually followed by the person and what you help with:

{你|nǐ}{能|néng}{帮|bāng}{我|wǒ}{拿|ná}{一下|yí xià}{吗|ma}？ — Could you hold this for me (for a moment)?

{我|wǒ}{帮|bāng}{妈妈|mā ma}{做饭|zuò fàn}。 — I help Mum cook.

{帮忙|bāng máng} is "to help out, do someone a favour". It's a separable verb, {帮|bāng} + {忙|máng}
(the {忙|máng} of "busy": think of it as helping with someone's busy work). So it doesn't take an
object; the person goes inside:

{你|nǐ}{能|néng}{帮|bāng}{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{忙|máng}{吗|ma}？ — Can you do me a favour?

{他|tā}{帮|bāng}{了|le}{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{忙|máng}。 — He helped me a lot.

{谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}{帮忙|bāng máng}！ — Thanks for your help!

~~{帮忙|bāng máng}{我|wǒ}~~ is a classic mistake: say {帮|bāng}{我|wǒ} or {帮|bāng}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{忙|máng}.

This is a **[[separable verb with a quantity]]**: the amount ({一|yí}{个|gè}, {很|hěn}{多|duō}) and the person go
between the two halves, and {了|le} goes after the first half. You saw the same thing in HSK 1's
{睡|shuì}{了|le}{八|bā}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{的|de}{觉|jiào} (slept for eight hours), and next lesson has
{游|yóu}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{的|de}{泳|yǒng}.

## Hoping and maybe: {希望|xī wàng}, {可能|kě néng}

{希望|xī wàng} is "to hope", usually followed by a whole clause:

{我|wǒ}{希望|xī wàng}{明天|míng tiān}{不|bú}{下雨|xià yǔ}。 — I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.

{希望|xī wàng}{你|nǐ}{考试|kǎo shì}{考|kǎo}{得|de}{好|hǎo}！ — Good luck in your exam! ("Hope you do well")

It's also a noun, "hope": {有|yǒu}{希望|xī wàng}, there's hope.

{可能|kě néng} is "maybe, possibly" before a verb, and "possible" on its own:

{他|tā}{可能|kě néng}{不|bù}{来|lái}{了|le}。 — He may not be coming after all.

{明天|míng tiān}{可能|kě néng}{会|huì}{下雨|xià yǔ}。 — It may well rain tomorrow.

{这|zhè}{不|bù}{可能|kě néng}！ — That's impossible!

Unlike English "maybe", {可能|kě néng} usually goes after the subject, before the verb, like other
adverbs: {他|tā}{可能|kě néng}{在|zài}{家|jiā} (maybe he's at home). It can also start the sentence:
{可能|kě néng}{他|tā}{在|zài}{家|jiā}.

## Already: {已经|yǐ jīng}…{了|le}

{已经|yǐ jīng} (already) goes before the verb, and the sentence usually ends with {了|le}:

{他|tā}{已经|yǐ jīng}{走|zǒu}{了|le}。 — He's already left.

{我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{吃|chī}{了|le}。 — I've already eaten.

{已经|yǐ jīng}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{了|le}！ — It's already ten o'clock!

{我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{学|xué}{了|le}{一|yì}{年|nián}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{了|le}。 — I've been learning Chinese for a year now.

The last one has two {了|le}: after the verb (completed amount) and at the end (and it's still going
on). {已经|yǐ jīng}…{了|le} comes back in lesson 26 with other time patterns.

## Right away, then: {就|jiù}

{就|jiù} is a short adverb with several jobs. Two matter now.

**Right away, soon.** {就|jiù} before the verb says it will happen very soon, or did happen early:

{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{来|lái}！ — I'm coming (right now)!

{你|nǐ}{等|děng}{一下|yí xià}，{他|tā}{就|jiù}{到|dào}。 — Wait a moment, he'll be here any minute.

{他|tā}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{就|jiù}{来|lái}{了|le}。 — He came as early as seven.

**Then, in that case.** After a condition or a first action, {就|jiù} says what follows:

{下课|xià kè}{以后|yǐ hòu}{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。 — After class I go straight home. ({以后|yǐ hòu}: HSK 3)

{你|nǐ}{去|qù}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{去|qù}。 — If you go, I'll go.

{那|nà}{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{不|bú}{去|qù}{了|le}。 — Then I won't go.

In these two uses {就|jiù} goes right before the verb (or before {不|bù} / {没|méi}), not at the start
of the sentence: ~~{就|jiù}{我|wǒ}{来|lái}~~.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 帮 (traditional 幫) | help | bāng | 巾 | 9 | {帮|bāng}, {帮忙|bāng máng} |
| 希 | hope; rare | xī | 巾 | 7 | {希望|xī wàng} |
| 望 | look into the distance; hope | wàng | 月 | 11 | {希望|xī wàng} |
| 已 | already | yǐ | 己 | 3 | {已经|yǐ jīng} |
| 就 | right away; then | jiù | 尢 | 12 | {就|jiù} |
| 让 (traditional 讓) | let, make | ràng | 讠 | 5 | {让|ràng} |

- 帮: 邦 *bāng* (an old word for a state) gives the sound exactly; 巾 (cloth) underneath. The
  traditional form 幫 has 封 on top and 帛 (silk) below.
- 希 and 望 only meet in {希望|xī wàng} at this level. 望: 亡 *wáng* on top gives the sound, with 月
  (moon) beside it and 王 below. A memory aid that fits the old forms: someone standing on the
  ground, gazing at the moon far away.
- 让: 讠 (speech) + 上 (up). Traditional 讓 has 言 + 襄 (*xiāng*), an old sound hint.
- 就: 京 (capital, as in 北京) + 尤. Make Me a Hanzi files it under 尢 (the shape of 尤 without its
  dot), as the old Kangxi dictionary did; some modern dictionaries use 亠 (the top of 京).
- 已 is the first of three characters that differ by one stroke's length. See below.

### 己, 已 and 巳

| Character | Top left | Meaning | Learned |
|---|---|---|---|
| 己 *jǐ* | open: the third stroke starts at the middle | self | lesson 01 ({自己|zì jǐ}) |
| 已 *yǐ* | half closed: the third stroke starts higher | already | now ({已经|yǐ jīng}) |
| 巳 *sì* | fully closed | the sixth earthly branch (in dates and the zodiac) | not taught |

All three have the same three strokes: a horizontal that turns down, a short horizontal, and a
vertical that bends right along the bottom and hooks up. Only the start of the last stroke moves.
A rhyme Chinese pupils learn says roughly: "open 己, half 已, closed 巳".

### Radical review: 巾, cloth

巾 (a cloth or towel hanging down) is the radical of 帮 and 希, and you know it from HSK 1 in 师
(teacher), 市 (in {超市|chāo shì}) and 常 (in {非常|fēi cháng}). In none of them does it give today's
meaning; it's a building block. Its three strokes: a short vertical, the stroke that goes across the top,
turns down and hooks, and the long vertical through the middle, last.

### Stroke order

- **帮**: the three horizontals of the top left, then the slash through them, then 阝 (the
  ear-shaped stroke and its vertical), then 巾.
- **希**: the cross at the top (a slash, then a dot falling right), the long horizontal, the long
  slash, then 巾.
- **望**: 亡 (dot, horizontal, the stroke that goes down and turns right), then 月 beside it, and 王
  across the bottom (horizontal, horizontal, vertical, the long bottom horizontal last).
- **就**: 京 first (dot, horizontal, 口, then the hooked vertical and the two short strokes of 小),
  then 尤: horizontal, slash, the long stroke that bends right and hooks up, and the dot last.
- **让**: 讠, then 上: the vertical, the short horizontal, the long horizontal.

```trace
帮希望已就让
```

## Dialogue: practising for tomorrow

{安娜|Ān nà} (Anna) has to read a text aloud in class tomorrow. She asks {王芳|Wáng Fāng} for help.

```dialogue
# Practising for tomorrow
安娜: {王芳|Wáng Fāng}，{你|nǐ}{能|néng}{帮|bāng}{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{忙|máng}{吗|ma}？
= Wang Fang, could you do me a favour?
王芳: {可以|kě yǐ}{啊|a}。{什么|shén me}{事|shì}？
= Sure. What is it?
安娜: {老师|lǎo shī}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{读|dú}{课文|kè wén}。{你|nǐ}{能|néng}{听|tīng}{我|wǒ}{读|dú}{一下|yí xià}{吗|ma}？
= The teacher wants me to read the text aloud tomorrow. Could you listen to me read it?
王芳: {好|hǎo}，{你|nǐ}{读|dú}{吧|ba}。{不要|bú yào}{急|jí}，{慢慢|màn màn}{地|de}{读|dú}。
= OK, go ahead. No hurry, read it slowly.
安娜: ……{我|wǒ}{读|dú}{得|de}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= … How did I do?
王芳: {你|nǐ}{读|dú}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}！{就|jiù}{一|yí}{个|gè}{字|zì}{读|dú}{错|cuò}{了|le}。
= You read it very well! You only got one character wrong.
安娜: {哪里|nǎ lǐ}{哪里|nǎ lǐ}。{我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{读|dú}{了|le}{十|shí}{次|cì}{了|le}。
= Oh, not really. I've already read it ten times.
王芳: {我|wǒ}{希望|xī wàng}{你|nǐ}{明天|míng tiān}{也|yě}{读|dú}{得|de}{这么|zhè me}{好|hǎo}。
= I hope you read it this well tomorrow too.
安娜: {谢谢|xiè xie}{你|nǐ}{帮忙|bāng máng}！{我|wǒ}{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}{吧|ba}。
= Thanks for your help! Let me buy you a tea.
王芳: {今天|jīn tiān}{可能|kě néng}{不|bù}{行|xíng}，{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{六|liù}{点|diǎn}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。{现在|xiàn zài}{已经|yǐ jīng}{五|wǔ}{点|diǎn}{半|bàn}{了|le}！
= Today's probably no good: my mum wants me home at six. It's already half past five!
安娜: {那|nà}{你|nǐ}{快|kuài}{走|zǒu}{吧|ba}，{明天|míng tiān}{见|jiàn}！
= Then off you go. See you tomorrow!
```

- {哪里|nǎ lǐ}{哪里|nǎ lǐ} ("where, where?") is a modest reply to praise, a little old-fashioned but
  still heard; many people now just say {谢谢|xiè xie}.
- {不要|bú yào}{急|jí}: don't hurry, don't worry ({急|jí}: HSK 3). {行|xíng}: OK, will do (HSK 3).
- {就|jiù}{一|yí}{个|gè}{字|zì}: "just one character". {就|jiù} also means "only, just" before a number; that use
  is taken further in HSK 3.
- {读|dú}{了|le}{十|shí}{次|cì}: {次|cì} (times) from lesson 10. {读|dú}{得|de}{这么|zhè me}{好|hǎo}, "read this well":
  {这么|zhè me} comes in lesson 22.

## Reading: my Chinese teacher

> {我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{老师|lǎo shī}{姓|xìng}{高|Gāo}。{高|Gāo}{老师|lǎo shī}{说话|shuō huà}{说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{慢|màn}，{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{能|néng}{听懂|tīng dǒng}。{她|tā}{让|ràng}{我们|wǒ men}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{读|dú}{课文|kè wén}、{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}。{上课|shàng kè}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{她|tā}{经常|jīng cháng}{让|ràng}{我们|wǒ men}{慢慢|màn màn}{地|de}{读|dú}，{我们|wǒ men}{读|dú}{错|cuò}{了|le}，{她|tā}{就|jiù}{帮|bāng}{我们|wǒ men}。{我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{学|xué}{了|le}{半|bàn}{年|nián}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{了|le}。{现在|xiàn zài}{我|wǒ}{说|shuō}{得|de}{不错|bú cuò}，{但是|dàn shì}{汉字|hàn zì}{写|xiě}{得|de}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}。{高|Gāo}{老师|lǎo shī}{说|shuō}{我|wǒ}{写|xiě}{得|de}{太|tài}{快|kuài}{了|le}。{我|wǒ}{希望|xī wàng}{明年|míng nián}{能|néng}{去|qù}{中国|Zhōng guó}，{可能|kě néng}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}。

2. What does she do when the students read something wrong?
3. What is the writer good at, and what not yet?

{地|de} before a verb ({慢慢|màn màn}{地|de}{读|dú}), and {得|de} after verbs ({说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{慢|màn}, {写|xiě}{得|de}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}).
