## Pronunciation

- {得|de} and {地|de} are both light and short, like the {的|de} you know. Don't give them a full
  tone in these uses.
- {让|ràng}: *r* is said with the tongue tip curled back, close to the *s* in "pleasure"; a full,
  falling fourth tone.
- {希望|xī wàng}: high level, then falling. {已经|yǐ jīng}: low, then high level. {可能|kě néng}: low, then
  rising.
- {就|jiù}: spelled *iu*, said *iou*, "jyoh" with a fall. The tone mark sits on the *u*.
- {帮忙|bāng máng}: both end in *-ang*; high level, then rising.
- {说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}: {很|hěn}{好|hǎo} is two third tones, so {很|hěn} rises (said *hén hǎo*).

## Common mistakes

- The object before {得|de}: ~~{他|tā}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}~~. Repeat the verb ({说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{说|shuō}{得|de}…)
  or move the object to the front ({他|tā}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{说|shuō}{得|de}…).
- {不|bù} before the verb in a degree complement: ~~{他|tā}{不|bù}{说|shuō}{得|de}{好|hǎo}~~. The description is
  negative: {说|shuō}{得|de}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}.
- The wrong *de* in writing: {慢慢|màn màn}{的|de}{说|shuō} and {说|shuō}{的|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo} are common in casual
  writing, but the standard forms are {慢慢|màn màn}{地|de}{说|shuō} and {说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}.
- {帮忙|bāng máng} with an object: ~~{帮忙|bāng máng}{我|wǒ}~~. Say {帮|bāng}{我|wǒ}, {帮|bāng}{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{忙|máng}.
- {就|jiù} (right away, then) at the start: ~~{就|jiù}{我|wǒ}{去|qù}~~. It goes right before the verb: {我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{去|qù}.
- English word order with {可能|kě néng}: {可能|kě néng}{他|tā}{不|bú}{是|shì} is possible, but the usual
  place is after the subject: {他|tā}{可能|kě néng}{不|bú}{是|shì}.
- Writing 已 like 己: the last stroke of 已 starts higher, closing half the top.

## Key points

- Degree complement: verb + {得|de} + ({很|hěn}) adjective: {说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}. Negative {说|shuō}{得|de}{不|bù}{好|hǎo};
  question {说|shuō}{得|de}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？ With an object: {说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{说|shuō}{得|de}… or {汉语|Hàn yǔ}{说|shuō}{得|de}….
- Adverbial {地|de}: description + {地|de} + verb: {慢慢|màn màn}{地|de}{说|shuō}.
- {的|de} + noun, {地|de} + verb, verb + {得|de}.
- Pivotal {让|ràng} / {请|qǐng}: {老师|lǎo shī}{让|ràng}{我们|wǒ men}{读|dú}; {我|wǒ}{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ}{吃饭|chī fàn}.
- {帮|bāng} + person + verb; {帮忙|bāng máng} is separable: {帮|bāng}{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{忙|máng}.
- {希望|xī wàng} + clause; {可能|kě néng} before the verb; {已经|yǐ jīng}…{了|le}; {就|jiù} right before the verb
  (right away; then).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Sport: 打篮球, 踢足球, 游泳
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

After school and exams, sport. This lesson gives you the ball games and the verbs that go with
them ({打|dǎ} for hands, {踢|tī} for feet), running and swimming, and the general word {运动|yùn dòng}
(sport, exercise). It also puts two earlier patterns to work: how long you did something
({游|yóu}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}: duration after the verb, like {次|cì} in lesson 10), and how well
({跑|pǎo}{得|de}{很|hěn}{快|kuài}: last lesson's {得|de}).

You'll learn:

- {打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú}, {踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}: which verb for which ball;
- {跑|pǎo} and {跑步|pǎo bù}, {={游|yóu}=} and {游泳|yóu yǒng}: the plain verb and the activity;
- how long: {游|yóu}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}, {踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}{踢|tī}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí};
- {运动|yùn dòng} as a noun and a verb; {球|qiú} on its own.

## Ball games: {打|dǎ} or {踢|tī}

{球|qiú} is a ball, and a ball game is named after its ball: {足球|zú qiú} is "foot ball", {篮球|lán qiú}
"basket ball". The verb depends on what you play with.

| Game | Verb | Play it | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| {篮球|lán qiú} basketball | {打|dǎ} (hit) | {打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú} | games you play with your hands or a racket take {打|dǎ} |
| {足球|zú qiú} football (soccer) | {踢|tī} (kick) | {踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú} | only football is kicked |
| {网球|wǎng qiú} tennis (HSK 3) | {打|dǎ} | {打|dǎ}{网球|wǎng qiú} | |
| {乒乓球|pīng pāng qiú} table tennis | {打|dǎ} | {打|dǎ}{乒乓球|pīng pāng qiú} | the honors lesson says more |

{他|tā}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú}。 — He plays basketball every afternoon.

{我们|wǒ men}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{去|qù}{踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}{吧|ba}！ — Let's go and play football on Saturday!

Don't say {玩|wán}{足球|zú qiú} for "play football". You may hear it among young people, but {玩|wán} is
"play, have fun", and Chinese usually uses the action verb instead. (A child can {玩|wán}{球|qiú}, "play with a ball".)

{打|dǎ} is the {打|dǎ} of {打电话|dǎ diàn huà} and {打车|dǎ chē}. Its basic meaning is "hit", and lesson 23
looks at its many uses. {踢|tī} (kick) has 足 (foot) on its left; it's shown with pinyin now and
taught as a character next lesson.

When the game is clear, {球|qiú} alone is enough: {打球|dǎ qiú} (play basketball, tennis, any ball game
with your hands), {踢球|tī qiú} (play football), {看球|kàn qiú} (watch a match).

{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{踢球|tī qiú}{吗|ma}？ — Do you like playing football?

{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{看球|kàn qiú}。 — My dad likes watching matches at home.

{足|zú} is "foot" in written words ({足球|zú qiú}); the everyday word for the foot is {脚|jiǎo}, in
HSK 3.

## Running and swimming: the verb and the activity

Two pairs work the same way. Each has a one-syllable verb and a two-syllable word for the
activity:

| Verb | Activity | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {跑|pǎo} run | {跑步|pǎo bù} | go running, jog (for exercise) |
| {={游|yóu}=} swim | {游泳|yóu yǒng} | swim, swimming |

The activity words are verb + object, like {睡觉|shuì jiào} and {吃饭|chī fàn}: {跑|pǎo} + {步|bù} (steps),
{={游|yóu}=} + {泳|yǒng} (swimming). Use them when you talk about the sport itself:

{我|wǒ}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{跑步|pǎo bù}。 — I go running every morning.

{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{游泳|yóu yǒng}{吗|ma}？ — Can you swim?

{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{游泳|yóu yǒng}{吧|ba}！ — Let's go swimming!

{她|tā}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{游泳|yóu yǒng}。 — She loves swimming.

Use the one-syllable verb when something else follows it: a complement, a direction, a
distance, a duration.

{他|tā}{跑|pǎo}{得|de}{很|hěn}{快|kuài}。 — He runs fast. (not ~~{跑步|pǎo bù}{得|de}{很|hěn}{快|kuài}~~)

{她|tā}{游|yóu}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 — She swims well.

{孩子|hái zi}{跑|pǎo}{过来|guò lái}{了|le}。 — The child came running over. ({过来|guò lái}: lesson 12)

{我|wǒ}{游|yóu}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — I swam for an hour.

{跑|pǎo} is also "run" in the sense of hurrying anywhere: {他|tā}{跑|pǎo}{到|dào}{车站|chē zhàn}{去|qù}{了|le}, "he ran
to the station". {跑步|pǎo bù} is only running as exercise.

{={游|yóu} has a second job in writing: it's the {游|yóu} of {旅游|lǚ yóu} (travel, lesson 10). In
traditional script the two split: swimming keeps 游 ({游泳|yóu yǒng}), travel is written 遊 ({旅遊|lǚ yóu}).=}

## How long: the duration after the verb

In lesson 10 you put {次|cì} after the verb to count times ({去|qù}{过|guo}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}). A duration goes
in the same place: after the verb, with {了|le} if it's finished.

{我|wǒ}{跑|pǎo}{了|le}{半|bàn}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — I ran for half an hour.

{他们|tā men}{打|dǎ}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{篮球|lán qiú}。 — They played basketball for two hours.

{我|wǒ}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{运动|yùn dòng}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — I exercise for an hour a day.

The time phrase never goes before the verb when it says how long: ~~{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{游泳|yóu yǒng}~~
is wrong. (Before the verb, a time word says *when*: {我|wǒ}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{游泳|yóu yǒng}, "I swim at eight".)

**With an object** there are two common orders:

| Order | Example |
|---|---|
| verb + duration (+ {的|de}) + object | {他们|tā men}{踢|tī}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{的|de}{足球|zú qiú}。 |
| verb + object, verb again + duration | {他们|tā men}{踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}{踢|tī}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 |

Both mean "they played football for two hours". The second repeats the verb, exactly as you did
with {得|de} in lesson 18 ({说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}).

**With {跑步|pǎo bù} and {游泳|yóu yǒng}.** These have their object built in, so the simplest way is the one-syllable
verb: {我|wǒ}{跑|pǎo}{了|le}{半|bàn}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}, {她|tā}{游|yóu}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}. You'll also hear
the separable form with the duration inside, {游|yóu}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{的|de}{泳|yǒng}, and the repeated
verb, {游泳|yóu yǒng}{游|yóu}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}. {游泳|yóu yǒng}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí} is heard in casual
speech, but it's less natural, and textbooks treat it as a learner's mistake: use one of the forms above.

Asking how long: {多|duō}{长|cháng}{时间|shí jiān} (how long a time).

{你|nǐ}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{跑|pǎo}{多|duō}{长|cháng}{时间|shí jiān}？ — How long do you run every day?
— {半|bàn}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — Half an hour.

## {运动|yùn dòng}: sport, exercise, to exercise

{运动|yùn dòng} is a noun, "sport, physical exercise":

{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{什么|shén me}{运动|yùn dòng}？ — What sports do you like?

{跑步|pǎo bù}{是|shì}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}{的|de}{运动|yùn dòng}。 — Running is good exercise.

It's also a verb, "to exercise, do sport", which takes no object:

{我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{都|dōu}{运动|yùn dòng}。 — My grandad exercises every morning.

{多|duō}{运动|yùn dòng}{对|duì}{身体|shēn tǐ}{好|hǎo}。 — Exercising more is good for you. ({对|duì}…{好|hǎo}, good for…;
{身体|shēn tǐ}, body, health: lesson 02)

The second character, {动|dòng}, means "to move". It comes back on its own in lesson 20.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 球 | ball | qiú | 王 | 11 | {球|qiú}, {足球|zú qiú}, {篮球|lán qiú} |
| 足 | foot; enough | zú | 足 | 7 | {足球|zú qiú} |
| 篮 (traditional 籃) | basket | lán | ⺮ | 16 | {篮球|lán qiú} |
| 运 (traditional 運) | move, carry | yùn | 辶 | 7 | {运动|yùn dòng} |
| 动 (traditional 動) | move | dòng | 力 | 6 | {运动|yùn dòng}, {动|dòng} (lesson 20) |
| 跑 | run | pǎo | 足 | 12 | {跑|pǎo}, {跑步|pǎo bù} |
| 步 | step | bù | 止 | 7 | {跑步|pǎo bù} |
| 泳 | swim | yǒng | 氵 | 8 | {游泳|yóu yǒng} |

- 球: on the left, the "jade" radical, written like 王 (as in 现, 班, 玩); on the right, 求 *qiú*, which
  gives the sound exactly. The character first had to do with jade (old dictionaries explain it as the sound of
  jade, or a fine jade); "ball" is a later meaning.
- 足: a drawing of a leg and foot: the knee on top (now 口), the foot below. On the left of a
  character it narrows to ⻊, and its last stroke becomes a rising stroke: 路, 跟, 跑, 踢 (next
  lesson), 跳 (next lesson). You met the radical in lesson 07; now 足 is a character in its own
  right.
- 篮: ⺮ (bamboo) on top: a basket was woven from bamboo. The part below gives the sound.
- 运 and 动 share 云. In 运 it gives the sound (*yún*, *yùn*); in 动 it's simply a shorter shape.
  动 adds 力 (strength): it takes strength to move. The traditional forms are quite different: 運
  has 軍 inside 辶, and 動 has 重 (heavy) beside 力.
- 跑: ⻊ (foot) + 包 *bāo*, an approximate sound hint.
- 步: two feet, one ahead of the other. The oldest forms draw them clearly; today the top is 止 (a
  foot) and the bottom is the other foot, turned round. It is not 少: there's no dot on the right.
- 泳: 氵 (water) + 永 *yǒng*, the sound.

### New radical: 力, strength

力 *lì* (strength, force) probably began as a drawing of a plough or a strong arm. It usually
stands on the right or at the bottom, and characters with it often have to do with effort: 动
(move) is the first of six in this track. HSK 3 brings 力 itself ({努力|nǔ lì}, work hard), 加 (add),
办 (do, handle), 努 (strive) and 助 (help). You already know one character with it at the bottom,
男 (man): 田 (field) over 力, strength in the fields, the traditional explanation. Make Me a Hanzi
files 男 under 田.

Two strokes: a horizontal that turns down and hooks left, and a long slash crossing it.

### Radical review: 辶, walking

辶 (HSK 1, lesson 03) is the "walking" radical of 这, 道, 边 and 还, and of this course's 远, 近, 进, 过
and 送. 运 (move, carry) joins them. Remember the stroke order: **辶 is written last**, after the part
it carries, even though it starts on the left: 云 first, then the dot, the zigzag and the long
sweep along the bottom.

### Stroke order

- **球**: the jade radical (horizontal, horizontal, vertical, rising stroke: the last stroke rises
  to the right), then 求: the horizontal, the hooked vertical, a dot and a rising stroke on the
  left, a short slash and a long falling stroke on the right, and the dot at the top right, last.
- **足**: 口, then the short vertical and horizontal on top of the foot, the slash, and the long
  falling stroke. In ⻊ the last stroke rises instead.
- **篮**: ⺮, then two short verticals, the slash with its horizontal and dot, and 皿 (the dish) at
  the bottom: vertical, the turning stroke, two short verticals, the long horizontal.
- **运**: 云 (two horizontals, the turning stroke, the dot), then 辶.
- **动**: 云, then 力: the turning hook, then the slash.
- **跑**: ⻊ (with its rising last stroke), then 包: the slash, the turning hook, then 巳 inside.
- **步**: 止 first (the middle vertical, the short horizontal on the right, the left vertical, the
  long horizontal), then below: the short vertical, the dot on the left, and the long slash.
- **泳**: 氵, then 永: the dot, the stroke that goes across, down and hooks, the stroke on the left,
  and the two strokes on the right.

```trace
球足篮运动跑步泳
```

### Handwriting review

Four HSK 1 handwriting characters for talking about sport and time: 打 (5 strokes), 时 (7), 间 (7),
半 (5).

```trace
打时间半
```
=}

In traditional script the pads show {+时+} (10 strokes) and {+间+} (12); {打|dǎ} and {半|bàn} are the same.

## Dialogue: what sport do you do?

{大卫|Dà wèi} (David) and {李明|Lǐ Míng} (Li Ming) on a Friday afternoon.

```dialogue
# What sport do you do?
李明: {大卫|Dà wèi}，{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{什么|shén me}{运动|yùn dòng}？
= David, what sports do you like?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}，{也|yě}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{游泳|yóu yǒng}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= I like playing football, and I like swimming too. And you?
李明: {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú}。{我们|wǒ men}{班|bān}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{都|dōu}{打|dǎ}{球|qiú}。
= I like basketball. People in our class play every afternoon.
大卫: {你们|nǐ men}{打|dǎ}{多|duō}{长|cháng}{时间|shí jiān}？
= How long do you play?
李明: {一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。{你|nǐ}{游泳|yóu yǒng}{游|yóu}{得|de}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= An hour. How good a swimmer are you?
大卫: {还|hái}{可以|kě yǐ}。{我|wǒ}{从|cóng}{小|xiǎo}{就|jiù}{会|huì}{游泳|yóu yǒng}。
= Not bad. I've been able to swim since I was little.
李明: {我|wǒ}{不|bú}{会|huì}，{你|nǐ}{能|néng}{教|jiāo}{我|wǒ}{吗|ma}？
= I can't. Could you teach me?
大卫: {可以|kě yǐ}{啊|a}！{星期六|xīng qī liù}{上午|shàng wǔ}{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{游泳|yóu yǒng}，{下午|xià wǔ}{去|qù}{踢|tī}{球|qiú}，{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= Sure! On Saturday morning we'll go swimming, and in the afternoon we'll play football. How's
that?
李明: {太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！{但是|dàn shì}{我|wǒ}{跑|pǎo}{得|de}{很|hěn}{慢|màn}……
= Great! But I'm a slow runner…
大卫: {没关系|méi guān xi}，{多|duō}{运动|yùn dòng}{就|jiù}{快|kuài}{了|le}。
= Never mind. Do more exercise and you'll get faster.
```

- {还|hái}{可以|kě yǐ}: "not bad, OK", a modest answer to "how good are you?".
- {从|cóng}{小|xiǎo}{就|jiù}{会|huì}: "could since I was small". {从小|cóng xiǎo} (since childhood) is lesson 25's
  word; here it's {从|cóng} (from, lesson 07) + {小|xiǎo}. {就|jiù} (lesson 18) stresses how early.
- {多|duō}{运动|yùn dòng}{就|jiù}{快|kuài}{了|le}: "exercise more and you'll be fast": {就|jiù} for the result,
  {了|le} for the change.

## Reading: the school sports club

The school's sports club puts up a notice.

> {学校|xué xiào}{运动|yùn dòng}{时间|shí jiān}：{星期一|xīng qī yī}{到|dào}{星期五|xīng qī wǔ}{下午|xià wǔ}{四|sì}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}{六|liù}{点|diǎn}。{星期一|xīng qī yī}、{星期三|xīng qī sān}{打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú}，{星期二|xīng qī èr}、{星期四|xīng qī sì}{踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}，{星期五|xīng qī wǔ}{游泳|yóu yǒng}。{踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{请|qǐng}{到|dào}{学校|xué xiào}{后面|hòu miàn}，{游泳|yóu yǒng}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{请|qǐng}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{门口|mén kǒu}{等|děng}，{老师|lǎo shī}{带|dài}{大家|dà jiā}{去|qù}。{不|bú}{会|huì}{游泳|yóu yǒng}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{也|yě}{可以|kě yǐ}{来|lái}，{杨|Yáng}{老师|lǎo shī}{教|jiāo}{你|nǐ}。{每|měi}{天|tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}，{我们|wǒ men}{也|yě}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{里|lǐ}{跑步|pǎo bù}，{跑|pǎo}{二十|èr shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。{多|duō}{运动|yùn dòng}，{身体|shēn tǐ}{好|hǎo}！

{等|děng}: to wait (lesson 20). {带|dài}: to take, lead (HSK 3).

1. On which days is there football, and where do the players meet?
2. Where should the swimmers wait, and who takes them?
3. Can students who can't swim come? Why?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Tuesdays and Thursdays; behind the school.
2. At the school gate; a teacher takes everyone there.
3. Yes: Teacher Yang will teach them.

"School sports times: Monday to Friday, 4 to 6 p.m. Mondays and Wednesdays basketball, Tuesdays
and Thursdays football, Fridays swimming. Football players, please come to the area behind the
school; swimmers, please wait at the school gate, and a teacher will take everyone there.
Students who can't swim can come too: Teacher Yang will teach you. Every morning at seven we also
run at school, for twenty minutes. Exercise more, stay healthy!"
</details>

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{什么|shén me}{运动|yùn dòng}？
= What sports do you like?
{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú}。
= I like playing basketball.
{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}{吧|ba}！
= Let's go and play football!
{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{游泳|yóu yǒng}{吗|ma}？
= Can you swim?
{我|wǒ}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{跑|pǎo}{半|bàn}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。
= I run for half an hour every day.
{他|tā}{跑|pǎo}{得|de}{很|hěn}{快|kuài}。
= He runs fast.
```

## Pronunciation

- {足球|zú qiú} and {篮球|lán qiú}: two rising tones in a row. Keep both rising; the second doesn't
  fall.
- {游泳|yóu yǒng}: rising, then low. *yong* is said like "yoong" with the lips rounded.
- {跑步|pǎo bù}: low, then falling. {跑|pǎo} has a puff of air on the *p*; {步|bù} has none.
- {运动|yùn dòng}: two falling tones. *yun* is the *ün* sound (lips rounded for *ü*), spelled *yun*.
- {踢|tī}: high and level, with a puff of air on the *t*.
- {球|qiú}: spelled *iu*, said *iou*; the mark sits on the *u*.

## Common mistakes

- {玩|wán} for playing a sport: {玩|wán}{篮球|lán qiú} is heard in casual speech, but the usual verbs are {打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú}, {踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}.
- {打|dǎ}{足球|zú qiú}: football is kicked, {踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}.
- The activity word before a complement: ~~{游泳|yóu yǒng}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}~~. Use the verb: {游|yóu}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}.
  With a duration, {游泳|yóu yǒng}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí} is heard but less natural than {游|yóu}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}.
- Duration before the verb, English-style "for an hour I swam": the duration follows the verb.
- An object after {运动|yùn dòng}: ~~{运动|yùn dòng}{足球|zú qiú}~~. Name the sport with its own verb.
- Writing the bottom of 步 as 少: it has no dot on the right.
- Writing 辶 first in 运: it comes last.

## Key points

- {打|dǎ} + ball games played with the hands ({打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú}); {踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}; {打球|dǎ qiú}, {踢球|tī qiú}, {看球|kàn qiú}.
- {跑步|pǎo bù} / {游泳|yóu yǒng} for the activity; {跑|pǎo} / {={游|yóu}=} before {得|de}, a duration or a direction.
- Duration after the verb: {游|yóu}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}; with an object, {踢|tī}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{的|de}{足球|zú qiú}
  or {踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}{踢|tī}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}. Ask with {多|duō}{长|cháng}{时间|shí jiān}.
- {运动|yùn dòng}: sport (noun) and to exercise (verb, no object).
- New radical 力 (strength); 辶 reviewed (written last).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Hobbies: 爱好, 一起, 开始, 一会儿
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last core lesson of the module is about free time: what your hobbies are, doing things
together, starting something new, and waiting a moment for someone. You'll use everything the
module has given you: {教|jiāo} someone a skill, {学会|xué huì} it, do it {得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}, and do it for
{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}.

You'll learn:

- {爱好|ài hào}: a hobby, and "to be keen on" in writing;
- {画|huà} and {画画儿|huà huàr} (draw, paint), {跳舞|tiào wǔ} (dance);
- {一起|yì qǐ} + verb, and {跟|gēn}…{一起|yì qǐ};
- {开始|kāi shǐ} + verb, and {开始|kāi shǐ} as "the beginning";
- {等|děng} (wait) and {一会儿|yí huìr} (a moment): {等|děng}{一会儿|yí huìr}, {等|děng}{我|wǒ}{一下|yí xià};
- {动|dòng} (move).

## Hobbies: {爱好|ài hào}

{爱好|ài hào} is "a hobby, an interest". It's built from {爱|ài} (to love) and {好|hào}, a fourth-tone
reading of the familiar {好|hǎo} that means "to like". Notice the tone: *ài hào*, not *ài hǎo*.

{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{什么|shén me}{爱好|ài hào}？ — What are your hobbies?

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{爱好|ài hào}{是|shì}{画画儿|huà huàr}。 — My hobby is drawing.

{他|tā}{的|de}{爱好|ài hào}{很|hěn}{多|duō}：{踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}、{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}、{唱歌|chàng gē}。 — He has lots of hobbies:
football, films, singing.

In writing, {爱好|ài hào} is also a verb, "to be keen on", followed by an activity: {他|tā}{爱好|ài hào}{运动|yùn dòng}
(he's keen on sport). In speech people more often say {喜欢|xǐ huan} or {爱|ài}: {他|tā}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{运动|yùn dòng},
{他|tā}{爱|ài}{运动|yùn dòng}.

## Drawing and dancing: {画|huà}, {跳舞|tiào wǔ}

{画|huà} is the verb "to draw, to paint", and also the picture you make. As a noun it's usually said
with erhua, {画儿|huàr}, so "to draw (pictures)" is {画画儿|huà huàr}: the verb {画|huà} + the noun {画儿|huàr}.

{我|wǒ}{妹妹|mèi mei}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{画画儿|huà huàr}。 — My younger sister loves drawing.

{你|nǐ}{画|huà}{的|de}{是|shì}{什么|shén me}？ — What's that you've drawn?

{这|zhè}{张|zhāng}{画儿|huàr}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{画|huà}{的|de}。 — My grandad painted this picture. ({张|zhāng}, the
measure word for flat things: HSK 3)

With a complement or a duration, use the verb alone: {他|tā}{画|huà}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo} (he draws well),
{我|wǒ}{画|huà}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí} (I drew for two hours), {画完|huà wán}{了|le} (finished drawing). It's the same
choice as {={游|yóu}=} / {游泳|yóu yǒng} last lesson. Speakers who use less erhua, especially in the south,
say {画画|huà huà}.

{跳舞|tiào wǔ} is "to dance": {跳|tiào} (jump; an HSK 3 word on its own) + {舞|wǔ} (a dance). Like
{跑步|pǎo bù} and {游泳|yóu yǒng} it's verb + object, so it separates:

{她|tā}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}{跳|tiào}{得|de}{非常|fēi cháng}{好|hǎo}。 — She dances extremely well.

{我们|wǒ men}{跳|tiào}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{的|de}{舞|wǔ}。 — We danced for an hour.

{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{会|huì}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}，{你|nǐ}{能|néng}{教|jiāo}{我|wǒ}{吗|ma}？ — I can't dance. Could you teach me?

Many older people in Chinese cities dance together in squares and parks in the evening:
{广场舞|guǎng chǎng wǔ} ("square dancing"). HSK 1's honors lesson on parks describes it.

## Together: {一起|yì qǐ}

{一起|yì qǐ} (together) goes before the verb, like other adverbs:

{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{吧|ba}！ — Let's go together!

{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{吃饭|chī fàn}{好|hǎo}{吗|ma}？ — Shall we eat together?

To say who with, put {跟|gēn} (lesson 14) + the person before {一起|yì qǐ}:

{我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{朋友|péng you}{一起|yì qǐ}{踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}。 — I play football with friends.

{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{跟|gēn}{我|wǒ}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}{吗|ma}？ — Would you like to go dancing with me?

{和|hé} works in place of {跟|gēn} here: {我|wǒ}{和|hé}{朋友|péng you}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}. Notice the order: who
with, then {一起|yì qǐ}, then the verb. English "I play football together with friends" puts it all
at the end; Chinese puts it before the verb.

The tone: {一|yì} before the third-tone {起|qǐ} is fourth, *yìqǐ* (HSK 1's rule).

## Beginning: {开始|kāi shǐ}

{开始|kāi shǐ} is "to begin, to start". It takes a verb (start doing), a noun, or nothing:

{我|wǒ}{去年|qù nián}{开始|kāi shǐ}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — I started learning Chinese last year.

{电影|diàn yǐng}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{开始|kāi shǐ}。 — The film starts at eight.

{开始|kāi shǐ}{了|le}！ — It's started!

{我们|wǒ men}{开始|kāi shǐ}{上课|shàng kè}{吧|ba}。 — Let's start the class.

It's also a noun, "the beginning": {开始|kāi shǐ}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}, "at the beginning, at first".

{开始|kāi shǐ}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{我|wǒ}{画|huà}{得|de}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}，{现在|xiàn zài}{好|hǎo}{多|duō}{了|le}。 — At first I didn't
draw well; now I'm much better.

Compare the words for starting you know: {开学|kāi xué} (school term starts, lesson 16), {上课|shàng kè}
(a class starts, or you go to class), and {开始|kāi shǐ}, which works for anything.

## Waiting a moment: {等|děng}, {一会儿|yí huìr}

{等|děng} is "to wait (for)". The person you wait for follows it directly; there's no word for
"for":

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{门口|mén kǒu}{等|děng}{你|nǐ}。 — I'll wait for you at the entrance.

{你|nǐ}{等|děng}{谁|shéi}？ — Who are you waiting for?

{请|qǐng}{等|děng}{一下|yí xià}。 — Please wait a moment.

{一会儿|yí huìr} is "a little while, a moment". After a verb it says how long, like any duration
(lesson 19):

{等|děng}{一会儿|yí huìr}！ — Wait a moment!

{我们|wǒ men}{休息|xiū xi}{一会儿|yí huìr}{吧|ba}。 — Let's rest for a bit.

{他|tā}{玩|wán}{了|le}{一会儿|yí huìr}{就|jiù}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{了|le}。 — He played for a little while and then went home.

With a person, {等|děng} + person + {一会儿|yí huìr} or {一下|yí xià}:

{你|nǐ}{等|děng}{我|wǒ}{一会儿|yí huìr}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{来|lái}。 — Wait for me a moment, I'm coming.

Before the verb, {一会儿|yí huìr} means "in a moment, soon": {我|wǒ}{一会儿|yí huìr}{就|jiù}{回来|huí lái} (I'll be back
in a moment). And {一会儿|yí huìr}{见|jiàn}! is "see you in a bit!"

{一下|yí xià} (HSK 1) and {一会儿|yí huìr} overlap: {等|děng}{一下|yí xià} softens the request ("just wait"),
{等|děng}{一会儿|yí huìr} says more about the time ("for a little while"). You'll also hear {一会儿|yí huìr} said
*yìhuǐr*, especially in Beijing; this course writes *yíhuìr*.

## Moving: {动|dòng}

{动|dòng} (to move) is the second half of {运动|yùn dòng}. On its own it's mostly used for small
movements, and in commands:

{不要|bú yào}{动|dòng}！ — Don't move! / Don't touch!

{你|nǐ}{动|dòng}{一下|yí xià}，{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{过去|guò qù}。 — Move a bit and let me past.

{我|wǒ}{太|tài}{累|lèi}{了|le}，{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{动|dòng}。 — I'm too tired, I don't want to move.

{动|dòng} for things: {这个|zhè ge}{东西|dōng xi}{你|nǐ}{动|dòng}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ ("Did you touch / move this?"). In
{运动|yùn dòng} it's exercise; on its own it's simply movement.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 踢 | kick | tī | 足 | 15 | {踢|tī}, {踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú} |
| 画 (traditional 畫) | draw; picture | huà | 田 | 8 | {画|huà}, {画画儿|huà huàr} |
| 跳 | jump | tiào | 足 | 13 | {跳舞|tiào wǔ}, {跳|tiào} (HSK 3) |
| 舞 | dance | wǔ | 舛 | 14 | {跳舞|tiào wǔ} |
| 始 | begin | shǐ | 女 | 8 | {开始|kāi shǐ} |
| 等 | wait; rank | děng | ⺮ | 12 | {等|děng} |

- 踢 and 跳: both have ⻊ (foot) on the left, and a sound hint on the right: 易 for 踢, 兆 *zhào* for
  跳. With 路, 跟, 跑 and 足 itself, that makes six characters with the foot radical in this course.
- 画: the traditional form 畫 shows it best: a hand holding a brush (聿) on top, drawing the borders
  of a field (田). The simplified form keeps the field and frames it with 凵 below and a line on top.
- 舞: in the oldest writing a person holding something in each hand, dancing. That shape was later
  borrowed for 無 (not have), and 舞 added 舛 (two feet) at the bottom for the dance. Make Me a Hanzi
  files it under 舛.
- 始: 女 (woman) + 台, an old sound hint.
- 等: ⺮ (bamboo) + 寺. The old dictionaries explain it as bamboo slips being sorted in order: rank,
  grade. "To wait" is a later meaning.

### Radical review: ⺮, bamboo

⺮ is 竹 (bamboo) squeezed onto the top of a character: two little "people" of three strokes each.
HSK 1 had 第; this course has added 笑 (lesson 05), 笔 (lesson 16), 篮 (lesson 19) and now 等. Bamboo
was used for writing slips, brushes and baskets, which is why 笔 and 篮 have it.

### Stroke order

- **画**: the top horizontal, then 田 (the left vertical, the top-and-right stroke, the middle
  horizontal, the middle vertical, the bottom), then 凵 last: the stroke that goes down the left and
  along the bottom, and the right vertical.
- **踢**: ⻊ (its last stroke rises), then 易: 日 on top, then the slash, the turning hook and two
  slashes inside it.
- **跳**: ⻊, then 兆: the long slash on the left, a dot and a rising stroke, the long stroke in the
  middle that bends right and hooks up, and a slash and a dot on the right.
- **舞**: the top slash and short horizontal, the long horizontal, four short verticals, the next
  horizontal; then 舛 at the bottom: on the left a shape like 夕, on the right the short horizontal,
  the turning stroke, and the long vertical last.
- **始**: 女 (the first stroke goes down and turns right; then the slash; then the horizontal),
  then 台 (the turning stroke and dot, then 口).
- **等**: ⺮, then 寺: 土 (horizontal, vertical, horizontal), then 寸 (the long horizontal, the
  hooked vertical, the dot).

```trace
踢画跳舞始等
```

### Handwriting review

Four more HSK 1 handwriting characters: 爱 (10 strokes), 下 (3), 午 (4), 么 (3). With the earlier
review boxes, that's twenty of HSK 1's handwriting characters practised in this module.

```trace
爱下午么
```
=}

In traditional script the pads show {+爱+} (13 strokes) and {+么+} (14); {下|xià} and {午|wǔ} are the same.

## Dialogue: what are you doing on Saturday?

{王芳|Wáng Fāng} (Wang Fang) and {安娜|Ān nà} (Anna) after class on Friday.

```dialogue
# What are you doing on Saturday?
王芳: {安娜|Ān nà}，{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{什么|shén me}{爱好|ài hào}？
= Anna, what are your hobbies?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{画画儿|huà huàr}，{也|yě}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}。{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= I like drawing, and I like dancing too. And you?
王芳: {我|wǒ}{也|yě}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}！{我|wǒ}{去年|qù nián}{开始|kāi shǐ}{学|xué}{的|de}。
= I like dancing too! I started learning last year.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{跳|tiào}{得|de}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= How good are you?
王芳: {开始|kāi shǐ}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{跳|tiào}{得|de}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}，{现在|xiàn zài}{还|hái}{可以|kě yǐ}。{星期六|xīng qī liù}{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}{吧|ba}？
= At first I wasn't good, now I'm OK. Shall we go dancing together on Saturday?
安娜: {好|hǎo}{啊|a}！{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{开始|kāi shǐ}？
= Sure! What time does it start?
王芳: {下午|xià wǔ}{三|sān}{点|diǎn}。{我|wǒ}{两|liǎng}{点|diǎn}{半|bàn}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{门口|mén kǒu}{等|děng}{你|nǐ}。
= Three in the afternoon. I'll wait for you at the school gate at half past two.
安娜: {我|wǒ}{可能|kě néng}{晚|wǎn}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{到|dào}，{你|nǐ}{等|děng}{我|wǒ}{一会儿|yí huìr}，{好|hǎo}{吗|ma}？
= I might be a bit late. Will you wait for me a moment?
王芳: {没问题|méi wèn tí}。{跳完|tiào wán}{舞|wǔ}，{你|nǐ}{教|jiāo}{我|wǒ}{画画儿|huà huàr}，{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= No problem. After dancing, you can teach me to draw, how's that?
安娜: {太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！{那|nà}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{见|jiàn}！
= Great! See you on Saturday, then!
```

- {我|wǒ}{去年|qù nián}{开始|kāi shǐ}{学|xué}{的|de}: the {是|shì}…{的|de} pattern of lesson 08 (with {是|shì} left out),
  stressing *when* she started.
- {晚|wǎn}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{到|dào}: "arrive a little late"; {晚|wǎn} (late) before the verb.
- {没问题|méi wèn tí}: "no problem", {没|méi} + {问题|wèn tí} (HSK 1).
- {跳完|tiào wán}{舞|wǔ}: the result complement {完|wán} goes between the two halves of {跳舞|tiào wǔ}, like a
  quantity does.

## Reading: plans in the group chat

Four friends plan their Saturday in a chat group.

> {王芳|Wáng Fāng}：{大家|dà jiā}{好|hǎo}！{星期六|xīng qī liù}{下午|xià wǔ}{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{公园|gōng yuán}{画画儿|huà huàr}{吧|ba}？
>
> {李明|Lǐ Míng}：{好|hǎo}{啊|a}！{但是|dàn shì}{我|wǒ}{画|huà}{得|de}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}……
>
> {安娜|Ān nà}：{没关系|méi guān xi}，{开始|kāi shǐ}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{画|huà}{得|de}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}。{我|wǒ}{可以|kě yǐ}{教|jiāo}{你|nǐ}。{我|wǒ}{可能|kě néng}{晚|wǎn}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{到|dào}，{你们|nǐ men}{等|děng}{我|wǒ}{一会儿|yí huìr}。
>
> {大卫|Dà wèi}：{我|wǒ}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{上午|shàng wǔ}{踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}，{十二|shí èr}{点|diǎn}{踢完|tī wán}，{下午|xià wǔ}{可以|kě yǐ}{去|qù}。{画完|huà wán}{以后|yǐ hòu}{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}，{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
>
> {王芳|Wáng Fāng}：{太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}！{那|nà}{我们|wǒ men}{两|liǎng}{点|diǎn}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{门口|mén kǒu}{见|jiàn}，{一起|yì qǐ}{走|zǒu}{过去|guò qù}。

{公园|gōng yuán}: park (HSK 3). {以后|yǐ hòu}: after (HSK 3).

1. What does Wang Fang suggest doing on Saturday?
2. Why does Li Ming hesitate, and what does Anna offer?
3. When is David free, and what does he suggest?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Going to the park together on Saturday afternoon to draw.
2. He doesn't draw well; Anna says everyone is bad at first and offers to teach him.
3. In the afternoon (football ends at twelve); he suggests going dancing after drawing.

Wang Fang: "Hi everyone! Shall we all go to the park and draw on Saturday afternoon?"
Li Ming: "Sure! But I'm bad at drawing…"
Anna: "Never mind, everyone draws badly at first. I can teach you. I might be a bit late, so wait
for me a moment."
David: "I'm playing football on Saturday morning; we finish at twelve, so I can come in the
afternoon. After drawing, how about we go dancing?"
Wang Fang: "Great! So let's meet at the school gate at two and walk over together."
</details>

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{什么|shén me}{爱好|ài hào}？
= What are your hobbies?
{我|wǒ}{的|de}{爱好|ài hào}{是|shì}{画画儿|huà huàr}。
= My hobby is drawing.
{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{吧|ba}！
= Let's go together!
{电影|diàn yǐng}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{开始|kāi shǐ}？
= What time does the film start?
{等|děng}{一会儿|yí huìr}！
= Wait a moment!
{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{门口|mén kǒu}{等|děng}{你|nǐ}。
= I'll wait for you at the entrance.
```

## Pronunciation

- {爱好|ài hào}: two falling tones. {好|hào} here is fourth tone; {好|hǎo} (good) is third.
- {画画儿|huà huàr}: two falling tones; the second has the *-r* ending (*huàr*).
- {一会儿|yí huìr}: *huìr* loses the *-i* sound in speech, close to *huèr*. {一|yí} rises before the
  fourth tone.
- {开始|kāi shǐ}: high level, then low. *shi* has the buzzing vowel after a curled-back *sh*.
- {跳舞|tiào wǔ}: falling, then low. {舞|wǔ} sounds like {五|wǔ} (five).
- {等|děng}: third tone, *-eng* as in {冷|lěng}.

## Common mistakes

- {爱好|ài hào} with the third tone: it's *ài hào*.
- {等|děng} + "for": ~~{等|děng}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}~~. The person follows {等|děng} directly: {等|děng}{你|nǐ}.
- {一起|yì qǐ} at the end, English-style: ~~{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{一起|yì qǐ}~~. It goes before the verb:
  {我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}.
- {一会儿|yí huìr} before the verb when you mean a duration: "wait a moment" is {等|děng}{一会儿|yí huìr},
  not ~~{一会儿|yí huìr}{等|děng}~~ (that would be "in a moment, wait").
- {跳舞|tiào wǔ} with a complement directly: ~~{跳舞|tiào wǔ}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}~~. Say {跳|tiào}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo} or
  {跳舞|tiào wǔ}{跳|tiào}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}.
- {=Writing 凵 of 画 first: the frame comes last.=}

## Key points

- {爱好|ài hào} *àihào*: hobby; {你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{什么|shén me}{爱好|ài hào}？ {我|wǒ}{的|de}{爱好|ài hào}{是|shì}….
- {画|huà} / {画画儿|huà huàr}; {跳舞|tiào wǔ} separates ({跳|tiào}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{的|de}{舞|wǔ}).
- ({跟|gēn} + person +) {一起|yì qǐ} + verb.
- {开始|kāi shǐ} + verb / noun / nothing; {开始|kāi shǐ}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}, at first.
- {等|děng} + person; {等|děng}{一会儿|yí huìr} (wait a while), {一会儿|yí huìr} + verb (in a moment).
- {动|dòng}: move; {不要|bú yào}{动|dòng}！
- ⺮ reviewed; 20 HSK 1 handwriting characters practised in this module.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Table tennis, badminton and the national sports
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 19 gave you {打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú} and {踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}. This honors lesson looks at the sports you
see every day in Chinese schools, parks and streets: table tennis, badminton, a kicking game with a
feathered shuttlecock, the exercises that whole schools do together, and the fans who follow
football and basketball. New words are glossed; none join your vocabulary reviews.

## Table tennis: {乒乓球|pīng pāng qiú}

The Chinese name copies the sound of the ball: *pīng*, *pāng*, back and forth. Table tennis was
invented in England in the early 1900s and first sold under the trade name "Ping-Pong"; it soon
spread to Japan and from there to China. Today it's so closely tied to China that it's often called
{国球|guó qiú}, "the national ball".

Part of the reason is how little it needs. Many schools, workplaces and parks have tables, often
made of concrete and left outside all year, and people bring their own bats. You'll see children
playing after school and older people playing in the morning, sometimes with a row of bricks for a
net.

{我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{在|zài}{公园|gōng yuán}{打|dǎ}{乒乓球|pīng pāng qiú}。 — My grandad plays table
tennis in the park every morning. ({公园|gōng yuán}: park, HSK 3)

{他|tā}{打|dǎ}{得|de}{非常|fēi cháng}{好|hǎo}，{我|wǒ}{打|dǎ}{不|bu}{过|guò}{他|tā}。 — He plays really well; I can't beat
him. ({打|dǎ}{不|bu}{过|guò}, "can't beat", is an HSK 3 pattern.)

Like every game played with a bat or the hands, it takes {打|dǎ}: {打|dǎ}{乒乓球|pīng pāng qiú}.

## Badminton: {羽毛球|yǔ máo qiú}

{羽毛球|yǔ máo qiú} is "feather ball", the shuttlecock, and the game played with it (an HSK 3 word).
Besides proper courts with a net, it's a favourite casual game: on a calm evening you'll often see
two people hitting a shuttlecock back and forth in a park, a courtyard or a quiet street, with no
net and no score, just keeping it in the air.

{晚上|wǎn shang}{我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{妈妈|mā ma}{在|zài}{楼|lóu}{下|xià}{打|dǎ}{羽毛球|yǔ máo qiú}。 — In the evening I play badminton
with my mum downstairs (outside our building).

## Kicking a shuttlecock: {踢|tī}{毽子|jiàn zi}

{毽子|jiàn zi} (*jianzi*) is a traditional game with a weighted shuttlecock, a few feathers fixed into a
small heavy base. The rule is simple: keep it in the air with any part of your body except your
hands, mostly your feet. Players kick it alone, counting how many times they keep it up, or stand
in a circle in a street or park and pass it round, showing off trick kicks. Because it's kicked,
the verb is {踢|tī}, as for football: {踢|tī}{毽子|jiàn zi}.

{你|nǐ}{能|néng}{踢|tī}{多少|duō shao}{个|gè}？ — How many (kicks) can you do?

## Exercising together: {广播体操|guǎng bō tǐ cāo}

{广播体操|guǎng bō tǐ cāo}, "broadcast exercises" or radio calisthenics, is a routine of movements done
to music and a counting voice, often from loudspeakers. China's first set was released in 1951, and
new sets have come out from time to time since; the ninth set was released in 2011. In many schools
the whole school lines up outside and does a set of exercises together every school day, usually in
a long break in the morning, and many adults remember the music from their own school days.

{我们|wǒ men}{学校|xué xiào}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{一起|yì qǐ}{做|zuò}{广播体操|guǎng bō tǐ cāo}。 — Our school does the
morning exercises together at ten every day.

Exercises are "done": {做|zuò}{操|cāo}, {做|zuò}{广播体操|guǎng bō tǐ cāo}. In the parks, older people have their
own morning routines: tai chi ({太极拳|tài jí quán}), walking, stretching, and in the evening dancing in
the square (lesson 20).

## Football and basketball fans

Football and basketball are hugely popular to play and to watch. China's professional basketball
league, the CBA, began with the 1995–96 season, and the top football league, the Chinese Super
League, in 2004. Many fans also follow foreign leagues and stay up late for matches played in
other time zones.

{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{还|hái}{没|méi}{睡觉|shuì jiào}，{在|zài}{看|kàn}{足球|zú qiú}{比赛|bǐ sài}。 — My dad hasn't gone to
bed yet: he's watching a football match. ({比赛|bǐ sài}: match, competition, HSK 3)

Fans say {看球|kàn qiú} (watch a match), and ask {谁|shéi}{赢|yíng}{了|le}？ (who won?: {赢|yíng}, to win).

## Reading: Grandad's table tennis

> {我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{今年|jīn nián}{七十|qī shí}{岁|suì}，{他|tā}{的|de}{爱好|ài hào}{是|shì}{打|dǎ}{乒乓球|pīng pāng qiú}。{他|tā}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{六|liù}{点|diǎn}{就|jiù}{起床|qǐ chuáng}，{跟|gēn}{朋友|péng you}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{公园|gōng yuán}{打|dǎ}{球|qiú}，{打|dǎ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。{公园|gōng yuán}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{人|rén}{运动|yùn dòng}：{有|yǒu}{的|de}{跑步|pǎo bù}，{有|yǒu}{的|de}{跳舞|tiào wǔ}，{也|yě}{有|yǒu}{踢|tī}{毽子|jiàn zi}{的|de}。{爷爷|yé ye}{打|dǎ}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{他|tā}{说|shuō}：“{多|duō}{运动|yùn dòng}，{身体|shēn tǐ}{就|jiù}{好|hǎo}。”{星期六|xīng qī liù}{他|tā}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{他|tā}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}，{他|tā}{教|jiāo}{我|wǒ}。

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

My grandad is seventy this year, and his hobby is table tennis. Every morning he gets up as early
as six and goes to the park with friends to play, for an hour. Lots of people exercise in the park:
some run, some dance, and some kick the shuttlecock. Grandad plays very well. He says: "Exercise
more and you'll be healthy." On Saturdays he has me go with him, and he teaches me.
</details>

## Words in this lesson

For recognition only; they aren't added to your vocabulary reviews.

| Word | Pinyin | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {乒乓球|pīng pāng qiú} | pīng pāng qiú | table tennis |
| {国球|guó qiú} | guó qiú | "national ball" (table tennis) |
| {羽毛球|yǔ máo qiú} | yǔ máo qiú | badminton; shuttlecock (HSK 3) |
| {毽子|jiàn zi} | jiàn zi | weighted shuttlecock for kicking |
| {广播体操|guǎng bō tǐ cāo} | guǎng bō tǐ cāo | radio calisthenics, school exercises |
| {太极拳|tài jí quán} | tài jí quán | tai chi |
| {公园|gōng yuán} | gōng yuán | park (HSK 3) |
| {比赛|bǐ sài} | bǐ sài | match, competition (HSK 3) |
| {赢|yíng} | yíng | to win |

lessons.title: School in China
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 16 gave you {高中|gāo zhōng}, {班|bān} and {开学|kāi xué}. This honors lesson follows a pupil through
the school system in mainland China: the stages, the school year, a school day, the uniform, and
the two big exams, one at the end of junior high school and the famous {高考|gāo kǎo} at the end of
senior high. Details vary from place to place, so take the times and dates as typical, not as
rules. New words are glossed; none join your vocabulary reviews.

## The stages: six, three, three

| Stage | Chinese | Usual length | Pupils |
|---|---|---|---|
| primary school | {小学|xiǎo xué} | 6 years, usually from age 6 | {小学生|xiǎo xué shēng} |
| junior high school | {初中|chū zhōng} (HSK 3) | 3 years | {初中生|chū zhōng shēng} |
| senior high school | {高中|gāo zhōng} | 3 years | {高中生|gāo zhōng shēng} |
| university | {大学|dà xué} | usually 4 years | {大学生|dà xué shēng} |

Primary and junior high school together make up nine years of compulsory education: every child
must have them. {初中|chū zhōng} and {高中|gāo zhōng} are the two halves of {中学|zhōng xué} (secondary school),
and many schools have both.

{我|wǒ}{弟弟|dì di}{上|shàng}{小学|xiǎo xué}，{我|wǒ}{上|shàng}{高中|gāo zhōng}。 — My little brother is at primary school, and
I'm at senior high.

Pupils talk about their year with {年级|nián jí} (grade, year; HSK 3): {我|wǒ}{上|shàng}{三|sān}{年级|nián jí}, "I'm in year
three". Within a year, pupils belong to a {班|bān}, a class that stays together for most lessons.

## The exam after junior high: {中考|zhōng kǎo}

At the end of junior high school, at about fifteen, pupils take an entrance exam set locally, by
their city or province: {中考|zhōng kǎo}. Its results decide which senior high school they can go to,
or whether they go to a vocational school ({职业学校|zhí yè xué xiào}) instead.

## The school year

The school year starts at the beginning of September ({九|jiǔ}{月|yuè}{一|yī}{号|hào}{开学|kāi xué} is typical)
and has two terms: an autumn term, then a spring term. Between them comes the winter holiday,
{寒假|hán jià}, a few weeks around the Spring Festival in January or February. The summer holiday,
{暑假|shǔ jià}, runs from early or mid July to the end of August. Beijing's calendar for 2023–24, for
example, started on 1 September and broke up for the summer in July (on 8 July for primary and junior high
schools, a week later for senior high).

{你们|nǐ men}{什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{放|fàng}{寒假|hán jià}？ — When does your winter holiday start? ({放|fàng}{假|jià}: to
break up for the holiday, HSK 3)

## A school day

A typical day starts early, often around half past seven, and is divided into lessons of about
forty-five minutes. Lessons are counted with {节|jié} (HSK 3): {今天|jīn tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}{有|yǒu}{四|sì}{节|jié}{课|kè},
"we have four lessons this morning".

Two things in the day surprise many visitors:

- **Exercises together.** In many schools, everyone goes out to the sports ground in a long morning
  break and does a set of exercises to music: the {广播体操|guǎng bō tǐ cāo} of the last honors lesson.
- **Eye exercises.** {眼保健操|yǎn bǎo jiàn cāo}, introduced in the 1960s: to recorded music and counting,
  pupils close their eyes and press and rub points around the eyes, meant to rest them after reading.

After school comes homework, {作业|zuò yè} (HSK 3), and for senior high pupils often more study in the
evening, at school or at home.

{下课|xià kè}{以后|yǐ hòu}{我|wǒ}{留|liú}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{写|xiě}{作业|zuò yè}。 — After class I stay at school and do my
homework. ({以后|yǐ hòu}, after: HSK 3)

## The uniform: {校服|xiào fú}

Most state schools have a uniform, {校服|xiào fú} ({校|xiào} from {学校|xué xiào} + {服|fú} from {衣服|yī fu}). The most
familiar style, common since the 1990s, is a loose tracksuit in the school's colours, worn every
day, not just for sport. Many pupils and former pupils joke about how shapeless it is. Some schools
have more formal uniforms with shirts and blazers.

{我们|wǒ men}{学校|xué xiào}{的|de}{校服|xiào fú}{是|shì}{蓝色|lán sè}{的|de}。 — Our school uniform is blue. ({蓝色|lán sè}, blue)

## {高考|gāo kǎo}: the college entrance exam

{高考|gāo kǎo} is short for the national college entrance examination, the main way into
university. It's held every year in early June, starting on 7 June, and lasts two days or more,
depending on the province. Every candidate takes Chinese, mathematics and a foreign language; the
other subjects depend on the province's rules and the pupil's choices. The exam in its present form
was restarted in 1977, after several years without it. It is taken very seriously: in 2025 about
13.35 million people registered for it, and families and schools do all they can to keep things
calm for the candidates during those days.

{我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge}{今年|jīn nián}{高考|gāo kǎo}，{我们|wǒ men}{家|jiā}{的|de}{人|rén}{都|dōu}{希望|xī wàng}{他|tā}{考|kǎo}{得|de}{好|hǎo}。 — My elder
brother takes the gaokao this year, and all of us at home hope he does well.

{高考|gāo kǎo} is {高|gāo} ("higher", for higher education: colleges and universities) + {考|kǎo}, the verb
of lesson 17. {中考|zhōng kǎo} is built the same way, with {中|zhōng} for secondary schools.

## Reading: a senior high pupil's day

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{林海|Lín Hǎi}，{是|shì}{高中生|gāo zhōng shēng}，{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{上|shàng}{高中|gāo zhōng}。{我们|wǒ men}{早上|zǎo shang}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{半|bàn}{到|dào}{学校|xué xiào}，{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{开始|kāi shǐ}{上课|shàng kè}。{上午|shàng wǔ}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}，{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{做|zuò}{广播体操|guǎng bō tǐ cāo}。{中午|zhōng wǔ}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}，{休息|xiū xi}{一会儿|yí huìr}。{下午|xià wǔ}{五|wǔ}{点|diǎn}{下课|xià kè}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{同学|tóng xué}{打|dǎ}{半|bàn}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{篮球|lán qiú}，{然后|rán hòu}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{写|xiě}{作业|zuò yè}。{我|wǒ}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}，{但是|dàn shì}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}。{明年|míng nián}{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{高考|gāo kǎo}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{希望|xī wàng}{能|néng}{上|shàng}{一|yí}{个|gè}{好|hǎo}{大学|dà xué}。

{然后|rán hòu}: then, after that; {以后|yǐ hòu}: after (both HSK 3).

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

My name is Lin Hai. I'm a senior high school pupil in Beijing. We get to school at half past seven
in the morning and lessons start at eight. At ten we do the exercises together. At noon we eat at
school and rest for a while. After lessons end at five, I play basketball with classmates for half
an hour, then go home and do my homework. I'm busy every day, but happy. Next year I'll take the
gaokao; I hope I can get into a good university.
</details>

## Words in this lesson

For recognition only; they aren't added to your vocabulary reviews.

| Word | Pinyin | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {初中|chū zhōng} | chū zhōng | junior high school (HSK 3) |
| {年级|nián jí} | nián jí | grade, year (HSK 3) |
| {中考|zhōng kǎo} | zhōng kǎo | senior high school entrance exam |
| {职业学校|zhí yè xué xiào} | zhí yè xué xiào | vocational school |
| {寒假|hán jià} | hán jià | winter holiday |
| {暑假|shǔ jià} | shǔ jià | summer holiday |
| {放假|fàng jià} | fàng jià | to be on holiday, break up (HSK 3) |
| {节|jié} | jié | (measure word for lessons) (HSK 3) |
| {眼保健操|yǎn bǎo jiàn cāo} | yǎn bǎo jiàn cāo | eye exercises |
| {作业|zuò yè} | zuò yè | homework (HSK 3) |
| {校服|xiào fú} | xiào fú | school uniform |
| {高考|gāo kǎo} | gāo kǎo | national college entrance exam |

lessons.title: At the café: 点, 还是, 别
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This module takes you out of the house: to cafés and restaurants, round a shopping centre, online
and out into the weather. It starts with something you'll do on your first day in any Chinese
city: buying a drink. You'll learn the words for coffee and three everyday teas, the verb
{点|diǎn} "to order", and two pieces of grammar you'll hear at every counter: questions that offer
a choice ("coffee or tea?") with {还是|hái shi}, and telling someone not to do something with
{别|bié} ("don't forget!"). By the end you can order for yourself and a friend, answer the
questions a server asks, and read a short message about meeting at a café.

## Drinks: {咖啡|kā fēi} and three kinds of tea

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {咖啡|kā fēi} | coffee | a loanword: the two syllables imitate the sound of "coffee" |
| {茶|chá} | tea | HSK 1 |
| {红茶|hóng chá} | black tea | literally "red tea": Chinese names it after the colour of the drink |
| {绿茶|lǜ chá} | green tea | {绿|lǜ} as in {绿色|lǜ sè} (green, lesson 03) |
| {奶茶|nǎi chá} | milk tea | tea with milk, usually sweet; {奶|nǎi} as in {牛奶|niú nǎi} |
| {牛奶|niú nǎi} | milk | HSK 1 |
| {水|shuǐ} | water | HSK 1 |

{红茶|hóng chá} trips up English speakers: what English calls "black tea" is "red tea" in Chinese,
because the tea in the cup is reddish brown. (Chinese also has a {黑茶|hēi chá}, "black tea" word for
word, but that's a different group of fermented teas, called "dark tea" in English.) So when a menu says {红茶|hóng chá}, expect an
ordinary cup of black tea.

{奶茶|nǎi chá} covers anything from tea with milk to the sweet, iced drinks sold at tea shops,
often with chewy tapioca balls: {珍珠|zhēn zhū}{奶茶|nǎi chá}, "pearl milk tea", known in English as
bubble tea.

Drinks are counted by the cup with {杯|bēi}, which you met as a measure word in HSK 1 ({杯子|bēi zi}
is a cup): {一|yì}{杯|bēi}{咖啡|kā fēi} (a coffee), {两|liǎng}{杯|bēi}{奶茶|nǎi chá} (two milk
teas). Cafés sell sizes the same way: {大杯|dà bēi} (large), {小杯|xiǎo bēi} (small), and in many
chains {中杯|zhōng bēi} (medium).

## Ordering: {点|diǎn}

You know {点|diǎn} as "o'clock" ({三|sān}{点|diǎn}) and from {一点儿|yì diǎnr} (a little). It is
also a verb, "to order" food or drink, choosing from a menu:

{我们|wǒ men}{点|diǎn}{菜|cài}{吧|ba}。 — Let's order (the dishes).
{你|nǐ}{点|diǎn}{什么|shén me}？ — What are you ordering?
{我|wǒ}{点|diǎn}{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{绿茶|lǜ chá}。 — I'll order a green tea.
{我|wǒ}{点|diǎn}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{菜|cài}。 — I've ordered two dishes.

{点|diǎn}{菜|cài} (to order dishes) is the set phrase in restaurants. The menu is
{菜单|cài dān} (an HSK 3 word).

{点|diǎn} and {要|yào} both work when you order. {要|yào} is "I'll have…" at the counter:
{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{咖啡|kā fēi}。 {点|diǎn} names the act of ordering, so you need it
when you talk *about* ordering: {你|nǐ}{点|diǎn}{了|le}{什么|shén me}？ (What did you order?),
{我|wǒ}{来|lái}{点|diǎn}。 (I'll order.) You'll hear a server ask
{您|nín}{要|yào}{点|diǎn}{什么|shén me}？ (What would you like to order?) with both.

On a phone or computer {点|diǎn} is "to tap, to click": {点|diǎn}{这儿|zhèr} (tap here),
{点|diǎn}{一下|yí xià} (give it a tap). It's the same verb: you pick something by touching it.

## Coffee or tea? Choice questions with {还是|hái shi}

A **[[choice question]]** offers two (or more) answers and asks the listener to pick one. Put
{还是|hái shi} ("or") between the options:

{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}{还是|hái shi}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}？ — Are you having coffee or tea?
{你|nǐ}{要|yào}{大杯|dà bēi}{还是|hái shi}{小杯|xiǎo bēi}？ — Do you want a large or a small?
{你|nǐ}{今天|jīn tiān}{去|qù}{还是|hái shi}{明天|míng tiān}{去|qù}？ — Are you going today or tomorrow?
{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{还是|hái shi}{他|tā}{去|qù}？ — Are you going, or is he?

Four rules:

1. **No {吗|ma}.** The {还是|hái shi} already makes it a question, so ~~{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}{还是|hái shi}{茶|chá}{吗|ma}？~~ is wrong.
   A soft {呢|ne} at the end is fine: {你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}{还是|hái shi}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}{呢|ne}？
2. **Each option can be a whole verb phrase**, and repeating the verb is common and clear:
   {喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}{还是|hái shi}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}. When only the object changes, you can drop the
   second verb: {你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}{还是|hái shi}{茶|chá}？
3. **With {是|shì}, don't double it.** {还是|hái shi} already ends in {是|shì}, so
   "Are you a teacher or a student?" is {你|nǐ}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}{还是|hái shi}{学生|xué sheng}？,
   never ~~{还是|hái shi}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}~~.
4. **Answer with your choice**, not "yes": {喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 or just {茶|chá}。 For "either is fine",
   say {都|dōu}{可以|kě yǐ}。

### {还是|hái shi} or {或者|huò zhě}?

English has one "or"; Chinese has two. {还是|hái shi} is the "or" of questions: you want the
listener to choose. In a statement ("tea or coffee, either is fine"), Chinese uses
{或者|huò zhě}, an HSK 3 word: {我|wǒ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}{或者|huò zhě}{咖啡|kā fēi}{都|dōu}{可以|kě yǐ}。 For
now, remember: a question that asks you to pick takes {还是|hái shi}.

{还是|hái shi} has two more uses, "still" and "had better", which lesson 26 covers. In this
lesson it's always the "or" of a question.

### Choice question or A-not-A?

Compare the two kinds of question you now have:

| Question | Kind | Expected answer |
|---|---|---|
| {你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{不|bu}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}？ | A-not-A: yes or no | {喝|hē}。/ {不|bù}{喝|hē}。 |
| {你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}{还是|hái shi}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}？ | choice: this or that | {喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}。/ {喝|hē}{茶|chá}。 |

## Don't! {别|bié} + verb

To tell someone not to do something, put {别|bié} before the verb. This is the
**[[imperative with 别]]**, the everyday spoken "don't":

{别|bié}{走|zǒu}！ — Don't go!
{别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le}！ — Don't forget!
{别|bié}{喝|hē}{太|tài}{多|duō}{咖啡|kā fēi}。 — Don't drink too much coffee.
{你|nǐ}{别|bié}{等|děng}{我|wǒ}。 — Don't wait for me.
{别|bié}{客气|kè qi}！ — Don't stand on ceremony! / Help yourself!

{别|bié}{客气|kè qi} is what a host says to a guest who holds back ({客气|kè qi}: polite, formal),
and also a reply to thanks, like {不客气|bú kè qi}.

**{别|bié}…{了|le}** means "stop…" or "don't bother any more": the {了|le} says the situation should
change. {别|bié}{说|shuō}{了|le}！ (Stop talking! / Say no more!), {别|bié}{看|kàn}{手机|shǒu jī}{了|le}！
(Put your phone away!), {你|nǐ}{别|bié}{来|lái}{了|le}。 (Don't come after all.)

**{别|bié} or {不要|bú yào}?** They mean the same: you learned {不要|bú yào} + verb in HSK 1.
{别|bié} is shorter and the usual choice in conversation; {不要|bú yào} sounds a little firmer, and
it's what you'll see on signs ({请|qǐng}{不要|bú yào}…, "please do not…"). Both soften with
{请|qǐng}: {请|qǐng}{别|bié}{走|zǒu}, {请|qǐng}{不要|bú yào}{走|zǒu}.

**Not {不|bù} or {没|méi}.** {不|bù}{走|zǒu} is a statement ("(I'm) not going"), not an order, and
{没|méi} is for what didn't happen. A command not to do something needs {别|bié} or {不要|bú yào}.

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 咖 | (the "ka" of coffee) | kā | 口 | 8 | {咖啡|kā fēi} |
| 啡 | (the "fei" of coffee) | fēi | 口 | 11 | {咖啡|kā fēi} |
| 别 (traditional 別) | don't; other; to part | bié | 刂 | 7 | {别|bié}, {别|bié}{客气|kè qi}, {别的|bié de} (other, HSK 3) |

咖 and 啡 are the same in traditional script.

### How the characters are built

- {咖啡|kā fēi}: two characters made to write a borrowed sound. Each has 口 (mouth) on the left, a
  sign used in many loanwords and sound words to say "read this for its sound", and a sound part
  on the right: {加|jiā} (to add, HSK 3) in 咖, {非|fēi} (as in {非常|fēi cháng}) in 啡. Neither
  character is used on its own, and {咖啡|kā fēi} is by far their most common word (咖 is also
  read *gā* in {咖喱|gā lí}, curry).
- {别|bié}: on the right is 刂, the "standing knife" ({立刀旁|lì dāo páng}) of {到|dào} and
  {前|qián}. The oldest meaning of 别 is "to separate, to divide", as a knife does; "other" and
  "don't" grew out of that. The traditional form 別 has the same parts; only the lower left is
  drawn a little differently.

Radical review: **口** ({口字旁|kǒu zì páng} on the left) marks things done with the mouth
({吃|chī}, {喝|hē}, {叫|jiào}) and sound words ({吗|ma}, {呢|ne}, {吧|ba}, {喂|wèi}), and now the sound
of a foreign word. **刂** (knife) is the radical of {到|dào}, {前|qián} and {别|bié}.

### Stroke order

- 啡: 口 first, small, then 非. In 非 the left half comes first: its vertical, the two short
  horizontals that run up to it, and the rising stroke at the bottom; then the right vertical and
  its three horizontals.
- 别: 口, then the hooked stroke and the left-falling stroke under it, then 刂: the short vertical
  before the long hooked one.

```trace
咖啡别
```

=}

## Dialogue: at a café

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) and {李明|Lǐ Míng} (李明) are at a café after class; the third speaker is the
{服务员|fú wù yuán} (服务员), the server (not a course word).

```dialogue
# At a café
服务员: {您好|nín hǎo}！{请问|qǐng wèn}，{您|nín}{要|yào}{点|diǎn}{什么|shén me}？
= Hello! What would you like to order?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{要|yào}{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{咖啡|kā fēi}。
= I'll have a coffee.
服务员: {大杯|dà bēi}{还是|hái shi}{小杯|xiǎo bēi}？
= Large or small?
安娜: {大杯|dà bēi}，{谢谢|xiè xie}。{李明|Lǐ Míng}，{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}{还是|hái shi}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}？
= Large, thanks. Li Ming, are you having coffee or tea?
李明: {我|wǒ}{晚上|wǎn shang}{不|bù}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}。{我|wǒ}{点|diǎn}{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{绿茶|lǜ chá}{吧|ba}。
= I don't drink coffee in the evening. I'll order a green tea.
服务员: {好|hǎo}。{你们|nǐ men}{还|hái}{要|yào}{什么|shén me}？
= OK. Anything else?
安娜: {你们|nǐ men}{有|yǒu}{奶茶|nǎi chá}{吗|ma}？
= Do you have milk tea?
服务员: {有|yǒu}。{红茶|hóng chá}{的|de}{还是|hái shi}{绿茶|lǜ chá}{的|de}？
= Yes. With black tea or green tea?
安娜: {红茶|hóng chá}{的|de}。
= Black tea.
李明: {安娜|Ān nà}，{别|bié}{点|diǎn}{太|tài}{多|duō}！{你|nǐ}{能|néng}{喝|hē}{两|liǎng}{杯|bēi}{吗|ma}？
= Anna, don't order too much! Can you drink two?
安娜: {奶茶|nǎi chá}{不|bú}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}，{是|shì}{王芳|Wáng Fāng}{的|de}。{她|tā}{一会儿|yí huìr}{就|jiù}{来|lái}。
= The milk tea isn't mine, it's Wang Fang's. She'll be here in a moment.
李明: {好|hǎo}。{别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}。
= OK. Don't forget, we're going to the cinema at seven.
```

Three choice questions, none with {吗|ma}, and each answered by naming the choice:
{大杯|dà bēi}, {红茶|hóng chá}{的|de}. {红茶|hóng chá}{的|de} is "the black-tea one", the {的|de}
phrase standing for a noun (lesson 03). Li Ming's {我|wǒ}{点|diǎn}…{吧|ba} makes a decision sound
easy-going: "I'll go for…".

## Reading: a message from Wang Fang

Anna gets this message on her phone.

> {安娜|Ān nà}，{我|wǒ}{到|dào}{咖啡|kā fēi}{店|diàn}{了|le}，{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{门口|mén kǒu}{旁边|páng biān}。{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{什么|shén me}？{咖啡|kā fēi}{还是|hái shi}{奶茶|nǎi chá}？{我|wǒ}{现在|xiàn zài}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{点|diǎn}。{这儿|zhèr}{的|de}{绿茶|lǜ chá}{也|yě}{不错|bú cuò}，{不|bú}{太|tài}{贵|guì}，{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{十五|shí wǔ}{块|kuài}。{你|nǐ}{别|bié}{坐|zuò}{公交车|gōng jiāo chē}{了|le}，{现在|xiàn zài}{路上|lù shang}{车|chē}{很|hěn}{多|duō}。{走路|zǒu lù}{来|lái}{吧|ba}，{十|shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}{就|jiù}{到|dào}。{我|wǒ}{五|wǔ}{点|diǎn}{要|yào}{上课|shàng kè}，{你|nǐ}{别|bié}{来|lái}{太|tài}{晚|wǎn}！

Read it once for the gist, then slowly. Then answer:

1. Where is the café?
2. What does Wang Fang say about the green tea?
3. How should Anna come, and why?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Next to the school gate ({在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{门口|mén kǒu}{旁边|páng biān}).
2. It's good too and not too expensive: fifteen kuai a cup.
3. On foot, not by bus: the roads are busy now, and it's only ten minutes' walk.

"Anna, I've got to the café; it's next to the school gate. What are you having? Coffee or milk
tea? I'll order for you now. The green tea here is good too, and not too expensive: fifteen kuai a
cup. Don't bother taking the bus, there's a lot of traffic right now. Walk here: you'll be here in
ten minutes. I have class at five, so don't be too late!"
</details>

{咖啡|kā fēi}{店|diàn} is "coffee shop": {店|diàn} makes shop names, as in {书店|shū diàn} and
{药店|yào diàn}. The {别|bié}…{了|le} in {你|nǐ}{别|bié}{坐|zuò}{公交车|gōng jiāo chē}{了|le} is the
"don't bother" use: Anna had probably planned to.

## Say it

```speak
{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{咖啡|kā fēi}。
= I'll have a coffee.
{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}{还是|hái shi}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}？
= Are you having coffee or tea?
{大杯|dà bēi}{还是|hái shi}{小杯|xiǎo bēi}？
= Large or small?
{我们|wǒ men}{点|diǎn}{菜|cài}{吧|ba}。
= Let's order.
{别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le}！
= Don't forget!
{别|bié}{客气|kè qi}！
= Make yourself at home!
```

## Pronunciation

- {咖啡|kā fēi}: two high, level first tones. Keep both up; English speakers tend to stress the
  first syllable and drop the second.
- {绿茶|lǜ chá}: *lǜ* has the rounded *ü* (say "ee" with your lips pushed forward). *lù* (road,
  {路|lù}) is a different syllable, so keep the dots: type `lv4` or `lu:4`.
- {还是|hái shi}: a rising *hái*, then a short, light *shi*. In {还是|hái shi} the {是|shì} loses its
  tone.
- {别|bié} rises, like a question: *bié*. Said sharply, {别|bié}{走|zǒu}！ is two quick syllables, a
  rising and then a dipping tone.
- {奶茶|nǎi chá}: a third tone before a second tone is said low, a "half third": the dip doesn't
  climb back up.
- {点|diǎn}{菜|cài} and {点|diǎn}{一下|yí xià}: *diǎn* before a fourth tone is also a low half
  third.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}{还是|hái shi}{茶|chá}{吗|ma}？~~: a choice question takes no {吗|ma}.
- ~~{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{学生|xué sheng}{还是|hái shi}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}？~~: the {是|shì} is already in
  {还是|hái shi}.
- Using {还是|hái shi} in a statement: "I'll drink tea or coffee" isn't a question, so it needs
  {或者|huò zhě} (HSK 3), not {还是|hái shi}.
- ~~{不|bù}{走|zǒu}！~~ or ~~{没|méi}{走|zǒu}！~~ for "Don't go!": the command is {别|bié}{走|zǒu}！
- Answering a choice question with "yes": answer with the thing you choose, {喝|hē}{茶|chá}。
- Translating {红茶|hóng chá} as "red tea": it's ordinary black tea.

## Key points

- Drinks: {咖啡|kā fēi}, {红茶|hóng chá} (black tea), {绿茶|lǜ chá}, {奶茶|nǎi chá}; count them with
  {杯|bēi}: {一|yì}{杯|bēi}{咖啡|kā fēi}.
- {点|diǎn} is "to order" ({点|diǎn}{菜|cài}, {点|diǎn}{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{茶|chá}) and "to tap, click" on a
  screen.
- Choice questions: A {还是|hái shi} B？ No {吗|ma}; answer by choosing. {或者|huò zhě} is the "or" of
  statements (HSK 3).
- {别|bié} + verb: "don't…"; {别|bié}…{了|le}: "stop…, don't bother". {不要|bú yào} means the same,
  a little firmer.
- {=Characters: 咖 and 啡 write the sound of "coffee"; 别 (traditional 別) has the knife radical 刂.=}

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Eating out: 这么, 那样 and approximate numbers
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 21 got you a drink; this one gets you a meal. You'll learn {饭馆|fàn guǎn} (a restaurant),
{肉|ròu} (meat) and {鱼|yú} (fish), the measure word {条|tiáo} for long, thin things such as fish,
trousers and roads, and two pairs of words that make your Chinese sound much more natural:
{这么|zhè me} / {那么|nà me} ("so": so tasty, so expensive) and {这样|zhè yàng} / {那样|nà yàng}
("like this, like that"). Then a skill you'll need for every price and every crowd:
**[[approximate numbers]]**, "a dozen or so", "twenty-odd", "two or three".

## Places to eat: {饭馆|fàn guǎn} and {饭店|fàn diàn}

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {饭馆|fàn guǎn} | restaurant (an everyday one) | a small or ordinary place to eat; very common in speech |
| {饭店|fàn diàn} | restaurant; hotel | HSK 1; often a bigger restaurant, and in names often a hotel |

{饭馆|fàn guǎn} is the everyday word for a place where you sit down to eat: a family-run
noodle shop, a local restaurant round the corner. {饭店|fàn diàn} can be a restaurant too, usually a
bigger one, but in names it is often a hotel. If you want somewhere to eat tonight, {饭馆|fàn guǎn}
is the safe word.

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{旁边|páng biān}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小|xiǎo}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}。 — There's a little restaurant next to my home.
{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吧|ba}。 — Let's go and eat at a restaurant.

The {馆|guǎn} in {饭馆|fàn guǎn} is a building for a purpose. You'll meet it again in HSK 3 in
{图书馆|tú shū guǎn} (library) and {宾馆|bīn guǎn} (hotel).

## Meat and fish: {肉|ròu}, {鱼|yú}

{肉|ròu} is meat. Put an animal in front to say which meat; you know two of the animals already:

| Word | Meaning | Built from |
|---|---|---|
| {牛肉|niú ròu} | beef | {牛|niú} (cow, as in {牛奶|niú nǎi}) + {肉|ròu} |
| {鸡肉|jī ròu} | chicken (the meat) | {鸡|jī} (chicken, as in {鸡蛋|jī dàn}) + {肉|ròu} |
| {猪肉|zhū ròu} | pork | {猪|zhū} (pig, not a course word) + {肉|ròu} |
| {鱼|yú} | fish | the animal and the food |

In much of China, {肉|ròu} on its own on a menu or in a recipe usually means pork, the most eaten
meat; when it's beef or lamb, the menu says so. {鱼|yú} is both the animal in the water and the
fish on the plate; there's no separate word as in "pig / pork".

{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{吃|chī}{肉|ròu}，{我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{鱼|yú}。 — I don't eat meat; I eat fish.
{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{牛肉|niú ròu}{还是|hái shi}{鸡肉|jī ròu}？ — Do you prefer beef or chicken?

## Long, thin things: {条|tiáo}

{条|tiáo} is the measure word for things that are long and thin, or that you think of that way.
You know the character from {面条儿|miàn tiáor} (noodles: "flour strips").

| | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| fish | {一|yì}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú} | a fish |
| trousers | {一|yì}{条|tiáo}{裤子|kù zi} | a pair of trousers |
| roads | {这|zhè}{条|tiáo}{路|lù} | this road |
| dogs (also {只|zhī}) | {一|yì}{条|tiáo}{狗|gǒu} | a dog |

A fish is long and thin; so are trousers (one pair, one {条|tiáo}: Chinese doesn't count the legs)
and roads. For dogs you learned {只|zhī} in HSK 1, and that's always right; {一|yì}{条|tiáo}{狗|gǒu},
seeing the dog as a long animal, is common in many places too.

{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{黑色|hēi sè}{的|de}{裤子|kù zi}。 — I bought a pair of black trousers.
{这|zhè}{条|tiáo}{路|lù}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}。 — There are lots of restaurants on this street.

## So tasty! {这么|zhè me} and {那么|nà me} + adjective

{这么|zhè me} and {那么|nà me} before an adjective mean "so", "this" or "that" in the sense of degree:

{这个|zhè ge}{菜|cài}{这么|zhè me}{好吃|hǎo chī}！ — This dish is so good!
{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú}{那么|nà me}{贵|guì}？ — A fish costs that much?
{今天|jīn tiān}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}{里|lǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{这么|zhè me}{多|duō}{人|rén}？ — Why are there so many people in the restaurant today?

{这么|zhè me} ("this") is for what's here or happening now; {那么|nà me} ("that") is for something
further away: what someone else just said, or another place or time.

{北京|Běi jīng}{这么|zhè me}{冷|lěng}！ — (said in Beijing) It's so cold here in Beijing!
{北京|Běi jīng}{那么|nà me}{冷|lěng}{吗|ma}？ — (said elsewhere) Is it that cold in Beijing?

They replace {很|hěn}: don't say ~~{这么|zhè me}{很|hěn}{好吃|hǎo chī}~~. And {怎么|zěn me}{这么|zhè me}… ("how
come it's so…?") is a very common way to show surprise, as in the third example.

{那么|nà me} has one more use, at the start of a sentence: "then, in that case".
{那么|nà me}，{我们|wǒ men}{明天|míng tiān}{去|qù}{吧|ba}。 — Then let's go tomorrow. In speech this is often
shortened to {那|nà}: {那|nà}{我们|wǒ men}{走|zǒu}{吧|ba}。

## Like this, like that: {这样|zhè yàng}, {那样|nà yàng}

{这样|zhè yàng} and {那样|nà yàng} describe a manner or a kind: "like this, this way", "like that,
that kind of". They go in three places:

| Where | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| before a verb (how) | {这样|zhè yàng}{做|zuò}{很|hěn}{好吃|hǎo chī}。 | Made this way, it's delicious. |
| before {的|de} + noun (what kind) | {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{买|mǎi}{那样|nà yàng}{的|de}{手表|shǒu biǎo}。 | I'd like to buy a watch like that. |
| as the predicate | {不|bú}{是|shì}{这样|zhè yàng}。 | It's not like that. / That's not how it is. |

{你|nǐ}{看|kàn}，{饺子|jiǎo zi}{要|yào}{这样|zhè yàng}{包|bāo}。 — Look, you wrap dumplings like this.
{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{想|xiǎng}{要|yào}{这样|zhè yàng}{的|de}{裤子|kù zi}。 — I'd like trousers like these too.
{晚上|wǎn shang}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{这样|zhè yàng}。 — It's always like this in the evening.

(The {包|bāo} "to wrap" in the first example is lesson 23's word.)

**{这么|zhè me} or {这样|zhè yàng}?** Before an adjective, use {这么|zhè me}: {这么|zhè me}{好吃|hǎo chī}
(so tasty). Before {的|de} and a noun, or as the predicate, use {这样|zhè yàng}. Before a verb, both
work: {这么|zhè me}{做|zuò} = {这样|zhè yàng}{做|zuò}, "do it like this".

## Approximate numbers

When you don't know or don't need the exact number, Chinese has three handy patterns. Together they
are the approximate numbers of this level.

### 1. {几|jǐ}: "a few", "-odd" in the teens and tens

You know {几|jǐ} as "how many?". In a statement it means "a few, several":

| Chinese | Meaning | Range |
|---|---|---|
| {几|jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén} | a few people | about 2–9 |
| {十几|shí jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén} | a dozen or so people, a few more than ten | 11–19 |
| {几十|jǐ shí}{个|gè}{人|rén} | dozens of people, several tens | 20–90 |
| {几|jǐ}{百|bǎi}{块|kuài} | a few hundred kuai | 200–900 |

{饭馆|fàn guǎn}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{十几|shí jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén}。 — There are a dozen or so people in the restaurant.
{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{中国|Zhōng guó}{朋友|péng you}。 — I have a few Chinese friends.

Only context tells you whether {几|jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén} asks ("how many people?", with a question
mark) or states ("a few people").

### 2. {多|duō} after a number: "and a bit", "-odd"

{多|duō} after a number means "more than, and a bit": {二十多|èr shí duō} is "twenty-odd", 21 to 29.
Where {多|duō} goes depends on the number:

| Number | {多|duō} goes | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| ends in zero (10, 20, 100…) | after the number, before the measure word | {二十多|èr shí duō}{块|kuài}{钱|qián} | twenty-odd kuai |
| | | {一百多|yì bǎi duō}{个|gè}{人|rén} | a hundred-odd people |
| 1–9 | after the measure word | {一|yí}{个|gè}{多|duō}{小时|xiǎo shí} | an hour and a bit |
| | | {三|sān}{块|kuài}{多|duō}{钱|qián} | three kuai and a bit (3.10, 3.50…) |

The difference matters: {十多|shí duō}{块|kuài} is 11 to 19 kuai, but {十|shí}{块|kuài}{多|duō} is ten
kuai and some change, 10.10 to 10.90.

### 3. Two numbers side by side: "two or three"

Two neighbouring numbers together give a rough guess, just like "two or three" or "five or six":
{两三|liǎng sān}{个|gè}{人|rén} (two or three people), {三四|sān sì}{天|tiān} (three or four days),
{七八|qī bā}{个|gè}{菜|cài} (seven or eight dishes). Use {两|liǎng}, not {二|èr}, at the start:
{两三|liǎng sān}{个|gè}. There's no comma and no "or" word between them.

{这|zhè}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú}{很|hěn}{大|dà}，{三四|sān sì}{个|gè}{人|rén}{吃|chī}{没|méi}{问题|wèn tí}。 — This fish is big: three or four people can eat it, no problem.

Don't combine the patterns: ~~{十几多|shí jǐ duō}~~ isn't a number. The reference sheet "Numbers in
HSK 2" has all three patterns with prices.

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 馆 (traditional 館) | building (for a purpose) | guǎn | 饣 | 11 | {饭馆|fàn guǎn}, {图书馆|tú shū guǎn} (library, HSK 3) |
| 肉 | meat | ròu | 肉 | 6 | {肉|ròu}, {牛肉|niú ròu}, {鸡肉|jī ròu} |
| 鱼 (traditional 魚) | fish | yú | 鱼 | 8 | {鱼|yú} |

### How the characters are built

- 馆 = 饣 (food) + {官|guān} (an official), which gives the sound: *guān* → *guǎn*. Old guesthouses
  where officials and travellers ate and slept were 馆, and the food radical fits a place to eat. In
  traditional script the radical is written in its full form, 食 squeezed onto the left: 館.
- 肉 began as a drawing of a piece of meat, with lines across it. As a part of other characters it
  is usually squeezed into the "meat moon" ⺼ you met in HSK 1 ({脑|nǎo} in {电脑|diàn nǎo}), which
  looks just like 月.
- 鱼 is a picture of a fish standing on its tail: the head at the top, the body with its scales in
  the middle (the 田 shape) and the tail at the bottom. Simplified script writes the tail as one
  long stroke; traditional 魚 keeps four dots there, the old fins of the tail. Those four dots
  look like the "fire" dots of {热|rè} and {点|diǎn}, but here they have nothing to do with fire.

Radical review: **饣**, the food radical ({食字旁|shí zì páng}), is on the left of {饭|fàn},
{饺|jiǎo} and now {馆|guǎn}. **月** and **⺼** look the same: the moon of {明|míng} and the meat of
{脑|nǎo}.

### Stroke order

- 肉: the frame first (the left vertical, then the top and right side with its hook), then the two
  人 inside, the upper one first. The upper 人's first stroke starts above the frame and cuts through
  its top.
- 鱼: the short left-falling stroke and the bent stroke at the top first, then 田 (left side, top
  and right side, the middle horizontal, the middle vertical, the bottom), and the long tail stroke
  last.
- 馆: 饣 first, three strokes (the last a vertical that turns up to the right), then 官 from the
  top down.

```trace
馆肉鱼
```

=}

## Dialogue: at a small restaurant

{王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) takes her classmate {大卫|Dà wèi} (大卫) to a restaurant near the school.
The {服务员|fú wù yuán} (服务员) is the server.

```dialogue
# At a small restaurant
服务员: {你们|nǐ men}{几|jǐ}{位|wèi}？
= How many of you?
大卫: {两|liǎng}{位|wèi}。
= Two.
服务员: {这边|zhè biān}{请|qǐng}。{这|zhè}{是|shì}{菜单|cài dān}。
= This way, please. Here's the menu.
王芳: {大卫|Dà wèi}，{你|nǐ}{吃|chī}{肉|ròu}{还是|hái shi}{吃|chī}{鱼|yú}？
= David, do you want meat or fish?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{都|dōu}{喜欢|xǐ huan}。{这儿|zhèr}{的|de}{鱼|yú}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= I like both. What's the fish like here?
王芳: {非常|fēi cháng}{好吃|hǎo chī}，{但是|dàn shì}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{贵|guì}，{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú}{一百多|yì bǎi duō}{块|kuài}。
= Really good, but a bit expensive: a hundred-odd kuai for a fish.
大卫: {一百多|yì bǎi duō}{块|kuài}？{这么|zhè me}{贵|guì}！
= Over a hundred kuai? That expensive!
王芳: {这儿|zhèr}{的|de}{鱼|yú}{很|hěn}{大|dà}，{三四|sān sì}{个|gè}{人|rén}{吃|chī}{都|dōu}{没|méi}{问题|wèn tí}。
= The fish here are big: three or four people could eat one.
大卫: {那么|nà me}，{我们|wǒ men}{点|diǎn}{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú}，{再|zài}{点|diǎn}{一|yí}{个|gè}{肉|ròu}{菜|cài}。
= Then let's order a fish, and a meat dish as well.
王芳: {好|hǎo}。{还|hái}{要|yào}{两|liǎng}{碗|wǎn}{米饭|mǐ fàn}。
= Good. And two bowls of rice.
大卫: {你|nǐ}{看|kàn}，{门口|mén kǒu}{有|yǒu}{十几|shí jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén}{在|zài}{等|děng}！
= Look, there are a dozen or so people waiting at the door!
王芳: {是|shì}{啊|a}，{晚上|wǎn shang}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{这样|zhè yàng}。
= Yes, it's always like this in the evening.
```

{你们|nǐ men}{几|jǐ}{位|wèi}？ is the polite question every restaurant asks at the door, with
{位|wèi}, the polite measure word for people (lesson 01). {碗|wǎn} (a bowl) is an HSK 3 measure
word. In {一|yí}{个|gè}{肉|ròu}{菜|cài} ("a meat dish"), {个|gè} counts dishes, the way people order.

## Reading: a restaurant near home

{李明|Lǐ Míng} writes about his favourite restaurant.

> {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{旁边|páng biān}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小|xiǎo}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}。{饭馆|fàn guǎn}{不|bú}{大|dà}，{能|néng}{坐|zuò}{二十多|èr shí duō}{个|gè}{人|rén}。{这儿|zhèr}{的|de}{肉|ròu}{和|hé}{鱼|yú}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{好吃|hǎo chī}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{菜|cài}{三十多|sān shí duō}{块|kuài}，{不|bú}{太|tài}{贵|guì}。{我|wǒ}{最|zuì}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{这儿|zhèr}{的|de}{鱼|yú}，{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú}{两三|liǎng sān}{个|gè}{人|rén}{吃|chī}。{鱼|yú}{这么|zhè me}{好吃|hǎo chī}，{我|wǒ}{每|měi}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī}{都|dōu}{来|lái}！{晚上|wǎn shang}{人|rén}{很|hěn}{多|duō}，{经常|jīng cháng}{要|yào}{等|děng}{半|bàn}{个|gè}{多|duō}{小时|xiǎo shí}。{你们|nǐ men}{别|bié}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{去|qù}，{那个|nà ge}{时候|shí hou}{人|rén}{太|tài}{多|duō}{了|le}。

Then answer:

1. How many people can the restaurant seat?
2. How much does a dish cost?
3. When does Li Ming tell you not to go, and why?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Twenty-odd ({二十多|èr shí duō}{个|gè}{人|rén}).
2. Thirty-something kuai ({三十多|sān shí duō}{块|kuài}).
3. At seven o'clock: there are too many people then.

"Next to my home there's a little restaurant. It isn't big; it seats twenty-odd people. The meat
and the fish here are both very good, and a dish is thirty-something kuai, not too expensive. I
like the fish best: one fish is enough for two or three people. The fish is so good that I come
every week! In the evening there are lots of people, and you often have to wait more than half an hour.
Don't go at seven: there are too many people then."
</details>

Notice {半|bàn}{个|gè}{多|duō}{小时|xiǎo shí}, "half an hour and a bit": {多|duō} goes after the
measure word, because the number ({半|bàn}) isn't a round ten.

## Say it

```speak
{你们|nǐ men}{几|jǐ}{位|wèi}？
= How many of you?
{我们|wǒ men}{点|diǎn}{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú}{吧|ba}。
= Let's order a fish.
{这个|zhè ge}{菜|cài}{这么|zhè me}{好吃|hǎo chī}！
= This dish is so good!
{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú}{一百多|yì bǎi duō}{块|kuài}。
= A fish is a hundred-odd kuai.
{饭馆|fàn guǎn}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{十几|shí jǐ}{个|gè}{人|rén}。
= There are a dozen or so people in the restaurant.
{晚上|wǎn shang}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{这样|zhè yàng}。
= It's always like this in the evening.
```

## Pronunciation

- {肉|ròu}: Chinese *r* is close to the "s" in "pleasure", with the tongue tip curled back. Say it
  with a strong fall.
- {鱼|yú} is written *yu* but has the rounded *ü* sound: after *y* (and *j q x*) the two dots are
  dropped, but the sound stays. It rises, like {别|bié}.
- {这么|zhè me}, {那么|nà me}: the *me* is light and short, as in {什么|shén me}.
- {这样|zhè yàng}, {那样|nà yàng}: two full tones, falling then falling. Compare {怎么样|zěn me yàng}
  from HSK 1.
- {饭馆|fàn guǎn}: a fall and then a dip; {馆|guǎn} ends in *-n*, as in {饭|fàn}.
- {十几|shí jǐ} rises and then dips; {几十|jǐ shí} dips and then rises. Say the pair aloud: the order
  of the tones is the order of the meaning.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{这么|zhè me}{很|hěn}{贵|guì}~~: {这么|zhè me} replaces {很|hěn}. Say {这么|zhè me}{贵|guì}.
- ~~{这么|zhè me}{的|de}{手表|shǒu biǎo}~~ for "a watch like this": before {的|de} + noun use
  {这样|zhè yàng}{的|de}{手表|shǒu biǎo}.
- ~~{一|yí}{个|gè}{鱼|yú}~~: a fish is {一|yì}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú}; trousers are {一|yì}{条|tiáo}{裤子|kù zi}.
- ~~{二十|èr shí}{块|kuài}{多|duō}~~ for "twenty-odd kuai": after a round number, {多|duō} goes before
  the measure word: {二十多|èr shí duō}{块|kuài}.
- ~~{二三|èr sān}{个|gè}{人|rén}~~: "two or three" starts with {两|liǎng}: {两三|liǎng sān}{个|gè}{人|rén}.
- {=Writing 鱼 with four dots at the bottom: that's the traditional 魚. Simplified 鱼 ends with one
  long horizontal.=}

## Key points

- {饭馆|fàn guǎn}: an everyday restaurant. {饭店|fàn diàn}: a restaurant, often bigger; in names often
  a hotel.
- {肉|ròu} (meat; alone it often means pork), {牛肉|niú ròu}, {鸡肉|jī ròu}; {鱼|yú} is fish, animal and
  food.
- {条|tiáo} counts long, thin things: fish, trousers, roads.
- {这么|zhè me} / {那么|nà me} + adjective: "so"; no {很|hěn}. {那么|nà me} at the start: "then".
- {这样|zhè yàng} / {那样|nà yàng}: "like this / that", before a verb, before {的|de} + noun, or as the
  predicate.
- Approximate numbers: {几|jǐ} ({十几|shí jǐ}, {几十|jǐ shí}), {多|duō} after a round number
  ({二十多|èr shí duō}{块|kuài}) or after the measure word ({一|yí}{个|gè}{多|duō}{小时|xiǎo shí}), and two
  neighbouring numbers ({两三|liǎng sān}{个|gè}).
- {=Characters: 馆 (館) with the food radical, 肉 (a piece of meat), 鱼 (魚, a fish on its tail).=}

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
