lessons.title: At the shopping centre: 花, 万, 快要
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

HSK 1 got you into a shop: {多少钱|duō shao qián}, {块|kuài}, {贵|guì} and {便宜|pián yi}. This
lesson takes you round a whole shopping centre, a {商场|shāng chǎng}. You'll learn to say what you
{花|huā} (spend), in money and in time; to read and say numbers up to the hundred thousands with
{万|wàn} (ten thousand), which Chinese counts in where English counts in thousands; to say that
something is about to happen with {快要|kuài yào}…{了|le} ("the shops are about to close"); and
three short words with many uses: {打|dǎ} (to hit, and the verb of phone calls, taxis and ball
games), {正|zhèng} (just, exactly) and {包|bāo} (a bag; to wrap). There's also a shop notice to
read, the kind of text the HSK 2 reading paper uses.

## Where to shop: {商场|shāng chǎng}

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {商场|shāng chǎng} | shopping centre, mall, department store | a big building of shops; {场|chǎng} as in {机场|jī chǎng} |
| {商店|shāng diàn} | shop | HSK 1 |
| {超市|chāo shì} | supermarket | HSK 1 |

{商场|shāng chǎng} is a large building with many shops (or one big store) on several floors, often
with restaurants and a cinema at the top. Things are *in* it: {在|zài}{商场|shāng chǎng}{里|lǐ}.

{我们|wǒ men}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{去|qù}{商场|shāng chǎng}{买|mǎi}{衣服|yī fu}{吧|ba}。 — Let's go to the shopping centre on Saturday to buy clothes.
{商场|shāng chǎng}{三|sān}{楼|lóu}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}。 — There are lots of restaurants on the third floor of the shopping centre.

## Spending money and time: {花|huā}

{花|huā} is "to spend". It takes money or time as its object:

{花|huā}{钱|qián} — to spend money
{花|huā}{时间|shí jiān} — to spend time, to take time
{你|nǐ}{花|huā}{了|le}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？ — How much did you spend?
{我|wǒ}{花|huā}{了|le}{两千|liǎng qiān}{块|kuài}。 — I spent two thousand kuai.
{做|zuò}{这个|zhè ge}{菜|cài}{要|yào}{花|huā}{一|yí}{个|gè}{多|duō}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — This dish takes over an hour to make.

When the amount is given, {了|le} follows {花|huā} (the completed action) and the amount comes after:
{花|huā}{了|le}{三百|sān bǎi}{块|kuài}. A general statement has no {了|le}:
{他|tā}{很|hěn}{爱|ài}{花|huā}{钱|qián}。 (He loves spending money.)

It's the same character, and the same sound, as {花|huā} "flower" (lesson 13). Context always tells
you which: you spend {钱|qián} and {时间|shí jiān}, and you give someone flowers.

## Ten thousand: {万|wàn}

English groups big numbers in threes (thousand, million); Chinese groups them in **fours**. After
{千|qiān} (1,000) comes {万|wàn} (10,000), and everything up to a hundred million is counted in
{万|wàn}:

| Number | Chinese | Word for word |
|---|---|---|
| 10,000 | {一万|yí wàn} | one ten-thousand |
| 20,000 | {两万|liǎng wàn} | two ten-thousands |
| 100,000 | {十万|shí wàn} | ten ten-thousands |
| 120,000 | {十二万|shí èr wàn} | twelve ten-thousands |
| 990,000 | {九十九万|jiǔ shí jiǔ wàn} | ninety-nine ten-thousands |

So "a hundred thousand" isn't "a hundred thousand" in Chinese but "ten {万|wàn}". The trick for
reading a big number: count four digits from the right and put {万|wàn} there.

| Number | Split | Chinese |
|---|---|---|
| 12,000 | 1 \| 2000 | {一万|yí wàn}{两千|liǎng qiān} |
| 25,000 | 2 \| 5000 | {两万|liǎng wàn}{五千|wǔ qiān} |
| 38,600 | 3 \| 8600 | {三万|sān wàn}{八千|bā qiān}{六百|liù bǎi} |
| 10,500 | 1 \| 0500 | {一万|yí wàn}{零|líng}{五百|wǔ bǎi} |
| 150,000 | 15 \| 0000 | {十五万|shí wǔ wàn} |

Three rules you know from HSK 1 still hold. {零|líng} fills an empty place inside the number
({一万|yí wàn}{零|líng}{五百|wǔ bǎi}); {两|liǎng}, not {二|èr}, goes before {万|wàn} and {千|qiān}
({两万|liǎng wàn}{两千|liǎng qiān}, 22,000); and {一|yī} changes tone: {一万|yí wàn}, because {万|wàn} is
fourth tone. In speech, a final round place is often dropped, as with prices: {两万五|liǎng wàn wǔ} is
25,000, just as {一千二|yì qiān èr} is 1,200.

A million is {一百万|yì bǎi wàn}, "a hundred ten-thousands".

{这|zhè}{个|gè}{电脑|diàn nǎo}{一万|yí wàn}{两千|liǎng qiān}{块|kuài}。 — This computer is twelve thousand kuai.
{这|zhè}{块|kuài}{手表|shǒu biǎo}{要|yào}{三万|sān wàn}{多|duō}。 — This watch costs over thirty thousand.

The second example uses lesson 22's {多|duō} after a round number: {三万多|sān wàn duō}, "thirty
thousand-odd". (And yes, {块|kuài} is also the measure word for a watch.)

## About to happen: {快要|kuài yào}…{了|le}

{快要|kuài yào} + verb (or adjective) + {了|le} says something will happen very soon:

{快要|kuài yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。 — It's about to rain.
{电影|diàn yǐng}{快要|kuài yào}{开始|kāi shǐ}{了|le}。 — The film is about to start.
{商场|shāng chǎng}{快要|kuài yào}{关门|guān mén}{了|le}。 — The shopping centre is about to close.
{我|wǒ}{快要|kuài yào}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}{了|le}。 — I'll soon be twenty.

The {了|le} at the end is the change-of-state {了|le} from HSK 1: a new situation is coming.
Don't leave it out. ({关门|guān mén}, "to close (for the day)", is {关|guān}, an HSK 3 word, + {门|mén}.)

Two limits:

- **No exact time with {快要|kuài yào}.** ~~{他|tā}{明天|míng tiān}{快要|kuài yào}{来|lái}{了|le}~~ is wrong:
  {快要|kuài yào} already says "very soon", so it doesn't go with a clock time or a day. Say
  {他|tā}{明天|míng tiān}{来|lái} or {他|tā}{快要|kuài yào}{来|lái}{了|le}.
- **Shorter forms.** You'll also hear {快|kuài}…{了|le} ({快|kuài}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{了|le}, it's nearly seven)
  and {要|yào}…{了|le}. Lesson 26 compares all three.

## Three busy words: {打|dǎ}, {正|zhèng}, {包|bāo}

### {打|dǎ}: to hit, and much more

On its own {打|dǎ} is "to hit, to strike": {别|bié}{打|dǎ}{他|tā}！ (Don't hit him!). But it's also the
verb of many everyday actions that have nothing to do with hitting, and these are what you'll use
most:

| Phrase | Meaning | Where you met it |
|---|---|---|
| {打电话|dǎ diàn huà} | to make a phone call | HSK 1 |
| {打车|dǎ chē} | to take a taxi | lesson 08 |
| {打开|dǎ kāi} | to open | lesson 12 |
| {打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú} | to play basketball | lesson 19 |
| {打|dǎ}{球|qiú} | to play ball (a ball game played with the hands or a racket) | lesson 19 |

Football is the exception: you kick it, {踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}. In shops you'll see one more:
{打|dǎ}{八|bā}{折|zhé} is "20% off", literally "strike to eight tenths": you pay 80% of the price.
{打|dǎ}{九|jiǔ}{折|zhé} is 10% off; {打|dǎ}{五|wǔ}{折|zhé}, half price. ({折|zhé} isn't a course word.)
The number is what you pay, not what you save, so {八|bā}{折|zhé} sounds like more than it is.

### {正|zhèng}: just, exactly

{正|zhèng} means "straight, upright", and as an adverb "just, exactly, right (then)". You know it
from {正在|zhèng zài}. Two more uses are common:

- {正|zhèng} + {想|xiǎng} / {要|yào}: "was just (about to)". {我|wǒ}{正|zhèng}{想|xiǎng}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}！
  (I was just going to call you!)
- {正好|zhèng hǎo}: "just right; exactly; as it happens" (an extra word, not in your reviews).
  {八十|bā shí}{块|kuài}，{正好|zhèng hǎo}。 (Eighty kuai, exactly. You hand over the exact money.)
  {这|zhè}{条|tiáo}{裤子|kù zi}{我|wǒ}{穿|chuān}{正好|zhèng hǎo}。 (These trousers fit me just right.)

### {包|bāo}: a bag, to wrap

{包|bāo} is a noun, "bag" (handbag, shoulder bag, backpack): {书包|shū bāo} (school bag, lesson
16) is one kind. It's also a verb, "to wrap", and a measure word, "a packet of":

{这|zhè}{个|gè}{包|bāo}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。 — This bag is lovely.
{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{包|bāo}{饺子|jiǎo zi}{吧|ba}！ — Let's make dumplings together!
{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yì}{包|bāo}{绿茶|lǜ chá}。 — I bought a packet of green tea.

{包|bāo}{饺子|jiǎo zi}, "wrap dumplings", is the normal way to say "make dumplings": you wrap the
filling in the dough. Now {包子|bāo zi} (a stuffed bun) makes sense too: a wrapped thing.

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 万 (traditional 萬) | ten thousand | wàn | 一 | 3 | {万|wàn}, {一万|yí wàn}, {十万|shí wàn} |

The other words of the lesson use characters you know: 商 (HSK 1) and 场 (lesson 08), 花 (lesson
13), 打 正 包 (HSK 1), 快 (lesson 13) and 要 (HSK 1).

- 万 is one of the oldest simplified forms: a short way of writing "ten thousand" that was in use
  for many centuries before the official simplified characters of the 1950s. The traditional form
  萬 began as a drawing of a scorpion, borrowed for its sound to write the number.
- Don't confuse 万 with 方 (as in {地方|dì fang}, place, HSK 3): 方 has a dot on top and a
  separate horizontal; 万 has no dot.

Radical review: **一** is filed as the radical of characters that have no clearer one, such as
{万|wàn}, {三|sān}, {下|xià} and {不|bù}.

### Stroke order

- 万: the horizontal first, then the stroke that goes right, turns down and hooks (it starts
  under the middle of the horizontal), and last the left-falling stroke. Three strokes; writing the
  left-falling stroke second is the usual mistake.

```trace
万
```

> **Handwriting review.** These 18 HSK 1 characters, all on the handwriting list, come up again and
> again in this module: 点 茶 还 要 多 两 百 打 时 现 在 上 家 半 少 书 天 分. Write each one three
> times from memory, then check it on a pad. Words to think of: {点|diǎn}{菜|cài}, {红茶|hóng chá},
> {还是|hái shi}, {快要|kuài yào}, {二十多|èr shí duō}, {两三|liǎng sān}, {一百多|yì bǎi duō},
> {打|dǎ}{球|qiú}, {小时|xiǎo shí}, {现在|xiàn zài}, {正在|zhèng zài}, {上面|shàng miàn},
> {家|jiā}, {半|bàn}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}, {多少|duō shao}, {书包|shū bāo}, {今天|jīn tiān}, {分钟|fēn zhōng}.

```trace
点茶还要多两
```

```trace
百打时现在上
```

```trace
家半少书天分
```

=}

## Dialogue: at the shopping centre

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) and {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) are on the second floor of a shopping centre. The
third speaker is a {店员|diàn yuán} (店员), a shop assistant (not a course word).

```dialogue
# At the shopping centre
王芳: {安娜|Ān nà}，{你|nǐ}{看|kàn}，{这|zhè}{个|gè}{包|bāo}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= Anna, look, what do you think of this bag?
安娜: {很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}！{多少钱|duō shao qián}？
= It's lovely! How much is it?
店员: {一千二|yì qiān èr}。{今天|jīn tiān}{打|dǎ}{八|bā}{折|zhé}，{九百六|jiǔ bǎi liù}。
= Twelve hundred. It's 20% off today, so nine hundred and sixty.
王芳: {九百六|jiǔ bǎi liù}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{贵|guì}{啊|a}。{这|zhè}{个|gè}{月|yuè}{我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{花|huā}{了|le}{三千多|sān qiān duō}{块|kuài}{了|le}。
= Nine sixty is still a lot. I've already spent over three thousand kuai this month.
安娜: {那|nà}{别|bié}{买|mǎi}{了|le}。{你|nǐ}{看|kàn}，{快要|kuài yào}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}{了|le}，{商场|shāng chǎng}{快要|kuài yào}{关门|guān mén}{了|le}。
= Then don't buy it. Look, it's nearly nine; the shopping centre's about to close.
王芳: {等|děng}{一下|yí xià}！{这|zhè}{个|gè}{手机|shǒu jī}{多少钱|duō shao qián}？
= Wait a moment! How much is this phone?
店员: {这|zhè}{是|shì}{新|xīn}{的|de}，{一万|yí wàn}{零|líng}{五百|wǔ bǎi}。
= This is the new one: ten thousand five hundred.
安娜: {一万多|yí wàn duō}！{走|zǒu}{吧|ba}，{别|bié}{看|kàn}{了|le}！
= Over ten thousand! Come on, stop looking!
王芳: {好|hǎo}{吧|ba}。{我们|wǒ men}{花|huā}{了|le}{三|sān}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}，{什么|shén me}{都|dōu}{没|méi}{买|mǎi}。
= All right. We spent three hours and didn't buy anything.
安娜: {没关系|méi guān xi}，{你|nǐ}{的|de}{钱|qián}{还|hái}{在|zài}！{我|wǒ}{正|zhèng}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}，{走|zǒu}{吧|ba}。
= Never mind, your money's still there! I was just thinking of going to eat. Let's go.
```

{一千二|yì qiān èr} and {九百六|jiǔ bǎi liù} drop the last round place, as prices often do: 1,200 and
960. {快要|kuài yào}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}{了|le} has a time in it, but that's fine: the time is what's about
to come, not when something happens. {什么|shén me}{都|dōu}{没|méi}{买|mǎi} ("didn't buy anything") puts
{什么|shén me} before {都|dōu} + {没|méi}: "anything at all… not".

## Reading: a notice in the shopping centre

This notice is on the door of the shopping centre.

> **{商场|shāng chǎng}{通知|tōng zhī}**
>
> {这|zhè}{个|gè}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{和|hé}{星期天|xīng qī tiān}，{商场|shāng chǎng}{里|lǐ}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}{都|dōu}{打|dǎ}{八|bā}{折|zhé}，{手表|shǒu biǎo}{打|dǎ}{九|jiǔ}{折|zhé}。{在|zài}{商场|shāng chǎng}{花|huā}{五百|wǔ bǎi}{块|kuài}，{送|sòng}{您|nín}{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{咖啡|kā fēi}。{一|yī}{楼|lóu}{有|yǒu}{咖啡|kā fēi}{店|diàn}，{三|sān}{楼|lóu}{有|yǒu}{二十多|èr shí duō}{个|gè}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}。{商场|shāng chǎng}{早上|zǎo shang}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{开门|kāi mén}，{晚上|wǎn shang}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{关门|guān mén}。{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{人|rén}{很|hěn}{多|duō}，{请|qǐng}{您|nín}{别|bié}{开车|kāi chē}{来|lái}，{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{很|hěn}{方便|fāng biàn}。

{通知|tōng zhī} is "notice" (not a course word) and {方便|fāng biàn} "convenient" (HSK 3). Then answer:

1. What is 20% off this weekend?
2. How do you get a free coffee?
3. Which floor has the restaurants, and about how many are there?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. All the clothes in the shopping centre ({衣服|yī fu}{都|dōu}{打|dǎ}{八|bā}{折|zhé}); watches are 10% off.
2. Spend five hundred kuai in the shopping centre.
3. The third floor: twenty-odd restaurants.

"**Shopping centre notice.** This Saturday and Sunday, all clothes in the shopping centre are 20%
off and watches 10% off. Spend five hundred kuai in the shopping centre and we'll give you a cup of
coffee. There's a café on the first floor, and twenty-odd restaurants on the third floor. The
shopping centre opens at ten in the morning and closes at ten in the evening. There are a lot of
people on Sunday evening, so please don't come by car: the metro is very convenient."
</details>

Notice {一|yī}{楼|lóu} with {一|yī} unchanged: floor numbers are ordinals, like dates, and keep
*yī*. In China the ground floor is {一|yī}{楼|lóu}, the "first floor" (lesson 11).

## Say it

```speak
{你|nǐ}{花|huā}{了|le}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？
= How much did you spend?
{这|zhè}{个|gè}{电脑|diàn nǎo}{一万|yí wàn}{两千|liǎng qiān}{块|kuài}。
= This computer is twelve thousand kuai.
{快要|kuài yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。
= It's about to rain.
{商场|shāng chǎng}{快要|kuài yào}{关门|guān mén}{了|le}。
= The shopping centre is about to close.
{今天|jīn tiān}{打|dǎ}{八|bā}{折|zhé}。
= It's 20% off today.
{我|wǒ}{正|zhèng}{想|xiǎng}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}！
= I was just going to call you!
```

## Pronunciation

- {万|wàn} falls; {玩|wán} (to play, HSK 1) rises; {晚|wǎn} (late) dips. Practise
  {一万|yí wàn}, {好玩儿|hǎo wánr}, {晚上|wǎn shang} in a row.
- {一万|yí wàn}: {一|yī} becomes *yí* before the fourth tone of {万|wàn}, as in {一个|yí gè}.
  {十万|shí wàn} has no change.
- {商场|shāng chǎng}: two *-ang* syllables, the first high, the second dipping. *sh* and *ch* both
  curl the tongue back.
- {花|huā}: *hu-* is a breathy *h* from the back of the mouth, then *ua* like "wah".
- {正|zhèng} and {正在|zhèng zài}: *zh* curled back, *z* flat behind the teeth. Keep them apart.
- {快要|kuài yào}: two falling tones; in quick speech the first is a little shorter.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{十千|shí qiān}~~ for 10,000: it's {一万|yí wàn}. And 100,000 is {十万|shí wàn}, not
  ~~{一百千|yì bǎi qiān}~~.
- ~~{二万|èr wàn}~~: before {万|wàn}, as before {千|qiān}, use {两|liǎng}: {两万|liǎng wàn}.
- Forgetting {零|líng}: 10,500 is {一万|yí wàn}{零|líng}{五百|wǔ bǎi}, not ~~{一万五百|yí wàn wǔ bǎi}~~. (And
  {一万五|yí wàn wǔ} on its own is 15,000, said short.)
- ~~{快要|kuài yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}~~ without {了|le}, or ~~{明天|míng tiān}{快要|kuài yào}…~~ with an exact
  time.
- ~~{花|huā}{钱|qián}{三百|sān bǎi}{块|kuài}~~: the amount replaces {钱|qián}: {花|huā}{了|le}{三百|sān bǎi}{块|kuài}{钱|qián}
  or {花|huā}{了|le}{三百|sān bǎi}{块|kuài}.
- Reading {打|dǎ}{八|bā}{折|zhé} as "80% off": it's 20% off (you pay eight tenths).
- {=Writing 万 with a dot on top: that's 方.=}

## Key points

- {商场|shāng chǎng}: a shopping centre; things are {在|zài}{商场|shāng chǎng}{里|lǐ}.
- {花|huā} + money or time: {花|huā}{钱|qián}, {花|huā}{时间|shí jiān}, {花|huā}{了|le}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}？
- Numbers in fours: {一万|yí wàn} (10,000), {十万|shí wàn} (100,000), {一万|yí wàn}{两千|liǎng qiān} (12,000),
  {两万|liǎng wàn}{五千|wǔ qiān} (25,000); {零|líng} for an empty place; {两|liǎng} before {万|wàn}.
- {快要|kuài yào} + verb + {了|le}: about to happen; no exact time with it.
- {打|dǎ}: to hit, and the verb of calls, taxis, ball games; {打|dǎ}{八|bā}{折|zhé} is 20% off.
- {正|zhèng}: just, exactly ({正|zhèng}{想|xiǎng}…, {正好|zhèng hǎo}); {包|bāo}: a bag, to wrap, a packet.
- {=Character: 万 (traditional 萬): horizontal, hooked stroke, left-falling stroke.=}

lessons.title: Online: 上网, 时, 周
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Much of daily life in China happens on the phone: shopping, paying, ordering food, chatting,
booking tickets. This lesson gives you the words to talk about it, {上网|shàng wǎng} (to go online)
and {网上|wǎng shàng} (online), and three words you'll read in every message and notice:
{时|shí}, the short written form of "when" ({上课|shàng kè}{时|shí}, "during class"), {周|zhōu},
the week of calendars and timetables ({这周|zhè zhōu}, {下周一|xià zhōu yī}), and
{事情|shì qing}, the full word for the {事|shì} (a matter, something to do) you know from HSK 1.
The reading is a group chat, the "electronic messages" of the HSK 2 reading tasks.

## Going online: {上网|shàng wǎng} and {网上|wǎng shàng}

{网|wǎng} is a net, and for nearly everyone now, *the* net. Two words are built from it, with the
same characters in the opposite order:

| Word | Part of speech | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {上网|shàng wǎng} | verb | to go online, to use the internet | {我|wǒ}{每天|měi tiān}{上网|shàng wǎng}。 |
| {网上|wǎng shàng} | place word | online, on the internet | {网上|wǎng shàng}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{中文|Zhōng wén}{书|shū}。 |

{上网|shàng wǎng} is built like {上课|shàng kè} and {上班|shàng bān}: {上|shàng} "go to" + the place.
It's an action, so it takes time words and durations like any verb:

{我|wǒ}{晚上|wǎn shang}{上网|shàng wǎng}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}。 — In the evening I go online and watch films.
{他|tā}{每天|měi tiān}{上网|shàng wǎng}{三四|sān sì}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — He's online three or four hours a day.

{网上|wǎng shàng} is a place, built like {桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng} ("on the table"): "on the net". Use
it where you'd use a place, often after {在|zài} and before the verb:

{我|wǒ}{经常|jīng cháng}{在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。 — I often buy things online.
{网上|wǎng shàng}{说|shuō}{明天|míng tiān}{下雨|xià yǔ}。 — It says online that it'll rain tomorrow.

So "I buy things online" is {在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{买|mǎi}, never ~~{在|zài}{上网|shàng wǎng}{买|mǎi}~~;
and "I'm online" is {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{上网|shàng wǎng} (in the middle of going online: {在|zài} as the
progressive), never ~~{我|wǒ}{网上|wǎng shàng}~~.

You'll see {网|wǎng} in more words later: {网站|wǎng zhàn} (website) and {网球|wǎng qiú} (tennis, a
game over a net) are HSK 3.

## When: …{的|de}{时候|shí hou} and …{时|shí}

HSK 1 taught …{的|de}{时候|shí hou} for "when…, while…": {上课|shàng kè}{的|de}{时候|shí hou} (in
class, when we have class). Written Chinese, and polite notices, often shorten it to …{时|shí}, with
no {的|de}:

| Spoken | Written | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {上课|shàng kè}{的|de}{时候|shí hou} | {上课|shàng kè}{时|shí} | during class |
| {吃饭|chī fàn}{的|de}{时候|shí hou} | {吃饭|chī fàn}{时|shí} | while eating, at meals |
| {我|wǒ}{来|lái}{中国|Zhōng guó}{的|de}{时候|shí hou} | {我|wǒ}{来|lái}{中国|Zhōng guó}{时|shí} | when I came to China |

{上课|shàng kè}{时|shí}{请|qǐng}{别|bié}{玩|wán}{手机|shǒu jī}。 — Please don't play with your phone during class.
{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{时|shí}，{请|qǐng}{别|bié}{在|zài}{车|chē}{上|shàng}{吃|chī}{东西|dōng xi}。 — On the metro, please don't eat on the train.

Both mean the same; {时|shí} sounds more written and concise, the way signs and messages like it.
In conversation, keep using {的|de}{时候|shí hou}.

{时|shí} is the character of {时间|shí jiān}, {小时|xiǎo shí} and {时候|shí hou}. As a word on its own it
is this written "when". Don't confuse the three time words you now have: {时间|shí jiān} is time you
have or spend ({没有|méi yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}), {小时|xiǎo shí} is an hour, and …{时|shí} / …{的|de}{时候|shí hou}
is "when".

## The week: {周|zhōu}

You know {星期|xīng qī} for "week". {周|zhōu} means the same and is the word of calendars,
timetables and notices; it's very common in speech too. It works without a
measure word:

| With {星期|xīng qī} | With {周|zhōu} | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {这|zhè}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī} | {这周|zhè zhōu} | this week |
| {上|shàng}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī} | {上周|shàng zhōu} | last week |
| {下|xià}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī} | {下周|xià zhōu} | next week |
| {一|yí}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī} | {一周|yì zhōu} | one week |
| {两|liǎng}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī} | {两周|liǎng zhōu} | two weeks |
| {星期一|xīng qī yī} | {周一|zhōu yī} | Monday |
| {星期天|xīng qī tiān} / {星期日|xīng qī rì} | {周日|zhōu rì} | Sunday |

Notice: {一周|yì zhōu}, {两周|liǎng zhōu} with no {个|gè}, unlike {星期|xīng qī}. The days are
{周一|zhōu yī} to {周六|zhōu liù}, and Sunday is {周日|zhōu rì} (not ~~{周天|zhōu tiān}~~, which you may hear
in casual speech but which isn't standard, and never ~~{周七|zhōu qī}~~). The weekend is {周末|zhōu mò}, an HSK 3 word.

{我们|wǒ men}{下周三|xià zhōu sān}{考试|kǎo shì}。 — We have an exam next Wednesday.
{我|wǒ}{一周|yì zhōu}{去|qù}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}{超市|chāo shì}。 — I go to the supermarket twice a week.

In traditional script "week" is written 週 (with the walking radical), while {=周=} stays for the
surname Zhou and the old sense "all around": {={周一|zhōu yī}=} appears as 週一.

## Things to deal with: {事情|shì qing} and {事|shì}

{事情|shì qing} and {事|shì} both mean "a matter, an affair, something that happens or needs doing".
They are the abstract "thing"; a thing you can hold is {东西|dōng xi}.

{事|shì} is the short, everyday form, and it's the one in set phrases:

- {有|yǒu}{事|shì} — to have something on, be busy: {我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{有|yǒu}{事|shì}。
- {没事|méi shì} — it's nothing, no problem (HSK 1)
- {什么|shén me}{事|shì}？ — What is it? (when someone calls or knocks)

{事情|shì qing} is the full word, natural where you'd use a whole noun phrase:

{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事情|shì qing}{你|nǐ}{别|bié}{告诉|gào su}{他|tā}。 — Don't tell him about this.
{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{事情|shì qing}{要|yào}{做|zuò}。 — I have a lot of things to do today.

Both are counted with {件|jiàn} (as clothes are): {一|yí}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}, {这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事情|shì qing}.
Often you can use either: {这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事|shì} = {这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事情|shì qing}. But keep the set phrases
short: {有|yǒu}{事|shì}, {没事|méi shì}.

## Messages on the phone

Chat messages are short and direct. A few habits:

- **Greetings and names first**: {大家好|dà jiā hǎo}！ (Hi everyone!), {安娜|Ān nà}，… .
- **Times, days and places in front**: {下周一|xià zhōu yī}{上午|shàng wǔ}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}，{学校|xué xiào}{门口|mén kǒu}。
- **{吧|ba} and {啊|a} to soften**, {别|bié}… for gentle warnings: {别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le}！
- **Short replies**: {好|hǎo}{的|de}！ (OK!), {没问题|méi wèn tí} (no problem), {谢谢|xiè xie}！

{好的|hǎo de} is the usual "OK" in messages, a little more polite than {好|hǎo} alone.

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 网 (traditional 網) | net; the internet | wǎng | 网 | 6 | {上网|shàng wǎng}, {网上|wǎng shàng}, {网球|wǎng qiú} (tennis, HSK 3) |
| 情 | feeling; situation | qíng (neutral in {事情|shì qing}) | 忄 | 11 | {事情|shì qing}, {热情|rè qíng} (warm, friendly; HSK 3) |
| 周 (traditional 週 for "week") | week; all round | zhōu | 口 | 8 | {周|zhōu}, {周一|zhōu yī}, {周末|zhōu mò} (weekend, HSK 3) |

情 is the same in both scripts. 周 stays 周 in traditional when it's a surname or means "all
round"; for "week" it becomes 週.

### How the characters are built

- 网 is a picture of a net: a frame with the crossed cords inside. Traditional 網 adds 糸 (silk,
  thread; simplified 纟) on the left and has a longer inner part; simplified script went back to
  the plain old drawing.
- 情 = 忄 (heart) + {青|qīng} (green, blue; not a course character) for the sound. You know two
  more characters with 青 as their sound part: {请|qǐng} (please) and {晴|qíng} (sunny, next lesson). All three sound
  *qing*, with different tones and radicals: speech for 请, the heart for 情 (feelings), the sun
  for 晴.
- 周: Make Me a Hanzi and the Kangxi dictionary file it under 口; some modern dictionaries put it
  under 冂, the frame. Look under either. 週 adds 辶, the "walking" radical of {这|zhè} and
  {还|hái}: 週 first meant "to go round", and a week is one round of days.

Radical review: **忄**, the heart on the left ({竖心旁|shù xīn páng}), is in {忙|máng}, {懂|dǒng}
(lesson 17) and now {情|qíng}; under a character, the heart is written 心 ({想|xiǎng}, {意|yì}).

### Stroke order

- 网: the frame first, left vertical then the top and right side with its hook. Then the two
  crosses inside, each left-falling stroke before its dot. The frame stays open at the bottom.
- 周: the left side first (a vertical that sweeps left at the bottom), then the top and right
  side with its hook; then 土 inside (horizontal, vertical, horizontal) and 口 last.
- 情: 忄 starts with its two dots, left then right, and the long vertical comes third. Then 青
  from the top: three horizontals and a vertical, then 月 at the bottom.

```trace
网情周
```

=}

## Dialogue: shopping online

{李明|Lǐ Míng} (李明) phones his friend {大卫|Dà wèi} (大卫).

```dialogue
# Shopping online
李明: {大卫|Dà wèi}，{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}？
= David, what are you doing?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{上网|shàng wǎng}，{在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。
= I'm online, buying something.
李明: {买|mǎi}{什么|shén me}？
= Buying what?
大卫: {一|yí}{个|gè}{新|xīn}{书包|shū bāo}。{网上|wǎng shàng}{的|de}{东西|dōng xi}{比|bǐ}{商场|shāng chǎng}{便宜|pián yi}。
= A new school bag. Things online are cheaper than at the shopping centre.
李明: {什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{能|néng}{到|dào}？
= When will it arrive?
大卫: {网上|wǎng shàng}{说|shuō}{三四|sān sì}{天|tiān}，{下周一|xià zhōu yī}{就|jiù}{到|dào}。
= It says three or four days online, so it'll be here by next Monday.
李明: {我|wǒ}{上周|shàng zhōu}{也|yě}{在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{裤子|kù zi}，{但是|dàn shì}{太|tài}{小|xiǎo}{了|le}。
= I bought a pair of trousers online last week too, but they're too small.
大卫: {那|nà}{你|nǐ}{别|bié}{在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{买|mǎi}{衣服|yī fu}{了|le}！
= Then stop buying clothes online!
李明: {对|duì}{了|le}，{你|nǐ}{这周六|zhè zhōu liù}{晚上|wǎn shang}{有|yǒu}{事|shì}{吗|ma}？
= Oh, by the way, are you doing anything this Saturday evening?
大卫: {没事|méi shì}。{什么|shén me}{事情|shì qing}？
= Nothing. What's up?
李明: {我们|wǒ men}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{同学|tóng xué}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}，{你|nǐ}{来|lái}{吗|ma}？
= A few of us from class are going for a meal together. Are you coming?
大卫: {好|hǎo}{啊|a}！{吃饭|chī fàn}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{玩|wán}{手机|shǒu jī}，{我|wǒ}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}！
= Great! At the meal I won't play with my phone; I'll speak Chinese!
```

{对了|duì le} ("oh, right", "by the way") changes the subject. {我们|wǒ men}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{同学|tóng xué},
"a few of us classmates", is lesson 22's {几|jǐ} meaning "a few".

## Reading: a group chat

Wang Fang writes in her class group chat. (The times are when each message was sent.)

> **{王芳|Wáng Fāng}** 09:15
> {大家好|dà jiā hǎo}！{这周六|zhè zhōu liù}{是|shì}{安娜|Ān nà}{的|de}{生日|shēng rì}，{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{给|gěi}{她|tā}{过|guò}{生日|shēng rì}{吧|ba}！
>
> **{李明|Lǐ Míng}** 09:20
> {好|hǎo}{啊|a}！{在|zài}{哪儿|nǎr}？
>
> **{王芳|Wáng Fāng}** 09:22
> {学校|xué xiào}{旁边|páng biān}{的|de}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}，{晚上|wǎn shang}{六|liù}{点|diǎn}。{别|bié}{告诉|gào su}{安娜|Ān nà}！
>
> **{大卫|Dà wèi}** 09:30
> {我|wǒ}{上网|shàng wǎng}{看|kàn}{了|le}，{那个|nà ge}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}{的|de}{鱼|yú}{很|hěn}{好吃|hǎo chī}。{我们|wǒ men}{点|diǎn}{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú}{吧|ba}。
>
> **{李明|Lǐ Míng}** 09:31
> {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{买|mǎi}{花|huā}。
>
> **{王芳|Wáng Fāng}** 09:40
> {好|hǎo}{的|de}！{上课|shàng kè}{时|shí}{别|bié}{说|shuō}{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事情|shì qing}，{安娜|Ān nà}{就|jiù}{在|zài}{我们|wǒ men}{班|bān}！

Then answer:

1. What is happening this Saturday, and where will they meet?
2. What will Li Ming do?
3. Why mustn't they talk about it in class?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Anna's birthday: they'll celebrate it at the restaurant next to the school, at six in the
   evening.
2. Buy flowers ({我|wǒ}{去|qù}{买|mǎi}{花|huā}).
3. Because Anna is in their class ({安娜|Ān nà}{就|jiù}{在|zài}{我们|wǒ men}{班|bān}).

**Wang Fang** 09:15 — Hi everyone! This Saturday is Anna's birthday. Let's celebrate it together!
**Li Ming** 09:20 — Great! Where?
**Wang Fang** 09:22 — The restaurant next to the school, at six in the evening. Don't tell Anna!
**David** 09:30 — I looked online: the fish at that restaurant is good. Let's order a fish.
**Li Ming** 09:31 — I'll buy flowers.
**Wang Fang** 09:40 — OK! Don't mention this in class: Anna's in our class, remember!
</details>

Wang Fang's last message uses the written {上课|shàng kè}{时|shí} where she might say
{上课|shàng kè}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}, and the {就|jiù} in {安娜|Ān nà}{就|jiù}{在|zài}{我们|wǒ men}{班|bān} stresses it:
"Anna is right there in our class".

## Say it

```speak
{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{上网|shàng wǎng}。
= I'm online.
{我|wǒ}{经常|jīng cháng}{在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}。
= I often buy things online.
{我们|wǒ men}{下周三|xià zhōu sān}{考试|kǎo shì}。
= We have an exam next Wednesday.
{上课|shàng kè}{时|shí}{请|qǐng}{别|bié}{玩|wán}{手机|shǒu jī}。
= Please don't play with your phone during class.
{你|nǐ}{这周六|zhè zhōu liù}{有|yǒu}{事|shì}{吗|ma}？
= Are you doing anything this Saturday?
{好|hǎo}{的|de}，{没问题|méi wèn tí}！
= OK, no problem!
```

## Pronunciation

- {网|wǎng} dips; {晚|wǎn} (late) dips too but ends in *-n*. {上网|shàng wǎng} and {晚上|wǎn shang}
  are a good pair to practise: *shàng* + *wǎng* against *wǎn* + a light *shang*, and *-ng* vs *-n*.
- {网上|wǎng shàng}: both syllables keep their tones; in {晚上|wǎn shang} the second one is light.
- {事情|shì qing}: *shì* falls, *qing* is light. The full tone of 情 is *qíng*.
- {周|zhōu}: *zh* (curled back) + *ou* said as "oh": the same final as {都|dōu}.
- {时|shí}: *sh* + the buzzing *-i*, rising. Not "she".

## Common mistakes

- ~~{在|zài}{上网|shàng wǎng}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}~~: the place is {网上|wǎng shàng}: {在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}.
- ~~{上课|shàng kè}{的|de}{时|shí}~~: {时|shí} takes no {的|de}. Say {上课|shàng kè}{时|shí} or
  {上课|shàng kè}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}.
- ~~{一|yí}{个|gè}{周|zhōu}~~: {周|zhōu} needs no measure word: {一周|yì zhōu}, {两周|liǎng zhōu}.
- ~~{周天|zhōu tiān}~~ (casual, not standard) or ~~{周七|zhōu qī}~~ for Sunday: it's {周日|zhōu rì}.
- Using {东西|dōng xi} for a matter: "I have something on" is {我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{事|shì}, not
  ~~{我|wǒ}{有|yǒu}{东西|dōng xi}~~ (which means "I have a thing", an object).

## Key points

- {上网|shàng wǎng} (verb): to go online. {网上|wǎng shàng} (place): online; {在|zài}{网上|wǎng shàng} + verb.
- …{时|shí} = …{的|de}{时候|shí hou} ("when, during"), more written; no {的|de} before {时|shí}.
- {周|zhōu} = week, no measure word: {这周|zhè zhōu}, {上周|shàng zhōu}, {下周|xià zhōu}, {一周|yì zhōu};
  {周一|zhōu yī} … {周日|zhōu rì}. Traditional 週.
- {事情|shì qing} = {事|shì} (a matter); set phrases keep {事|shì}: {有|yǒu}{事|shì}, {没事|méi shì}; both counted
  with {件|jiàn}.
- {=Characters: 网 (網, a net), 情 (heart + 青 for the sound), 周 (週 for "week").=}

lessons.title: Weather and childhood: 晴, 阴, 从小
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

HSK 1 gave you hot and cold, rain and snow. This lesson adds the two words of every weather
forecast, {晴|qíng} (sunny, clear) and {阴|yīn} (overcast), and the way forecasts are written. Then
it looks back in time: {小时候|xiǎo shí hou} (when I was little) and {从小|cóng xiǎo} (ever since I was
little) look alike in English but are built differently in Chinese, and this lesson shows you
which is which. Along the way you'll meet {鸟|niǎo} (a bird) and a handy way to end a list,
…{什么|shén me}{的|de} ("and so on, and things like that"). It's the last core lesson of the module.

## Sunny or overcast: {晴|qíng}, {阴|yīn}

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {晴|qíng} | sunny, clear | no clouds, or few; the sun is out |
| {阴|yīn} | overcast, dull | the sky is grey with cloud |
| {晴天|qíng tiān} | a sunny day; fine weather | extra word, not in your reviews |
| {阴天|yīn tiān} | an overcast day | extra word, not in your reviews |
| {下雨|xià yǔ}, {下雪|xià xuě} | to rain, to snow | HSK 1 |
| {冷|lěng}, {热|rè} | cold, hot | HSK 1 |

{晴|qíng} and {阴|yīn} are adjectives, so they describe the sky or the day directly:

{今天|jīn tiān}{天|tiān}{很|hěn}{晴|qíng}。 — The sky is very clear today.
{明天|míng tiān}{阴|yīn}，{不|bú}{太|tài}{冷|lěng}。 — Tomorrow will be overcast and not too cold.
{天|tiān}{晴|qíng}{了|le}！ — The sky's cleared! (change-of-state {了|le})
{天|tiān}{阴|yīn}{了|le}，{快要|kuài yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。 — It's clouded over; it's about to rain.

{天|tiān} here is the sky, as in {天气|tiān qì} (weather, "sky air"). {天|tiān}{晴|qíng}{了|le} and
{天|tiān}{阴|yīn}{了|le} are the everyday ways to say the weather has changed.

The nouns {晴天|qíng tiān} and {阴天|yīn tiān} name the kind of day: {今天|jīn tiān}{是|shì}{阴天|yīn tiān}。
(Today is an overcast day.) {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{晴天|qíng tiān}。 (I like sunny days.) A light cloud
cover, "partly cloudy", is {多云|duō yún} in forecasts, another extra.

### Reading a forecast

Weather forecasts in apps and on television are written in a compressed style: the day, then the
weather words, with no {很|hěn} and no verb. Temperatures are in {度|dù}, degrees (Celsius in
China; an extra word).

| | Weather | Temperature |
|---|---|---|
| {今天|jīn tiān} {周三|zhōu sān} | {晴|qíng} | 5–15{度|dù} |
| {明天|míng tiān} {周四|zhōu sì} | {阴|yīn} | 3–10{度|dù} |
| {周五|zhōu wǔ} | {阴|yīn}，{下午|xià wǔ}{有|yǒu}{雨|yǔ} | 2–8{度|dù} |
| {周六|zhōu liù} | {晴|qíng} | 1–9{度|dù} |

{有|yǒu}{雨|yǔ} ("there will be rain") and {有|yǒu}{雪|xuě} are forecast style for {下雨|xià yǔ} and
{下雪|xià xuě}. Read the table aloud: {明天|míng tiān}{周四|zhōu sì}，{阴|yīn}，{三|sān}{到|dào}{十|shí}{度|dù}。
Temperatures below zero use {零下|líng xià}: {零下|líng xià}{五|wǔ}{度|dù}, minus five.

## A bird: {鸟|niǎo}

{鸟|niǎo} is a bird. Like cats and dogs, birds are counted with {只|zhī}: {一只|yì zhī}{鸟|niǎo},
{两只|liǎng zhī}{小|xiǎo}{鸟|niǎo}. {小鸟|xiǎo niǎo}, "little bird", is the friendly word for small birds
in general.

{天|tiān}{晴|qíng}{了|le}，{外面|wài miàn}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{鸟|niǎo}。 — The sky has cleared, and there are lots of birds outside.
{你|nǐ}{听|tīng}，{小|xiǎo}{鸟|niǎo}{在|zài}{叫|jiào}。 — Listen, the birds are singing.

{叫|jiào} (to call, to be called) is what animals do when they make their sound: birds sing,
dogs bark and cats miaow with {叫|jiào}.

## When I was little: {小时候|xiǎo shí hou} and {从小|cóng xiǎo}

Both are about childhood, but they are different kinds of word and go in different places.

**{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}** is a time word: "(in the time) when someone was little". Like
{昨天|zuó tiān} or {去年|qù nián}, it goes before the verb, either before or after the subject:

{我|wǒ}{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}。 — When I was little I lived in Beijing.
{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{画|huà}{画儿|huàr}。 — As a child I loved drawing.
{我|wǒ}{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{的|de}{家|jiā}{很|hěn}{小|xiǎo}。 — The home I grew up in was small.

It talks about the past as a time, and usually implies "back then": it may be different now.
Literally it's {小|xiǎo} (small) + {时候|shí hou} (the time when): "the time when (I was) small".

**{从小|cóng xiǎo}** is an adverb: "since childhood, from an early age". It says something began in
childhood and has lasted. It usually goes after the subject, right before the verb, very often
with {就|jiù} for "already then":

{他|tā}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{就|jiù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{踢|tī}{足球|zú qiú}。 — He's loved football ever since he was little.
{我|wǒ}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{长大|zhǎng dà}。 — I grew up in Beijing (from childhood on).

It's {从|cóng} (from, lesson 07) + {小|xiǎo}: "from small". ({长大|zhǎng dà}, "to grow up", uses
the {长|zhǎng} of HSK 3; here it's an extra word.)

Compare:

| Sentence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {我|wǒ}{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{鸟|niǎo}。 | When I was little I liked birds. (then; maybe not now) |
| {我|wǒ}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{就|jiù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{鸟|niǎo}。 | I've liked birds ever since I was little. (and still do) |

Two traps: {从小|cóng xiǎo} isn't a time word, so ~~{我|wǒ}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{的|de}{家|jiā}~~ is wrong (it's
{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{的|de}{家|jiā}); and {小时候|xiǎo shí hou} isn't {小时|xiǎo shí} (an hour) + {候|hou}:
read it as one word.

## And so on: …{什么|shén me}{的|de}

At the end of a list, {什么|shén me}{的|de} means "and so on, and things like that". It's a fixed
phrase of everyday speech:

{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}、{奶茶|nǎi chá}{什么|shén me}{的|de}。 — I like coffee, milk tea, that kind of thing.
{商场|shāng chǎng}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{衣服|yī fu}、{手表|shǒu biǎo}、{包|bāo}{什么|shén me}{的|de}。 — The shopping centre has clothes, watches, bags and so on.
{周六|zhōu liù}{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{看|kàn}{看|kan}{书|shū}、{上|shàng}{上|shang}{网|wǎng}{什么|shén me}{的|de}。 — On Saturdays I read a bit, go online a bit, that sort of thing.

- It goes right after the last item, with no {和|hé} before it.
- It can follow one item: {看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}{什么|shén me}{的|de} (watching films or something).
- The items are often separated by the enumeration comma 、 (a short slanted comma used only
  between items of a list), not by ，.
- In writing, {等|děng} does the same job: {咖啡|kā fēi}、{奶茶|nǎi chá}{等|děng}. You know {等|děng} as "to
  wait"; this "etc." is another use of the character.

The third example uses verb reduplication ({看看|kàn kan}, {上上网|shàng shang wǎng}: "a bit of", lesson 01).

## Characters

{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 晴 | sunny, clear | qíng | 日 | 12 | {晴|qíng}, {晴天|qíng tiān} |
| 阴 (traditional 陰) | overcast; shade | yīn | 阝 | 6 | {阴|yīn}, {阴天|yīn tiān} |
| 鸟 (traditional 鳥) | bird | niǎo | 鸟 | 5 | {鸟|niǎo}, {小鸟|xiǎo niǎo} |

晴 is the same in both scripts.

### How the characters are built

- 晴 = 日 (sun) + {青|qīng} for the sound: a sunny sky. It's the third *qing* character you know
  with 青 on the right, after {请|qǐng} (please) and {情|qíng} (in {事情|shì qing}, lesson 24).
- 阴 = 阝 + 月 (moon) in simplified script: the moon instead of the sun, shade instead of light. Its
  opposite, {阳|yáng} (sun, as in {太阳|tài yang}, HSK 3), is 阝 + 日. Traditional 陰 has a different
  right side: 今 over 云 (cloud).
- 鸟 is a drawing of a bird: the head with its eye (the dot), the body, and the tail at the bottom.
  Like 鱼 (lesson 22), traditional 鳥 ends in four dots where simplified has one stroke. You've seen
  鸟 before, on the right of {鸡|jī} in {鸡蛋|jī dàn}: a chicken is a bird.
- Memory aid: {乌|wū} (a crow; not a course character) is 鸟 without the dot, and people joke that the
  crow is so black you can't see its eye.

Radical review: **日** (sun) on the left is in {明|míng}, {昨|zuó}, {晚|wǎn}, {时|shí} and now {晴|qíng}: time
and light. **阝** on the left (from a word for a hill) is in {院|yuàn} and {阴|yīn}; the same shape on
the right (from a word for a town) is in {都|dōu} and {那|nà}.

### Stroke order

- 鸟: the short left-falling stroke at the top, then the stroke that goes right and hooks down,
  then the dot (the eye), then the long stroke down the body that bends right, bends down and hooks,
  and last the bottom horizontal. Five strokes.
- 阴: 阝 first: the "ear" in one stroke (right, then a curve down to the left and back), then the
  vertical; then 月.
- 晴: a narrow 日 on the left, then 青: two horizontals, the vertical through them, the long
  horizontal, then 月 below.

```trace
晴阴鸟
```

=}

## Dialogue: planning a day out

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) and {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) plan Saturday.

```dialogue
# Planning a day out
安娜: {王芳|Wáng Fāng}，{周六|zhōu liù}{天气|tiān qì}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？
= Wang Fang, what's the weather like on Saturday?
王芳: {网上|wǎng shàng}{说|shuō}{上午|shàng wǔ}{晴|qíng}，{下午|xià wǔ}{阴|yīn}，{晚上|wǎn shang}{可能|kě néng}{下雨|xià yǔ}。
= It says online it'll be sunny in the morning, overcast in the afternoon, and maybe rain in the evening.
安娜: {那|nà}{我们|wǒ men}{上午|shàng wǔ}{去|qù}{公园|gōng yuán}{吧|ba}。
= Then let's go to the park in the morning.
王芳: {好|hǎo}{啊|a}！{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{鸟|niǎo}、{画|huà}{画儿|huàr}{什么|shén me}{的|de}。
= Great! We can look at birds, do some drawing, that kind of thing.
安娜: {你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{鸟|niǎo}{吗|ma}？
= Do you like birds?
王芳: {很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}！{我|wǒ}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{就|jiù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{鸟|niǎo}。{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{两只|liǎng zhī}{小|xiǎo}{鸟|niǎo}。
= Very much! I've loved birds ever since I was little. When I was a child we had two little birds at home.
安娜: {我|wǒ}{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{也|yě}{想|xiǎng}{要|yào}{一只|yì zhī}{鸟|niǎo}，{但是|dàn shì}{妈妈|mā ma}{不|bú}{让|ràng}。
= When I was little I wanted a bird too, but Mum wouldn't let me.
王芳: {为什么|wèi shén me}？
= Why?
安娜: {因为|yīn wèi}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{两只|liǎng zhī}{猫|māo}！
= Because we had two cats!
王芳: {是|shì}{啊|a}，{猫|māo}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{鸟|niǎo}！{周六|zhōu liù}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}{见|jiàn}，{别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{带|dài}{伞|sǎn}。
= Yes, cats love birds too! See you at nine on Saturday; don't forget to bring an umbrella.
```

{公园|gōng yuán} (park), {带|dài} (to bring) and {伞|sǎn} (umbrella) are HSK 3 words. {周六|zhōu liù}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}{见|jiàn},
"Saturday nine o'clock see", is the usual short way to fix a time: day, time, {见|jiàn}.

## Reading: David's birds

{大卫|Dà wèi} writes about something he has loved since he was a child.

> {我|wǒ}{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{英国|Yīng guó}。{那儿|nàr}{经常|jīng cháng}{下雨|xià yǔ}，{晴天|qíng tiān}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}。{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{旁边|páng biān}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{公园|gōng yuán}，{里面|lǐ miàn}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{鸟|niǎo}。{我|wǒ}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{就|jiù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{鸟|niǎo}，{每|měi}{个|gè}{星期六|xīng qī liù}{都|dōu}{跟|gēn}{爷爷|yé ye}{去|qù}{公园|gōng yuán}{看|kàn}{鸟|niǎo}。{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}、{黑色|hēi sè}{的|de}、{白色|bái sè}{的|de}{什么|shén me}{的|de}，{爷爷|yé ye}{都|dōu}{知道|zhī dào}{它们|tā men}{叫|jiào}{什么|shén me}{名字|míng zi}。{现在|xiàn zài}{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{上|shàng}{大学|dà xué}。{北京|Běi jīng}{的|de}{晴天|qíng tiān}{比|bǐ}{英国|Yīng guó}{多|duō}，{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{经常|jīng cháng}{去|qù}{公园|gōng yuán}{看|kàn}{鸟|niǎo}。{上|shàng}{个|gè}{星期天|xīng qī tiān}{是|shì}{阴天|yīn tiān}，{但是|dàn shì}{我|wǒ}{看见|kàn jiàn}{了|le}{一只|yì zhī}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}{的|de}{鸟|niǎo}。{我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{爷爷|yé ye}{打|dǎ}{了|le}{电话|diàn huà}，{他|tā}{非常|fēi cháng}{高兴|gāo xìng}。

{英国|Yīng guó} is Britain (an extra word). Then answer:

1. What was the weather like where David grew up?
2. Who did he go to the park with, and how often?
3. What happened last Sunday?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. It often rained, and sunny days were rare ({晴天|qíng tiān}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}).
2. With his grandfather, every Saturday.
3. It was overcast, but he saw a beautiful bird, and he phoned his grandfather, who was very happy.

"When I was little I lived in Britain. It often rained there, and there weren't many sunny days.
Next to our house there was a park with lots of birds in it. I've loved birds since I was little,
and every Saturday I went to the park with my grandfather to look at them. Red ones, black ones,
white ones and so on: Grandpa knew the names of them all. Now I'm at university in Beijing.
Beijing has more sunny days than Britain, and I often go to the park to watch birds here too. Last
Sunday was overcast, but I saw a really beautiful bird. I phoned Grandpa, and he was very happy."
</details>

Notice both childhood words in one text: {我|wǒ}{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{英国|Yīng guó}
(back then, not now) and {我|wǒ}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{就|jiù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{鸟|niǎo} (since then, and still). The
list {红色|hóng sè}{的|de}、{黑色|hēi sè}{的|de}、{白色|bái sè}{的|de}{什么|shén me}{的|de} ends with …{什么|shén me}{的|de}, and
its items are separated by 、.

## Say it

```speak
{今天|jīn tiān}{是|shì}{晴天|qíng tiān}。
= It's a sunny day today.
{天|tiān}{阴|yīn}{了|le}，{快要|kuài yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。
= It's clouded over; it's about to rain.
{我|wǒ}{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}。
= When I was little I lived in Beijing.
{我|wǒ}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{就|jiù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{鸟|niǎo}。
= I've loved birds ever since I was little.
{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}、{奶茶|nǎi chá}{什么|shén me}{的|de}。
= I like coffee, milk tea, that kind of thing.
```

## Pronunciation

- {晴|qíng} rises; {请|qǐng} (please) dips; {情|qíng} in {事情|shì qing} is light. Same syllable, three
  ways.
- {阴|yīn}: high and level, ending in *-n*. {因为|yīn wèi} starts with the same syllable.
- {鸟|niǎo}: *n* + *iao*, a third tone. Don't drop the *i*: *nǎo* is {脑|nǎo} in {电脑|diàn nǎo}.
- {小鸟|xiǎo niǎo}: two third tones, so the first is said rising: *xiáo niǎo*.
- {小时候|xiǎo shí hou}: a dip, a rise, and a light *hou*. {从小|cóng xiǎo}: a rise, then a dip.
- {什么的|shén me de}: all after the first syllable is light and quick.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{今天|jīn tiān}{是|shì}{晴|qíng}~~: {晴|qíng} is an adjective, so no {是|shì}: {天|tiān}{很|hěn}{晴|qíng}, or,
  more usually, the noun: {今天|jīn tiān}{是|shì}{晴天|qíng tiān}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}~~: mixing the two. Say {我|wǒ}{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{从小|cóng xiǎo}~~ (English order): {从小|cóng xiǎo} goes before the
  verb: {我|wǒ}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}.
- ~~{什么|shén me}{的|de}{咖啡|kā fēi}、{奶茶|nǎi chá}~~: {什么|shén me}{的|de} comes after the list, never before it.
- ~~{一|yí}{个|gè}{鸟|niǎo}~~: birds take {只|zhī}: {一只|yì zhī}{鸟|niǎo}.
- {=Writing 鸟 without its dot: that's {乌|wū}, a crow.=}

## Key points

- {晴|qíng} (sunny, clear) and {阴|yīn} (overcast) are adjectives: {天|tiān}{很|hěn}{晴|qíng},
  {天|tiān}{阴|yīn}{了|le}; {晴天|qíng tiān} / {阴天|yīn tiān} are the nouns.
- Forecasts: day + weather words, no {很|hěn}; {有|yǒu}{雨|yǔ} for rain; {度|dù} for degrees.
- {鸟|niǎo}: a bird, counted with {只|zhī}.
- {小时候|xiǎo shí hou}: a time word, "when I was little" (then). {从小|cóng xiǎo}: an adverb before the verb,
  "ever since childhood" (and still), often with {就|jiù}.
- …{什么|shén me}{的|de} at the end of a list: "and so on"; items separated by 、.
- {=Characters: 晴 (sun + 青), 阴 (陰), 鸟 (鳥).=}

lessons.title: Chinese cuisines
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

"Chinese food" is many cuisines. A meal in Chengdu, in Guangzhou and in Qingdao can share almost
nothing but the chopsticks: one fiery and numbing, one light and fresh, one built on seafood. This
honors lesson introduces the regional styles that Chinese people themselves talk about, a few
famous dishes from each, and how a meal with friends works when everyone shares. You'll use this
module's grammar along the way: {这么|zhè me}, choice questions with {还是|hái shi}, {别|bié},
approximate numbers and {什么|shén me}{的|de}. The new words here are glossed, not added to your
reviews.

## Cuisines: {菜|cài} after a region

You know {菜|cài} as a dish and {中国|Zhōng guó}{菜|cài} as Chinese food. Put a region in front and it
names a regional cuisine. Each province also has a one-character short name, and the cuisines are
usually called by it. (Jiangsu's best-known style is the exception: it is named after a region,
{淮扬|huái yáng}, the area of Huai'an and Yangzhou.)

| Cuisine | Short name | Region | Known for |
|---|---|---|---|
| {川菜|chuān cài} | {川|chuān} | {四川|Sì chuān}, Sichuan (south-west) | chilli, garlic and Sichuan pepper; bold, hot flavours |
| {粤菜|yuè cài} | {粤|yuè} | {广东|Guǎng dōng}, Guangdong (south) | light sauces that let fresh ingredients taste of themselves; dim sum |
| {鲁菜|lǔ cài} | {鲁|lǔ} | {山东|Shān dōng}, Shandong (east coast) | seafood; salty, fresh and crisp; braising |
| {淮扬菜|huái yáng cài} | {淮扬|huái yáng} | {江苏|Jiāng sū}, Jiangsu (east) | braising and stewing; mild, slightly sweet |

These four are often called the "four great cuisines". In modern times the list is usually
extended to **eight**, adding Zhejiang ({浙|zhè}), Fujian ({闽|mǐn}), Hunan ({湘|xiāng}, known for
being very hot and sour) and Anhui ({徽|huī}, from the old region of Huizhou rather than the
province's short name). Treat these as a common way of grouping, not a fixed
rule: they leave out plenty of other well-loved styles, including Beijing's (home of
{北京|Běi jīng}{烤鸭|kǎo yā}, Peking roast duck), and every city has its own favourites.

## Hot, light, sweet: the words for taste

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {辣|là} | (chilli) hot, spicy | {很|hěn}{辣|là}, {不|bú}{辣|là} |
| {麻|má} | numbing, tingly | the feeling of Sichuan pepper on the tongue |
| {甜|tián} | sweet | an HSK 3 word |
| {酸|suān} | sour | as in vinegar |
| {清淡|qīng dàn} | light, mild | not oily, not strongly seasoned |

{麻|má} and {辣|là} together, {麻辣|má là}, are the signature of Sichuan cooking: chillies for the
heat, Sichuan pepper for a tingling numbness. If you can't take the heat, the phrase to learn is

{别|bié}{放|fàng}{辣|là}，{谢谢|xiè xie}！ — No chilli, please! ({放|fàng}: to put in, HSK 3)

or ask {这个|zhè ge}{菜|cài}{辣|là}{不|bu}{辣|là}？ (Is this dish spicy?). A server may ask you a choice
question back: {微辣|wēi là}{还是|hái shi}{特辣|tè là}？ (mild or extra hot?).

## Some famous dishes

| Dish | Cuisine | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| {麻婆豆腐|má pó dòu fu} | {川菜|chuān cài} | tofu in a hot, numbing sauce with a little minced meat; it comes from Chengdu |
| {宫保鸡丁|gōng bǎo jī dīng} | {川菜|chuān cài} | diced chicken stir-fried with chillies and peanuts (kung pao chicken) |
| {点心|diǎn xin} | {粤菜|yuè cài} | dim sum: small dishes such as steamed shrimp dumplings, rice-noodle rolls and turnip cake |
| {糖醋鲤鱼|táng cù lǐ yú} | {鲁菜|lǔ cài} | a whole carp, fried, in sweet and sour sauce |
| {北京|Běi jīng}{烤鸭|kǎo yā} | Beijing | roast duck, sliced and wrapped in thin pancakes |

{点心|diǎn xin} has the {点|diǎn} of this module's {点|diǎn}{菜|cài}, but here it's part of a word: "dim
sum" is the Cantonese pronunciation of the same two characters. In Guangdong people
often call a dim sum meal {喝|hē}{早茶|zǎo chá}, "drinking morning tea": you go for the tea and stay
for the food.

{糖醋鲤鱼|táng cù lǐ yú} is counted like any fish: {一|yì}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú}. And when the menu just says
{肉|ròu}, remember lesson 22: it's very often pork.

## Eating together

A meal with family or friends in China is shared. The dishes go in the middle of the table, often on
a turntable in restaurants, and everyone has their own bowl of rice and takes a little from each
dish. So you don't order one main course each: the group orders several dishes together. A common
rule of thumb is one dish per person, and one more.

{我们|wǒ men}{五|wǔ}{个|gè}{人|rén}，{点|diǎn}{六七|liù qī}{个|gè}{菜|cài}{吧|ba}。 — There are five of us; let's order six or seven dishes.

At more formal meals there are serving chopsticks, {公筷|gōng kuài} ("public chopsticks"), used only
to take food from the shared dishes. When in doubt, watch what your hosts do.

A typical order mixes kinds and tastes: a meat dish, a fish, a vegetable dish, a soup, some spicy
and some mild ones.

{我们|wǒ men}{点|diǎn}{一|yí}{个|gè}{肉|ròu}{菜|cài}、{一|yì}{条|tiáo}{鱼|yú}、{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{青菜|qīng cài}{什么|shén me}{的|de}。 — Let's order a meat dish, a fish, two green vegetable dishes and so on.

({青菜|qīng cài}: green vegetables, a common menu word.)

## Dialogue: what shall we order?

{大卫|Dà wèi} (大卫) and {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) are at a Sichuan restaurant with three friends.

```dialogue
# What shall we order?
王芳: {我们|wǒ men}{五|wǔ}{个|gè}{人|rén}，{点|diǎn}{六七|liù qī}{个|gè}{菜|cài}{吧|ba}。
= There are five of us; let's order six or seven dishes.
大卫: {好|hǎo}。{你们|nǐ men}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{辣|là}{的|de}{还是|hái shi}{不|bú}{辣|là}{的|de}？
= OK. Do you like spicy or not spicy?
王芳: {我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{爱|ài}{吃|chī}{辣|là}！{你|nǐ}{呢|ne}？
= We all love spicy food! What about you?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{就|jiù}{不|bù}{能|néng}{吃|chī}{辣|là}{的|de}。
= I've never been able to eat spicy food, ever since I was little.
王芳: {那|nà}{我们|wǒ men}{点|diǎn}{一|yí}{个|gè}{麻婆豆腐|má pó dòu fu}，{再|zài}{点|diǎn}{两三|liǎng sān}{个|gè}{不|bú}{辣|là}{的|de}{菜|cài}。
= Then we'll order a mapo tofu, and two or three dishes that aren't spicy.
大卫: {麻婆豆腐|má pó dòu fu}{辣|là}{不|bu}{辣|là}？
= Is mapo tofu spicy?
王芳: {又|yòu}{麻|má}{又|yòu}{辣|là}，{你|nǐ}{别|bié}{吃|chī}{了|le}！
= Numbing and hot: you'd better not eat it!
大卫: {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{试试|shì shi}。
= I'd like to try it anyway.
```

{又|yòu}…{又|yòu}… ("both… and…") is an HSK 3 pattern, and {试|shì} (to try; {试试|shì shi}, have a try) an HSK 3 word. {我|wǒ}{从小|cóng xiǎo}{就|jiù}{不|bù}{能|néng}{吃|chī}{辣|là}{的|de}
uses lesson 25's {从小|cóng xiǎo}: it has been true all his life.

## Reading: a menu

> **{四川|Sì chuān}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}**
>
> | {菜|cài} | {辣|là} | {元|yuán} |
> |---|---|---|
> | {麻婆豆腐|má pó dòu fu} | {很|hěn}{辣|là} | 28 |
> | {宫保鸡丁|gōng bǎo jī dīng} | {辣|là} | 38 |
> | {糖醋|táng cù}{鱼|yú} | — | 68 |
> | {青菜|qīng cài} | — | 18 |
> | {米饭|mǐ fàn} | — | 2 |

1. Which dish is the hottest?
2. You order a mapo tofu, a kung pao chicken and two bowls of rice. About how much is it, using
   {多|duō}?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. {麻婆豆腐|má pó dòu fu}: {很|hěn}{辣|là}.
2. 28 + 38 + 2 + 2 = 70 {元|yuán} exactly, so no {多|duō} needed: {七十|qī shí}{块|kuài}. Without the rice it
   would be 66, {六十多|liù shí duō}{块|kuài}, sixty-odd kuai.
</details>

## Key points

- Regional cuisines are named with a region's short name + {菜|cài}: {川菜|chuān cài} (Sichuan),
  {粤菜|yuè cài} (Cantonese), {鲁菜|lǔ cài} (Shandong), {淮扬菜|huái yáng cài} (Jiangsu).
- "Four great" and "eight great" cuisines are common groupings, not the whole picture.
- Sichuan cooking is {麻辣|má là}, numbing and hot; Cantonese cooking is light and fresh, with dim sum.
- Dishes are shared; order about one per person, mixing tastes; {公筷|gōng kuài} are serving
  chopsticks.

lessons.title: The Mid-Autumn Festival and the moon
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Like the Spring Festival, the Mid-Autumn Festival is one of the best-loved festivals of the
Chinese year: a night for family, mooncakes and the full moon. This honors lesson tells you when
it is and what people do, retells the story of Chang'e, the woman who flew to the moon, and ends
with the most famous moon poem in Chinese, Li Bai's "Quiet Night Thoughts", four short lines that
many Chinese children learn by heart. The new words here are glossed, not added to your reviews.

## When it is: {中秋节|Zhōng qiū jié}

{中秋节|Zhōng qiū jié} means "the mid-autumn festival": {中|zhōng} (middle) + {秋|qiū} (autumn) +
{节|jié} (festival). In the traditional calendar, autumn is the seventh, eighth and ninth months, and
the festival falls in the very middle: **the 15th day of the 8th month**, the night of the full
moon. In the Gregorian calendar the date moves, landing in September or early October.

{中秋节|Zhōng qiū jié}{是|shì}{八|bā}{月|yuè}{十五|shí wǔ}。 — The Mid-Autumn Festival is on the fifteenth of the eighth month.

People simply call the date {八|bā}{月|yuè}{十五|shí wǔ}, "the eighth month, fifteenth": everyone knows
which calendar is meant. In mainland China the festival has been a public holiday since 2008.

The greeting is {中秋节|Zhōng qiū jié}{快乐|kuài lè}！ (Happy Mid-Autumn Festival!), built like
{生日快乐|shēng rì kuài lè} (lesson 13).

## Moon, mooncakes and family

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {月亮|yuè liang} | the moon | an HSK 3 word; {月|yuè} alone in poems and set phrases |
| {月饼|yuè bǐng} | mooncake | a round pastry with a sweet or savoury filling |
| {赏月|shǎng yuè} | to admire the moon | the festival's main activity |
| {团圆|tuán yuán} | (family) reunion, being together | the festival's main idea |

The full moon is round, and a round moon stands for a family that is whole, everyone together.
That's why the festival is above all a family night: people travel home if they can, eat dinner
together, then go outside, or up on the roof or balcony, to look at the moon and eat mooncakes.

{月饼|yuè bǐng} are round too. Classic fillings are lotus-seed paste, sweet bean paste and a salted
egg yolk in the middle (the yolk looks like a little moon), but there are many regional kinds,
and every year brings new flavours. Boxes of mooncakes are a usual gift to family, friends and
colleagues in the weeks before the festival.

{中秋节|Zhōng qiū jié}{晚上|wǎn shang}，{我们|wǒ men}{一|yì}{家|jiā}{人|rén}{一起|yì qǐ}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}、{吃|chī}{月饼|yuè bǐng}、{看|kàn}{月亮|yuè liang}。 — On the night of the festival, our whole family eats dinner together, eats mooncakes and looks at the moon.

{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{甜|tián}{的|de}{月饼|yuè bǐng}{还是|hái shi}{咸|xián}{的|de}？ — Do you prefer sweet mooncakes or savoury ones?

Children often carry paper lanterns, {灯笼|dēng long}, especially in the south. And on a clear night
the weather word of lesson 25 matters: everyone hopes it's {晴|qíng}, not {阴|yīn}.

## Chang'e, the woman in the moon

The story behind the festival has many versions. Here is a common one, in simple Chinese and then
in English.

> {古时候|gǔ shí hou}，{天|tiān}{上|shàng}{有|yǒu}{十|shí}{个|gè}{太阳|tài yang}，{天气|tiān qì}{非常|fēi cháng}{热|rè}。{一|yí}{个|gè}{叫|jiào}{后羿|Hòu Yì}{的|de}{人|rén}{射|shè}{下|xià}{了|le}{九|jiǔ}{个|gè}{太阳|tài yang}。{有|yǒu}{人|rén}{送|sòng}{他|tā}{一|yì}{种|zhǒng}{药|yào}，{吃|chī}{了|le}{就|jiù}{能|néng}{长生不老|cháng shēng bù lǎo}。{后羿|Hòu Yì}{的|de}{妻子|qī zi}{叫|jiào}{嫦娥|Cháng'é}。{一|yì}{天|tiān}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{坏|huài}{人|rén}{想|xiǎng}{拿|ná}{走|zǒu}{这|zhè}{个|gè}{药|yào}。{嫦娥|Cháng'é}{没|méi}{有|yǒu}{办法|bàn fǎ}，{就|jiù}{自己|zì jǐ}{吃|chī}{了|le}{药|yào}。{她|tā}{飞|fēi}{起来|qǐ lái}{了|le}，{飞|fēi}{到|dào}{了|le}{月亮|yuè liang}{上|shàng}。{现在|xiàn zài}，{很|hěn}{多|duō}{人|rén}{说|shuō}，{月亮|yuè liang}{上|shàng}{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{一只|yì zhī}{白色|bái sè}{的|de}{小|xiǎo}{兔子|tù zi}。

Words: {古时候|gǔ shí hou} long ago, {太阳|tài yang} sun, {射|shè} to shoot (with a bow),
{种|zhǒng} kind (HSK 3), {长生不老|cháng shēng bù lǎo} to live forever, {嫦娥|Cháng'é} Chang'e,
{办法|bàn fǎ} a way out (HSK 3), {兔子|tù zi} rabbit.

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

"Long ago there were ten suns in the sky, and it was terribly hot. A man called Hou Yi shot down
nine of the suns. Someone gave him a medicine: whoever took it would live forever. Hou Yi's wife
was called Chang'e. One day a bad man tried to take the medicine away. Chang'e saw no other way, so
she took the medicine herself. She rose into the air and flew all the way to the moon. Today many
people say there's a little white rabbit on the moon, too."
</details>

In other versions the medicine comes from the Queen Mother of the West, a goddess; or Hou Yi has
become a cruel ruler, and Chang'e drinks it so that he can't live forever. In all of them she ends up
on the moon, and on festival night people look up and think of her. The rabbit, the {玉兔|yù tù}
("jade rabbit"), is said to pound medicine in a mortar there.

Notice the HSK 2 grammar in the story: {射|shè}{下|xià}{了|le} (a direction complement: shot *down*),
{飞|fēi}{起来|qǐ lái} (rose up into the air) and {飞|fēi}{到|dào}{了|le}{月亮|yuè liang}{上|shàng} (flew to the moon:
{到|dào} as a result).

## Li Bai: "Quiet Night Thoughts"

{李白|Lǐ Bái} (Li Bai) is one of the great poets of the Tang dynasty (618–907), famous for poems about
wine, mountains, friendship and the moon. This short poem, 《{静夜思|jìng yè sī}》, "Quiet Night
Thoughts", isn't about the festival itself, but it is the poem people think of when they see a full
moon far from home. Each line has five characters.

> {床前明月光|chuáng qián míng yuè guāng}，
> {疑是地上霜|yí shì dì shàng shuāng}。
> {举头望明月|jǔ tóu wàng míng yuè}，
> {低头思故乡|dī tóu sī gù xiāng}。

Our translation:

> Before my bed, the moonlight shines so bright,
> I wonder: is it frost upon the ground?
> I raise my head and gaze at the bright moon,
> then bow my head and think of home.

You know more of these characters than you might expect:

| Characters | Reading | Meaning here | You know it from |
|---|---|---|---|
| 床前 | chuáng qián | in front of the bed | {起床|qǐ chuáng}, {前面|qián miàn} |
| 明月光 | míng yuè guāng | the bright moon's light | {明天|míng tiān}, {月|yuè} |
| 疑是 | yí shì | (I) suspect it is, wonder if it is | {是|shì} |
| 地上霜 | dì shàng shuāng | frost on the ground | {地铁|dì tiě}, {上|shàng} |
| 举头 | jǔ tóu | to raise the head | {头|tóu} (lesson 02) |
| 望 | wàng | to gaze into the distance | {希望|xī wàng} (lesson 18) |
| 低头 | dī tóu | to lower the head | {头|tóu} |
| 思故乡 | sī gù xiāng | to think of (my) home town | {意思|yì si} (lesson 15) |

Scholars still discuss what exactly 床 means here: a bed, or (some argue) the railing around a well
or a low seat. Either way, the speaker is awake at night, sees moonlight so white it looks like frost,
looks up at the moon and thinks of home, the same moon that shines there.

### The poem's other text

The four lines above are the text everyone learns today; they're the wording in popular
Qing-dynasty anthologies such as 《{唐诗三百首|Táng shī sān bǎi shǒu}》 (*Three Hundred Tang Poems*). Older
collections, such as the Song-dynasty anthology 《{乐府诗集|Yuè fǔ shī jí}》 (*Collection of Yuefu
Poems*), have two different words:

> {床前看月光|chuáng qián kàn yuè guāng}，{疑是地上霜|yí shì dì shàng shuāng}。
> {举头望山月|jǔ tóu wàng shān yuè}，{低头思故乡|dī tóu sī gù xiāng}。

"Before my bed I see the moonlight… I raise my head and gaze at the mountain moon." Which wording
Li Bai himself wrote can't be known for certain, and both have their defenders; this course teaches
the familiar one and mentions the other.

## Reading: a message on festival night

> {妈妈|mā ma}，{中秋节|Zhōng qiū jié}{快乐|kuài lè}！{我|wǒ}{今年|jīn nián}{不|bù}{能|néng}{回|huí}{家|jiā}，{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{几|jǐ}{个|gè}{同学|tóng xué}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{过|guò}{节|jié}。{我们|wǒ men}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{十几|shí jǐ}{个|gè}{月饼|yuè bǐng}，{有|yǒu}{甜|tián}{的|de}，{也|yě}{有|yǒu}{咸|xián}{的|de}。{今天|jīn tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{很|hěn}{晴|qíng}，{月亮|yuè liang}{这么|zhè me}{大|dà}！{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{起|qǐ}{了|le}{李白|Lǐ Bái}{的|de}{诗|shī}：“{举头望明月|jǔ tóu wàng míng yuè}，{低头思故乡|dī tóu sī gù xiāng}。”{你们|nǐ men}{别|bié}{太|tài}{晚|wǎn}{睡|shuì}，{早|zǎo}{点儿|diǎnr}{休息|xiū xi}{吧|ba}。

{过|guò}{节|jié}: to spend a festival (HSK 3); {诗|shī}: poem; {想|xiǎng}{起|qǐ}: to be reminded of.

1. Where is the writer spending the festival, and with whom?
2. What is the weather like tonight?
3. Which two lines of the poem does the writer quote?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. At school, with a few classmates ({几|jǐ}{个|gè}{同学|tóng xué}).
2. Clear ({很|hěn}{晴|qíng}), and the moon is big.
3. The last two: "I raise my head and gaze at the bright moon, then bow my head and think of home."

"Mum, happy Mid-Autumn Festival! I can't come home this year; I'm spending the festival at school
with a few classmates. We bought a dozen or so mooncakes, some sweet and some savoury. It's very
clear tonight, and the moon is so big! It made me think of Li Bai's poem: 'I raise my head and gaze
at the bright moon, then bow my head and think of home.' Don't stay up too late: get to bed early."
</details>

## Key points

- {中秋节|Zhōng qiū jié}: the 15th day of the 8th lunar month ({八|bā}{月|yuè}{十五|shí wǔ}), at full moon;
  September or early October.
- Family reunion ({团圆|tuán yuán}), mooncakes ({月饼|yuè bǐng}), admiring the moon ({赏月|shǎng yuè}).
  Greeting: {中秋节|Zhōng qiū jié}{快乐|kuài lè}！
- Chang'e took the medicine of immortality and flew to the moon; the versions differ on why.
- Li Bai's 《{静夜思|jìng yè sī}》: {床前明月光|chuáng qián míng yuè guāng}，{疑是地上霜|yí shì dì shàng shuāng}。{举头望明月|jǔ tóu wàng míng yuè}，{低头思故乡|dī tóu sī gù xiāng}。
  Older texts read {看月光|kàn yuè guāng} and {望山月|wàng shān yuè}.

lessons.title: Already, about to, still
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last module of HSK 2. It adds no new words: it puts together what you know and
practises the tasks of the level, reading notices and messages, listening, writing short notes and
the exam itself. It starts with a group of patterns you've met one by one in modules 4 and 5 and
that you'll hear many times a day: how to say that something has *already* happened, is *about to*
happen, *still* hasn't happened, or that it's *already that late*.

Each of them is a **[[fixed pattern]]**: two parts that always go together, with the verb or the time
word between them, such as {快要|kuài yào}……{了|le} (about to…). You learn the frame once and fill it with any
words. You know other fixed patterns already: {因为|yīn wèi}……{所以|suǒ yǐ}, {虽然|suī rán}……{但是|dàn shì}, {从|cóng}……{到|dào}…… and {什么|shén me}{的|de} at the end of
a list (lesson 25).

At the end of the lesson you'll find a time line with all of them on it. Keep it in mind as you
read: *done*, *happening now*, *about to happen*, *not yet*.

## Done: {已经|yǐ jīng}……{了|le}

You learned {已经|yǐ jīng} (already) in lesson 18. It goes before the verb, and the sentence usually ends
with {了|le}:

{我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}。 — I've already eaten.
{他们|tā men}{已经|yǐ jīng}{走|zǒu}{了|le}。 — They've already left.
{电影|diàn yǐng}{已经|yǐ jīng}{开始|kāi shǐ}{了|le}。 — The film has already started.

{已经|yǐ jīng} also goes before a time, an age or an amount, with {了|le} at the end. There's no verb: the time
word is the predicate, as in {现在|xiàn zài}{十|shí}{点|diǎn} (lesson 07 of HSK 1).

{已经|yǐ jīng}{十二|shí èr}{点|diǎn}{了|le}。 — It's already twelve o'clock.
{我|wǒ}{妹妹|mèi mei}{已经|yǐ jīng}{十八|shí bā}{岁|suì}{了|le}。 — My younger sister is already eighteen.
{已经|yǐ jīng}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{了|le}。 — It's been two hours already.

The negative of "already done" is "not yet": {还|hái}{没|méi} + verb, and *no* {了|le} (see "Not yet" below).
Never ~~{已经|yǐ jīng}{没|méi}~~ for "not yet".

## About to happen: {快要|kuài yào}……{了|le}, {快|kuài}……{了|le}, {要|yào}……{了|le}

Lesson 23 taught {快要|kuài yào} (about to, soon). All of these mean "something is about to happen", and all
of them end with {了|le}:

| Pattern | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {快要|kuài yào} + verb + {了|le} | {快要|kuài yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。 | It's about to rain. |
| {快|kuài} + verb + {了|le} | {快|kuài}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。 | It's going to rain soon. |
| {要|yào} + verb + {了|le} | {要|yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。 | It's going to rain. |
| {快|kuài} + time / number + {了|le} | {快|kuài}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{了|le}。 | It's nearly ten o'clock. |
| {就|jiù}{要|yào} + verb + {了|le} | {我们|wǒ men}{明天|míng tiān}{就|jiù}{要|yào}{考试|kǎo shì}{了|le}。 | We have our exam tomorrow (it's very close). |

{快要|kuài yào}, {快|kuài} and {要|yào} mean almost the same before a verb; {快要|kuài yào} and {快|kuài} stress that it's very soon.
The {了|le} at the end is the "change" {了|le} of HSK 1 lesson 20: a new situation is coming.

{火车|huǒ chē}{快要|kuài yào}{开|kāi}{了|le}！ — The train is about to leave!
{我|wǒ}{快要|kuài yào}{到|dào}{了|le}，{你|nǐ}{在|zài}{门口|mén kǒu}{等|děng}{我|wǒ}{吧|ba}。 — I'm almost there; wait for me at the door.
{他|tā}{快|kuài}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}{了|le}。 — He's nearly twenty.
{快|kuài}{十二|shí èr}{点|diǎn}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吧|ba}。 — It's nearly twelve: let's go and eat.

Before a time or a number, {快|kuài} is the usual choice: {快|kuài}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{了|le}. You'll also hear
{快要|kuài yào} there, as in lesson 23's {我|wǒ}{快要|kuài yào}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}{了|le}.

### With a time word: {就|jiù}{要|yào}……{了|le}

When the sentence says *when* ({明天|míng tiān}, {下|xià}{个|gè}{月|yuè}, {九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}), use {就|jiù}{要|yào}……{了|le} instead of {快要|kuài yào}……{了|le}. {就|jiù} (lesson 18)
here stresses that it's soon:

{下|xià}{个|gè}{月|yuè}{我们|wǒ men}{就|jiù}{要|yào}{开学|kāi xué}{了|le}。 — School starts next month.
{电影|diàn yǐng}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}{就|jiù}{要|yào}{开始|kāi shǐ}{了|le}。 — The film starts at nine.

Saying ~~{明天|míng tiān}{快要|kuài yào}{考试|kǎo shì}{了|le}~~ is a classic mistake: {快要|kuài yào} already means "very soon", and a time word on top
of it doesn't fit. Say {明天|míng tiān}{就|jiù}{要|yào}{考试|kǎo shì}{了|le}, or just {明天|míng tiān}{考试|kǎo shì}.

### Asking and answering

{你们|nǐ men}{快要|kuài yào}{到|dào}{了|le}{吗|ma}？ — Are you nearly there?
{快|kuài}{到|dào}{了|le}。 — Nearly.
{还|hái}{没|méi}{呢|ne}，{我们|wǒ men}{还|hái}{在|zài}{路上|lù shang}。 — Not yet, we're still on the way.

## "Already!": {都|dōu}……{了|le}

{都|dōu} (all, lesson 02 of HSK 1) has a second use: in {都|dōu} + time / age + {了|le} it means "already", with a
feeling. The speaker finds it late, a lot, or surprising:

{都|dōu}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{了|le}！{他|tā}{怎么|zěn me}{还|hái}{没|méi}{起来|qǐ lái}？ — It's already ten! Why isn't he up yet?
{你|nǐ}{都|dōu}{二十|èr shí}{岁|suì}{了|le}，{自己|zì jǐ}{洗|xǐ}{衣服|yī fu}{吧|ba}。 — You're twenty now: wash your own clothes.
{我|wǒ}{都|dōu}{等|děng}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{了|le}！ — I've been waiting for a whole hour!

Compare:

| | |
|---|---|
| {已经|yǐ jīng}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{了|le}。 | It's (already) ten o'clock. *a fact* |
| {都|dōu}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{了|le}！ | It's ten o'clock already! *too late, I'm surprised or annoyed* |

You can use both together for extra force: {都|dōu}{已经|yǐ jīng}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{了|le}！ In speech, {都|dōu} here is usually light;
the time after it carries the stress.

Don't confuse this {都|dōu} with {都|dōu} "all": {我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{十八|shí bā}{岁|suì} (we're all eighteen) has no {了|le} and is a plain
statement. {我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{十八|shí bā}{岁|suì}{了|le} can mean either "we're all eighteen now" or "we're already eighteen!":
the tone of voice and the situation decide.

## Not yet, still: {还|hái} + negative

{还|hái} (still, HSK 1 lesson 24) with {没|méi} gives "not yet":

{他|tā}{还|hái}{没|méi}{来|lái}。 — He hasn't come yet.
{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{没|méi}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{呢|ne}。 — I haven't eaten yet.
—{你|nǐ}{考|kǎo}{完|wán}{了|le}{吗|ma}？—{还|hái}{没|méi}{呢|ne}。 — "Have you finished your exam?" "Not yet."

- {还|hái}{没|méi} + verb has *no* {了|le}: the action hasn't happened, so there's nothing completed or changed.
  {呢|ne} at the end is common in speech and makes it softer.
- {他|tā}{没|méi}{来|lái} just says he didn't come; {他|tā}{还|hái}{没|méi}{来|lái} says you're still waiting for him.
- {还|hái}{没|méi}{呢|ne} is the usual short answer to a ……{了|le}{吗|ma}？ question when the answer is "not yet".

With {不|bù} instead of {没|méi}, {还|hái} says something *still isn't so*, or someone *still won't* do it:

{他|tā}{还|hái}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}。 — He still doesn't know.
{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。 — I don't want to go to bed yet.

And with an ordinary verb, {还|hái} is "still": {外面|wài miàn}{还|hái}{在|zài}{下雨|xià yǔ} (it's still raining outside), {他|tā}{还|hái}{在|zài}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{呢|ne}
(he's still asleep).

## Happening now: {正在|zhèng zài} / {在|zài} / {正|zhèng}……{呢|ne} (review)

You learned the progressive in HSK 1 lesson 10: {正在|zhèng zài}, {在|zài} or {正|zhèng} before the verb, often {呢|ne} at the end.

{我|wǒ}{正在|zhèng zài}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}{呢|ne}，{一会儿|yí huìr}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{打|dǎ}。 — I'm on the phone; I'll call you back in a moment.
{他们|tā men}{在|zài}{上课|shàng kè}。 — They're in class.

{正|zhèng} (just, exactly: lesson 23) also goes before {要|yào}: {正|zhèng}{要|yào} + verb is "just about to" at this very
moment:

{我|wǒ}{正|zhèng}{要|yào}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}！ — I was just going to call you!

## Better do this: {还是|hái shi}……{吧|ba}

In lesson 21 {还是|hái shi} was "or" in questions: {咖啡|kā fēi}{还是|hái shi}{茶|chá}？ In a statement with {吧|ba} at the end, {还是|hái shi} means
"had better", "it would be better to". You use it after thinking about the choices:

{外面|wài miàn}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{还是|hái shi}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{吧|ba}。 — It's raining outside: we'd better take the metro.
{太|tài}{晚|wǎn}{了|le}，{你|nǐ}{还是|hái shi}{别|bié}{走|zǒu}{了|le}，{在|zài}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{住|zhù}{吧|ba}。 — It's too late: you'd better not leave; stay at my place.
{我们|wǒ men}{还是|hái shi}{明天|míng tiān}{去|qù}{吧|ba}。 — Let's go tomorrow instead.

The {吧|ba} is the suggestion {吧|ba} of HSK 1 lesson 12. Without it, {还是|hái shi} + verb is "still": {他|tā}{还是|hái shi}{没|méi}{来|lái} (he
still didn't come). So listen for the {吧|ba}.

## The time line

| Already done | Happening now | About to happen | Not yet |
|---|---|---|---|
| {已经|yǐ jīng}……{了|le} | {正在|zhèng zài} / {在|zài} / {正|zhèng}……{呢|ne} | {快要|kuài yào} / {快|kuài} / {要|yào}……{了|le} | {还|hái}{没|méi}……（{呢|ne}） |
| {他|tā}{已经|yǐ jīng}{到|dào}{了|le}。 | {他|tā}{正在|zhèng zài}{路上|lù shang}{呢|ne}。 | {他|tā}{快要|kuài yào}{到|dào}{了|le}。 | {他|tā}{还|hái}{没|méi}{到|dào}{呢|ne}。 |
| He's arrived. | He's on his way. | He's almost here. | He isn't here yet. |

And two for feelings and decisions: {都|dōu}……{了|le} ("already!", it's late) and {还是|hái shi}……{吧|ba} ("we'd better").


## Dialogue: we're going to be late

The speakers are {小兰|Xiǎo Lán} and her younger brother {小明|Xiǎo Míng}; their names label the lines.

```dialogue
# We're going to be late
小兰: {小明|Xiǎo Míng}，{都|dōu}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{了|le}！{你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{还|hái}{没|méi}{起来|qǐ lái}？
= Xiaoming, it's eight o'clock already! Why aren't you up yet?
小明: {我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{起来|qǐ lái}{了|le}，{正在|zhèng zài}{洗|xǐ}{手|shǒu}{呢|ne}。
= I'm already up, I'm washing my hands.
小兰: {快|kuài}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}！{电影|diàn yǐng}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}{就|jiù}{要|yào}{开始|kāi shǐ}{了|le}。
= Hurry up! The film starts at nine.
小明: {我们|wǒ men}{坐|zuò}{公交车|gōng jiāo chē}{去|qù}{吗|ma}？
= Are we taking the bus?
小兰: {公交车|gōng jiāo chē}{太|tài}{慢|màn}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{还是|hái shi}{打车|dǎ chē}{吧|ba}。
= The bus is too slow; we'd better take a taxi.
小明: {好|hǎo}。{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手表|shǒu biǎo}{呢|ne}？{我|wǒ}{找不到|zhǎo bu dào}{了|le}……{啊|a}，{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}！
= OK. Where's my watch? I can't find... ah, here it is!
小兰: {车|chē}{快要|kuài yào}{到|dào}{门口|mén kǒu}{了|le}，{走|zǒu}{吧|ba}！
= The taxi's almost at the door. Let's go!
小明: {等|děng}{一下|yí xià}，{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{没|méi}{吃|chī}{早饭|zǎo fàn}{呢|ne}！
= Wait a moment, I haven't had breakfast yet!
小兰: {路上|lù shang}{吃|chī}{吧|ba}！
= Eat on the way!
```

{找不到|zhǎo bu dào} (can't find) is a pattern you'll learn in HSK 3: {找|zhǎo} (to look for) + {不|bú}{到|dào} (not reach). Here
just recognise it.

## Reading: a message from David

> {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}，{您|nín}{好|hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{大卫|Dà wèi}。{我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{到|dào}{北京|Běi jīng}{了|le}，{现在|xiàn zài}{在|zài}{机场|jī chǎng}。{外面|wài miàn}{在|zài}{下雨|xià yǔ}，{路上|lù shang}{车|chē}{很|hěn}{多|duō}，{所以|suǒ yǐ}{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{没|méi}{到|dào}{酒店|jiǔ diàn}。{我|wǒ}{快要|kuài yào}{到|dào}{了|le}，{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}{能|néng}{到|dào}。{明天|míng tiān}{就|jiù}{要|yào}{开始|kāi shǐ}{上课|shàng kè}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{准备|zhǔn bèi}{好|hǎo}{了|le}。{您|nín}{明天|míng tiān}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}{学校|xué xiào}？{我|wǒ}{还是|hái shi}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{去|qù}{吧|ba}，{因为|yīn wèi}{地铁|dì tiě}{比|bǐ}{打车|dǎ chē}{快|kuài}。{谢谢|xiè xie}{您|nín}！

1. Where is David now?
2. Has he reached his hotel?
3. How will he go to school tomorrow, and why?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. At the airport in Beijing ({现在|xiàn zài}{在|zài}{机场|jī chǎng}).
2. Not yet ({我|wǒ}{还|hái}{没|méi}{到|dào}{酒店|jiǔ diàn}), but he's nearly there and can be there by nine.
3. By metro, because it's faster than a taxi ({地铁|dì tiě}{比|bǐ}{打车|dǎ chē}{快|kuài}).

"Hello, Teacher Wang! This is David. I've arrived in Beijing, and I'm at the airport now. It's
raining outside and there's a lot of traffic, so I haven't got to the hotel yet. I'm nearly there:
I can be there by nine. Classes start tomorrow, and I'm ready. What time will you get to the
school tomorrow? I think I'll take the metro, because it's faster than a taxi. Thank you!"
</details>

## Say it

```speak
{都|dōu}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{了|le}！
= It's ten o'clock already!
{我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}。
= I've already eaten.
{快要|kuài yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。
= It's about to rain.
{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{没|méi}{准备|zhǔn bèi}{好|hǎo}{呢|ne}。
= I'm not ready yet.
{我们|wǒ men}{还是|hái shi}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{吧|ba}。
= We'd better take the metro.
```

## Common mistakes

- ~~{明天|míng tiān}{快要|kuài yào}{考试|kǎo shì}{了|le}~~: with a time word, say {明天|míng tiān}{就|jiù}{要|yào}{考试|kǎo shì}{了|le}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{没|méi}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le}~~: "not yet" has no {了|le}: {我|wǒ}{还|hái}{没|méi}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}（{呢|ne}）.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{没|méi}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}~~ for "I haven't eaten yet": {我|wǒ}{还|hái}{没|méi}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}.
- Leaving out the {了|le}: ~~{快要|kuài yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}~~ and ~~{都|dōu}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}~~ sound unfinished. The {了|le} belongs to the pattern.
- Taking {还是|hái shi} for "or" in a statement: {我们|wǒ men}{还是|hái shi}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{吧|ba} is a suggestion, not a question.

## Key points

- A **[[fixed pattern]]** is a two-part frame: learn it whole and fill it in.
- {已经|yǐ jīng}……{了|le}: already done. Not yet: {还|hái}{没|méi} + verb (+ {呢|ne}), without {了|le}.
- {快要|kuài yào} / {快|kuài} / {要|yào} + verb + {了|le}: about to; {快|kuài} + time + {了|le}: nearly (that time); with a time word,
  {就|jiù}{要|yào}……{了|le}.
- {都|dōu} + time / age + {了|le}: "already!", with a feeling that it's late or a lot.
- {还是|hái shi} + verb + {吧|ba}: "we'd better…", a suggestion after weighing the choices.
- {正在|zhèng zài} / {在|zài} / {正|zhèng}……{呢|ne}: happening now; {正|zhèng}{要|yào}: just about to.

This lesson has no new words.

lessons.title: Reading notices and messages
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

HSK 1 asked you to read signs, menus and name cards. HSK 2 asks for a little more: notices on a
wall or a door, text and chat messages, simple forms, timetables and menus, and short texts of up
to about 200 characters. These are also the texts you meet first when you live or travel in China:
the school notice about the first day, the shop's opening times, the group chat about a birthday
dinner.

This lesson gives you one of each, all written for this course, and the strategies to read them
fast. Read each one first with pinyin on, then turn pinyin off with the switch at the top of the
lesson and read it again. The character list in the Study tools box has all 371 characters of
HSK 1 and 2.

## Strategies: skim, then scan

You don't read a notice the way you read a story. Two kinds of reading help:

- **[[Skimming]]**: reading the whole text quickly for the general idea. What kind of text is it, who
  wrote it, and to whom? A line at the top saying {通知|tōng zhī} (notice) and a name and date
  at the bottom tell you it's a notice before you've read a word of the middle.
- **[[Scanning]]**: looking for one fact, such as a time, a place or a name, without reading
  everything. Read the question first, then let your eyes run over the text until you see the
  characters you need.

What to scan for:

| You want | Look for |
|---|---|
| when | numbers with {点|diǎn}, {号|hào}, {月|yuè}, {星期|xīng qī}, {周|zhōu}; {上午|shàng wǔ} / {下午|xià wǔ} / {晚上|wǎn shang}; {从|cóng}……{到|dào}…… |
| where | {在|zài} + place; {楼|lóu}, {教室|jiào shì}, {门口|mén kǒu}, {旁边|páng biān}, {左边|zuǒ bian} / {右边|yòu bian}, {里面|lǐ miàn} / {外面|wài miàn} |
| who | names (surname first), {老师|lǎo shī}, {同学|tóng xué}, {大家|dà jiā}, the name at the end of a message |
| what to do | {请|qǐng} + verb, {别|bié} / {不要|bú yào} + verb, {要|yào}, {准备|zhǔn bèi} |
| how much | numbers with {块|kuài} / {元|yuán}, measure words, {多|duō} / {几|jǐ} ({二十|èr shí}{多|duō}, {十|shí}{几|jǐ}) |

Then read the sentence around what you found, to the end: {不|bù}, {没|méi}, {别|bié}, {还|hái}{没|méi} and {已经|yǐ jīng} can turn the
meaning around. {星期|xīng qī}{一|yī}{休息|xiū xi} says the shop is *closed* on Monday.


## A notice

Notices from schools, buildings and offices start with {通知|tōng zhī} and end with who wrote it and the
date. The middle says what will happen, when and where, and what you need to do.

> **{通知|tōng zhī}**
>
> {下|xià}{星期|xīng qī}{一|yī}（3{月|yuè}2{号|hào}）{开学|kāi xué}。{请|qǐng}{大家|dà jiā}{上午|shàng wǔ}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{到|dào}{学校|xué xiào}，{在|zài}{三|sān}{楼|lóu}{的|de}302{教室|jiào shì}{上课|shàng kè}。{请|qǐng}{准备|zhǔn bèi}{好|hǎo}{本子|běn zi}{和|hé}{笔|bǐ}。
>
> {下午|xià wǔ}{三|sān}{点|diǎn}，{我们|wǒ men}{一起|yì qǐ}{去|qù}{打|dǎ}{篮球|lán qiú}，{请|qǐng}{别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{带|dài}{运动服|yùn dòng fú}。
>
> {有|yǒu}{问题|wèn tí}，{请|qǐng}{给|gěi}{黄老师|Huáng lǎo shī}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà}：125 0000 5678。
>
> {高中|gāo zhōng}{一|yī}{班|bān} {黄老师|Huáng lǎo shī}
>
> 2{月|yuè}25{号|hào}

{带|dài} (to bring) is an HSK 3 word, and {运动服|yùn dòng fú} are sports clothes: {运动|yùn dòng} + {服|fú} as in {衣服|yī fu}.

Skim: it's a notice from a teacher to a class. Scan for the answers:

- When does school start? 3{月|yuè}2{号|hào}, next Monday, at eight in the morning.
- Where? Room 302 on the third floor ({三|sān}{楼|lóu}{的|de}302{教室|jiào shì}). Floors use {楼|lóu} without {第|dì}: {三|sān}{楼|lóu} is "the
  third floor".
- What do the students need? A notebook and a pen ({本子|běn zi}{和|hé}{笔|bǐ}), and sports clothes for the afternoon ({运动服|yùn dòng fú}).

The phone number is read digit by digit, with 1 as *yāo*: *yāo èr wǔ, líng líng líng líng…*

## Opening times

> **{商场|shāng chǎng}{时间|shí jiān}**
>
> {星期|xīng qī}{一|yī}{到|dào}{星期|xīng qī}{五|wǔ}：10:00—21:00
>
> {星期|xīng qī}{六|liù}、{星期日|xīng qī rì}：9:00—22:00
>
> 1{月|yuè}1{号|hào}{休息|xiū xi}

Times on notices use the 24-hour clock and a long dash for "from… to…". Said aloud, 21:00 is
{晚上|wǎn shang}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}. {休息|xiū xi} on a notice means "closed".

Check yourself: can you go shopping there at half past nine on a Saturday morning? (Yes: on
Saturdays it opens at 9:00.) On a Tuesday? (No: it opens at 10:00 on weekdays.)

## A text message

Short messages leave out what both people know. The name of the person comes first, the name of
the writer last (or not at all, since the phone shows it).
